feat(crabbox): protect cloud setup secrets through egress (#171073)

Cloud setup used to forward host environment values through plaintext `setupEnv`, which disabled automatic snapshots and prepared workers. `settings.setupSecrets` replaces it: up to 16 POSIX environment names mapped to protected shared-store SecretRefs. One job-scoped egress owner gives profile setup, recipe preparation and postCreate/postStart commands only sentinels plus public CA trust; Crabbox native egress keeps the authenticated upstream proxy on the Gateway host, allows public HTTPS package downloads, and substitutes each secret only for its store-bound destinations. Grants revoke before process termination on cancellation.

Devcontainer `secrets` requests resolve only through the operator-approved map; unmapped requests fail once, before repository commands run. Setup secrets no longer disable snapshots or prepared workers; images captured with protected egress use a distinct compatibility identity, so older plaintext images are never adopted.

Requirements: an owned coordinator Linux lease and Crabbox 0.77.0 or newer with its matching runtime helper. Unsupported targets, a missing helper or login, an unavailable proxy, missing bindings and old CLIs fail visibly; there is no plaintext or direct-egress fallback.

Update behavior: the Crabbox plugin's Doctor health repair migrates each `setupEnv` profile atomically, and only when every same-name protected store entry already has destination bindings and there is no conflicting host value or mapping. It writes through Doctor's backed-up config writer, never writes store values, never invents destinations, and stays lazy when no profile needs migration. Unrepaired profiles report a remedy (`openclaw doctor --fix`) instead of forwarding plaintext. No SQLite schema change.

Merged with main after #170929 (empty-workspace cloud sessions): empty workspaces still require project-preparation support, so they stay cold on setup-command-only providers.

fix: tool call text no longer leaks into chat output when provider chunks split a call marker (#169172)

* fix(tool-call-repair): keep call text private when chunks split a call marker

A buffered tail that is still an unfinished call marker ("<funct", "<|channel|>")
was replayed as a false-positive prefix when a complete call preceded it, so the
rest of the call arrived mid-buffer and was emitted as visible text. Hold the
buffer while the tail can still complete into a call, replay only decided
false-positive prefixes, and route trim bookkeeping through one helper so the
done/error/EOF paths share the same chunk-independent decision.

Regression tests cover a replayed false prefix, a stacked function call, and a
stacked Harmony call split across chunks.

Refs #169161

* fix(tool-call-repair): align split-stream replay with the block origin

The split-marker buffering added in the previous commit diverged from the
unsplit stream when an authoritative text_end extended the same content block
("hello\n[read]\n{}\nX\n  " lost the call placeholder). Classify
delta-path buffers with the same finalize context as snapshots, keep the block
offset when a text_end extends a buffered snapshot, and track per-content-index
consumed input length so non-authoritative replays slice from the right origin.

Adds three regression tests (plain text and Harmony, delta and text_end split
shapes); stream-normalizer suite 58/58 and packages/tool-call-repair +
normalization-core 445/445 pass, fuzz seed=1 20k iters failures 71 -> 56 and
leakToSplit 18 -> 10 versus the previous commit.

Refs #169161

* chore(tool-call-repair): store the touched files with LF line endings

The previous uploads kept a CRLF final newline captured from the local
working copy; the repository stores these files as LF, so the PR diff
picked up a spurious trailing-line change on both files. No code changes.

Refs #169161

* style(tool-call-repair): format the new test cases with oxfmt

check-lint failed on the previous commit because the three added it.each
rows exceeded the formatter width; run oxfmt's default formatting on the
test file (source file already clean). No behavior change.

Refs #169161

* fix(tool-call-repair): keep trim replay order and drain buffered aux

Replays each false-positive prefix segment with its own content block template and unit accounting instead of the latest template, and interleaves the replayed text with queued reasoning in arrival order. Every trim path (delta, done, error, queue overflow, EOF) now drains buffered auxiliary events before clearing the candidate queue. Adds regression tests for the three review repros.

* test(tool-call-repair): cover terminal trim drains for done, error, and queue cap

* fix(tool-call-repair): keep trimmed snapshot offsets local to their block

A trim can drop earlier content blocks whole, so the retained suffix can
start inside a later block. Advancing snapshotOffset by the concatenated
buffer's removed length made authoritative text_end reconciliation slice
at the wrong origin: the f865603 review repro ('[read]' then
'x\n<function=read>' plus text_end) leaked 'ion=read></function>' as
visible text.

Derive the new origin from the original part that contains the retained
suffix so replay slicing and cumulative snapshots agree, and add the
cross-block cumulative-snapshot case to the block-index regression.

* refactor(tool-call-repair): isolate bounded stream suppression

Keep the stream coordinator below its inherited line budget by moving the existing oversized-payload state machine into a sibling module. Preserve the shared grammar and request tool allowlist, and strengthen marker-split regressions with independent visible-text expectations.

* fix(pr-wrapper): list the extracted suppression module in the wrapper inventory

6caf20c moved the bounded stream suppression state machine into packages/tool-call-repair/src/stream-normalizer-suppression.ts, but scripts/pr only extracts scripts/pr, scripts/pr-lib, and the paths listed in wrapper-components.txt. Without the entry the extracted anchor cannot resolve ./stream-normalizer-suppression.js, so eager-import-closure fails on the PR wrapper inventory and on the extracted dependency context.

fix(skills): keep background reviews out of user reply hooks (#171651)

## What Problem This Solves

Detached Skill Workshop reviews inherit the foreground user trigger, so user-only reply hooks can mistake background maintenance for a new user turn.

## User Impact

Background learning no longer starts user-only reply hooks such as Advisor. Foreground user turns remain eligible; the review's model, tools, source snapshot, and permission checks are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The review is admitted as system work but reuses the foreground prompt context. Clear its inherited trigger at the producer so every hook sees the correct distinction, rather than adding session-key exclusions to individual plugins. The trigger taxonomy has no generic system-maintenance value, so this run leaves the optional trigger unset.

## Evidence

- Production experience-review regression proves a user-eligible claiming hook handles the foreground turn, then does not dispatch for the detached review through the real review forwarding and reply-hook dispatcher; review model work proceeds.
- 33 focused tests passed: experience review (9), review scheduler (12), and reply-hook boundaries (12).
- Scoped Oxfmt and Oxlint passed.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json` passed.
- Madge import-cycle check: 0 cycles.
- Documented that background reviews are internal system work, not user turns.

fix(codex): project raw outer tool-call lifecycles (#171661)

## What Problem This Solves

The Codex harness projects native app-server items (`commandExecution`, `dynamicToolCall`, and so on) to the `codex_app_server.item` agent-event stream with `started`/`completed` phases. Outer model tool calls that Codex records as raw response items have no projected lifecycle: function calls, custom tool calls (for example the code-mode JS `exec` wrapper), local shell calls and tool-search calls. A plugin that must know whether any tool call is still running therefore sees the run as idle while an outer code-mode call is still open, because its child shell commands have already completed.

This was found live with the Advisor plugin (#169564). It must not fork a session while a call is still open, because codex-rs normalization then fabricates an `aborted` output for the open call.

## Fix

`handleRawResponseItemCompleted` now also projects raw call receipts as `codex_app_server.item` `{ phase: "started", itemId: call_id, type }`, and their recorded outputs as `{ phase: "completed", itemId: call_id, type }`. Only phase, id and type are copied, never arguments or results. The app-server forwards raw response items after codex-rs records them in history, so `completed` means the output is persisted. Call and output receipts share `call_id` (codex-rs `protocol/src/models.rs`).

## User Impact

None by itself. Plugins that track in-flight work on Codex runs (with `payload: "metadata"`) can now see outer tool calls start and finish. The existing subscriber (`run-attempt.steering-settlement`) is unaffected.

## Evidence

- Projector test: raw function, custom, local-shell and tool-search calls produce paired started/completed events with ids and types only.
- The steering-settlement subscriber tests still pass.
- Live (Advisor, Codex runtime): before this change, a review boundary was reached while the outer code-mode call was open, and the Gateway logged a missing custom-tool output. Advisor's regression, an outer call open while its children are complete, holds the review until the outer output is recorded.

fix(ai): turns fail without compaction when Hugging Face TGI rejects an over-long prompt (#158161)

* fix(ai): reject exhausted proxy completions budgets in every thinking mode

When the estimated input leaves no room for output, the openai-completions
request builder falls back to max_completion_tokens=1 and still sends the
request. #157673 turned that into a context overflow for thinking-enabled
reasoning models; non-reasoning models and thinking-off requests still send
the one-token request, which cannot hold a useful reply and comes back cut
off by length.

Throw the same context_length_exceeded error for those requests when the
estimate leaves zero or negative output space, so the existing overflow
recovery compacts instead. Positive short budgets (1-15 tokens that fit the
estimate) and their insufficient_output_budget warning are unchanged for
non-reasoning and thinking-off requests, and deliberately short requested
budgets are untouched.

Refs #157307

* fix(ai): budget exhausted non-thinking proxy requests without the estimate margin

The openai-completions request builder estimates input as chars/4 with a
1.25 safety margin. Against a real tokenizer (Qwen3) that estimate is
1.4-1.6x the true count for prose, code, tool schemas and CJK text, so a
fixed prompt that really fills about 65-73% of the context was refused
before provider I/O, with nothing for compaction to recover.

When the margined estimate leaves no room and thinking is off (or the
model is non-reasoning), budget from the unmargined chars/4 estimate
instead and refuse only when that also leaves no room. If the unmargined
estimate undercounts, the provider's own context-length rejection enters
the same overflow recovery. Thinking-enabled requests keep the margined
estimate and the 16-token floor from #157673.

The runtime's required-maintenance test now passes unchanged: its
foreground requests go out with roughly 700 and 4,400 output tokens
instead of triggering an extra overflow compaction. The refusal fixtures move to estimates of at
least 1.25x the context, and an explicit one-token request at an
exhausted estimate is still sent.

* fix(ai): hold proxy completions caps to the useful floor on both estimates

The unmargined fallback only fired once the margined estimate left no room
at all, so a non-thinking request whose margined room was 1-15 tokens was
still sent with that cap (down to 1, the original one-token defect), and
the cap then jumped back up once the margin was fully exhausted.

For requests without thinking, budget from the unmargined estimate as soon
as the margined estimate leaves fewer than 16 output tokens, and refuse
with context_length_exceeded when the unmargined room is also under 16.
Every cap that context pressure reduces is now at least 16 tokens, caps
fall steadily within each estimate, and refusal is terminal as the prompt
grows. Thinking-enabled requests keep the margined estimate and the
16-token floor from #157673 unchanged. A caller's own maxTokens that fits
the room (1, 2, 16) is still sent as requested; only budgets that context
pressure cuts are held to the floor.

The refusal now says which estimate it used and how many of the 16
tokens remain, instead of "leaves only 1 output tokens" for an exhausted
prompt. The margin drop is logged as keep_max_tokens when a caller's cap
is honored without clamping, and the insufficient_output_budget warning
is removed because no reduced cap under the floor is sent any more.

* fix(ai): warn when proxy completions fall back to the unmargined estimate

Budgets taken from the unmargined estimate were logged only at debug
level, so the warn-level signal operators used to spot prompts at the
context cap (the insufficient_output_budget lines) disappeared by
default. Log those clamp_max_tokens and keep_max_tokens lines at warn
level, with the margined estimate alongside, since the provider may
still reject the request. Ordinary clamping stays at debug level.

Document the requested-cap rule exactly: the room never counts below one
token, so a requested cap of 1 is sent in every mode even when the
estimate already exceeds the context, and a prompt that really does is
rejected by the provider and enters overflow recovery. Any other

## Problem

Meta Muse Code needed terminal setup: `muse login`, `openclaw plugins enable muse`, and a hand-written `agentRuntime: { id: "muse" }` on the Meta model. Model Setup offered only "Meta: API key". Other subscription logins (xAI, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex) already work from the Models page.

## Solution

- **Meta provider owns a "Muse Code" device-code choice** (`extensions/meta/muse-login.ts`). It runs `muse login` under supervision, shows the device code in the wizard, honors cancel, and gives an install hint when `muse` is missing. The Gateway login always uses Muse's file credential store under `<stateDir>/muse`, so one browser approval is enough. The macOS Keychain write fails for background Gateway processes.
- **The credential stays Muse-owned.** No fake OpenClaw profile is written. The muse harness uses the managed credential when present and otherwise falls back to Muse's own store. Model availability uses the harness's existing catalog/readiness hooks over the same authenticated MSP `model/list`; it does not grant the direct Meta Responses route.
- **Setup installs and routes the runtime.** `runtime-plugin-install.ts` gains a Muse descriptor beside Codex and Copilot. The auth result enables `muse` and returns an `agentRuntimeId: "muse"` hint; setup writes it only to the activated agent's model entry (`agents.entries.<agent>.models[<model>]`). Global `agents.defaults.models` rows, including an explicit `openclaw` policy, and other agents are unchanged.
- **Activation verification without a tool-free turn.** Muse cannot guarantee a zero-tool turn (MSP has no all-tools-off switch), so activation's `disableTools` probe cannot pass honestly. This adds an optional, activation-only harness `verifySetup`, used only for profileless native auth. Muse checks MSP `model/list` and requires `source: "providerCatalog"` that contains the selected model. A rejected credential returns a bundled catalog and fails setup. Core binds the plugin owner/artifact fingerprints and re-runs the check before commit. Other runtimes keep the existing probe.
- **Live authority.** The `models.authLogin` setup branch carries the existing connection/choice guard through activation; an invalidated device token stops the flow before `muse login`, verification or runtime install run.
- **Catalog/UI.** The provider-login catalog marks native-setup choices `requiresSetup`. AI Setup → Connect provider lists them and dispatches through setup activation with connection-owned cancellation. The plain Provider Access list stays credential-only.

feat(sessions): run sessions in existing folders on paired devices (#169722)

Related: #136048 (non-Git directory semantics) and #142521 (non-Git worker workspace context; this PR does not implement ephemeral cloud workspaces).

## What Problem This Solves

Device-hosted sessions required a Git repository or managed worktree, a constraint inherited from ephemeral cloud sessions, even when a paired personal machine should simply work in an existing non-Git folder.

## User Impact

Users can choose **Existing folder on device** in New Session and run a session directly in an existing folder on a paired session-host device. OpenClaw does not create Git metadata, copy the folder to the Gateway, or sync, reconcile, reset, or delete it.

- `nodeHost.workerRuns.folders` is node-local consent: unset allows existing directories, a non-empty list restricts selection to those roots and their descendants, and `[]` disables the feature and its capability advertisement.
- The session stays pinned to that device: Auto/cloud dispatch, Move, and Continue on Gateway are refused. Attachment staging and the Gateway Files panel are unavailable for these sessions.
- Worker HOME stays in private node storage. Files are not locked against external changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

- `sessions.create` accepts `deviceFolder: { deviceId, path }` (requires `operator.write`); the binding is stored on the existing session entry and the `device-folder` workspace kind reuses the worker execution and lifecycle owners.
- The node owns folder policy and re-validates on every use: absolute or `~` paths only, realpath resolution (symlinks cannot escape a root), no filesystem root, no overlap with private worker storage, and a dev/ino fence between acquisition and execution. One shared rule in `node-workspace-protocol.ts` forbids preparing, resetting, transferring, seeding, or quiescing a device folder, for both ingress parsing and direct node execution.
- Gateway shutdown reads the teardown scope from the durable placement, so stopping an attachment with no in-memory tunnel no longer reaches closed worktree admission.
- A restored existing-folder create retry is owned by its frozen request; current device capacity or runtime no longer blocks it.
- Attachments are refused for device-folder sessions before anything is persisted: `chat.send` rejects them with a clear message, New Session blocks Send while attachments are attached, and worker media preparation never restages historical attachments into a device folder, so one refused file cannot make later turns fail.
- Security tradeoff: a session-host node already runs operator-directed agents with exec, so the allow-all default does not widen that boundary. The folder list is a selection guardrail, not an exec sandbox or a boundary against a compromised Gateway. Deployments that contain `operator.write` with `tools.fs.workspaceOnly` should also set a root list; the docs say so.
- Control UI selection/path input, plus docs for node configuration, session hosting, operator scopes, and workspace behavior.

## Screenshots

**After — desktop existing-folder input**

## Evidence
- **Cross-machine E2E on the final feature code:** a disposable Gateway on one Mac (tailnet TLS, token auth, QA mock model) and a session-host node on a second Mac, both on the same exact head, with `folders` unset and an existing non-Git target folder on the second Mac. Pairing and capability advertisement; create + explicit dispatch (`active`, workspace = the device folder); hosted exec wrote `pwd` and `hostname` into the folder, confirmed by independent readback on that Mac; node restart and an unclean Gateway restart, then a second turn appended to the same file; `~` and a Gateway-only path rejected; reclaim + delete left the folder, sentinel, and absence of `.git` unchanged with no copy in Gateway state.
- **Isolated single-host E2E (25 checks, all pass):** missing/root/file/relative/private-storage rejections; auto-dispatch rejection; node restarts; clean Gateway shutdown with a live tunnel and with a durable attachment but no tunnel; Gateway restart and resume; symlink escape and outside-root rejection under a root list; `[]` disables the capability.
- **Attachment refusal, live:** on the isolated Gateway, a `chat.send` with a text attachment to a device-folder session returns the refusal, the attachment never enters history, and the next text turn and later turns after node and Gateway restarts complete in the folder.
- **Authority, live (real Gateway WebSocket, no mocks):** an operator client granted only `operator.read` + `operator.sessions.write` sends `sessions.create` with `deviceFolder` and gets `FORBIDDEN` / `missingScope: operator.write`; no session row exists afterwards and a debugger logpoint on the node records no workspace command for that request. The full `operator.write` client creates and dispatches the same folder (`active`).
- **Device revocation during awaited admission, live:** with the node process tree stopped (`SIGSTOP`) while `sessions.create` and `sessions.dispatch` wait on it, `devices remove` succeeds, then `SIGCONT`. Create fails with `Selected device changed during folder validation; retry` and leaves no row; dispatch fails with `Device worker installation connection is no longer current`; the node is then disconnected and its old token is rejected. Known bounded behavior: the read-only folder validation request already delivered to the stopped node still runs once on resume (1 ms after removal) before the close frame arrives; its result is discarded, nothing is persisted, and no session command runs. Unit coverage also revokes the caller (real `captureGatewayDeviceRevocation` capture) and the device during validation.
- **Requesting-operator revocation during awaited admission, live:** separate signed operator devices with `operator.write`, real paired node stopped with `SIGSTOP`. Removing the operator while `sessions.create` waits on folder validation: the client gets `gateway closed (4001): device removed`, `sessions.describe` returns `{"session":null}`, the key is absent from `sessions.list`, and the node trace has no worker execution command. Removing a different operator while `sessions.dispatch` waits: the session moves from `provisioning` to `{"state":"failed","terminalReason":"Gateway requester authority changed"}`, `hasActiveRun` is false, and no worker command runs. As with device revocation, one already-delivered read-only folder validation runs on resume and its result is discarded.
- **Inline initial turns are refused:** `sessions.create` with `deviceFolder` plus `message`, `task` or `attachments` is rejected before node I/O; the UI already sends the first message through `sessions.send` after dispatch. The three new cases fail with the validator removed (`3 failed | 12 passed`) and pass with it (`25 passed`).
- **Upgrade compatibility, live:** the `main` merge-base build created a plain session and an explicit-cwd session (turn `ok`); the PR build on the same state dir lists and describes both with their original IDs, a new turn on the old session completes `ok`, and Doctor exits 0 with no session-row load errors.
- **Upgrade from stable `v2026.10.3`, live:** the stable build created a plain session with a completed turn, an explicit-cwd session, a custom model alias and a non-default `thinkingDefault`. Direct startup on the new build exits 78 with "uses schema version 24; … run openclaw doctor --fix" on both this PR and the plain `main` merge base (inherited). After `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive` (`v24 -> v26`), the PR Gateway starts, both old sessions list and describe with their original IDs, both settings read back unchanged, a new turn on the old session returns `ok`, and a new device-folder session created after the upgrade dispatches and runs a turn in the folder. One session-event publication warning about an unsettled worker-environment mutation appeared during that dispatch; the turn still succeeded.
- **Focused tests:** device-folder node, tunnel, create, protocol, media, submit-gate and draft-state suites pass; the restored-retry and history-restage regressions fail before their fixes.
- **Hosted CI:** on the exact head `364a000`, every job passes on the first attempt, and so does the Security Review, except `checks-ui-e2e (8/9)`. That job runs `plugins-lifecycle.e2e.test.ts`, which also fails the same way on plain `main` (see the maintainer override comment). Earlier heads hit flaky qa-lab E2E tests and `main`-side ratchet failures that plain `main` also reproduces.

## Merge Danger

Additive optional protocol field and session-entry JSON field; no SQL schema change. Older Gateways reject the new `sessions.create` parameter; older nodes do not advertise the capability, so the option is not offered. Revert removes the feature; existing device-folder sessions would then be unrecognized but their folders are untouched.

fix(agents): keep in-flight tool calls pending in session forks (#171580)

Related: #169564

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes read-only built-in session forks reporting a still-running tool call as aborted, which can make a background reviewer recommend repeating successful work.

## User Impact

A fork taken during tool execution now describes the result as pending, not as a tool error. Parent execution and persisted results are unchanged. Ordinary `/btw` and normal-run transcript repair keep their existing behavior.

## Why This Change Was Made

The built-in fork retains the last prepared request and appends subsequently published messages. When an assistant tool call has been published but its result has not, provider replay pairing repair inserts an error result (`aborted` for OpenAI Responses). The fork now supplies a non-error pending result only for those new, unmatched publications, before provider serialization. It keeps the actual prepared request prefix unchanged and never writes the placeholder back to the parent snapshot.

Known limitation: Codex has its own upstream missing-result repair (`codex-rs/core/src/context_manager/normalize.rs:104-107`, `CustomToolCallOutput` with `output: "aborted"`; function calls at lines 59-64). This PR does not rewrite native Codex tool outputs. Mid-call Codex forks remain subject to that upstream behavior; consumers should review at a settled boundary.

## Evidence

- Live evidence from Advisor #169564 at `1b75f3ab75f4e77a349387ef26f661e491ffa922`: six requested sequential `echo N; sleep 10` calls became ten actual executions after three false-abort corrections passed verification. All ten persisted tool results were successful. A captured verification request contained `function_call_output` with `output: "aborted"` for the still-running third call.
- Root cause: `packages/ai/src/transcript-transform.ts:154-170` synthesizes the error while replaying the fork, not in the parent's persisted transcript or its original prepared request. The assistant publication is appended by `src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.ts:82-91`.
- Regression covers synchronous and asynchronous pending calls through the real OpenAI Responses and Anthropic transports, and verifies a later fork sees the genuine completed result instead of retaining the placeholder. All four cases failed before the fix for the intended missing-pending-result reason.
- Focused tests: **26 passed across 3 files** (13 fork boundary tests, 2 tool-ID preservation tests, 11 replay sanitization tests).
- Scoped TypeScript project, changed-file oxlint and oxfmt checks passed; `check:madge-import-cycles` reported **0 cycles**. No full typecheck, broad suite, `check-changed`, or autoreview was run.
- Live re-proof: cherry-picked onto the Advisor head as `b31c3fcf879eda6cf23c3b409b6d548571b7b78e` (local only), retaining its old tool-start scheduler. The identical six-command built-in case completed with **exactly 6 successful exec calls**. Reviews during calls 3 and 6 both returned **NO_CHANGE** (3013 ms and 1982 ms); no verification or steering occurred. Both captured fork input arrays contain the pending call's result as `This tool call is still running. Its result is not available yet.`, with no `aborted` tool output. All six genuine persisted results are successful and the parent transcript contains no pending placeholders. Gateway and isolated temporary state were cleaned up.

* fix(hooks): dispatch the SessionStart hook via Git Bash on Windows

The SessionStart command string starts with a quoted path, which breaks
both Windows shells Claude Code may hand it to: PowerShell parses the
leading quoted string as an expression and dies on the next bareword
('Unexpected token session-start', #1751), and cmd.exe's /c quote rule
drops the outer quotes when the path contains a metacharacter, so a
profile dir like C:\Users\Name(External) truncates the command at the
'(' (#1918). Either way the bootstrap silently never loads.

Declare shell: "bash" on the hook. Claude Code >= 2.1.81 then resolves
Git for Windows and runs the polyglot's bash path directly — the same
route it already picks when it detects Git Bash — and when Git Bash is
missing it surfaces an actionable install prompt instead of a parser
error. Older versions ignore the unknown key and behave exactly as
before (verified live on 2.0.77 and 2.1.80).

Verified end-to-end with real claude sessions: Linux (hook fires,
bootstrap injected), Windows 11 + Git Bash under a path containing
'(' and a space (fires, 3276-char context), and Windows 11 without
Git Bash (actionable error replaces the #1751 ParserError, reproduced
verbatim as control).

* fix(codex): make package script and its test portable beyond macOS/bsdtar

The packaging pipeline only worked on a Mac with default umask, for
three stacked reasons:

- The deterministic-metadata tar flags (--uid/--gid/--uname/--gname)
  are bsdtar spellings; GNU tar rejects them, so the tar.gz archive
  step died on Linux. Detect the tar flavor and use --owner=:0
  --group=:0 --numeric-owner on GNU tar, which writes byte-identical
  ustar headers (uid/gid 0, empty uname/gname).
- Staged file modes depended on two umasks canceling out: git archive
  masks entry modes with tar.umask (git default 0002 -> 775), and the
  unflagged tar extraction re-masked with the process umask (022 on
  macOS -> 755, but 002 elsewhere -> 775). Pin tar.umask=0022 on the
  archive call and extract with -p so staged modes are canonical
  755/644 on every machine.
- The test's timestamp assertion parsed bsdtar's -tv column layout and
  expected epoch 0 rendered in a US timezone ("Dec 31 1969"); GNU tar
  uses different columns and UTC hosts render "1970-01-01". Assert
  mtime == 0 via python3 tarfile instead, matching how the test
  already checks zip timestamps.

the bsdtar branch preserves the exact flags that passed on macOS.

* fix(sdd): batch reviews check the diff against the brief's file list

Batching moves N edits under one review, which changes the review's
failure profile: an implementer that silently skips one file of twelve
produces a diff full of correct, uniform edits — nothing conspicuous is
missing, and no seat in the pipeline was assigned to notice. The single
combined review is the only net for a dropped edit, but the reviewer

reconciles the diff against that list file by file; a listed file with no
hunk is a Missing finding regardless of how clean the rest of the batch
looks. Conditional on a multi-file brief, so single-task reviews are
unchanged.

The '# or origin/main' alternative fed a moving ref into the reviewer's

* fix(sdd): invoke sdd-workspace via bash so helpers survive stripped exec bits

Codex marketplace users hit 'Permission denied' running SDD helpers:
some extractors (Python zipfile) discard Unix mode attributes when
unpacking the package, so task-brief's and review-package's direct exec
of their sibling sdd-workspace fails. Our packaging preserves 0755
(git archive | tar -xpf, asserted by the existing packaging test) — the
bits are lost on the consumer side, which no packaging change can reach.

* fix(sdd): reject empty or non-descendant BASE..HEAD ranges in review-package

When an SDD implementer commits to the wrong branch (#2050), the
BASE..HEAD range handed to review-package is either empty or not rooted

an empty one lets the reviewer approve "clean" work that isn't there.

for usage errors) so callers can distinguish range problems:

- git merge-base --is-ancestor BASE HEAD, else "HEAD is not a

- git rev-list --count BASE..HEAD > 0, else "empty commit range"

* fix(hooks): dispatch the SessionStart hook via Git Bash on Windows

The SessionStart command string starts with a quoted path, which breaks
both Windows shells Claude Code may hand it to: PowerShell parses the
leading quoted string as an expression and dies on the next bareword
('Unexpected token session-start', #1751), and cmd.exe's /c quote rule
drops the outer quotes when the path contains a metacharacter, so a
profile dir like C:\Users\Name(External) truncates the command at the
'(' (#1918). Either way the bootstrap silently never loads.

Declare shell: "bash" on the hook. Claude Code >= 2.1.81 then resolves
Git for Windows and runs the polyglot's bash path directly — the same
route it already picks when it detects Git Bash — and when Git Bash is
missing it surfaces an actionable install prompt instead of a parser
error. Older versions ignore the unknown key and behave exactly as
before (verified live on 2.0.77 and 2.1.80).

Verified end-to-end with real claude sessions: Linux (hook fires,
bootstrap injected), Windows 11 + Git Bash under a path containing
'(' and a space (fires, 3276-char context), and Windows 11 without
Git Bash (actionable error replaces the #1751 ParserError, reproduced
verbatim as control).

* fix(codex): make package script and its test portable beyond macOS/bsdtar

The packaging pipeline only worked on a Mac with default umask, for
three stacked reasons:

- The deterministic-metadata tar flags (--uid/--gid/--uname/--gname)
  are bsdtar spellings; GNU tar rejects them, so the tar.gz archive
  step died on Linux. Detect the tar flavor and use --owner=:0
  --group=:0 --numeric-owner on GNU tar, which writes byte-identical
  ustar headers (uid/gid 0, empty uname/gname).
- Staged file modes depended on two umasks canceling out: git archive
  masks entry modes with tar.umask (git default 0002 -> 775), and the
  unflagged tar extraction re-masked with the process umask (022 on
  macOS -> 755, but 002 elsewhere -> 775). Pin tar.umask=0022 on the
  archive call and extract with -p so staged modes are canonical
  755/644 on every machine.
- The test's timestamp assertion parsed bsdtar's -tv column layout and
  expected epoch 0 rendered in a US timezone ("Dec 31 1969"); GNU tar
  uses different columns and UTC hosts render "1970-01-01". Assert
  mtime == 0 via python3 tarfile instead, matching how the test
  already checks zip timestamps.

the bsdtar branch preserves the exact flags that passed on macOS.

* fix(codex): suppress SessionStart hook auto-discovery with empty hooks object

Codex auto-discovers a plugin's hooks/hooks.json whenever the Codex
manifest has no `hooks` field: load_plugin_hooks falls back to a
hardcoded DEFAULT_HOOKS_CONFIG_FILE = "hooks/hooks.json" and registers
it. hooks/hooks.json is the Claude Code SessionStart hook, it is tracked
in this repo, and the Codex marketplace installs the whole repo root
(source url "./"), so the fallback re-registered the SessionStart hook
and its install-time trust prompt on Codex.

Removing the Codex hook file and the manifest `hooks` pointer (commit
"Remove Codex hooks") did not disable the hook on Codex — it removed the
explicit declaration that was overriding the fallback, so the fallback
took over and found the Claude hooks/hooks.json.

Declare an empty inline hooks object ({}) in .codex-plugin/plugin.json.
It parses as an empty inline hook set and stops Codex reaching the
auto-discovery fallback. An absent field, an empty array ([]), and an
empty inline list all collapse back to the fallback, so the value must
be exactly {}.

Update the test to assert the manifest declares hooks: {} (and that
hooks/hooks.json exists, which is what makes the declaration necessary),
replacing the prior assertion that the field was absent — which passed
while the hook was still being auto-discovered.

* fix(hooks): dispatch the SessionStart hook via Git Bash on Windows

The SessionStart command string starts with a quoted path, which breaks
both Windows shells Claude Code may hand it to: PowerShell parses the
leading quoted string as an expression and dies on the next bareword
('Unexpected token session-start', #1751), and cmd.exe's /c quote rule
drops the outer quotes when the path contains a metacharacter, so a
profile dir like C:\Users\Name(External) truncates the command at the
'(' (#1918). Either way the bootstrap silently never loads.

Declare shell: "bash" on the hook. Claude Code >= 2.1.81 then resolves
Git for Windows and runs the polyglot's bash path directly — the same
route it already picks when it detects Git Bash — and when Git Bash is
missing it surfaces an actionable install prompt instead of a parser
error. Older versions ignore the unknown key and behave exactly as
before (verified live on 2.0.77 and 2.1.80).

Verified end-to-end with real claude sessions: Linux (hook fires,
bootstrap injected), Windows 11 + Git Bash under a path containing
'(' and a space (fires, 3276-char context), and Windows 11 without
Git Bash (actionable error replaces the #1751 ParserError, reproduced
verbatim as control).

* fix(codex): make package script and its test portable beyond macOS/bsdtar

The packaging pipeline only worked on a Mac with default umask, for
three stacked reasons:

- The deterministic-metadata tar flags (--uid/--gid/--uname/--gname)
  are bsdtar spellings; GNU tar rejects them, so the tar.gz archive
  step died on Linux. Detect the tar flavor and use --owner=:0
  --group=:0 --numeric-owner on GNU tar, which writes byte-identical
  ustar headers (uid/gid 0, empty uname/gname).
- Staged file modes depended on two umasks canceling out: git archive
  masks entry modes with tar.umask (git default 0002 -> 775), and the
  unflagged tar extraction re-masked with the process umask (022 on
  macOS -> 755, but 002 elsewhere -> 775). Pin tar.umask=0022 on the
  archive call and extract with -p so staged modes are canonical
  755/644 on every machine.
- The test's timestamp assertion parsed bsdtar's -tv column layout and
  expected epoch 0 rendered in a US timezone ("Dec 31 1969"); GNU tar
  uses different columns and UTC hosts render "1970-01-01". Assert
  mtime == 0 via python3 tarfile instead, matching how the test
  already checks zip timestamps.

failure profile: an implementer that silently skips one file of twelve

auto-discovery fallback. An absent field, an empty array ([]), and an
empty inline list all collapse back to the fallback, so the value must
be exactly {}.

replacing the prior assertion that the field was absent — which passed

* fix(hooks): dispatch the SessionStart hook via Git Bash on Windows

The SessionStart command string starts with a quoted path, which breaks
both Windows shells Claude Code may hand it to: PowerShell parses the
leading quoted string as an expression and dies on the next bareword
('Unexpected token session-start', #1751), and cmd.exe's /c quote rule
drops the outer quotes when the path contains a metacharacter, so a
profile dir like C:\Users\Name(External) truncates the command at the
'(' (#1918). Either way the bootstrap silently never loads.

Declare shell: "bash" on the hook. Claude Code >= 2.1.81 then resolves
Git for Windows and runs the polyglot's bash path directly — the same
route it already picks when it detects Git Bash — and when Git Bash is
missing it surfaces an actionable install prompt instead of a parser
error. Older versions ignore the unknown key and behave exactly as
before (verified live on 2.0.77 and 2.1.80).

Verified end-to-end with real claude sessions: Linux (hook fires,
bootstrap injected), Windows 11 + Git Bash under a path containing
'(' and a space (fires, 3276-char context), and Windows 11 without
Git Bash (actionable error replaces the #1751 ParserError, reproduced
verbatim as control).

* fix(codex): make package script and its test portable beyond macOS/bsdtar

The packaging pipeline only worked on a Mac with default umask, for
three stacked reasons:

- The deterministic-metadata tar flags (--uid/--gid/--uname/--gname)
  are bsdtar spellings; GNU tar rejects them, so the tar.gz archive
  step died on Linux. Detect the tar flavor and use --owner=:0
  --group=:0 --numeric-owner on GNU tar, which writes byte-identical
  ustar headers (uid/gid 0, empty uname/gname).
- Staged file modes depended on two umasks canceling out: git archive
  masks entry modes with tar.umask (git default 0002 -> 775), and the
  unflagged tar extraction re-masked with the process umask (022 on
  macOS -> 755, but 002 elsewhere -> 775). Pin tar.umask=0022 on the
  archive call and extract with -p so staged modes are canonical
  755/644 on every machine.
- The test's timestamp assertion parsed bsdtar's -tv column layout and
  expected epoch 0 rendered in a US timezone ("Dec 31 1969"); GNU tar
  uses different columns and UTC hosts render "1970-01-01". Assert
  mtime == 0 via python3 tarfile instead, matching how the test
  already checks zip timestamps.

the bsdtar branch preserves the exact flags that passed on macOS.

  expected epoch 0 rendered in a US timezone ("Dec 31 1969"); GNU tar
  uses different columns and UTC hosts render "1970-01-01". Assert

fix(hooks): dispatch the SessionStart hook via Git Bash on Windows

The SessionStart command string starts with a quoted path, which breaks
both Windows shells Claude Code may hand it to: PowerShell parses the
leading quoted string as an expression and dies on the next bareword
('Unexpected token session-start', #1751), and cmd.exe's /c quote rule
drops the outer quotes when the path contains a metacharacter, so a
profile dir like C:\Users\Name(External) truncates the command at the
'(' (#1918). Either way the bootstrap silently never loads.

Declare shell: "bash" on the hook. Claude Code >= 2.1.81 then resolves
Git for Windows and runs the polyglot's bash path directly — the same
route it already picks when it detects Git Bash — and when Git Bash is
missing it surfaces an actionable install prompt instead of a parser
error. Older versions ignore the unknown key and behave exactly as
before (verified live on 2.0.77 and 2.1.80).

Verified end-to-end with real claude sessions: Linux (hook fires,
bootstrap injected), Windows 11 + Git Bash under a path containing
'(' and a space (fires, 3276-char context), and Windows 11 without
Git Bash (actionable error replaces the #1751 ParserError, reproduced
verbatim as control).

fix(windows): an MSIX with no Node to copy runs npx MCP servers on its packaged node

With no host Node and lazy installs off, the payload's own npx is the
only npx a bare `command: npx` can resolve to. Every package bin it
starts goes through cmd.exe, which cannot start the packaged node.exe,
so the server dies with "Access is denied".

The payload's Python can start the packaged node.exe. In this case
the MCP preflight installs the package with npm's own npm-cli.js
under <HERMES_HOME>/cache/mcp-npx/<spec hash>, with install scripts
off (npm runs those through cmd.exe too). It then spawns the bin's
script on that node. The OSV malware check still sees the original
npx argv. Any other argv shape, a failed install, or a manifest with
no clear bin keeps plain npx.

alias-started process tree, python -> packaged node.exe starts, and
cmd.exe -> packaged node.exe gets "Access is denied".

fix(windows): MSIX terminal and MCP children get node, npm and python copied outside the package

program whose own executable is outside WindowsApps cannot start one
inside it. cmd.exe gets "Access is denied" from the packaged node.exe,
and npm starts every package bin through cmd.exe. So every npx MCP
server died, and so did each `npm exec` in the terminal on a machine
without its own Node. A venv's Scripts\python.exe redirector exits 101
when it starts the packaged interpreter, which broke `python -m venv`.

A copy of the same files in the writable store starts without error.
PM already makes one for Python builds (#135236). That code moves from
pm._uv._toolchain to pm.user_facing.writable_copy. pm.user_facing.copies
swaps each packaged npm, node and python dir for that copy, made on
first use from the verified entry: a copy plus a digest check, no
download. Two places use it:

- the terminal's fallback dirs (user_facing_path), behind the user's
  own tools;
- Hermes's npx/npm/node for a bare `command: npx` MCP server, which
  stays Hermes's own as on main.

When lazy installs are off, PM makes no copy and the packaged dir stays.

alias-started process tree: cmd.exe -> npx.cmd -> node.exe fails with

fix(gemini): resume a dropped long-decode stream from its last checkpoint

Past 32,768 output tokens a Gemini 4 stream sends a continuationToken
every ~5,000 tokens, riding on the event whose text it commits. Google's
contract: if the stream drops, resend the SAME request with the last
checkpoint token instead of starting over (the dropped stream is billed
up to that checkpoint, so restarting pays for it twice and redoes minutes
of decoding).

The native client ignored mid-stream checkpoints and turned any
mid-stream httpx error into gemini_stream_error, so the agent retried the
whole request from token 0.

  token (never one on a real, non-CONTINUATION finish).
- _stream_completion keeps the latest token with nothing yielded after
  it. On an httpx drop it resends request + that token; with no token,
  or once any chunk was yielded after it, it raises as before (resuming
  would duplicate or lose shown text). One token rides at most 3
  requests, so a network that keeps dropping still ends in an error.

- ONBOARDING_DECIDE_DEADLINE_MS is deleted. The stale comments about
  deadlines are fixed.

perf(onboarding): the due answer is worked out at serve boot and served from a cache

The desktop asks onboarding.state at launch. The handler recomputed
everything inline, on the connection's serial queue, while boot threads
did the same provider reads. A slow answer missed the desktop's deadline,
and onboarding was skipped for that launch.

- hermes_cli/onboarding_due.py keeps the answer (run, eligible). A
  reader waits a bounded time (8 s) for a boot computation in flight,
  then answers live and caches that.
- The serve lifespan starts the computation on the desktop's local
  backend (start_due_boot), after the setup bootstrap has recorded a
  fresh install and kept an existing guest's trial.
- Every writer that can move the answer drops the cache: set_run, the OS
  user's marker, and the setup record's refresh and reconcile. A stamp of
  the files the answer reads catches edits made outside the process.
- onboarding.state runs on the RPC pool (_LONG_HANDLERS), so its wait
  never holds the connection's queue. Remote backends answer eligible:
  false at once, and --fresh-install still asks live.

fix(serve): the desktop backend's first-install check runs before its state.db is touched

The install check reads the default root's state.db. At serve boot the
same process starts creating or healing that database on another thread,
so the check could meet it mid-write. On the desktop's local backend the
check now runs once in the lifespan, before the state.db reconcile thread
starts, and its answer is cached for the process.

perf(onboarding): one provider walk per due answer, one AWS chain walk, no IMDS on the desktop backend

On a fresh machine every `onboarding.state` walked the whole provider
ladder twice (inference_available, then claim_blocker), and each walk ran
the boto3 credential chain twice (has_aws_credentials asked
resolve_aws_auth_env_var, which walked it, and then walked it again).
Where botocore is installed and no AWS credentials exist, each walk also
waited on the EC2 instance-metadata lookup.

- inference_available asks provider_configured() once and hands the
  answer to claim_blocker.
- has_aws_credentials walks the chain once.
- The auto-detect rung skips the instance-metadata lookup on the
  desktop's local backend (a botocore session setting, not os.environ).
  The backend runs on the user's own computer there.

Test fakes of has_aws_credentials take the new keyword.

feat(onboarding): the first desktop boot records that onboarding is due and the trial reserved

Whether onboarding is due fell back to a live install probe on every
launch. If the first launch missed the run (a late answer, the app closed
early), the user's first chat or key made the next launch read "used",
and onboarding and the trial were gone for good.

On the desktop's local backend, the serve bootstrap now writes
`onboarding.run: true` to the root config once, when the flag is unset
and the install is fresh, and reserves the trial in the OS user's marker.
A missed launch stays due until a run ends or is skipped (both write
`false`, as today). The claim checks the reservation instead of a later
probe, and the claim consumes it, so a lost trial is still never claimed
again.

fix(install-state): a locked state.db is not prior use

The probe read a state.db that another process held locked as
"unreadable", which counts as used, and cached that for the process. On a
first boot the backend is creating or healing that same database while
the probe runs, so a new user could lose the trial and onboarding. A
busy/locked database (after sqlite's own retry window) now adds no
evidence; any other sqlite error still counts as used.

docs(free-tier): the trial is once per OS user, not once per machine

The marker and every evidence source live in the OS user's home, so a
second account on the same computer is a separate first install. The
module docstrings now say so.

fix(onboarding): claim the trial after the run record, so a crash keeps onboarding due

onboarding.start claimed the welcome trial (mint the guest, mark the
machine) before start() wrote the run record and `onboarding.run: true`.
A crash in between left a guest and the marker, both of which make the
next launch's machine check read "used", with `onboarding.run` still
unset: auto-onboarding never opened again.

The run record and `onboarding.run: true` are now written first, then the
claim, so the marker only lands once the run is on disk and a crash at any
later point reopens onboarding. A refused claim (5079) still leaves no
guest and no chat: the just-created run is discarded.

fix(free-tier): the guest token seam mints inference only for the welcome trial

Review question on #137807: can a connector-only guest get an inference
token with model.provider: nous? The runtime resolver already refuses such
a guest before the exchange (resolve_nous_runtime_credentials), so the
pinned-provider case stays refused; a test now pins that. But the
exchange seam itself, refresh_guest_state(purpose="inference"), minted an
inference token for any guest it was handed.

The seam now refuses purpose="inference" unless the guest carries the
welcome trial (claimed or grandfathered) on the desktop's local backend.
Every other guest gets no inference token, whichever caller asks (Q4).

fix(desktop): type the onboarding params so tsc accepts them

The generated OnboardingStartParams / OnboardingStateParams interfaces have
no index signature, so passing them to the requester (Record<string,
unknown>) failed the desktop typecheck lane. Intersect them with the
requester's own param type.

fix(auth): the no-provider error no longer promises a free Nous tier

trial, so "the free Nous tier needs no API key" pointed users at nothing.

fix(free-tier): the shared store keeps welcome_claim; a guest pool row is not a Portal login

Found in the live E2E run of this PR.

- The shared Nous store dropped `welcome_claim`. A connector guest (False)
  adopted into another profile then arrived with no key, which since the
  previous commit reads as "minted before the trial" and can be
  grandfathered, bringing back a trial the machine already used. The key
  now travels with the identity. WELCOME_CLAIM_FLAG moves to auth_constants
  so auth_nous can name it without an import cycle.
- When `providers.nous` was gone, the auth status fell back to the
  credential pool and reported a leftover guest row as `logged_in`, so

fix(install-state): shared .env tokenizer, atomic marker write, no reads in protected folders

- `.env` keys go through agent.secret_scope.load_env_file, so
  `KEY="" # comment` is empty here too. The size and read checks still run
  first, so an unreadable .env still counts as used.
- The machine marker is written with atomic_json_write (unique temp name),
  so two backends marking at once cannot fail each other.
- A launcher that resolves into a macOS protected folder is reported by
  folder and never opened, so the probe cannot raise a permission prompt.

fix(onboarding): eligibility reads the default profile; a claim refreshes the setup record

onboarding.state computed `eligible` in the launch profile, though
onboarding runs in `default`. A desktop launched under an unconfigured
profile, with the key only in default's .env, never reopened the run. The
check now runs in the same default-profile scope onboarding.start uses.

A successful claim in onboarding.start now refreshes the serve boot record,
so setup.status stops reporting no provider and no free-tier account.

fix(free-tier): stamp the trial in the mint's own write; grandfather only pre-change guests

A claim saved the new guest, then stamped `welcome_claim` in a second write.
A crash between the two left an unstamped guest that claim_blocker refused
forever. Grandfathering could not tell an old free-model guest from a new
connector guest, so after a reaped claim, a connector mint plus the old
nous/welcome history brought the trial back (against the rule that a lost
trial is never claimed again).

Every mint now writes `welcome_claim` in the same save: True for the
desktop claim, False for connector mints. Only a guest with no key (minted
before this change) can be grandfathered, and free inference requires
`welcome_claim is True`.

fix(desktop): send assume_fresh only on a --fresh-install launch

The renderer sent `assume_fresh` on every onboarding.state and
onboarding.start, as `false` when the switch was off. The rule is that the
field is present only when it is true, and only an unpackaged build started
with --fresh-install can make it true. Packaged launches and Settings reruns
now send requests without the field.

fix(speech-to-text-sensevoice): restore the onset a cold VAD drops

Silero cannot back-date the first segment of a cold detector, so it
reports a start index several frames after speech actually began. Every
recording therefore lost its opening audio: measured across 50
utterances the median loss was 102 ms and the worst 230 ms — a full
syllable, which surfaced as dropped leading words ("麻烦把发票…" →
"把发票…", "用 Python…" → "写一个 Python…").

Only the first segment is affected; later segments aligned within 3 ms
because the detector retains history by then. Tuning cannot fix it:
lowering minSpeechSeconds from 0.25 s to 0.05 s left the median loss at
110 ms, and lowering the threshold to 0.2 still lost up to 174 ms while
risking false triggers.

Restore the dropped onset from the recording itself, bounded by the new
vadOnsetPaddingSeconds (default 0.3 s, zero disables). Measured on the
same corpus with identical DSH settings, this recovers the full no-VAD
accuracy and in the technical domain exceeds it, since segmentation also
trims silence:

  语料        条件     无VAD    VAD丢起音  VAD+回填   改善
  audio      clean   12.50%    16.33%    12.50%   23.5%
  audio      noisy10 17.74%    19.15%    17.94%    6.3%
  audio_tech clean   10.34%    15.65%     9.81%   37.3%
  audio_tech noisy10 25.73%    30.50%    26.26%   13.9%

Inference cost is unchanged (2.6 s vs 2.6 s on both clean corpora).

fix(coverage): keep attributing a worker exit that raced a teardown

An unexpected fork exit can close the worker's channel under a send, which
Vitest reports as a runner-level worker error instead of the clean exit. It
then tears the worker down before the ChildProcess exit event, and
DiagnosticForkWorker treated that teardown as an orderly shutdown: it cleared
the observer and marked the exit expected, so the coverage log lost the pid,
file, code and signal it exists to report.

A worker error observed before a stop now keeps the observer, and a stop
requested after that error no longer marks the exit as expected.

Vitest reports one such exit either as the clean exit path or as a
runner-level worker error, so the spec accepts both forms and compares the
record against whichever appeared.

fix(capture): end special-scheme URL authorities at a backslash (#2767)

* fix(capture): end special-scheme URL authorities at a backslash

The native mitmproxy adapter removed transport userinfo with
`^(...//)[^/?#]*@`, so the authority ran to the last "@" before "/", "?"
or "#". For `https://example.test\part@tail` it treated
`example.test\part` as userinfo, reported `https://tail` as the
Location, and withdrew the original bytes as a transport credential.
WHATWG URL parsing, used by the shared TypeScript owner
(recordedTransportUrl.ts) and by HAR captures, ends a special-scheme or
scheme-relative authority at a backslash, so that "@" is ordinary path
text.

Locate the authority with the same boundary rule before removing
userinfo. Bytes are handled as Latin-1 text so unrelated bytes stay
identical. Userinfo before the backslash is still removed and redacted.
Add source unit tests for the adapter projection to test:python.

Fixes #2671

* fix(capture): skip special-scheme leading slashes before userinfo

Ending the authority at a backslash exposed a credential: for

or "\" after a special scheme (and in scheme-relative references), so

backslash and found no "@". The same applied to `https:\\user:pass@host`
and `https:user:pass@host`.

schemes and scheme-relative references. File URLs keep their "//"
boundary because they carry no userinfo. Load the adapter in tests with

in sys.modules.

* fix(reference): report entries beyond the path limit as I/O failures

Reference-source traversal joins each child onto the root path. A valid
tree whose nested entries exceed the platform's absolute path limit

reader's filesystem error allow-list lacked that code, so
filesystemFailureDetail returned undefined and the native rejection
escaped both readReferenceSource and importReferenceSource instead of
becoming the existing failed `io` entry.

Add ENAMETOOLONG to the allow-list, matching the JavaScript application
reader's list. Readable siblings stay in the graph and the unreachable
entry is recorded with its OS message.

Fixes #2652

🤖 Generated with Claude Code (Sonnet 5.5, verified by Opus 5.5) 🦊

* fix(electron): absorb only this launch's orphaned rejections

The listener around the launch dropped every rejection with a
playwright-core stack, so an unrelated Playwright failure during the
launch window would vanish. Hold those rejections instead. When the
launch settles, drop only the ones whose message is part of the launch's
own error (the orphans of a failed launch). Raise every other one again
through the unhandledRejection path, so the process still fails. A launch
that succeeds raises all of them. Rejections without a Playwright stack
still fail at once.

One setImmediate turn before the decision lets rejections queued by the
settling tick arrive first. It is a single turn, not a timer. A shared
set of absorbed errors stops overlapping launches from raising each
other's orphans. The listener is removed on every path.

* fix(cli): refuse an integrity policy the binary analyze lane cannot honor

`analyze` declares --integrity-policy for its JavaScript lane and forwards it
only there. On a binary target the flag was accepted and then dropped:
inspect_artifact-style integrity handling does not exist on this path, and
binary_overview is a strictObject with no input at all, so the request could
never take effect and the run proceeded as if the caller had not asked.

The same branch already refuses source_paths on a binary target with a typed
AnalysisInputError, and the sibling `inspect` command refuses the flag outright,
so the refusal is the established handling here. The policy option carries a
default, so the check keys off a value that differs from the owner schema's own
default rather than the flag's presence; otherwise every binary analyze would be
refused. The default is read from the schema instead of being restated.

Verified with 5 integrity policy CLI cases, check:fast and
verify:test-discovery (1023 files) on macOS arm64, and by running the built CLI
for the no-flag, explicit-default and record-and-continue cases. The regression
case failed with the command reaching the binary lane before the change.

* fix(cli): reject explicit default integrity policies for binaries

* fix(cli): keep an omitted integrity policy absent on the binary lane

`javascriptApplicationOptions.shape.integrityPolicy` fills an omission with its
default, and `.optional()` keeps reporting that parsed value, so
`options.integrityPolicy !== undefined` was true for every `analyze <target>`
call: ordinary binary analysis was rejected before the target was even read.

List `z.undefined()` first in a union so an omitted option stays absent while
the owner still validates a supplied value, and reapply the owner's metadata so
help and `--schema` keep describing the option.

1 failed | 5 passed without this change (the case "still routes a binary
analyze target without an integrity policy" returned invalid_request for
integrity_policy instead of reaching the target) and 6 passed with it;
`npm run check:fast` passes on macOS 26.5.1 arm64 with Node.js 24.18.0.

fix(managed): pair members by declared identity before name-free remaps (#2116)

* fix(managed): pair members by declared identity before name-free remaps

The first matching round keyed methods on signature and normalized CIL,
and fields on signature, without the declared type or name. Identical
members of different types fell into one ambiguous group, so a file
compared with itself reported unknowns, and a lone match across types
was reported as an unchanged exact pair while the member's own
counterpart went unpaired.

Pair by declared type, name, and exact CIL/signature first, then by
declared type, name, and raw signature. The name-free CIL/signature,
field-signature, and structural rounds now run last, as remaps, and
skip a pair across declared identities while either member's own type
and name remain unpaired on the other side.

Nested types that share a bare name still share one declared identity,
so their identical members stay ambiguous in a self-comparison.

* fix(managed): keep members with kept identities out of remap rounds

The cross-identity check applied only to one-to-one groups. A member
whose own declared type and name were still unpaired on the other side
could fall into a larger remap group and be reported ambiguous, and a
blocked candidate could make an otherwise unique remap ambiguous.

A remap round now drops such members before grouping, along with
members whose declaring type is unresolved. Same-identity structural
pairs get their own round before the remaps. Each member's declared
identity is computed once.

Ambiguity limitations now name the evidence a group shares, which
stays true whether the round keyed on names or not.

* fix(managed): keep names in unresolved identities and hold ambiguous ones

A member of an unresolved declaring type had no declared identity, so
the declared-identity rounds keyed it by CIL or signature alone. Two
unresolved members with different names paired as an exact match, and
a file compared with itself reported unresolved members ambiguous.

The declared identity now always includes the name, with a null type
for an unresolved one. Remap rounds still leave such members out.

A remap round now also leaves out a member whose own identity sits in
an ambiguous group on the other side, not only one left one-sided.

The undecoded-counterpart check uses the same declared identity.

* fix(managed): keep remap groups with unresolved owners ambiguous

Remap rounds dropped members of an unresolved declaring type before
grouping. Such a member can be another member's own counterpart, so a
resolved member could remap to a copy in another type while its
unresolved counterpart was reported added.

Unresolved members now join remap grouping, and a group that contains
one stays ambiguous instead of pairing.

The undecoded-counterpart set reuses each member's computed identity.

* fix(managed): keep ownerless members out of declared rounds when shared

A member whose declaring type did not resolve has a declared identity
of a null type and its name. The declared rounds paired two such
same-named members even when the other side also held a resolved
member with the same CIL and signature, which could be the owner. The
old name-free first round reported that group as ambiguous.

An ownerless member now enters the declared rounds only when no other
member on either side shares its exact CIL/signature key, and never
the declared structural round. Otherwise it reaches the remap rounds,
which keep any group with an unresolved member ambiguous.

* fix(managed): keep competitors of an ownerless member out of the declared round

When an ownerless member shares its exact CIL/signature key with another
member on the same side, its owner may be that member. The resolved
members holding the key now stay out of the declared round too, so they
cannot pair and consume the candidate the ownerless member may own, and
the remap round keeps the whole group ambiguous as main does. A lone
ownerless member still pairs with its lone counterpart.

* test(managed): split the ownerless comparison tests under the function length limit

The ownerless describe block reached 181 lines, past oxlint's
max-lines-per-function limit of 150. Move the structural-competitor
case into its own block.

* fix(managed): contest signatures and remap only open candidates

* fix(managed): retain blocked raw-signature choices as unknown

* fix(managed): keep member names in signature contention

ownerlessContested applies competitionIdentityKey itself, but

name-scoped, so the contested set never matched the groups and the

matchObserved passes its items to matchByKeys, which needs Declared, so

language set through REA_GHIDRA_LANGUAGE_ID still replaces the lane default.

fix: isolate OPENAI_BASE_URL in provider hint test to prevent environment pollution (#3347)

The test explicit_model_provider_hint_controls_runtime_provider_dispatch
was failing when OPENAI_BASE_URL was set in the environment to a non-standard
URL (e.g., api.layofflabs.com). The test expects the OpenAI provider to use
the default base URL (api.openai.com) when no explicit base_url is provided
in the ProviderConfig.

This fix adds an EnvVarGuard struct to the tests module and uses it to

feat(cli): press Esc to interrupt a running turn

While a turn runs the main thread is blocked in the conversation loop,
so nothing reads the keyboard. Add an EscapeInterruptMonitor that, for
the duration of a turn on an interactive terminal, switches stdin to a

a lease the listener restores canonical mode and stops consuming bytes.

fix(runtime): keep a failed turn's tool results, and size guards from the real context window

Five defects found by auditing the agent stack, all of which let the harness act
confidently on a wrong picture of its own state.

1. A turn that errored discarded the record of tools that had already run. The CLI
   hands run_turn a CLONE of the session; the turn appends the user message, each
   assistant reply, and a tool_result per executed tool to that clone alone. The error
   path dropped it while the side effects of those tools remained on disk, and the
   recovery path then replayed the same user input against a session showing no sign
   they had ever run — inviting a second execution of tools that are not idempotent.
   The clone is now adopted before teardown, and recovery resumes the turn instead of
   replaying it (new ConversationRuntime::resume_turn).

2. Every sizing guard was computed against the model NAME's context window. With a
   local server behind a cloud model alias that is 200k against a much smaller
   backend, which does not make the preflights inaccurate — it makes them unreachable.
   CLAW_CONTEXT_WINDOW now declares the real window; model_token_limit honours it and
   returns a limit for unrecognised models instead of None, max_tokens is capped to a
   quarter of it, and the auto-compaction threshold derives from it (70%) rather than
   defaulting to a 200k-window constant.

3. Whether to recover by discarding conversation history was decided by substring
   matching on rendered error prose, including strings that ordinary transport and
   decode failures also produce — so a dropped connection cost the session its
   transcript. Classification now happens in the API layer, where the error still has
   its type and the request is still in hand: typed overflow errors, plus ambiguous
   transport failures only when the request actually filled the window. The two
   copy-pasted detection blocks are gone.

4. The top-level agent loop had no iteration ceiling (usize::MAX) while spawned
   subagents were bounded at 32. It now gets the same bound, overridable with
   CLAW_MAX_TURN_ITERATIONS.

5. Auto-continue nudges were injected as USER turns, so harness-authored text was
   persisted, re-sent on every later request, and folded into compaction summaries as
   something the user had said. They are recorded as system turns now; the wire
   payload is unchanged.

Also replaces the repository's own self-host section, which described a translator
and a serving stack no longer in the request path. That file is folded into the
system prompt verbatim, so it was briefing the model with an architecture that does
not exist.

refactor(cli): let the emitter report the output tail it leaves behind (#3304)

refactor(cli): let the emitter report the output tail it leaves behind

Two places believed they owned terminal output: consume_stream streams
assistant deltas live while emit_output = true, and run_turn decided
whether to emit a separating newline before spinner.finish by guessing
from final_assistant_text(&summary).

That guess agrees with reality only because every *other* writer happens to
terminate its output with a newline — tool results go through
stream_markdown (which appends one), thinking summaries are written with a
trailing newline, and tool-call headers use writeln! — so the assistant
text path is the only one that can leave a partial line. That is a property
of the current renderers rather than of the streaming protocol, and it is
not enforced anywhere.

TerminalTail is state the emitter records into as it writes: both live
writers (AnthropicRuntimeClient::consume_stream and the tool-result blocks
in CliToolExecutor::execute) now push bytes through a TailTrackingWriter
that reports the last byte written, and the caller that ends a turn asks
where the emitter stopped instead of inferring it.

The heuristic also left the failure arm unguarded. A turn that streamed text
and then errored called spinner.fail on a partial line, which the line
clear then erased; that arm now carries the same guard.

Also gate the animated spinner.tick frame on is_terminal(). That frame is
pure cursor control (save, rewrite line, restore) and emits no newline, so
down a pipe it leaves an unterminated banner that the first streamed delta
then continues on the same physical line.

fix: handle DOCX files with inconsistent ZIP filename casing (#1812) (#2016)

* fix: handle DOCX files with inconsistent ZIP filename casing (#1812)

Some document generators (e.g. certain Microsoft Word versions, legal
document systems) produce .docx files where the central directory records
one casing (e.g. 'customXml/item2.xml') but the local file headers record
another (e.g. 'customXML/item2.xml'). Python's zipfile module raises
BadZipFile when reading such files.

Add _fix_zip_filename_casing() to patch local file header filenames to
match the central directory before any ZIP processing occurs.

* test: register DOCX zip casing test in __main__ runner list

* fix: encode central directory filenames with the ZIP's actual charset

ZIP filenames are stored as cp437 unless general purpose flag bit 11
(0x800) marks them UTF-8, which is how zipfile decoded orig_filename.
Re-encoding unconditionally as UTF-8 produced the wrong bytes for
non-ASCII cp437 names, so a local header could be skipped or patched
with mismatched bytes.

* fix(ocr): pre-process the DOCX before reading it in DocxConverterWithOCR

convert() read the caller's stream twice before repairing it: once for the
embedded style map, and once to extract images for OCR. A .docx whose ZIP
local file headers disagree with the central directory on casing would then
fail those reads. The image extraction swallows every exception, so the
result was an empty OCR map and silently missing OCR blocks -- output
identical to the no-OCR path, with no error.

Call pre_process_docx() once at the top and feed the repaired stream to
every read, matching the ordering the base DocxConverter already uses. This
also drops a redundant second rebuild of the archive on both branches.

* Improve name comparison for casing mismatch

* test: assert non-case ZIP filename mismatches are still rejected

Equal encoded length does not imply two filenames differ only in case, so
the local file header repair must not wave through archives whose local and
central directory names genuinely disagree. Cover an unrelated same-length
name, a single differing character, and a difference outside the cased
characters, alongside the case-only mismatch that should still be repaired.

fix(outlook): read .msg string properties saved in the non-Unicode format (#2295)

* fix: read .msg string properties saved in the non-Unicode format

Every string property in a .msg lives under a stream whose name ends in its
MAPI type: 001F for PT_UNICODE (UTF-16LE) or 001E for PT_STRING8, written in
the message's code page. Outlook writes one or the other for a given message,
never both, so a message saved in the legacy non-Unicode format carries no
001F streams at all.

The converter addressed only the 001F names. Such a message therefore came
out as bare scaffolding -- "# Email Message" followed by "## Content" -- with
From, To, Subject and the body all silently dropped, and no error raised.

Each property is now read from the 001F stream and, failing that, from its
001E counterpart. PT_STRING8 streams record no encoding of their own, so the
charset is detected with charset_normalizer, as is already done for other
8-bit sources in the codebase. The Unicode path is unchanged.

* Read code page info once.

fix: remove extra closing brace from caron and ring-above accents (#2279)

`CHR["\u030c"]` and `CHR["\u030a"]` each carried a fourth `}`, so the
templates read `\check{{{0}}}}` and `\ocirc{{{0}}}}`. Every other accent
in the table is `\name{{{0}}}`. `oMath2Latex.do_acc` applies these with
`latex_s.format(c_dict["e"])`, and an unbalanced template raises
`ValueError: Single '}' encountered in format string`.

The damage is not limited to the accented equation. `pre_process_docx`
runs `_pre_process_math` over the whole of `word/document.xml` inside a
blanket `except Exception` and, on error, writes the *original*
unprocessed XML back. Mammoth does not render OMML, so a single caron or
ring-above accent silently removes **every** equation in the document,
with no error and a zero exit code.

Both are standard entries in Word's Equation > Accent gallery
(U+030C COMBINING CARON, U+030A COMBINING RING ABOVE).

Measured on the repo's own `equations.docx` fixture: 2 equations
recovered normally, 0 after appending one caron-accented equation, 3
with this fix applied.

Adds `test_docx_math_accents.py`: a table-wide guard asserting every
`{0}` template survives `.format()`, plus direct coverage of the two
affected accents and an unaffected control.

fix: correct \underleftarrow macro and map math italic h in equation conversion (#2293)

U+20EE COMBINING LEFT ARROW BELOW mapped to \underledtarrow, which is not a
LaTeX macro -- the name is a scrambled \underleftarrow. The two neighbouring
entries in the same table show the intent: U+20D6 -> \overleftarrow and
U+20EF -> \underrightarrow. The template still formats, so nothing raises;
the equation just ends up with an undefined control sequence.

T normalizes the Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols back to ASCII, but skipped
math italic small h. That letter has no codepoint of its own: U+1D455 is
permanently reserved because Unicode unifies it with U+210E PLANCK CONSTANT.
Following the contiguous block left h as the only Latin letter to survive
untranslated, so an equation reading h(x)=g(x) converted to "ℎ(x)=g(x)".
