Syncs the claude-api skill with the current upstream source.

## Managed Agents — five new features

- `effort` on the agent's `model` object (a level string or `{"type": "<level>"}`).
  It is agent-configuration only: setting it in a per-session `model` override is
  silently ignored.
- Optional `version` on agent update, for optimistic concurrency. Omit it for
  last-write-wins.
- `initial_events` on session create, collapsing create plus first send into one
  call. Validation is all-or-nothing and only `user.message` and
  `user.define_outcome` are accepted.
- Environment and memory-store webhooks: four `environment.*` events and three
  `memory_store.*` events.
- Event deltas on per-thread streams. Previews are thread-scoped, so a child
  thread's previews never reach the session-level stream.

## Corrections to behavior the skill already documented

- Tool output offload triggers at 100,000 characters (~25k tokens), not 100K
  tokens, and covers built-in tools rather than MCP alone.
- `system.message` works on four models, checks only the primary model, appends
  system context instead of replacing the prompt, and is accepted during a
  `requires_action` idle when it trails a tool result in the same request.
- Vault-to-MCP credential matching is normalized (scheme and host lowercased,
  default ports and trailing slashes stripped), not byte-exact.
- Multiagent depth greater than 1 is a validation error, not silently ignored.
- Outcome `interrupted` fires even when evaluation never started, and then
  carries an empty-string `outcome_evaluation_start_id`.
- Deployment jitter is 15% of the run interval, floor 5s, cap 9 minutes.
- Webhooks retry three times with jittered 5-120s backoff, then drop silently.
  Auto-disable is duration-based with three named triggers.
- `session.status_terminated` means completion or error.
- `agent.thinking` is a progress signal and carries no thinking content.
- `processed_at` is already populated on first sighting for
  `user.define_outcome`, `user.custom_tool_result`, and `user.tool_result`.
- Session creation does not provision the sandbox.
- Skill `version` applies to Anthropic-authored skills too.
- Console-created vault credentials are header-injection only, and vault
  environment-variable substitution skips secrets in URL paths.
- Console trace URLs need the real workspace ID when the API key is not in the
  Default workspace.

## Elsewhere in the skill

- Note partner pricing under the first-party price table: Microsoft Foundry
  bills at standard API rates, while Amazon Bedrock and Vertex AI are
  partner-operated with separate pricing.
- Correct the tool-runner human-in-the-loop guidance, which previously pointed
  readers at the manual loop for approval gates the runner's per-turn hooks
  already cover.

SessionStart also fires on compact, and the activate hook always reset
the flag to the default level. A session switched to /ponytail ultra fell

was switched back on. Codex fires the same compact source.

Startup, resume and clear still start at the default level. Like the
mode tracker, it never waits on stdin for more than a second and falls

The hook entry itself is unchanged: Codex trusts a hook by a hash of its

fix(map): keep repo-controlled text and symlinked files out of the SessionStart map (#1070)

ponytail-map.js forwarded raw text from the opened repo into the model
context and followed any tracked symlink.

Injection: the `export { ... }` capture spans newlines and keeps any text up
to `}`, and directory names go in unfiltered. A cloned repo could plant
arbitrary sentences in the hidden session context (export list; folder name
with spaces/colons via git ls-files; folder name with newlines via the
git-less walk).

Symlinks: readFileSync followed tracked symlinks. One pointing at /dev/zero
never returns, so Claude Code's 5 s hook timeout kills the hook with no
output (no ruleset, no map) on every session start in that repo, while the
flag file already says ponytail is on; one pointing outside the repo leaks
that file's top-level names into the context.

- NAME: an export entry is kept only if it is a whole identifier, `type X`,
  `a as b`, or one dotted receiver (`self.helper`). Also fixes `type Foo`
  being listed verbatim.
- SAFE_PATH: files whose path has spaces, quotes, control or non-ASCII chars
  are left out of the map.
- lstat: anything that is not a regular file is skipped.
- tests/map.test.js: regression test for the payloads and the symlink.

fix(hooks): keep hook launchers loadable on Node 12 (#1072) (#1078)

The launchers used `replaceAll` (Node 15+) and `require('node:path')`
(Node 14.18+), so any project that pins an older Node in `.nvmrc` fails
every hook before the script loads. `split().join()` and `require('path')`
do the same on any Node; the hook scripts themselves already run on 12.

Fixes #1072

Claude Code prunes old plugin versions, so a statusLine pointing into the versioned plugin cache went blank after an update. The per-project mode file name replaced every path separator with '_', so <root>/project/nested and <root>/project_nested shared one mode file. The name is now a SHA-256 of the normalized project path.

test(hermes): isolate the Python helper from the developer's ponytail config (#1025)

The Hermes test helper passed the real environment through, so a developer whose own default mode is off saw a failing test. The helper now starts with an empty config dir and no PONYTAIL_DEFAULT_MODE.

fix(hermes): honor default-mode config with a UTF-8 BOM (#873)

Hermes read config.json as plain utf-8, so a BOM-prefixed file failed to parse and the configured default (even off) was ignored. It now reads utf-8-sig, like the JS side (#478).

fix(hermes): reject review as a default mode (#700)

Hermes validated PONYTAIL_DEFAULT_MODE and config.defaultMode against the config modes, which include the session-only review, so review could become the default. It now uses the runtime modes, like the JS hooks (#377).

fix(qoder): expand ${QODER_PLUGIN_ROOT} in plugin hook commands (#598)

The Qoder plugin manifest loads hooks/qoder-hooks.json directly, but its commands held the literal PONYTAIL_DIR placeholder, so both hooks failed on every prompt. Qoder expands ${QODER_PLUGIN_ROOT} in plugin hook commands.

fix(pi): show the off notice when ponytail is stopped by phrase (#636)

fix(pi): restore branch mode after /tree navigation (#828)

Pi only restored the mode from the session branch on session_start, so jumping back with /tree to a branch that ran in lite left ponytail off. The same restore now also runs on session_tree.

fix(pi-extension): clear disabled footer status (#850)

In off mode the Pi footer entry was set to an empty string, which keeps it registered and can leave a trailing separator. Pi clears a status entry with undefined.

On Pi the /ponytail-* aliases sent the literal /skill:ponytail-review text without the skill body, because sendUserMessage only expands skill commands with expandPromptTemplates, and they dropped anything typed after the command. Both fixed in sendAlias.

fix(uninstall): remove the statusline nudge flag (#680)

fix(config): normalize default-mode parsing (#716)

A default mode with stray whitespace, like PONYTAIL_DEFAULT_MODE=' lite ' or a config value ending in a newline, was silently ignored and fell back to full. getDefaultMode() now reuses normalizeMode(), so whitespace and case are handled and review is still rejected as a default.

fix(hooks): silence off-mode SessionStart (#687)

Qoder has no SessionStart, so a missing mode file means first run and the hook switches the default on. Turning ponytail off deleted that file, so the next prompt switched it back on. On Qoder, off is now written as 'off' instead of deleting the file.

fix(hooks): don't emit a second JSON object on Qoder report-only /ponytail (#617)

fix(hooks): preserve mode on invalid arguments (#677)

fix(hermes): match config items with inline comments (#1030)

* fix(hermes): match config items with inline comments

The plugins.enabled / plugins.disabled item scan compared raw line text, so
a YAML inline comment became part of the value it matched against. Three
concrete failures followed on configs users can edit by hand:

- an existing enabled entry carrying a comment ("agency-agents-router # x")
  was not recognized, so the plugin was appended a second time;
- a stale disabled entry carrying a comment was not removed, so the
  installer reported "enabled plugin ... in config.yaml" while the plugin
  stayed disabled;
- the corrupted-glue repair counted "- " in the whole line, so a comment
  containing " - " was split into fake list entries: the installer silently
  rewrote a comment such as "# keep - rotate this one first" into two
  enabled entries.

Strip a trailing YAML comment ("#" only starts one after whitespace) before
matching, counting, and splitting, and use the same value helper in the
post-repair re-check so a quoted entry is recognized too. No config format
or install behavior change beyond those shapes.

check-hermes-config-rewrite.py gains four cases for them plus two general
invariants: the plugin appears exactly once, and the writer may not gain or
lose unrelated enabled entries outside the documented glue repair. The
suite fails on the previous code with exactly those four cases and passes
with this patch.

* test(hermes): pin a quoted entry that also carries a comment

Independent verification on the PR (phant0um) covered an existing quoted
entry with an inline comment (`- "agency-agents-router"  # quoted`). The fix
recognizes it through the comment-stripped item value; pin that shape so it
cannot regress. On the previous code the extended suite fails with this case
plus the original four; with the fix all 21 cases pass.

fix(lib): an indented closing fence closes the block (CommonMark/GitHub parity) (#1028)

fence_closes_p() required a closing fence's indent to be <= the opener's.
That is not a CommonMark rule and not how GitHub renders: a closing fence
may be indented up to three spaces regardless of the opener. A GitHub-valid
document was therefore read as still open, so lint reported a false
"does not nest" (and a false "never closed") and the OpenClaw split kept the
next "##" heading inside the previous section, leaving AGENTS.md empty.

The closing rule is now exactly the four conditions already enforced: same
character, run at least as long as the opener, indent 0-3, and nothing but
whitespace after the run. Callers still pass the opener's indent as the
optional fourth argument; it is documented as deliberately not consulted.

Regression fixtures in test-lint-fences.sh pin the helper boundaries (2- and
3-space closers close; a shorter or 4-space-indented run does not; tilde
closers follow the same rule), a lint run on the GitHub-valid document, and
the OpenClaw split. They fail on the previous code at the first new
assertion: "fence_closes_p rejected a bare closer indented 2 spaces under
an unindented opener".

feat(deployments): declare and provision what a flow's MCP servers need (#15668)

* feat(deployments): declare required MCP variables and projects in deploy artifacts

A deployed flow reaches an MCP server through config the deploy target may not
be able to satisfy: an external server resolves its credential from a global
variable only that environment can supply, and an internal one calls a sibling
project that has to already be deployed there. Neither was declared, so both
failed at the first tool call rather than at deploy.

Collected from the flow the same way model providers are, by both deploy paths,
because a precheck whose answer depended on whether the caller packaged a zip or
captured a snapshot would pass a project one way and refuse it the other. The
manifest steps to schema_version 6 when either list is populated, so an older
reader refuses the artifact instead of deploying it unprovisioned; a project with
no MCP servers packages byte-identically to before.

A sibling project is declared as the name the flow calls it by together with the
project id, not the id alone. The name is carried rather than derived because a
server can be added under any name, and the component resolves by name, preferring
the stored row over the embedded config -- so a rebuilt connection written under a
derived name is a row the flow never finds, and that fails at the first tool call
rather than at deploy, which is the failure this exists to remove.

Two helpers carry the rules so they live in one place. project_id_from_mcp_url
answers which project a URL names, matched against the parsed path rather than
the raw string: searched raw, a query string could carry the shape and an
external server would have read as one of our own. It answers "names project X"
and never "is ours" -- the caller confirms a sibling by looking the id up
locally, since a rebuilt connection carries the target's own address and discards
whatever origin was configured. variable_reference_name returns the name a config
value defers to, and _is_variable_reference now delegates to it rather than
restating the rule.

Nothing counts configs that still hold a literal secret: a strict snapshot
already refuses to capture one, so that state cannot reach the collector.

* fix(deployments): declare and carry what a flow's MCP servers actually need

Both halves of this came out of running the feature end to end against a live
three-plane stack. Every unit test passed before either was found.

A sibling project no longer declares the credential beside it. Saving a flow
scrubs the author's key out of the MCP config into a generated MCP_* name, so an
internal server reaches the collector carrying both a project URL and a
credential reference, and declaring the reference refused the deploy over a
variable the target must never hold -- it is the authoring plane's key, and the
rebuilt connection discards it for one minted on the target. Every internal
connection was undeployable. The test that should have caught this passed
because its fixture had no headers; it now carries the real scrubbed shape.

External server configs are now returned beside the archive, never inside it.
The packaged graph keeps only each server's name, deliberately and by test,
because an lfpkg is a file people store and move. The configuration still has to
reach a deploy target, so it rides on the returned object to whoever is
deploying and no further. Only a config whose every credential is already a
variable reference is handed on, so no secret can travel; a config still holding
a literal is left out.

The two readers of MCP fields now share one walk, so a server one of them sees
the other sees too. A config the requirements declared but the carried list
omitted would ask an operator for a credential that nothing then resolves.

* fix(deployments): resolve an MCP server by name against the owner's address book

Selecting a registered MCP server stores only its name in the flow. The url and
credentials live in the owner's `mcp_server` row, and `resolve_mcp_config`
prefers that row over anything inline when the flow runs. Reading only what was
inline meant such a flow declared nothing and provisioned nothing: the deploy
wrote an empty config on the target, which the component then resolved through
in preference to everything else. Inline config is the exception, so this was
the common case failing, not an edge one.

Reading the row here also makes the two sides agree. With the precedence the
other way round, a deploy can provision the project a stale inline config names
while the flow calls the one the row names.

Three things follow from reading the row rather than the flow.

The url is now read from `config["url"]` or out of the stdio `args`, because the
`lf-<project>` entry Langflow seeds for a project puts it there. Without that, a
sibling configured that way was classified external and the deploy tried to
carry a subprocess command to a pod.

A credential read from the row is rewritten into the deterministic name the
save-time scrubber would have given it before anything is carried, so the row's
real secrets never cross planes, and the requirements declare exactly those
names. A carried reference the declaration never mentions leaves the target
holding a configuration nothing resolves, and a readiness check that never asked.

A config with no address is no longer carried at all. That is what produced the
empty row on the target, and an empty row is worse than none: the component
prefers it.

A credential inside stdio `args` after `--headers` is still not carried.
Rewriting positional arguments is guesswork, so such a config is left behind
rather than moved with the value in it.

* fix: fail safely when packaging MCP deployment connections

* refactor(deployments): share the MCP config readers with the Editor's deploy gate

The Editor's cycle check reads a flow's MCP fields to answer whether a sibling
project points back at the one being deployed. It did that by reaching into
`field["value"]["config"]["url"]` itself, which sees only one of the shapes a
server is stored in: not the usual name-only field whose config lives in the
owner's address book, not the stdio entry with the url among its arguments, and
nothing inside a grouped node. A check that knows fewer shapes than the builder
misses the cycles it exists to catch, and they surface later as a missing
dependency instead.

Make the three readers it needs public, the way `iter_mcp_field_values` already
is, so the gate can share them rather than keep a second copy that drifts:

  _effective_mcp_config   -> effective_mcp_config
  _mcp_config_url         -> mcp_config_url
  _registered_mcp_servers -> load_registered_mcp_servers

The last one is renamed rather than just unprefixed because
`registered_mcp_servers` is already a local at two call sites in the builder.

No behaviour change here. The gate that uses them lives in the Editor
distribution and lands separately.

fix(tests): keep the client database template readable on SQLite 3.54 (#15725)

DatabaseTemplate backs up a WAL-mode database, so each copy inherits the
WAL flag in its header but none of the -wal/-shm files. SQLite 3.54.0
refuses to open such a file with mode=ro (SQLITE_CANTOPEN), so every

pages, and Langflow re-enables WAL through sqlite_pragmas on connect.

* test(api): list the GET routes that a migration pause lets through

A migration pause lets every GET through as a read. A route that changes

accepts: what signing in counts, the authorization audit log when it is
on, and values that are worked out again. A route that is added later
fails the test until it is on the list or takes the dependency.

* test(api): cover disabled deployment reads in migration guard

* test(api): list the audit trail's GET routes as reads

The release branch gained five GET routes that read the audit trail of
flows and projects. Each one was read to its end. The route files and
the feed helpers behind them write nothing, and their permission check
is not recorded, because reading a trail must not add to it.

* test(api): list the data subject routes among the GET routes of a migration pause

Four GET routes of the data subject feature leave the instance as it is: the
list of requests, one request, the dry run, and a user's own deletion request.
Each was read to its end with what it depends on. The admin check on them
builds a 403 and records nothing.

Three add a row to the audit log and say so with changes_the_instance: the
export of a request, the search for end users, and a user's own data export.

* refactor(api): share how a migration command's environment is built

A copy starts from the server's environment without the settings that
say where this instance keeps its data, and a files copy adds the keys
of the destination bucket. The check of the new instance needs both, so
each is now a function of its own. copy_environment builds the same
environment as before.

* feat(api): let the migration page check the copy and start the new instance

The page had no server side for its last two steps, so a move could not
be finished on it.

Check the copy (check_target, now the step after the copies):
- POST steps/check_target/runs starts Langflow's integrity check as a
  detached run, pointed at what the copies wrote, with this instance's
  key and an empty folder in place of this instance's own. It reads and
  writes nothing. It is followed and stopped through the run routes of
  the copies.
- It runs before any new instance has started on the destination. A new
  instance writes rows of its own at its first start, so a check made
  after it differs on a clean move, and a newer Langflow moves the
  schema, which this Langflow then cannot read.
- The record keeps each check beside what the first step said of this
  instance. Two results are the same when status and summary are. A
  report where every pair is the same makes the step done.
- A report with a difference keeps the start waiting. The admin copies
  again, which is still allowed, or accepts it with the run_id of the
  report they read: POST steps/check_target/confirm (409 not_checked,
  differences, report_changed).
- A check counts for the pause it ran in and for the parts of the
  destination it read, which are the ones this instance needs. A copy
  that starts takes it off the record. GET hands it out only while it
  counts or still runs.
- The check keeps what this instance had to move, as it stood then. On
  PostgreSQL the new instance writes to the database this server reads
  that from, and the admin starts it before saying so.

Start the new instance (start_target, the last step):
- GET /migration carries start.settings once the copy was checked: the
  settings the new instance starts with, with a placeholder wherever a
  password or a key goes. No secret is in them.
- POST steps/start_target/confirm records the admin's word that the new
  instance was started. It is the one-way point, and it ends the move.
- From then on the record of the move is closed. No copy and no check
  starts, the destination cannot be saved again, and no finding, key
  answer, backup confirmation or decision is taken (each answers 409
  new_instance_started): the new instance runs on what was checked, and
  a copy would write over what it has written since.
- From then on changes come back on only when the admin says that the
  new instance is stopped, and on PostgreSQL that the database is
  restored (409 new_instance_running), because both instances would
  take changes.

The server never calls the new instance. The check reads the
destination's data with this instance's key, so it proves the copy and
says nothing of how the new instance is configured.

* feat(frontend): list what a move needs at the top of the migration page

The page asked for each thing only when its step came: a database and a bucket at step 2, a place
for the backup after people were already locked out. An admin found out one step at a time, and
the last of it after the pause.

A short list above the steps now says what has to be ready elsewhere, each thing only when this
instance's move calls for it. It is open until the check is done, then closed and one click away.

* feat(frontend): add the check of the copy, the start and the way back to the migration page

The page stopped after the copies. It now carries a move to its end.

"Check the copy" runs the checks of the first step on the copied data and
sets each result beside this instance's. It runs before the new instance
starts, so what is missing can still be copied again. A copy that matches
needs nothing more. With a difference, the admin goes on only after saying
that it is expected, and that word names the check they read.

"Start the new instance" says that the move is one-way from there, shows the
settings to start the new instance with, what that list can't print, and what
to try on the new instance. The admin's word that it runs ends the move, and
a closing panel says what to keep.

Once the new instance has started, nothing is copied or checked again and the
destination can't be changed. Turning changes back on is then a way back that
loses what the new instance wrote. So the banner drops its button, and "If
something goes wrong" opens with what going back takes and asks for the
admin's word before the button works.

* fix(api): give the migration page the stores the check of the copy read

A part of the destination that was saved for an earlier move stays in the
record. The settings for the new instance were built from every saved part,
so they could name a bucket or a knowledge base store that no copy of this
move wrote to and that the check of the copy never read:

- This instance keeps its files in a bucket of its own by now. The settings
  named the bucket that the earlier move had saved.
- No knowledge base is left on this instance's disk, and the others are in
  the server's own pgvector store. The settings sent the new instance to the
  destination database for them.

The instance's own bucket is given whenever its files are in one. The
destination database is given for knowledge bases only while this move
copies them, or when the server has no store of its own.

A bucket that the admin saved is still given when this instance has no file
left to copy.

* test(frontend): pin what the migration page does while it is switched off

The page is off by default. Opened by its address with the flag off, it
sends the admin to the settings and asks the server nothing. While the
server's flags have not arrived it shows a spinner, stays where it is and
asks nothing, and it reads the move once the flag turns out to be on.

No test said so: every test of the page set the flag on. Each of the three
guards fails one of the two new tests when it is taken out.

* fix: guard migration cutover and preserve remote store settings

* fix: keep the copy check when a copy's command cannot be started

A copy start takes the check of the copy off the record before it spawns
its command, so the start of the new instance waits for another check.
When the command could not be started at all, nothing wrote to the
destination and the check was lost all the same: the admin had to run it
again to get the start back.

The admission now hands back a call that puts the check back, and
start_run calls it, still under the start lock, when the spawn fails with
an error that names a file. Such an error comes from before the command
runs: from the open of /dev/null, or from the spawn or the exec of the
command.

Any other failure keeps the check off. Out of file descriptors, a spawn
can fail with an error that names no file, and on Linux that error can
come after the child was made, with the child still running. A request
that is cancelled during the spawn may have started its child as well.

The tests also hold three things the copy start already does. A second
start is refused before it is admitted while a run is live. A copy that
is stopped after its command started leaves its audit line. A command
that ran and whose run could not be recorded keeps what admission saved.

* fix: print no empty, protected or secret-bearing value in the start settings

The settings of the new instance gained the server's host policies and
the variable names of OpenSearch knowledge bases. Four things came with
that:

- A policy that is set and empty printed a line with nothing after the
  equals sign.
- A host list that holds a URL printed the URL, with any user and
  password in it.
- A host list written over several lines printed over several lines, and
  a file made from the list kept only its first line.
- A knowledge base row that names a protected variable, such as
  LANGFLOW_CONFIG_DIR, printed a line for it. A knowledge base never
  reads such a name from the environment.

A policy is now printed as its readers take it: the entries between the
commas, on one line with no space in it, and no line when there is none.
A policy with an entry that is anything but a switch, a host, an address
or a range prints the placeholder in place of the value. A protected
name prints no line.

The test that compares the whole list no longer reads these policies
from the shell that runs it.

feat(api): run the database copy from the migration endpoints (#15610)

* feat(api): run the database copy from the migration endpoints

Add the endpoints that start, follow and stop a copy step of the migration,
with the first of the three copies: the SQLite database into the new
instance's PostgreSQL database.

POST /migration/steps/{id}/runs starts the command with the step runner and
records the run under the step. GET .../runs/{run_id}/events streams the run's
events from a given seq, and DELETE .../runs/{run_id} stops it. A run belongs
to no request, so how it ended is written to the record the first time
anything reads the record afterwards.

The command gets its addresses from the environment, never the command line.
Its environment is the server's without any LANGFLOW_, AWS_ or PGVECTOR_
variable, plus the ones the copy is given by name, so it cannot write to
this instance by following the server's own settings.

A copy step is done when its run was made during the pause that is on now
and reported ok. Otherwise it is blocked with the command's own code, or
crashed, cancelled or interrupted.

* fix(api): count a migration copy only for the pause that let it in

A copy was checked against the pause and the steps before it, and then its
command was started. Changes turned back on and paused again in between
left a copy that started during the new pause, and its step read done
though that pause had checked and backed up nothing.

The run's entry now keeps the pause that let it in, and the step counts the
run only for that pause, whenever it started. Once the command has started,
the record is read again: if the pause or the saved destination is no
longer the one the copy was let in for, the run is stopped and the request
answers 409 state_changed.

A copy is also let in only when this worker's secrets are for the
destination that is saved. A worker that holds the secrets of an earlier
one answers 409 secrets_missing, as one that holds none does.

* fix(api): hold a migration copy to the steps before it once it has run

A step that has run keeps saying where it stands when an earlier step
opens again, and a copy was let in on what its own step said. So a copy
that had been made could be started again while the check or the pause
before it was blocked, where a copy that had never run was refused.

A copy is now let in only when every step before it is done or skipped,
whatever its own step says. Otherwise it answers 409 locked with
earlier_step, like a step that has not started.

* fix(api): refuse a save of the migration record that another worker has overtaken

A request reads the record, changes it and saves it. Two workers that
did so at the same moment each held what they read, and the second save
undid the first. A copy that started could put back a pause that another
worker had just ended, while its command kept running.

Every save now counts the record's generation up, under a short lock,
and a save of a record that is behind is refused. The start of a copy
takes its last look again on what the other worker saved, and stops its
command when it is no longer let in. Turning changes back on, the
pause's own saves, the outcome of a run or of a check and the stamp of
a backup are made again on the newer record. Any other save answers 409
with record_changed.

* fix(api): stop a copy's command when the save of its run does not go through

A copy start begins its command, then saves the run into the record. When that
save was refused five times in a row, or failed for another reason, the route
answered with the error and left the command running. The record said nothing
of it, so the page offered no way to stop it, and a second start answered that
a run was active.

The route now stops the command before it passes the error on.

A new test holds the record's lock from a second descriptor and shows that a
save waits for it. The tests of the overtaken save run their two saves one
after the other, so they pass without the lock.

* test(api): wait for a stopped copy's end before reading how it ended

The stop returns once the command is gone, and the run's last status is written
a moment later. The test of a copy start whose save is refused read the status
at once. It now waits for the run's end, as the tests beside it do.

The route logs that it stopped the command, and the thread of the lock test is
a daemon, so a failing assertion cannot keep the process from ending.

* fix(api): keep a running copy followable when a step before it opens again

A copy whose command was still running read locked with earlier_step as soon as a resume or a failed recheck reopened an earlier step. The page draws a copy's progress and its stop only for a live step, so the admin lost both while the command kept writing to the destination. A running copy now keeps reading current; a new start is still refused by the earlier-step check.

* test(api): cover a copy outcome that must not overwrite a newer run

_settle_copies writes how a run ended only when the record still names that run. Without that check, a worker that read the record before another worker started a newer copy would overwrite the newer running entry, leaving its command with nothing to follow or stop it. Replacing the check with True left the suite green; this test fails on it.

* fix(api): keep a run live for the worker that reads it when the clock is set

A run read as interrupted when neither its worker nor its child matched what the status file had
recorded. A process is told apart by when it started, and on macOS that time moves when the system
clock is set: psutil shifts it once the boot time differs by a second or more from the one it read
at import. After such an update a run read as interrupted while both processes were alive, it then
ended done, and a second run could be started on top of the live one.

The worker that started a run knows it is live without asking the system: it is the one reading
the child. read_run now asks that first.

* fix(api): let the worker that reads a run stop it when the clock is set

A cancel found the child through what the status file had recorded of it. After a clock update on
macOS that matches no process, so stopping a run did nothing until the run ended by itself.

When the recorded identity finds nothing, the worker that reads the child now uses the child it
holds. The handle says the child has not exited until one loop turn after it was reaped, and in
that gap its pid may be free, so the process with that pid must also have this worker as its
parent. Every other case finds the child as before.

fix(data-subjects): erase legacy knowledge base directories under dot-prefixed usernames (#15684)

* fix(data-subjects): erase legacy knowledge base directories under dot-prefixed usernames

A username may start with a dot, and the storage upgrade reads such a
builder's `<username>/<name>` directories. The builder erase skipped every
folder whose name starts with a dot, so that it never took the internal
`.migration` folder for an owner's. A builder named `.bob` therefore kept
their upgraded base's original directory, and their empty folder, after
an erase.

Only `.migration` and the SQLite stores in `sqlite/<owner id>` are now
treated as internal. The erase scan and its plan skip both, as the
upgrade's own scan does, and the two scans share the SQLite store rule.
Usernames are unique regardless of case, and macOS and Windows match
folder names the same way, so `.migration` is matched regardless of case.
Every other folder goes through the existing checks: a directory tied to
another account, or one that is unreadable or a symbolic link, is still
kept and counted. Every candidate directory is checked against the
internal locations, and so is each planned removal when it runs.

This also stops a builder named `sqlite` from removing another account's
SQLite store when that store holds a `.kb_deleted` file.

* fix(data-subjects): match the SQLite store folder regardless of case

macOS and Windows match folder names regardless of case, so once a user
named `SQLite` has a legacy folder, the 1.13 SQLite stores are written into
it under that spelling. The exact-case check then took `SQLite/<owner id>`
for a legacy directory: erasing that builder could remove another account's
SQLite store, and the adoption scan surveyed the stores as legacy sources.

Compare the folder with casefold, as `is_owner_folder` already does for
`.migration`.

fix(knowledge-bases): find legacy directories by evidence, not the current username (#15683)

A legacy local Chroma base lives in <knowledge_bases_dir>/<username>/<name>,
under the username its owner had when the directory was written, and
renaming a user does not move it. The upgrade resolved it from the owner's
current username. A base renamed before 1.13 stayed needs_attention and its
only copy was never upgraded. Startup adoption gave the old directory to
whoever took the name. Deleting a base could retire another account's
directory and hide it from the inventory. A renamed owner's old directories
did not reserve their names.

The new legacy_sources module ties each <folder>/<name> directory to bases
by evidence: the ledger's source_identity, the base id that an
embedding_metadata.json sidecar records when that base exists, and the
folder of the owner's current username or of a former one that this
evidence shows. A directory that more than one base may hold, or a base
with more than one directory, fails closed with legacy_source_ambiguous,
and a base with none fails with legacy_source_missing. A folder-name claim
is contested by a same-named base that holds data but found no directory.

migrate_one records the located directory in the ledger before anything
can fail, so a later rename cannot move it, and locates it again only if
it moved away before the snapshot. Adoption records its ledger run, and
adopts a directory for its folder's holder only when the sidecar records a
base id and a creation time no earlier than the holder's account, nothing
shows that another account held the name, and no same-named base is still
missing its data. Otherwise the inventory reports
unattributed_legacy_source. retire_legacy_source binds only the
directories that are the base's alone, and ensure_legacy_name_available
also reserves names under former usernames.

One attribution is shared per upgrade pass, and creating a base scans the
storage root only when a directory of that name exists. The upgrade notice
shows guidance for the two new error codes.

fix(data-subjects): erase only the builder's own legacy knowledge base directories (#15682)

A builder erase removed <knowledge_bases_dir>/<username> whole. Usernames
can change and be taken again, and legacy Chroma directories stay under
the name their owner had when they were written, so erasing whoever took
a name deleted the former holder's directories, which are the only copy
of a base whose upgrade is still needs_attention or migrating. Erasing a
builder named "sqlite" deleted every account's SQLite stores, and a
username with a slash pointed into another account's folder.

The plan now lists one <owner>/<name> directory per item, and only when
the builder's ledger row, one of their Chroma bases under their current
name, or the base id in the directory's sidecar ties it to them, and no
ledger row or sidecar ties it to another account. A ledger row older
than the builder's account belongs to a former holder of the name. Only
directories that look like a legacy store are removed, through the
retained-source path. Unreadable or symlinked directories are kept and
counted in a warning. A binding is forgotten only once its directory is
gone, and the folder named after the builder is removed once empty.

fix(data-subjects): delete the storage upgrade's application backup once it has finished (#15681)

The automatic Chroma-to-SQLite upgrade takes one consistent backup of a
SQLite application database under
.migration/application-backups/. Nothing ever removed it, and
data-subject erases delete rows from the live database only, so every
erased message, trace, transaction, job, memory row and account stayed
in the backup while the erase reported done.

Nothing reads the backup back: a retried base uses its own routing
record and source snapshot. So it now lasts only while the upgrade
does:

- A coordinator pass deletes this database's backup, its interrupted
  .incomplete copy and their SQLite journals when it ends with the
  upgrade finished: discovery is complete and no base is on Chroma,
  migrating or needs attention (the query strict readiness now shares).
- Before an erase finishes, it does the same, unless a pass is running.
  Passes and erases are serialized by a per-event-loop lock, and backups
  are created only inside a pass.
- Whatever remains is recorded as counts.retained_backups and as
  backups_not_reached on the dsar:erase audit event, including a backup
  that cannot be deleted. That case no longer blocks the erase.
  rows_deleted excludes the new count.

PostgreSQL application databases get no local backup and report 0.
The upgrade guide now says the backup supports recovery only while the
upgrade runs, and explains how erases treat it.

fix: accept dictionary input in Type Convert JSON and Message outputs (LE-3003) (#15680)

* fix: preserve dictionary payloads in Type Convert JSON output

* fix: accept dictionary input for Type Convert Message output

convert_to_message called dict.to_message(), raising AttributeError even
though the helper documents dictionary support. Wrap the dictionary in
Data(data=v) first so it converts the same way a JSON input with that
payload does. Regenerate the component index for the new code hash.

The regression test follows the dict-to-JSON test from #15536: the same
model-field-name payload, and checks that the input is not mutated and
that component status holds the result.

feat(frontend): add the pause step to the migration page (#15608)

* feat(frontend): add the pause step to the migration page

"Pause changes" asks before it pauses. When the server refuses because
something is still writing, the step lists each run with its owner, its
state and its own cancel action, and each trigger listener process that
is still up, with a button to check again. Once the pause is on, the
page runs the check again with the saved version, and the step stays
blocked until that run passes.

While changes are paused a banner stays in view, with a button that
turns them back on after a confirmation. The confirmation says that the
backup and the copies made so far go out of date. "If something goes
wrong" says how to go back from where the move stands.

For the banner to stick, the two boxes the settings shell wraps every
page in now clip their overflow where they hid it. Neither box scrolls,
and a hidden one is what a sticky element inside a page sticks to. No
other settings page changes.

* fix(frontend): show a pause that still waits as changes being refused

The record holds "pausing" from the moment a pause is asked for until the
changes that were under way have ended. Changes are refused in that time. When
the server stops in it, "pausing" stays, and the page showed no banner and no
way to turn changes back on.

The banner and "If something goes wrong" now read "pausing" as they read
"pause". Turning changes back on ends both.

* fix(frontend): say that a waiting pause has not begun, and that an ended one did not

The banner read "Changes are paused on this instance" for a pause that still
waits. The server takes such a pause for no backup and no copy, so the banner
now says that changes are refused and that the pause has not begun, with who
asked for it and when.

A request for a pause that was ended while it waited is answered 409 with
pause_ended. The page showed "Something went wrong" for it. It now says that
the pause did not begin, and why.

feat(frontend): add the secret key step to the migration page (#15607)

* feat(frontend): add the secret key step to the migration page

"Hand over the secret key" says where this instance's key is and tells
the admin to set it on the new instance. The admin proves it with the
first 12 characters of the key's SHA-256, which a one-line command
prints where the new instance's key is set. The key itself never enters
the page, and the field has no room for it.

The server keeps the last answer, so a mismatch still shows after a
reload. A request that never reached the server shows as failed, and
the last mismatch is not shown as its outcome.

* fix(frontend): let the fingerprint command wrap in the secret key step

In a narrow window, or at 250% zoom and above, the command box scrolled sideways. Not every
browser lets the keyboard reach a scrolling box, so the end of the command could go unread
without a mouse. The command now wraps and fits, and nothing scrolls.

feat(frontend): add the destinations step to the migration page (#15606)

"Where your data goes" asks only for what this instance keeps on its own
server: the address of an empty PostgreSQL database for a SQLite
instance, and an S3 bucket with its keys for local files. Knowledge
bases go into the new instance's database, so that section only says
so. Saving tests each destination, and a refused one says why next to
its own fields, in the page's words and then in the server's. A saved
step shows where the data goes and never a password or a key. Those
stay in the server's memory, so the step can ask for them again.

A save that never reached the server shows as failed, and what the last
test found is not shown as its outcome.

A step shows its form only when the server says the admin has reached
it and can do it. When a step finishes, focus moves to the heading of
the next one.

feat(flow-versions): keep versions an extension marks as retained (#15638)

* feat(flow-versions): keep versions an extension marks as retained

Add a `retained` flag (and `retained_reason`) to flow versions for versions
something outside OSS depends on, such as an Editor deployment that shipped
them.

- Pruning skips retained versions, and re-checks the flag in its DELETE so a
  version retained mid-prune survives.
- Deleting a retained version answers 409 with the reason.
- `set_flow_version_retained` sets or clears the flag in the caller's
  transaction.
- Version reads expose `retained` and `retained_reason`.
- Migration adds both columns; existing versions read as not retained.

* fix(flow-versions): rebase retained migration onto release-1.13.0 head

Repoint e5a7c9b1d3f2 from d42f18a9b760 to d4f1a6c8e2b7 to resolve the
multiple-heads conflict after merging release-1.13.0.

fix(data-subjects): erase the Chroma copies kept by the storage upgrade (#15676)

The automatic Chroma-to-SQLite upgrade keeps the original store directory and
a snapshot under .migration/<kb_id>/<run_id>/source for rollback, and deleting
the base keeps them too. An end-user erase only reached the live SQLite store,
so a finished erase left the person's Memory Base chunks in both copies. A
builder erase removed the original directory but orphaned the snapshot.

End-user erase: a new memory_legacy_copies step after memory_vectors walks the
upgrade ledger and removes each retained copy, and a failed run's export, that
may hold the person's chunks. It only removes copies that no longer back live
data, and waits for a base whose deletion has not finished. Detection matches
the end_user_id key and value, never the bare id, and errs toward removal.
Copies are renamed out of the inventory scan's sight before deletion.

Builder erase: the storage plan also removes the builder's .migration/<kb_id>
directories, sources kept under a former username, and source bindings. Ledger
rows are matched by the builder's bases as well as by name, and rows of a base
someone else owns after a rename are left alone, in the plan and in the
knowledge_base_upgrades step.

fix(api): fail knowledge bases as their database did when it is refused (#15605)

PUT /api/v1/migration/destinations forgets a database address that fails
its test. Knowledge bases sent in the same request then found no address
to be tested in and answered secrets_missing, which tells the admin to
enter again an address that was just entered.

They now answer what the database answered, with its code and reason.
secrets_missing is left for knowledge bases that are sent alone while
this worker holds no address, as after a restart.

feat(api): back up an instance before its migration (#15604)

* feat(api): back up an instance before its migration

POST /api/v1/migration/backup/database sends a consistent copy of a
SQLite database, made with VACUUM INTO while changes are paused. The
copy is deleted when the download ends, whether or not it finished. A
streamed response does not close its source when the client goes away,
so the download uses a response that does.

POST /api/v1/migration/steps/backup/confirm records where the admin put
the backup. On SQLite it answers 409 database_not_downloaded until the
copy was downloaded during the current pause. A PostgreSQL database is
backed up with its own tools, so there is nothing to wait for.

A backup from before the current pause no longer counts, because it
lacks whatever changed since.

* fix(api): bind migration backups to their original pause

feat(api): confirm the secret key reached the new instance (#15603)

POST /api/v1/migration/secret-key/verify takes the fingerprint the admin
read on the new instance, the first 12 hex characters of the key's
SHA-256, and compares it in constant time. A match is recorded with who
and when. Anything else answers 400 fingerprint_mismatch and is recorded
too, so the step reads as blocked until a fingerprint matches.

GET /migration says whether the key lives in a file or in the
environment, so the page can tell the admin how to carry it over. It
never returns the key or its fingerprint: a fingerprint that is handed
out would pass the check without anyone reading the new instance.

feat(api): test and save the destination of a migration (#15602)

* feat(api): test and save the destination of a migration

PUT /api/v1/migration/destinations tests each part of the destination it
is sent and saves how the test ended: the database (a new, empty
PostgreSQL database the user can create tables in), the vector extension
for knowledge bases, and a bucket the keys can write to. A part the
instance does not need is refused, and an instance that keeps nothing on
its own disk skips the step.

The bucket is tested with the keys it was given and nothing else. The
session reads no variable of the server's environment, no AWS config
file and no shared credentials file, so a profile named there cannot
fail the test. A bucket that answers 404 is missing, one that answers
403 is denied, and anything else never got an answer about the bucket.

The record keeps where each part is and never a user, a password or a
key. The password and the keys stay in this worker's memory, for the
copies to use. The route reads and checks its own body, so a body that
fails is answered without its values and is never logged. It reads the
record only once the tests are over, so what another request saved
meanwhile is kept.

* fix(api): hold a destination's secrets in the step that saves it

PUT /migration/destinations changed what this worker holds as soon as
the database test ended, and wrote the record only after the tests of
the other parts. A save that waited on its bucket test could end after
a second save: the record then named the first database while the
worker held the address of the second, and a copy would have written to
one while the record reported the other.

Each test now runs on what its own request brought, and nothing is held
until the tests are over. The record is written and the secrets are
changed in one step, with nothing awaited in between, so whichever save
ends last decides both. The secrets also say which saved part they
belong to, in _secrets["for"], which lets a copy refuse a secret that
is not the one of the saved destination, in any worker.

* fix(api): tie what knowledge bases found to the database it was found in

A saved knowledge base test stayed when another database address was
saved without it. The step then read done on the strength of a database
nobody had tested for the vector extension.

The saved database now carries an identity beside its location: a short
digest of the user, the host, the port, the name and every option of
the address, without the driver and without any password. The location
leaves the options out, and a host or a search_path given there changes
where a copy lands. When a database with another identity is saved and
knowledge bases are not sent with it, their saved test is dropped and
the step waits for it again. The same database saved again keeps it.

* refactor(api): hold or forget a destination's secret through _hold again

The step that saves a destination did by hand what _hold does. It calls
_hold again, once the tests are over, so the helper is unchanged and
stays the one place where a secret is held or forgotten. No change in
behaviour.

* fix(api): read a destination that failed as blocked while another part is missing

The step for the destinations answered "current" whenever a part the
instance needs was not saved, before it looked at how the saved parts
had fared. Since a database saved alone drops what knowledge bases found
in the one before it, a database that cannot be reached then read as
"current", and the admin lost the reason.

A part that was saved and failed now decides first: the step reads
blocked with its code. Only when none failed does a missing part make
the step current.

* fix(api): drop what knowledge bases found in a database replaced meanwhile

Knowledge bases sent without a database are tested in the database this
worker holds. A test takes a while, and another save could replace the
database before this one wrote: the record then named the new database
next to what the knowledge bases had found in the old one.

The save now compares the database the test ran in with the saved one
when it writes. If they differ, the result is not kept, as when a new
database is saved alone.

* fix(api): name the missing pgvector package apart from the missing extension

The knowledge base test answered pgvector_missing in three cases. Two
are about the destination database and are for its admin to fix. The
third is this server's own Python package, which a plain install of
Langflow does not include, and it is fixed by whoever runs Langflow.

That case now answers pgvector_package_missing, with the reason it had.

* fix(api): test knowledge bases where a PostgreSQL instance's own variable points

An instance that already runs on PostgreSQL keeps its database, and its
knowledge bases move into pgvector. After the copy the server reads
them through its own PGVECTOR_CONNECTION_STRING, so the copy has to
write where that variable points. The destination test asked the
instance's database address, and said nothing when the variable was
missing.

The test now asks the database the variable names. Without the variable
it answers pgvector_env_missing and says to set it and restart, so the
admin learns it at this step and not after the pause. The value of the
variable holds a password: it goes to the test and is neither saved nor
returned. An instance on SQLite is tested as before.

* fix(api): give one database on an IPv6 host one identity

An IPv6 host can be written in several ways: in upper or lower case,
with or without its zeros. Each spelling gave the destination database
another identity, so the same database entered again read as a new one.

The host now goes into the identity by its one canonical spelling. Other
hosts, and what the page shows as the location, are as before.

* fix(api): keep a password with an "@" in it out of a destination's location

A database password with an "@" that is typed as it is, and not as %40,
ends at that "@" where the address is read. The rest of it is taken for
the host, and for the database or an option when it also holds a "/" or
a "?". The location that is saved and shown is built from those parts,
so it held a part of the password. So did the driver's message about a
host it could not find, which goes back in the response.

Nothing tells such a part from a real one, so an address with an "@"
after what is read as its password is not read at all. No location and
no identity is kept for it, and its test answers at once that an "@" in
the password has to be written as %40, and asks no driver.

A user name with an "@" in it, as some servers name their users, is
read as before.

* fix(api): handle malformed migration destination hosts

* fix(api): test and keep a bucket's endpoint only when it is a plain address

The record kept the bucket's endpoint as it was sent. An endpoint with a
user and a password in it, or with a token after a "?" or a "#", left them
in migration.json, in the answers of the migration routes and in the record
an admin downloads for support. The bucket's client also wrote the endpoint
to the debug log, and repeated one it could not read in its error.

An endpoint is now tested and kept only when it is http or https, a host,
and at most a port and a path. The path takes no "%", which could spell the
"@" and the "?" that are refused before it. Any other endpoint is neither
tested nor kept: the answer for the bucket is bucket_unreachable and says
how to enter it, the way an address of the database with an "@" in its
password is handled.

Nothing can tell a token from a host name or from a path, so those are kept
as typed.

feat(api): pause and resume changes from the migration endpoints (#15601)

* feat(api): pause and resume changes from the migration endpoints

POST /api/v1/migration/pause writes the pause into the migration record,
and from that moment every worker refuses changes. DELETE removes it.

The pause is refused while anything is still writing: a job that is
queued, running or suspended, a knowledge base marked as ingesting, or a
trigger listener process that is alive. The 409 lists each one. A job's
cancel route answers only the job's owner, so the admin gets the whole
request that cancels each of their own jobs (method, URL and body) and
the owner's name for every other job. Nothing is cancelled for the
admin, because a suspended job holds a person's pending decision.

The pause step is done only once a check that started during the pause
has passed. Until then it reads as blocked, with recheck_pending or
recheck_failed. The page starts that check. A check from before the
current pause no longer counts.

A step that has started now keeps its own state when an earlier step
reopens, so a failed re-check shows on both the check and the pause.

The two steps before the pause get their routes in the next change. Until
then only the record can say they are done, so the pause stays locked on
a real instance.

* fix(api): let the changes already let in end before a pause counts

A request that the pause middleware had let in could still be writing
when POST /migration/pause wrote the pause and answered 200: a long
upload finished its file and its row while the instance read as paused.
The look for jobs also came before the write, so a job that a request
queued in between was missed.

The pause is now written first, which closes the door in every worker.
Then it waits for the changes that were let in before. Each one holds a
place for as long as it runs: a count in its own worker, and a shared
lock on CONFIG_DIR/migrations/pause.lock that the other workers see and
the kernel lets go of when a process dies. The place is taken before the
pause is asked about, so no change can slip between the two. Only when
no place is held does the pause look for jobs and listeners.

If changes are still going after five seconds the pause is taken out
again and the route answers 409 requests_active. It is also taken out
when jobs or listeners are found, and when the request is cut off while
it waits. A pause that another request made is left alone. Once the
instance is still, frozen_at is stamped again, so that a check or a copy
counted "after the pause" cannot have started while a change was still
going.

Where there is no flock (Windows) only this worker's changes are
counted. With the feature off the middleware is not installed, and
nothing takes the lock.

* fix(api): keep a trigger listener idle while the instance is paused

A langflow listeners process that started during a pause announced its
lease and claimed its connections, and would then write the events it
received. The pause route refuses to begin while a listener is alive,
but it cannot see one that starts afterwards, such as the child that
LANGFLOW_LISTENERS_MODE=subprocess starts again whenever it exits.

A reconcile pass now holds a place among the changes a pause waits for,
and does nothing while the instance is paused. A pause that is written
during a pass waits for it and then finds the listener's lease. With the
feature off the pass loads nothing and takes no lock.

* test(api): give the paused record a bucket for the file the upload adds

The upload tests leave a file on the instance's own disk. Once the
destinations step exists, such an instance has to name a bucket before
it can pause, so the record these tests start from now names one.

* fix(api): wait for a flow sync pass that began before the pause

The loop that reads flows from disk asked whether the pause was on when
a pass began, and then read and wrote for the rest of the pass. A pause
that was written in between did not wait for it, so the pass could end a
write after the pause counted. The app under test runs this loop too,
which is why test_the_flow_sync_from_disk_waits_out_the_pause failed
now and then.

A pass now holds a place among the changes a pause waits for, as a
request does, and lets go of it before it sleeps. The test pauses the
way the route does: it writes the pause, waits for the passes that began
before it, and only then adds the flow. A new test holds a pass open on
an event and shows that the pause waits for it.

The trigger dispatcher, the telemetry writer and the audit cleanup still
ask at the start of a pass and hold no place.

* fix(api): stop holding the migration pause for a run that waits for a person

A suspended run held the pause. One that was not started in the
background has no cancel route (the stop route takes background runs
only), so POST /pause answered 409 with nothing to send for as long as
the run waited.

Such a run cannot write while changes are paused: the answer it waits
for is a change, and the pause refuses it with 503. The run is copied
with the rest of the data. So it no longer holds the pause and is not
listed among the jobs.

* fix(api): wait for the other loops' passes that began before the pause

The trigger dispatcher, the audit log cleanup and the telemetry writer
write with no request around them. Each asked whether the pause was on
when a pass began and held no place, so the pause could count while a
pass that began just before it was still writing, as the flow sync
could before the last fix.

Each of their passes now holds a place for as long as it runs: the two
ticks of the dispatcher, the audit sweep, and the flush and the
retention sweep of the telemetry writer. The calls are wrapped where
the loops make them, so a pass that is called directly behaves as
before.

* fix(api): keep a running trigger listener's lease alive while a pause is tried

A reconcile pass that is not let in did nothing at all, and the lease a
pause finds a listener by is renewed only in a pass. A pause that is
refused over a change still under way stays written while it waits. An
admin who tried it again for longer than a lease lasts let the lease run
out, and the next pause went through with the listener still connected
and writing the events it received.

A listener that has already reconciled now renews its lease on such a
pass and does nothing else. One that starts during a pause still
announces nothing.

* fix(api): say what a migration pause is still waiting for

A pause that gave up waiting answered 409 requests_active and nothing
else, so the admin learned only that something was still under way.

Each place among the changes a pause waits for now says what holds it
and since when: a request by its method and path, a live connection by
its path, a loop by its name. A refusal carries the places of this
worker as "changes", and "elsewhere" when another worker holds one,
which the shared lock cannot name.

The order stays as it was. The changes under way end first, and the
jobs and listeners are looked for after the wait, so a request that
runs a flow does not refuse the pause with a job that ends with it. A
change that outlasted the wait is told together with the jobs.

* fix(api): keep work that outlives its request visible to a migration pause

A request holds its place among the changes a pause waits for only
until it answers. A webhook answers 202 and runs its flow in a task of
its own. A Playground build answers with its id and runs in a task of
the job queue, and the memory capture after a run is started the same
way. Each writes its job only once its graph is built, if it writes one
at all. A pause that landed in between found no place and no job and
went through, and the run then wrote during the pause.

writing_on() takes a place for such a task while the request still
holds its own, and lets it go when the task ends. The job queue calls
it for every task it starts, and the webhook route for its run.

Three more runs go on with no request around them. The task of a
background run holds a place as well: a run that is told to stop is
marked as cancelled at once and still writes until its task ends, so a
pause asked for right after the cancel went through under it. A tool
call over the MCP SSE transport runs in the task of the open stream,
after the POST that carried it has answered 202. An A2A run goes on in
a task of the SDK after its request has answered. Each holds a place
from where it begins, and the tool call is refused when the pause came
first.

A task that is a job by the time a pause gives up is told as that job,
with who can cancel it. One that is not is told as work a request left
running.

With the feature off nothing is taken.

* fix(api): refuse a GET that changes the instance while it is paused

The pause middleware lets every GET through as a read. The route an
OAuth provider sends the browser back to is a GET, and it stores the
tokens of a connection. A consent that was begun before the pause and
came back during it wrote those tokens after the database copy, so the
new instance never got them.

A route that changes the instance on a GET now says so with the
dependency changes_the_instance(). Its request holds a place like any
other change and is refused with 503 while the pause is on. The two
browser routes of the OAuth flow take it. The refusal uses up nothing
of the consent, so the same answer of the provider completes it after
the pause.

* fix(api): keep a pause that still waits from counting as a pause

The pause route wrote the pause first and then waited for the changes
that were let in before it. While it waited, the record already read as
paused. A second pause request was answered with success, and a check
that passed in that time finished the pause step, though a change was
still writing.

A pause that still waits is now written as "pausing". It refuses new
changes as a pause does, and no check or copy is measured against it. It
becomes the pause once every change before it has ended. A second
request waits for those changes as well. One that a stopped worker left
behind is finished by the next request, and turning changes back on ends
it.

* fix(api): keep an A2A run's place until its last state is saved

A run held its place among the changes a migration pause waits for
while its executor ran. The SDK reads the last event of a run after the
executor has returned, and saves the task then. A pause that came in
between was confirmed, and the task went from working to its final
state while changes were paused.

The place is now kept until the task store has written a state that
ends the run, and until the executor has returned, because a cancel
writes its state while the run still goes. If that save never comes,
the place is given up after a minute, so a run whose reader is gone
cannot hold every pause off.

* fix(api): refuse a pause request whose pause was ended while it waited

A request for a pause waits for the changes that are still under way. While it
waits, changes can be turned back on, or another request for the same pause
can be refused or cut off. The request then answered 200 with no pause in the
record, and the page went on as if the pause had begun.

It now answers 409 with code pause_ended.

Five tests looked only for "pause" after a request was refused or cut off.
What such a request can leave is "pausing", so they look for both.

* fix(api): keep the place of an A2A run that goes on with a waiting task

An answer to a task that waits for a person goes on with its run. The SDK
first saves the task once more in the state it already has, with the answer in
it. The task store took that save for the end of the run, so the place was let
go as soon as the run returned, and the saves that followed had none. A pause
could begin while the task was still working, and the task completed during it.

The store now tells the run only of a save that moves the task into a state
that ends a run.

The wait for that save also starts again at each save of the task. A reader
that is slow, because it sends a push to the caller between two saves, keeps
the place for as long as it still saves. The timer is kept on the place and
cancelled with it, and it no longer holds the request context.

* fix(api): wait for an erase under way and refuse the audited data subject reads while paused

The data subject feature merged after this layer was written.

An erase pass now holds a place, like the other background loops, so a pause
waits for the erase that is under way.

* fix(data-subjects): erase end-user memory on SQLite and refresh the counts

The end-user erase built its backend with a raw create_backend call and no
SQLite storage context. On SQLite, the default store in 1.13, it raised
ValueError at the memory_vectors step, so the erase never finished. It now
builds the backend through the storage runtime (backend_for_record), as the
session purge does.

After the delete, the erase now refreshes the knowledge_base row's cached
chunks, words and characters. The refresh goes through
refresh_metrics_after_purge, which this change factors out of the session
purge, and stays best-effort: a failure only logs a warning. Before, the
row recorded more chunks than the store held. check-integrity reported it
as mismatched, and relocate-kb --verify-skipped failed it with
kb_target_short.

A store that is migrating, needs attention, is detached or is still
deleting now raises StorageUnavailableError. The engine retries the request
instead of finishing it with the person's chunks still in place. A
tombstoned (deleted) store is skipped. Legacy local Chroma handling is
unchanged.

* fix(data-subjects): keep an erase open when the upgrade copied a missing legacy source

The end-user erase skips a legacy local Chroma Memory Base whose directory
is missing, because a store that was never written holds no chunks. But
the SQLite upgrade snapshots the source and imports it into an unpublished
SQLite generation before it switches routing. If the source directory
disappears after that point, the copied chunks remain, and the skip let
the request finish anyway.

The skip now also requires that the upgrade never captured the source,
which means the run never recorded a source_fingerprint. Otherwise the
erase reaches the storage runtime, raises StorageUnavailableError, and is
retried.

The storage state alone cannot tell the two cases apart. At startup every
ready legacy row is fenced to migrating, and the upgrade sends a
never-written row to needs_attention. Skipping on state would therefore
never skip, and erases over those Memory Bases would stay open for good.

* fix(jobs): rebind append_event's lock to its running event loop

JobService is a service-manager singleton whose asyncio.Lock was created
eagerly in __init__. asyncio.Lock only binds to a loop on its contended
path (creating a waiter future) -- the uncontended fast acquire never
touches the loop -- so the bind happens silently the first time two
appends actually overlap, and the lock is then stuck to that loop for the
service's lifetime. A singleton that outlives its first loop (e.g. the
real-service suite, a fresh event loop per test) hits "<Lock> is bound to
a different event loop" the next time append_event is contended, and the
caller's job gets marked failed with no error detail.

Lazily (re)create the lock -- and drop any queued items, which belonged
to a loop that's already gone -- whenever the running loop differs from
the one it's bound to. In production there's one loop for the process's
life, so this binds once and never again; it only matters when the
service instance is reused across loops.

Fixes the intermittent test_facade_real_services.py failures reported on
LE-2617 (2 of 3 runs failing); verified fixed via 3x re-run against real
Postgres (94 passed each run).

* fix(jobs): skip the append_event batching window when nothing to batch

append_event unconditionally slept _APPEND_EVENT_BATCH_WINDOW_S (10ms)
before every flush, even when the caller was the only one in the queue
-- a pure latency tax with nothing to batch against. Rafael's benchmark
on LE-2617 showed a lone job's DB time roughly doubling (0.84s -> 1.61s
for 46 events) for only an 11-14% jobs/s gain at saturation, where the
window actually pays for itself.

Give the window owner a free, zero-wall-clock yield (asyncio.sleep(0))
right after acquiring the lock -- enough for any already-scheduled
concurrent appender to join the queue, since asyncio.sleep(0) only lets
ready callbacks run, it doesn't wait in real time -- then only pay the
real window if that check finds company. A solo append (nothing ready
to join) flushes immediately; a genuinely concurrent one still shares a
transaction exactly as before.

test_cancelled_window_owner_hands_off_to_waiter needed its task
creation reordered: it relied on the old unconditional wait to give
itself room to cancel the leader before any flush started, which no
longer holds once a solo owner can flush immediately -- creating leader
and follower back-to-back (instead of yielding between them) restores
genuine lock contention so the cancel still lands before the flush.

and WebSocketRequestValidationError too. ResponseValidationError is a server
bug and is still logged.

fix(kb): treat a process reaped during its identity read as gone (#15566)

On Linux, process_identity opens /proc/<pid>/stat and then reads it. When
the process is reaped between the two calls, the read fails with
ProcessLookupError (ESRCH). Only FileNotFoundError was translated to
psutil.NoSuchProcess, so the error escaped through identity_matches into
the upgrade controller's stop loop, which polls for exactly that exit.

Catch ProcessLookupError as well. The new test starts a real child and
reaps it between the real open and the real read, so the error comes from
the kernel.

fix(jobs): keep in-request runs alive so orphan sweeps cannot fail them (#15665)

v1 /run, v2 sync workflows, playground builds and memory-base ingestion
mark their job IN_PROGRESS through execute_with_status but never
heartbeat it. Any orphan sweep that runs while one is in flight (the
Redis-fallback watchdog, or a sibling's startup sweep) fails it as
worker_lost with a run_failed event, which stay on the job after the
run ends COMPLETED.

execute_with_status(keep_alive=True) now keeps the job alive while the
run executes, stopping before the terminal status write and on a pause.
Each path inserts its job heartbeated, so the first heartbeat waits one
interval and a short run writes none: a v2 sync run is still one INSERT
and one UPDATE on the job table.

fix(knowledge): show orphaned ingestion runs as failed and keep live runs from being swept (#15664)

Run history read job_metadata.status, which only the ingestion's own
finalize_run sets to a terminal value. A run whose job the orphan sweep
failed after its worker died read RUNNING forever.

- Run history now follows the job once it has ended without the run
  finalizing (sweep, timeout, cancel, lost finalize write). A terminal
  status the run recorded itself still wins.
- KB ingestion jobs (API and flow component) now heartbeat while they
  run, so a sibling's startup sweep or the Redis-fallback watchdog can no
  longer fail a live run. The heartbeat starts after mark_running and
  stops before finalize_run, since both rewrite job_metadata.
- An API ingestion interrupted by a shutdown is recorded as failed
  instead of the SUCCEEDED it was initialized to.

  run whose worker died just before a restart is still reconciled. That
  pass skips rows with no heartbeat, which may be live synchronous runs.

fix(knowledge): finalize runs on repeated cancels and keep KB status on cancel (#15661)

Leaving a flow mid-ingestion drops the Playground stream. The response
generator then awaits the run task inside Starlette's cancelled AnyIO
scope, so the Knowledge task is natively cancelled on every loop tick.
The shield from the previous fix only blocks AnyIO cancellation, so the
writes that make the run terminal were interrupted and the run stayed
RUNNING. Those writes and the backend teardowns now run in their own
task and survive repeated cancels.

the list endpoint mapped a cancelled job to failed, the upload cancel
branch wrote FAILED, and a flow run never noticed the cancel. The list
no longer maps cancelled jobs, an upload cancel restores the KB's prior
status, and the component polls its job during the embedding call and

written.

MCP tools/list and the A2A agent card derive each flow's input schema by
building its graph, and the build instantiated every component, evaluating
the node's stored source (module-level assignments included). Both surfaces
answer callers who cannot build the flow themselves: tools/list on a project
shared with auth_type="none" runs for anonymous clients, and the agent card
is unauthenticated by spec. The public call paths refuse flows carrying
executable custom code, so listing handed an anonymous caller the execution
