advertised fields from the saved template. Build the graph without
instantiating components. The derived schema is unchanged for every shipped
starter project.

fix(workflow): cancel a disconnected stream's run task only once (#15662)

* fix(workflow): cancel a disconnected stream's run task only once

When a client drops a v2 workflow stream, Starlette cancels the response's
AnyIO task-group scope. The generator's finally then cancelled run_task and
awaited it inside that cancelled scope. AnyIO cancellation is level-triggered
and asyncio forwards a cancel of a waiting task to the task it awaits, so the
run received a fresh cancel on every event-loop tick: component cleanup was
cut short at its next await, and execute_with_status could lose its FAILED
write and leave the job row IN_PROGRESS. lfx's stream_workflow_frames had the
same pattern.

Add lfx.utils.async_helpers.cancel_and_wait: cancel once, then wait in a
shielded scope through asyncio.wait, which neither forwards a cancel nor
cancels on timeout. The wait is bounded (RUN_CANCEL_GRACE_SECONDS, 30s) so a
component that swallows its cancellation cannot pin the request forever; past
the grace period the run finishes unobserved and a late failure is logged.
Both stream generators use it and close their queue in a finally.

* fix(workflow): close the event queue before cancelling a stream's run task

terminal sentinel put on a full queue (lfx: drive()'s finally after the one
cancel; backend: generate_flow_events' success put after a swallowed cancel)
blocked forever and outlived the cancel grace period. The consumer now closes the
queue first: later puts return at once and a blocked put is released.

feat(api): run migration commands as child processes that outlive a request (#15580)

* feat(api): run migration commands as child processes that outlive a request

The migration page will run three long copy commands. A copy can take hours,
so a run cannot belong to the request that started it: the admin may reload
the page, or a second admin may open it, and both must follow the same run.

This adds the runner and nothing that calls it yet. It takes an argv and an
environment, spawns the child, and keeps two files per run under
CONFIG_DIR/migrations/runs: an append-only NDJSON log of the JSON objects the
child printed, each given a seq, and a small status file. Following,
cancelling and listing read those files and the pids in them, so any worker
process can serve a run that another worker started. One run is live at a
time. The environment and the argv are never written or logged.

* fix(api): skip an overlong line, ignore an unreadable run status, and test the edges

A stdout line longer than the stream limit used to end the reader with an
unhandled ValueError: the child was killed and its later report was never
read. The line is now skipped like any other line that is not JSON.

A status file that is not JSON, which a machine that lost power can leave,
used to make every listing and every start raise. It is now no run.

The tests gain the cases the first draft could not fail on: a follower that
starts after a long run is over, a half-written last line, a cancel that
arrives after the child exited, and a start from a worker that logs at DEBUG,
so the environment and the argv are looked for in the application log too.

* fix(api): treat a process reaped mid-read as gone, and test what a dead worker leaves

On Linux the shared process identity helper reads /proc/<pid>/stat itself.
When the process is reaped between the open and the read, the kernel answers
ESRCH, and that ProcessLookupError escaped into cancel_run, read_run and
start_run. Both places that ask about a process now read it as gone.

The half-written line test now uses a process that nothing reaps, so a
process that died but still holds its pid is covered on every platform. A
new test makes the log unwritable in the middle of a run: the child is
stopped and a follower still gets the end, from the status file.

* test(api): prove the child's environment, and stop racing SIGINT and the grace period

Nothing checked that the child runs with the environment it was given. A new
test does, and it fails when the server's own environment leaks in.

The two tests that stop a worker with Ctrl-C hung when pytest itself had been
started with SIGINT ignored, as a process started in the background of a shell
script is. The worker now sets the default handler, and its exit is awaited
with the same bound as every other wait.

The SIGTERM test gave the child one second to answer before it was killed,
which a busy machine can miss. The grace period there is now as long as the
other waits, and the test lets it run out only after it has seen the child's
answer.

* test(api): start the stranger a tenth of a second before the run it is mistaken for

The pid-reuse test handed the run's recorded pids to a process spawned right
after the run's child was killed. A process is told apart by its start time, to
within a clock tick, so a stranger born a few milliseconds from the child or the
worker was taken for it and the run read as running. It failed about one run in
four on a fast machine. The stranger now starts first and the run's processes
start a tenth of a second later.

* fix(api): discard oversized migration output lines completely

Preserve stdout line boundaries across stream overruns and cover split writes, EOF, and following events. Use a monotonic timer to separate process birth ticks in the PID-reuse test.

feat(kb): add --json output to relocate-kb and keep stored content out of errors (#15527)

* feat(kb): add --json to relocate-kb for a UI that runs it as a child process

An admin UI that starts relocate-kb has to parse its text to show anything,
and the text only appears once every knowledge base is done.

With --json, stdout carries one JSON object per line and logs go to stderr:
progress per batch of chunks copied, an item as each knowledge base finishes,
and a closing report with the counts and the knowledge bases that failed. A
run refused before it starts (a --target-config it cannot use, a database at
another revision) writes one error event. Exit codes are the same.

Each failure gets a stable code on the result, set where the failure is
raised, so a caller does not have to match on the reason text. A metric
refusal also names its way out: the flag that accepts the change, or the
target config that avoids it.

The target's connection settings are now resolved before the copy starts
instead of inside the first write, which is what lets a target that is not
set up be told apart from a write that failed.

Output without --json is unchanged.

* fix(kb): keep chunk text out of a failed relocation's reason and log

A failed write to Postgres surfaces as a SQLAlchemy error, whose message ends
with the statement and its parameters. For the copy those parameters are the
chunks of the batch, so one chunk Postgres refuses (a NUL byte Chroma had
stored, say) printed the batch's text in the knowledge base's reason and in
the warning logged next to it. The driver's own message can quote the value
too, on its later lines.

For a SQLAlchemy error the reason is now the driver error's class and first
line, and the log line carries the same text. Other errors read as before.

* fix(kb): keep documents out of a refused OpenSearch write's error

When OpenSearch refuses documents in a bulk write, opensearch-py raises a
BulkIndexError that carries each refused document next to the reason, and its
message prints all of it: chunk text, metadata and vector. That message became
a relocation's reason and log line, and ingestion logged it on every retry.

Both write paths (ingestion and the precomputed-vector copy) now raise an
error that says how many documents were refused and, for each kind of error,
what OpenSearch said about the first one. The original is not chained, since a
traceback would print the documents again.

* feat(kb): report a target that drops during the copy as unreachable

A real run first connects to the target when it writes, so a target that is
down or misaddressed failed there with the catch-all kb_failed, while the same
target in a dry run was kb_target_unreachable.

A write that fails with the driver's own connection error now gets
kb_target_unreachable: SQLAlchemy's OperationalError for Postgres and
opensearch-py's ConnectionError (its timeout and TLS errors included) for
OpenSearch. The match is on the exception type alone. Chroma has no such type,
so a Chroma Cloud target that drops still reads as kb_failed, and so does a
write the target refuses because of the data.

* feat(kb): name the phase in relocate-kb's progress events

The other commands a UI runs this way put a phase on each progress event, and
a reader that handles all of them expects the field. relocate-kb has one
phase, the copy, so every progress event now says "phase": "copying".

* feat(kb): code relocate-kb's upgrade and routing refusals for --json

Two refusals came in with SQLite sources after the codes were set: a
knowledge base whose storage upgrade has not finished, and one whose row
changed while it was copied. Both left code null, so a UI reading --json
could only match on the reason text.

kb_upgrade_pending marks a row still on Chroma or whose storage is not
ready; the way past it is to let 1.13 finish the upgrade. kb_routing_changed
marks a repoint that found the row's backend, generation or storage state
moved on. It is not kb_changed, which means the source's chunks changed and
asks for ingestion to stop; here the row itself was rerouted, often by
Langflow's own storage operations, and a re-run copies what it routes to now.

* fix(kb): report a knowledge base deleted mid-copy as kb_deleted

On 1.13, deleting a knowledge base tombstones its SQLite store before the
row is removed, so a relocation still copying it fails on its next read
("SQLite storage generation has been deleted") before the repoint can find
the row gone. That came out as kb_failed, which reads as something to
investigate, when the knowledge base was simply deleted.

A failure that no narrower code has named now checks the row: if it is
gone, or its storage_state is deleting or deleted, the result is kb_deleted
with the same reason the repoint gives. A database that cannot answer
leaves it kb_failed.

target that drops mid-copy is reported describes nothing that can happen.

small opensearch-py module. Embedded writes now catch BulkIndexError to keep
refused documents out of the error, and importing it from the stub raised

in a venv without opensearch-py and passed in one with it.

* fix(kb): code what relocate-kb's metric check refuses besides a metric change

The metric check now reads every source vector before anything is copied, so
it can refuse for two reasons the copy also has: a chunk stored without a
vector, and a read that returns fewer chunks than the source counted. The
caller coded whatever the check returned as kb_metric_change, which told a UI
to offer --allow-metric-change for something the flag does not get past.

The check sets the code with each reason it returns. A chunk without a vector
is kb_no_vectors and a short read is kb_read_short, the codes the copy gives
the same findings.

* fix(kb): report an OpenSearch target the metric check cannot reach as unreachable

An OpenSearch target now reads its metric from its index's mapping before
anything is copied. That is the first time a relocation resolves the target's
settings and connects to it, so a target that is not set up or not there now
fails in the metric check. The copy used to find both and report them as
kb_target_unreachable. The metric check reported them as the catch-all
kb_failed.

The target's metric lookup now gives kb_target_unreachable as well.

* feat(kb): code an index that cannot say its metric as kb_metric_unknown

OpenSearch now reads the metric of an existing index from its mapping, and
raises a configuration error when the mapping does not give one, for example
when the index has no vector field. For a target that came out as
kb_target_unreachable, which sends someone to check a connection that is
fine. For a source it was the catch-all kb_failed.

Both now get kb_metric_unknown. --allow-metric-change does not get past it,
because there is no known change to accept. The index has to be fixed or
removed.

* fix(kb): carry --allow-metric-change on an OpenSearch metric refusal too

An OpenSearch target's metric now comes from its index's mapping when the
index exists, and target config cannot change that. The refusal's reason says
so and names --allow-metric-change as the way through. The result carried only
the space_type suggestion, so a UI offering what the result names would send
someone to set a config that changes nothing.

The refusal now carries the flag for every target. An OpenSearch target keeps
the space_type suggestion as well, which works for an index that does not
exist yet.

* fix(kb): code a row the storage lock finds rerouted as kb_routing_changed

The relocation now takes the storage lock with the row it read, and the lock
refuses a row whose generation, backend or configuration has moved on. That is
the change the repoint used to find and report as kb_routing_changed. The lock
raises the same error for it as for a row it cannot use for any other reason,
so it came out as the catch-all kb_failed.

A failure that no narrower code has named already asks the row whether it was
deleted. It now also asks whether the row still routes where it did when it
was read, and reports kb_routing_changed when it does not. The reason is still
the error that stopped the copy.

The kb_metric_unknown test hands the metric check a store that raises the
error itself. This one leaves a real index with no vector field where the
target would go, so it also holds OpenSearch to raising the error type the
code is matched on.

* fix(kb): report a target that drops before the count as unreachable

A knowledge base with no chunks has nothing to write, so a real run first
connects to a Postgres target when it counts what arrived. That failed with
the catch-all kb_failed, in the same run that reported every knowledge base
with chunks as kb_target_unreachable.

driver's connection error, like the write.

The storage lock raises one error type for a row that was rerouted and for a
lock it could not get in time. Only the first is kb_routing_changed, and this
holds the lock through a move to show the second stays kb_failed.

different metrics, so it now finds the chunk this test stores without a
vector, and the copy's own check went untested. The test now runs against a
target with each metric, one the check reads the source for and one it does
not.

* feat(api): add audit events table and helpers

Adds the audit_events table from the audit log data contract and the
shared helpers every producer and reader goes through. Nothing produces
events yet; the flow and project write paths are wired separately.

The row describes an operation, never resource state: resource identity
and event-time name, the Langflow account, the authenticating credential,
an on-behalf-of pair, permission-level action, operation shape, event
type and result, a safe error code, a server-generated request id, and
details validated per resource type and schema version. No column has a
foreign key, so an event outlives the resource, user and API key it names.

The database constrains only the closed pairings: event type with result,
and the acting issuer with its subject. Action, operation and error code
are validated in the application so a new value is never a migration.

A succeeded event is staged in the mutation's own transaction, so neither
can commit without the other. A failure or denial is written after the
mutation rolled back, in its own transaction, bounded to four concurrent
connections; a storage outage there is logged, never raised into a
caller that is already failing. A draft that breaks the contract raises
before anything touches the database.

Reads are keyset-paginated on (timestamp DESC, id DESC) with a cursor
bound to its filters and no total. Retention deletes by age only,
90 days by default, at startup and on the existing cleanup cadence.

Indexes use ascending keys: DESC keys reflect as expressions and produce
a phantom autogenerate diff, while a B-tree serves the descending order
by backward scan. Migration df1410b1eefa is EXPAND and reversible.

holds the write lock.

spreadsheet does not need and rarely shows. The CSV column is now UTC to
the second; the JSON feed and the NDJSON export keep full precision, which
clients use to order rows exactly.

* fix(api): fold non-ascii case in audit search on sqlite

SQLite's LIKE folds ASCII only, so searching the audit feed for "äöü"
missed "ÄÖÜ" there while PostgreSQL found it. SQLite also reads stored
details JSON with non-ASCII letters escaped, so those never matched.

On SQLite the search now compares both sides through Python casefold and
unescapes details first, using functions registered on each connection.
PostgreSQL keeps its ILIKE unchanged (US-12 AC6, US-07 AC1).

* feat(api): let the audit feed jump to a page by offset

The console could only step one page at a time because the feed paged
by cursor alone. GET /api/v1/audits now also takes offset: the database
finds the row just before that position across both stores and the page
is read from that key like a cursor, so a jump pays for its depth once
and next_cursor keeps the following pages keyset-cheap. offset cannot be
combined with cursor; the export does not take it.

* fix(api): read a comma in the audit search as one phrase

Review follow-up on the unified audit feed and export (PR #15243).

- flatten_query_string_lists hands `q` over whole. It splits every value
  on `,` so a repeatable filter can be sent as one key; applied to a free
  text search, `q=invoice, q3` reached both routes as a repeated key and
  answered 400, raw or percent-encoded. `q` is the only key exempted and
  no other route declares one.
- /audits and /audits/export publish their query parameters. They read the
  query string themselves, so FastAPI had no signature to publish and the
  served spec listed none at all while /flows/audits listed all 14; they
  now cover every filter and page key, plus `format` on the export.
- iter_feed and iter_feed_batches are gone. Nothing called them once the
  export moved to iter_feed_batches_per_session, and they yielded with the
  caller's session still open — the pattern we moved away from.
- The export's connection test asserts on the pool. expunge_all() detaches
  the rows before the scope closes either way, so the old assertion held

* fix(db): merge the audit events and storage heads

release-1.13.0 advanced to d42f18a9b760 while the audit events table and
its timeline index were written on top of the earlier head, so meeting the
branches left two heads and every test that initialises the database
failed with "Multiple head revisions are present for given argument
'head'". The new revision joins the parents and changes nothing.

* fix(api): keep a project create rollbackable

release-1.13.0 (#15541) gave `_new_project` an `owns_transaction` flag and
threads it to the MCP registration, which is the helper's only commit. Both
create routes took the default, so the project committed before the flow
moves and the audit event were staged: a guard that refused a move answered
409 and left the project and its MCP server behind, and the audit event and
its mutation no longer committed or rolled back together.

Both routes now pass `owns_transaction=False`, which is what the flag is
documented for — a caller that makes further writes in the same transaction
and must be able to take the project back with them.

* fix(api): give MCP registration its own savepoint

A project create or rename hands `update_server` a transaction it does not
own, and on that path `update_server` re-raises the duplicate-name
`IntegrityError` rather than rolling back, because a rollback there would
discard the caller's work. The failed flush still leaves the session needing
one, and both registration helpers treat a failure as best effort, so the
swallowed error poisoned the caller's transaction: the next statement of the
create raised `PendingRollbackError` and the client got a 500 for a request
that had only lost a server name to a concurrent one.

Both helpers now run inside `session.begin_nested()` when the transaction is
borrowed, so the API key and the server write unwind together and the caller
gets its transaction back intact. A caller that owns the transaction lets
`update_server` commit, which no savepoint can contain, and keeps the plain
path.

* fix(audit): search non-ASCII details on postgresql

The module unescapes the stored `details` JSON on SQLite and read the column
as plain text on PostgreSQL, where `json` keeps exactly the text it was handed
and the column's serializer escapes every non-ASCII letter. So a search for
"Ärger" matched a row stored as `{"...": "Ärger"}` on SQLite and missed it
on PostgreSQL - the bug the module says it fixes, with tests that only cover
SQLite.

PostgreSQL now reads the column through `jsonb`, whose output function writes
the letters themselves. Verified against PostgreSQL 17: the row is missed by
`CAST(details AS TEXT) ILIKE '%équipe%'` and found through the cast, and a
project created with an accented description is returned by `?q=` on the live
feed.

* fix(audit): bound details, scope a project read

Three findings from the review of #15082, in the same read and record path.

A written project description was copied into `details` whole. The column it
comes from is free text of any length, and the row outlives the project,
stays for the retention period and is readable and searchable, so a secret or
a personal detail pasted into a description was kept there after the project
was edited or deleted. The producer now trims it to 255 characters and the
contract refuses anything longer, as it already does for a name.

`/projects/audits?project_id=X` passed no `resource_id`, so under an
authorization plugin it returned every past life of that id. The reasoning
for the asymmetry with the Flow read does not hold: a plugin that cannot
decide `project:X` outright resolves it through the workspace X is in *now*,
which a caller names when they re-create a freed id. Both named-resource
reads now keep the resource's current life, and the unfiltered feed stays
where a grant meant to read every life reads them all.

`build_audit_event` runs outside the write's `try`, so a draft that breaks the
contract raised through the route's own `except` and replaced its 4xx with a
500. The staged path still raises where a test sees it; the failure record
now logs the bug instead of answering with it.

* fix(audit): preserve lifecycle history and record MCP failures

perf(tray): cache speed-text attributes and derive width arithmetically

Every traffic refresh rebuilt the attributed-string dictionary (font,
color, paragraph style, baseline number, dict) and ran a CoreText layout
via NSAttributedString::size() just to size the status item, although
both depend only on the button height and the glyph advance.

The dictionary and the monospaced per-glyph advance (measured once
through the same layout engine with a "0" probe) are now cached keyed by
button height, and the width is computed as longest-line length times
the advance. The speed charset is pure ASCII on a monospaced font, so
the arithmetic width matched the layout width exactly (max deviation
0.000pt over 2000 realistic samples).

Standalone A/B over 43,200 updates (12h at 1 Hz), same hot path:

| variant | mean | p95 | phys_footprint after |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| rebuild + layout (old) | 6.89us | 7.8us | 19.8MB |
| cached attrs | 4.71us | 5.0us | 7.8MB |
| cached + arithmetic width | 0.27us | 0.3us | 6.0MB |

The retained-memory delta is malloc-zone fragmentation from the churn,
which this removes at the source.

perf(runtime): cap tokio workers at 4

The cap of 8 was a conservative pick from 8ccb0b9a; that commit's own
setup benchmark had the 4-worker / 8-blocking row as the best config:
639.3ms avg / 645.5ms max setup time and 22.1 avg threads, ahead of the
adopted 8-worker row (650.1ms / 662.4ms, 26.0 threads).

Startup parallelism is unaffected in practice: the setup join! polls
cooperatively on one task, and CPU work (validation, script eval, YAML
parse) runs on the spawn_blocking pool, which keeps its 8-thread cap
through the existing 2x invariant. A 12h live session showed the 8 idle
workers accumulating under 0.5s CPU total, so four parked stacks
(~0.4MB dirty) are pure overhead.

feat(core,anthropic,openai): declare mid-conversation support in model profiles (#41180)

Alternative to #41175 (#41150).

`ChatAnthropic` decides whether to keep a mid-conversation
`SystemMessage` in place by matching model names. That misses Bedrock
model IDs, and it makes callers such as deepagents keep their own model
and class allowlists. This PR moves the decision into the model profile.

- `ModelProfile` gets two fields, `mid_conversation_system_messages` and
`mid_conversation_tools`. The second covers adding a tool by full
definition or by reference. The block format stays provider-specific.
- `ChatAnthropic` reads `mid_conversation_system_messages` from its
profile instead of a list of model names.
- A chat model whose API can't send a capability turns it off in
`_resolve_model_profile`. `ChatOpenAI` does this when it isn't on the
Responses API, and `_ChatOpenAICodex` does it for both fields.
`AzureChatOpenAI` makes no claim, because the live API tests didn't
cover Azure.
- The profile data comes from the live API tests in #41175 and
langchain-ai/deepagents#6874.

A caller then checks one field:

```python
if (model.profile or {}).get("mid_conversation_tools"):
    ...  # add the tool in a message
```

## Review notes

- Bedrock still needs the same two fields in langchain-aws's profile
data, in a follow-up PR there.
- A new model ID now needs a profile entry. The old prefix list matched
new releases automatically.
- Passing `profile=` replaces the resolved profile, so it drops these
flags, as it already drops `reasoning_effort_levels`.
- The partners need a langchain-core release with the new fields first.
Otherwise they warn about unknown profile keys.

## Release note

`ModelProfile` gains `mid_conversation_system_messages` and
`mid_conversation_tools`. `ChatAnthropic` now decides whether to keep a
mid-conversation `SystemMessage` in place from its profile, not its
model name. Claude Sonnet 5 and Haiku 5.5 now keep it in place. Claude
Haiku 5.5 also gets a profile, so its default `max_tokens` rises from
4096 to 128000.

fix(fireworks): preserve reasoning in streaming and tool loops (#41093)

Fixes #40367

`ChatFireworks` now preserves streamed reasoning, replays assistant
reasoning in tool loops, and reports reasoning-token usage. V1 streams
keep reasoning, text, and tool-call content blocks separate.

---

`ChatFireworks` drops streamed reasoning and omits it from subsequent
tool-loop requests. Preserve `reasoning_content` so reasoning models
retain their context across tool calls.

- Replay string reasoning from Fireworks-tagged or untagged assistant
messages; exclude explicitly foreign-provider reasoning and incompatible
content blocks.
- Keep reasoning, text, and tool-call blocks separate in v1 streams
without changing raw tool-call indices.
- Expose reasoning-token counts in
`usage_metadata.output_token_details.reasoning` without changing
reported token totals.

([#38042](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/pull/38042)).

([#40085](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain/pull/40085),

fix(ollama): raise ollama floor to 0.6.3 for thinking levels (#40986)

Fixes #40985

---

`ChatOllama(reasoning="xhigh")` currently raises a Pydantic
`ValidationError` instead of reaching Ollama, because the `ollama` floor
still admits clients that reject model-defined thinking levels.

`ChatOllama.reasoning` is `bool | str | None` and `_chat_params()`
forwards the string verbatim as `think`. Since ollama 0.6.3
(ollama/ollama-python#744) `ChatRequest.think` is `Optional[Union[bool,
str]]`, matching the Ollama Go backend. But the declared range
`ollama>=0.6.1,<1.0.0` still admits 0.6.1 and 0.6.2, where the
annotation is `Optional[Union[bool, Literal["low", "medium", "high"]]]`
and `"xhigh"` or `"max"` fails validation client-side.

Verified both directions on the same snippet —
`ChatOllama(reasoning="xhigh")._chat_params(...)["think"] == "xhigh"`,
then constructing `ChatRequest(..., think=...)`:

- ollama 0.6.2 → `ValidationError` on `think.bool` and
`think.literal['low','medium','high']`
- ollama 0.6.3 → validates

This raises the floor only; no `ChatOllama` code path changes. Narrowing
`reasoning` inside `ChatOllama` instead would reject levels the Ollama
backend accepts and duplicate type logic the client now owns.

Per the PR template I'm opening this alongside the issue rather than
pre-approved, so please assign it to me if the approach looks right.

## Release note

`langchain-ollama` now requires `ollama>=0.6.3`, fixing a
`ValidationError` when `ChatOllama` is configured with a model-defined
reasoning level such as `"xhigh"` or `"max"`.

Release notes

Sourced from urllib3's releases.

2.8.0

🚀 urllib3 is fundraising for HTTP/2 support

urllib3 is raising ~$40,000 USD to release HTTP/2 support and ensure long-term sustainable maintenance of the project. If your company or organization uses Python and would benefit from HTTP/2 support in Requests, pip, cloud SDKs, and thousands of other projects please consider contributing financially to ensure HTTP/2 support is developed sustainably and maintained for the long-haul.

Thank you for your support.

Security

Fixed the following security issues:

  • The TLS configuration for HTTPS proxies could be ignored or overridden. (High severity, GHSA-8988-9cw3-xx77)
  • HTTPResponse.stream() and read_chunked() could buffer a chunk-size line of unbounded length in memory. (High severity, GHSA-vxq7-64xx-v4gw)
  • Chunked Deflate streaming could enter an infinite loop. (Medium severity, GHSA-gh4c-6fx4-qh6g)

[!IMPORTANT] urllib3 2.8.0 fixes HTTPS proxy TLS configuration being ignored or overridden by destination settings. Configurations relying on that behavior may require changes.

Configure proxy CA certificates and client certificates in proxy_ssl_context, and proxy identity checks with proxy_assert_hostname or proxy_assert_fingerprint. Destination client certificates and identity overrides no longer apply to HTTPS forwarding proxy connections.

[!NOTE] CVE IDs had not yet been assigned to these advisories at the time of release due to a backlog at GitHub's CNA.

Deprecations & Removals

  • Deprecated using an empty collection as the Retry option allowed_methods to retry any verb. (#5044)

Features

  • Added Url.auth_decoded and Url.auth_decoded_joined convenience properties to the result of parse_url(). (#4945)
  • Added basic_auth_encoding and proxy_basic_auth_encoding parameters to urllib3.util.make_headers(). (#5092)

Bugfixes

  • Fixed response header handling to replace obsolete folded header lines (obs-fold) with spaces in accordance with RFC 9112, preventing raw CRLF sequences from appearing in header values such as Set-Cookie. (#1362)

  • Fixed usage of proxy_ssl_context with ProxyManager when use_forwarding_for_https=True. Passing ssl_context instead of proxy_ssl_context for HTTPS proxies in this configuration now emits a FutureWarning and will raise an error in v3.0. (#2577)

  • Changed behavior of the default ConnectionPool.pool initialization. LifoQueue is now resolved from the queue module after the ConnectionPool is instantiated instead of using the default cached QueueCls class property. This is done because sometimes the queue.LifoQueue is monkey-patched late in the program, such as by gevent. (#3289)

  • Raised UnrewindableBodyError instead of ValueError when retrying a request whose body had tell() but not seek(). (#3779)

  • Decoded percent-encoded SOCKS proxy credentials before authenticating with the proxy server. (#3785)

  • Fixed HTTPResponse.drain_conn() to discard unread response data in 64 KiB chunks (same as the default amt when doing HTTPResponse.stream(...)). (#5019)

  • Fixed is_ipaddress() to detect non-standard IPv4 forms accepted by socket.connect, such as hex (0x7f000001), octal (0177.0.0.1), and decimal integers (2130706433), ensuring SSL certificate verification uses the correct mode for these addresses. (#5029)

  • Fixed HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen raising a misleading FullPoolError instead of ValueError when called with an invalid timeout argument on a pool created with block=True. (#5059)

  • Fixed port-zero handling to preserve explicit :0 values instead of substituting the default ports 80 or 443 in URL parsing, pool selection, proxy configuration, connection_from_url(), and HTTP/2 request authority. (#5071, #5101)

  • Fixed a bug where PoolManager passed the assert_hostname and assert_fingerprint parameters to HTTP connection pools. (#5077)

  • Fixed HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen() and HTTP proxy forwarding to strip URL fragments from absolute request targets before sending requests. (#5079)

  • Added safeguards to the proxy tunneling code to prevent potential security issues when handling invalid characters in the proxy host and HTTP headers. This change affects users of Python 3.10, Python 3.11, and Python 3.12 when the standard library does not contain the fix; those on newer Python versions should upgrade to 3.13.14+ or 3.14.5+ to get the same security fixes. (#5091)

  • Fixed HTTPSConnection.connect() overriding ProxyConfig.ssl_context's certificate policy and proxy identity checks with the target connection's TLS settings when forwarding through an HTTPS proxy.

    HTTPSConnection no longer applies target SNI, assertions, or client credentials to forwarding proxy handshakes and continues to use its ssl_context as a fallback when an HTTPS proxy forwards an HTTP target. (#5093)

  • Fixed URL parsing to more strictly enforce RFC 3986 host syntax, rejecting invalid host input such as raw spaces and control characters, malformed percent-encodings, and percent-encoded control characters in HTTP(S) hosts and IPv6 zone identifiers, including proxy CONNECT tunnel targets. Host normalization now also follows RFC 3986 normalization rules for percent-encoded octets by decoding percent-encoded unreserved characters and uppercasing the hexadecimal digits of retained percent-encoded octets. (#5095)

This minor version is a correctness- and robustness-focused release. It fixes a silent scoring bug for causal-LM rerankers, corrects several hard-negative mining and GIST loss edge cases, restores TSDAE on transformers v5, and adds Apple Silicon (MPS) support for the cached losses.

The headline fix affects chat-template models that read the final token position, i.e. causal-LM rerankers (like Qwen3-Reranker) and last-token-pooling embedders: when an over-long input was truncated, the chat template's trailing suffix (e.g. the assistant prefill the model scores from) was silently dropped, producing wrong scores with no error. There's also a forward-looking deprecation: loading local custom code without trust_remote_code=True now warns, and will require it from v6.0.

Install this version with

# Training + Inference
pip install sentence-transformers[train]==5.6.0

Inference only, use one of:


pip install sentence-transformers==5.6.0
pip install sentence-transformers[onnx-gpu]==5.6.0
pip install sentence-transformers[onnx]==5.6.0
pip install sentence-transformers[openvino]==5.6.0


Multimodal dependencies (optional):


pip install sentence-transformers[image]==5.6.0
pip install sentence-transformers[audio]==5.6.0
pip install sentence-transformers[video]==5.6.0


Or combine as needed:


pip install sentence-transformers[train,onnx,image]==5.6.0

Fixed silently wrong scores when truncation drops chat-template suffixes (#3787)

Chat-template models render the full conversation to a flat string before tokenizing, so when the rendered input is longer than the tokenizer's model_max_length, the tokenizer truncates it from the right and drops the template's trailing suffix: the fixed tokens a template appends after the content, e.g. a prompt, instruction, [/INST], or a trailing EOS. For models that read the final token position, this silently corrupted the result:

  • causal-LM rerankers (e.g. Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B) score a pair from the last token's yes/no logits, and
  • last-token-pooling embedders read the final hidden state.

When the suffix was truncated away, that final position landed mid-document instead of after the prefill, so the score or embedding came from the wrong place.

Transformer.preprocess now detects when truncation drops the suffix and splices it back onto the tail of each truncated row. Because the fix lives in the shared base Transformer, it applies across SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder, and SparseEncoder. It's enabled by default and saved to the model configuration. Pass processing_kwargs={"chat_template": {"restore_suffix": False}} to opt back into raw truncation.

Hard-negative mining and GIST loss correctness (#3821, #3817, #3816)

A trio of correctness and scalability fixes for hard-negative mining and the GIST losses:

  • Sign-independent relative margin: mine_hard_negatives(relative_margin=...) and the margin_strategy="relative" branch of GISTEmbedLoss / CachedGISTEmbedLoss used a multiplicative threshold (positive * (1 - margin)) that only behaves correctly when the positive-pair similarity is positive. When that similarity was negative, the threshold moved the wrong way and let through false negatives: candidates more similar to the anchor than the true positive. The threshold is now positive - |positive| * margin, identical to before for positive scores but correct for negative ones.
  • Distributed positive masking in the GIST losses: with gather_across_devices=True and a non-zero margin, the false-negative suppression mask protected the wrong columns on ranks beyond the first (it ignored the per-rank offset into the gathered batch), which set the true positive's logit to -inf and produced a +inf loss. The mask now accounts for the cross-rank offset, so multi-GPU GIST training stays finite.
  • Memory-bounded mining without FAISS: mine_hard_negatives(use_faiss=False) (the default) materialized the full (queries × corpus) similarity matrix at once, which could OOM on large corpora. It now batches over the query axis (controlled by faiss_batch_size, default 16384), bounding peak memory while producing identical results.

TSDAE weight tying restored on transformers v5 (#3781)

transformers v5 removed the private PreTrainedModel._tie_encoder_decoder_weights helper that DenoisingAutoEncoderLoss (TSDAE) used to tie its separate encoder and decoder. As a stopgap, v5.5 raised a RuntimeError for the default tie_encoder_decoder=True on transformers >= 5.0.0, effectively breaking TSDAE there unless you pinned an older transformers or disabled tying. TSDAE now ships its own tying routine that shares storage between encoder and decoder, so it works on both transformers <5 and >=5 with the default settings.

Release notes

Sourced from urllib3's releases.

2.8.0

🚀 urllib3 is fundraising for HTTP/2 support

urllib3 is raising ~$40,000 USD to release HTTP/2 support and ensure long-term sustainable maintenance of the project. If your company or organization uses Python and would benefit from HTTP/2 support in Requests, pip, cloud SDKs, and thousands of other projects please consider contributing financially to ensure HTTP/2 support is developed sustainably and maintained for the long-haul.

Thank you for your support.

Security

Fixed the following security issues:

  • The TLS configuration for HTTPS proxies could be ignored or overridden. (High severity, GHSA-8988-9cw3-xx77)
  • HTTPResponse.stream() and read_chunked() could buffer a chunk-size line of unbounded length in memory. (High severity, GHSA-vxq7-64xx-v4gw)
  • Chunked Deflate streaming could enter an infinite loop. (Medium severity, GHSA-gh4c-6fx4-qh6g)

[!IMPORTANT] urllib3 2.8.0 fixes HTTPS proxy TLS configuration being ignored or overridden by destination settings. Configurations relying on that behavior may require changes.

Configure proxy CA certificates and client certificates in proxy_ssl_context, and proxy identity checks with proxy_assert_hostname or proxy_assert_fingerprint. Destination client certificates and identity overrides no longer apply to HTTPS forwarding proxy connections.

[!NOTE] CVE IDs had not yet been assigned to these advisories at the time of release due to a backlog at GitHub's CNA.

Deprecations & Removals

  • Deprecated using an empty collection as the Retry option allowed_methods to retry any verb. (#5044)

Features

  • Added Url.auth_decoded and Url.auth_decoded_joined convenience properties to the result of parse_url(). (#4945)
  • Added basic_auth_encoding and proxy_basic_auth_encoding parameters to urllib3.util.make_headers(). (#5092)

Bugfixes

  • Fixed response header handling to replace obsolete folded header lines (obs-fold) with spaces in accordance with RFC 9112, preventing raw CRLF sequences from appearing in header values such as Set-Cookie. (#1362)

  • Fixed usage of proxy_ssl_context with ProxyManager when use_forwarding_for_https=True. Passing ssl_context instead of proxy_ssl_context for HTTPS proxies in this configuration now emits a FutureWarning and will raise an error in v3.0. (#2577)

  • Changed behavior of the default ConnectionPool.pool initialization. LifoQueue is now resolved from the queue module after the ConnectionPool is instantiated instead of using the default cached QueueCls class property. This is done because sometimes the queue.LifoQueue is monkey-patched late in the program, such as by gevent. (#3289)

  • Raised UnrewindableBodyError instead of ValueError when retrying a request whose body had tell() but not seek(). (#3779)

  • Decoded percent-encoded SOCKS proxy credentials before authenticating with the proxy server. (#3785)

  • Fixed HTTPResponse.drain_conn() to discard unread response data in 64 KiB chunks (same as the default amt when doing HTTPResponse.stream(...)). (#5019)

  • Fixed is_ipaddress() to detect non-standard IPv4 forms accepted by socket.connect, such as hex (0x7f000001), octal (0177.0.0.1), and decimal integers (2130706433), ensuring SSL certificate verification uses the correct mode for these addresses. (#5029)

  • Fixed HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen raising a misleading FullPoolError instead of ValueError when called with an invalid timeout argument on a pool created with block=True. (#5059)

  • Fixed port-zero handling to preserve explicit :0 values instead of substituting the default ports 80 or 443 in URL parsing, pool selection, proxy configuration, connection_from_url(), and HTTP/2 request authority. (#5071, #5101)

  • Fixed a bug where PoolManager passed the assert_hostname and assert_fingerprint parameters to HTTP connection pools. (#5077)

  • Fixed HTTPConnectionPool.urlopen() and HTTP proxy forwarding to strip URL fragments from absolute request targets before sending requests. (#5079)

  • Added safeguards to the proxy tunneling code to prevent potential security issues when handling invalid characters in the proxy host and HTTP headers. This change affects users of Python 3.10, Python 3.11, and Python 3.12 when the standard library does not contain the fix; those on newer Python versions should upgrade to 3.13.14+ or 3.14.5+ to get the same security fixes. (#5091)

  • Fixed HTTPSConnection.connect() overriding ProxyConfig.ssl_context's certificate policy and proxy identity checks with the target connection's TLS settings when forwarding through an HTTPS proxy.

    HTTPSConnection no longer applies target SNI, assertions, or client credentials to forwarding proxy handshakes and continues to use its ssl_context as a fallback when an HTTPS proxy forwards an HTTP target. (#5093)

  • Fixed URL parsing to more strictly enforce RFC 3986 host syntax, rejecting invalid host input such as raw spaces and control characters, malformed percent-encodings, and percent-encoded control characters in HTTP(S) hosts and IPv6 zone identifiers, including proxy CONNECT tunnel targets. Host normalization now also follows RFC 3986 normalization rules for percent-encoded octets by decoding percent-encoded unreserved characters and uppercasing the hexadecimal digits of retained percent-encoded octets. (#5095)

perf(plugins): filter agent event subscriptions by phase before cloning (#171534)

## Problem

Agent-event subscriptions can filter by stream, but not by phase. A plugin interested only in tool starts still receives cloned tool update and result payloads before its handler can ignore them. Each matching subscription also allocates callback context and tracks handler settlement.

## Fix

- Add optional `phases: string[]` to agent-event subscription registrations.
- Validate and trim phase names with the same string-list normalizer used for streams; reject non-arrays and empty/non-string entries.
- Apply the phase filter immediately after the stream filter, before callback context allocation, event cloning, and promise bookkeeping.
- Keep terminal-run bookkeeping and bounded run-context cleanup outside subscription delivery so filtering terminal events cannot leak or resurrect run state.
- Document narrow subscriptions, defaults, and per-matching-subscription cloning costs.

## Impact

Plugins can avoid subscriber-side work for unwanted phases without changing event production or delivery to other subscriptions. Omitted or empty `phases` preserves existing behavior. Non-empty lists deliver only events whose object payload has a matching string `phase`.

No performance percentage is claimed: the regression proves skipped payloads are not read/cloned, rather than benchmarking whole-run CPU or memory.

## Evidence

- Before the runtime fix, the focused regression run failed all nine new filtering/validation cases; omitted and empty phase-list compatibility cases passed.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/contracts/run-context-lifecycle.contract.test.ts src/plugins/contracts/host-hooks.contract.test.ts` — 80 tests passed across both owner files.
- After trimming redundant assertions to stay within the existing file-length limit, `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/contracts/run-context-lifecycle.contract.test.ts -t 'filters event phases|cleans up a filtered terminal'` — all 5 cases passed.
- Getter-based payload evidence confirms unmatched phases are never cloned; terminal end/error cases confirm pending handlers settle before cleanup and closed runs cannot regain state.
- `pnpm exec oxlint src/plugins/host-hooks.ts src/plugins/host-hook-runtime.ts src/plugins/registry-registrars-host.ts src/plugins/contracts/run-context-lifecycle.contract.test.ts src/plugins/contracts/host-hooks.contract.test.ts` — passed.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json` — passed.
- Changed files formatted with Oxfmt. No imports added, so the import-cycle gate was not needed.
- Fresh parent review found no issues in filter placement, registration validation, terminal cleanup independence, or behavior-based tests.

* feat(diagnostics): capture model prompt and response on message and run spans

With diagnostics.otel.captureContent enabled, openclaw.message.processed,

input.value (turn prompt / inbound text) and output.value (the model's own

channel and the exporter re-checks policy before writing a span attribute.

output.value contract: model-authored text only.
- The model's raw final text (sentinels such as NO_REPLY kept verbatim;
  genuine partial output from errored runs kept).
- For tool-only turns, the text the model passed to the message tool as its
  confirmed final reply to the source conversation. Progress sends
  (final: false) and sends to other destinations are excluded.
- Never delivered, hook, or host text: before_dispatch / before_agent_reply
  hook replies (hook-handled turns record providerStarted: false),
  no-visible-reply fallbacks, continuation statuses, failure texts, restart
  notices, and the CLI delivery mirror are not captured.
- Webchat/Control UI tool-only replies carry marker-stripped text; the exact
  tool arguments are on openclaw.tool.execution for the built-in runtime.

Covers the built-in embedded runner, the Claude CLI runner (including
publication before backend/session cleanup), agent harnesses (completed and
error spans), and isolated cron runs. Capture work is skipped when output
capture is disabled.

rounds; the per-commit history is preserved on

* fix(diagnostics): output.value is the model's own final message only

Text the model passes to the message tool is a tool-call argument, not its
final message; treating the send as "the reply" is OpenClaw's delivery
layer, not the model's response. For scoring (e.g. Langfuse top-level
output), output.value must be what the model itself ended the turn with.

- Remove the message-tool fallback from every capture path (message.processed
  via resolveDiagnosticModelResponse, embedded run span, harness run and
  completion spans). Tool-only turns record the model's closing message
  (usually NO_REPLY verbatim) or nothing.
- Terminal preparation marks finalAssistantRawTextIsFallback when the model's
  actual last message has no text and the raw field was filled from earlier
  turn text; capture never reports that narration as the final response.
  Harnesses that project their answer only through assistantTexts are not
  marked.
- Docs: the sent text lives on openclaw.model.call output messages and, for
  the built-in runtime, openclaw.tool.execution arguments; CLI backends do
  not export tool arguments.

  runner fallback when the last completed message ended in a tool call, and
  the embedded run and harness spans use the same check. This covers a later
  message that timed out before message_end, which previously left the
  earlier "Checking now" narration as output.value.
- CLI raw text is cumulative across results ("Checking now\nDone").
  transformCliResultText records the last result's raw text as rawFinalText,
  CLI settlement carries it as finalAssistantMessageRawText, and the
  diagnostic resolver prefers it. finalAssistantRawText keeps its cumulative

feat: run Meta models through the Muse Code CLI agent runtime (#170487)

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw cannot run agents through Meta's Muse Code CLI. Muse has no ACP support, so the acpx route does not work, and `meta/*` models only run on the built-in runtime.

## User Impact

Users can install the external `@openclaw/muse` plugin and set `agentRuntime: { id: "muse" }` on a `meta/*` model or on the `meta` provider. Turns then run through `muse serve`, using Muse's own sign-in (subscription browser login, stored key, or `META_API_KEY`). Muse owns its native tools, sandbox, MCP servers and session state. OpenClaw keeps channels, approvals, the transcript and session mapping. The runtime is opt-in and never auto-selected.

## Why This Change Was Made

- New external plugin `extensions/muse`. It registers an `AgentHarnessV2` with id `muse` and talks to Muse through the official `@muse-code/sdk` over the Muse Session Protocol. The SDK is pinned to 1.4.2, the newest version the repo's `minimumReleaseAge` policy admits.
- **Exec policy.** The effective policy is resolved through the SDK `execPolicy` contract across the global, agent and override layers, including `tools.exec.mode`, then tightened by the host-local exec-approval floors (`loadExecApprovalsReadOnlyAsync`, `minSecurity`/`maxAsk`). An explicit full-session elevation is the only bypass. Deny becomes `muse serve --disable-shell --disable-write` with `denyUnmatched`. Full with `ask: off` becomes `allowAll`. Everything else becomes `promptUnmatched`, and each Muse request goes to OpenClaw's approval flow (allow-once or deny, server-offered choices only, 120-second wait). Exec allowlist, `ask: always`, OpenClaw sandbox, workspace-only file access, restricted tool policy and `adaptive` thinking are refused before Muse starts, with a user-visible message.
- **Settlement.** On abort, timeout, approval failure or transcript failure, the harness interrupts and then waits for the native turn's terminal outcome before releasing the attempt. If no terminal arrives, it closes the host after 5 seconds.
- **Sessions.**
  - Bindings live in plugin keyed state (SQLite) and are published only after Muse accepts the turn. A Muse session is resumed only when workspace, model, credential, read-only posture and approval mode are unchanged.
  - A server-authored resume refusal starts a new session and logs why. Muse ran nothing in that case.
  - `reset` and `withSessionContextReset` (after a committed history cut) drop the binding.
- **Context.** A fresh Muse session (first turn, model change, refused resume, or committed context reset) is seeded once with OpenClaw workspace bootstrap context (`resolveBootstrapContextForRun`) and the retained conversation (`openModelContextAsync`, bounded by `resolveAgentHarnessHistoryLimits`). If the retained context cannot be read, the turn fails visibly before anything is dispatched.
- **Input and results.** Prepared images are forwarded as MSP image parts. Native tool failures carry `lastToolError` back to core.
- **Failure reporting.** Failures are logged to the Gateway log with Muse's stderr tail. Muse's `authRequired` failure becomes "not signed in on the Gateway host; run `muse login`".
- **Config baseline (maintainer-approved).** The plugin config budget goes from 4553 to 4575. 21 entries are the generic `plugins.entries.muse.*` entries every plugin gets; 1 is `binaryPath`, which is needed when the Gateway service's PATH lacks `~/.local/bin`.
- **Data-model compatibility.** The plugin is new. It adds no tables or columns and uses only its own plugin keyed-state namespace, so there is no existing stored data to migrate.

Known gaps (documented in `docs/plugins/muse.md`):

## What Problem This Solves

Prepared entry-only authority checks reread session fields through native SQLite at synchronous effect boundaries and through a worker on repeated asynchronous checks. These rereads duplicate facts already published by the session entry owner.

## User Impact

Prepare the selected entry fields once with the existing worker reader, then validate them against the existing retained-predicate publication owner. Unrelated metadata writes keep the predicate current; reset, deletion, recreation, and changes to selected policy fields revoke it before a subsequent effect check. No schema, retention, SDK, or update contract changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Register with the entry-publication owner before the initial worker read yields, acknowledge the selected fields against its existing revision, and release on checker disposal or failed preparation. Native and worker writers feed this same owner. Unknown actor settlement now also invalidates retained entry predicates: a durable commit without its receipt cannot leave an old authority check current. No new cache, generation, fencing protocol, synchronous bridge, or authority owner is introduced.

Removed checks and accepted edges:

- Entry-only synchronous source checks no longer reread the durable entry. In-process writer receipts are authoritative under exclusive Gateway custody; foreign writers remain unsupported.
- Repeated entry-only asynchronous checks no longer dispatch another worker read. A write overlapping initial preparation can still refuse that preparation through the owner's existing acknowledgement contract.

Final live authority and physical-source checks remain because they protect actual execution and disclosure. Conversation-bound checks remain held: conversation selection is derived from associations, node recency, generation validity, and primary-pointer precedence, and those writers do not yet publish a complete binding postimage. No partial publication is used to authorize an effect.

The real-writer regression covers unrelated native/worker edits, awaited policy revocation, native reset, worker deletion/recreation, and caller-local mutation of the returned entry. It asserts zero host SQL during both synchronous and asynchronous entry-only checks. The existing actor transport failure regression also proves that a lost settlement revokes retained authority even when the selected generation did not change, while rollback preserves it.

fix(plugins): allow admitted hooks to share run context (#171307)

## What Problem This Solves

`api.runContext` is the documented way for a plugin to share per-run data between its agent hooks and its Gateway service. In a running Gateway, agent-run hooks (`llm_input`, `agent_end`, …) dispatch from the agent's prepared, scoped plugin registry. That registry is loaded without global side effects, so `setRunContext` returned `stored: false` and `getRunContext` returned `undefined` there. The plugin's service runs in the root registry and never saw anything the hooks recorded.

Found while proving the Advisor plugin (#169564) live. Its `llm_input` hook records which runs are user-triggered, and its service counts tool starts for those runs. On a real Gateway, `setRunContext` from the hook returned `stored: false` on both Codex and the built-in runtime, so Advisor never reviewed anything.

## Fix

`setRunContext`, `getRunContext` and `clearRunContext` now require the plugin's existing lifecycle authority: `registration` plus `admittedRuntime`. They no longer use the blanket `activateGlobalSideEffects` denial.

- Allowed: active root registrations, and scoped hook registrations while their invocation is admitted.
- Still denied: plugins loaded only for inspection, and retired registrations.
- Unchanged: steering, prompt injection, agent-event emission and session attachments keep the old gate.

Run context is plugin-owned scratch data keyed by run ID, plugin ID and namespace. This change lets separate registrations of the same plugin exchange it; it grants no new authority.

## User Impact

Plugins that pair agent hooks with a service can share per-run data, as the SDK docs describe. No new API, config or protocol field.

## Evidence

- New contract regression in `src/plugins/contracts/host-hooks.contract.test.ts` uses real registries. A hook in the scoped agent-prepared registry writes run context, and the plugin's root service reads it. A registry loaded only for inspection is denied, and so is a retired registration. Before the fix the scoped write returned `false`.
- `host-hooks.contract.test.ts`: 53/53 pass. Scoped typecheck, oxlint and the import-cycle check are clean.
- Live, isolated Gateway: before the fix, the hook's `setRunContext` returned `stored: false` on both Codex and built-in runs. The live run after the fix is in #169564.
- Docs: `docs/plugins/sdk-overview/host-hooks.md` states what run context allows and does not allow.

fix(agents): deliver plugin next-turn context on Codex and other harness runtimes (#169558)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: context a plugin queues for a conversation's next turn (`api.session.workflow.enqueueNextTurnInjection`) is silently dropped when that turn runs on a harness runtime (Codex app-server, ACPX, Agents API, Copilot). OpenAI models use the Codex runtime by default, so most installs never receive these injections.

## User Impact

Plugins that queue next-turn context now reach the agent on every runtime, not only the built-in one. Turns with nothing queued produce byte-identical prompts, so prompt caching is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Only the built-in runner drained the durable injection queue and ran `agent_turn_prepare`. The harness prompt builder skipped both, and returned early when no prompt hooks were registered. One module now owns queue draining, the per-run retry cache, and `agent_turn_prepare`. The built-in runner and the harness prompt builder both use it, in the existing order: queued injections, `agent_turn_prepare`, heartbeat contribution, `before_prompt_build`. Harness runs release the retry cache when the run ends. History is still loaded only when a prompt hook needs it.

## Evidence

- **Live, real OpenAI API, isolated Gateway, Codex runtime (default for `openai/gpt-6.1-sol`):** a plugin queued a correction after a turn, and the next turn was asked to quote any note it received.
  - Before (current `main`): the agent answered "No, my context for this turn does not include a note starting with 'Progress review (OpenClaw Labs)'."
  - After: the agent quoted the queued note verbatim.
- **Regression test:** `src/agents/harness/prompt-compaction-hook-helpers.test.ts` "delivers queued injections". With a real enqueued injection and no prompt hooks registered, the prompt contains the text once, a same-run retry reuses it, and the queue is drained. It fails on `main` (`prompt.match(...)` is null) and passes with this change.
- **Focused tests:** harness helper 12/12, embedded prompt helpers 6/6, host-hook contract injection cases 7/7.
- Maintainer-intent check: #159779 and #159375 shaped this helper and the Agents API hooks. This change keeps their contract: no-hook and heartbeat-only attempts still do not read history, and the Agents API `config` move only places it in the shared host-side context (`buildAgentHookContext` does not forward `config` to plugins).
- Not run locally: full lint (the plugin-SDK boundary declaration prep timed out on a loaded host). Left to hosted CI.

**Merge danger:** two-way door; a revert restores the old behavior. Blast radius: harness runtimes now drain the injection queue, so plugins that already queue next-turn context (for example on Codex) will start seeing it delivered.

GitHub's statusCheckRollup and mergeStateStatus keep cancelled runs that a
newer run of the same workflow/event/job name superseded on the same head

after `ready_for_review`, and Labeler). After openclaw/ci-gate passes, those

at the exact prepared head exits GREEN. The watcher's classifyRollup stays
the single supersession owner and the pass also requires the attached ci.yml
run to succeed; any unsuperseded failure, hidden or paginated context, missing
run identity, pending check, moved head, or watcher error keeps refusing.

without waiting, with --timeout bounding only that pass's evidence reads.

This is a one-shot admission predicate, not a pinned snapshot fact: required
checks stay server-enforced at dispatch, the exact-head mutation pins the
head, and the final stability reread pins the UNSTABLE projection. Pinning
rollup contexts would extend the Octopool-allowlisted landing snapshot and
the retained-outcome schema. Accepted edge case, documented in
merge-admission.md: a new non-required failure on the same head between the
pass and dispatch is not rechecked.

feat(plugins): let plugins steer a session's active run (#170152)

Related: #170146 (session fork), #169564 (Advisor, the first consumer)

## What Problem This Solves

Plugins that notice a problem while an agent is still working can only queue context for the agent's next turn (`api.session.workflow.enqueueNextTurnInjection`). By then the run has already finished, so the agent spends the rest of the turn on the wasteful path. Core already lets users and `sessions_send` steer an active run; plugins have no access to it.

## Fix

Adds `api.session.workflow.steerActiveRun({ sessionKey, text, idempotencyKey? })`, returning `{ steered: true, runId? }` or `{ steered: false, reason }`.

- Uses the existing steering owner (`queueEmbeddedAgentMessageWithOutcomeAsync`) with the same call shape as `sessions_send` steer mode, so the built-in runner injects before the next model step and Codex receives native `turn/steer`.
- Plugin-authored and hidden: `internal_system` provenance with `sourceTool: "plugin:<id>"`, no sender or owner authority, never answers a pending user question.
- Requires the existing prompt-injection grant (`plugins.entries.<id>.hooks.allowPromptInjection`).
- Never throws for "no run accepts it": no active run, not streaming, backend rejection and missing grant return `steered: false` with the reason, so callers can fall back to `enqueueNextTurnInjection`.
- Respects plugin lifetime: the caller's plugin instance is revalidated after the lazy import and immediately before dispatch.

## User Impact

None by default; no core feature calls it. Plugins that opt in can correct an agent mid-run instead of after it finishes.

## Evidence

- Contract tests through the real plugin API factory and embedded steering queue: an active run receives the steer with plugin provenance and no sender/owner authority and does not answer a pending question; no active run returns `steered: false`; a plugin with `allowPromptInjection=false` is refused; an expired plugin instance cannot dispatch.
- Live (Codex runtime, real OpenAI API, isolated Gateway, via the Advisor plugin in #169564): a plugin steer issued mid-run was accepted (`steered: true`) and appears in the running turn's native rollout as a user item before the turn's next model request. Not observed live: the built-in runtime path, and whether the agent then changed course.
- Plugin revocation reaches final native admission (fix: `message-injection-target.ts` now composes the plugin lifetime assertion into the guard handed to V2 sinks; Codex already rechecks that guard after recorder persistence and right before the physical write, `attempt-steering.ts:302-304,350-359`). Real Codex client against a synthetic native app-server (`run-attempt.plugin-steering.test.ts`):
  - allowed guidance reaches the native server;
  - plugin disposed after the recorder persisted the item, before dispatch: rejected, `{ steered: false, reason: "runtime_rejected" }`, nothing written. Before the fix this returned `{ steered: true, runId: "run-1" }`;
  - an already-disabled plugin is rejected before queueing.
  - Totals: 3 native + 6 steering contract + 21 API lifecycle tests pass.
- Only source-guarded (V2) sinks accept plugin steering: `steerActiveRun` uses `queueGuardedEmbeddedAgentMessageWithOutcomeAsync`, so the plugin-lifetime assertion is checked up to native dispatch. A run whose runtime only has a legacy V1 sink (for example Copilot) returns `{ steered: false, reason: "active runtime does not support guarded steering" }` and nothing is queued; the caller can use next-turn injection instead. Regression: before the fix, a V1 run returned `{ steered: true }`. Totals: 62 tests across steering contract (7), `runs.steering` (31), API lifecycle (21), Codex plugin steering (3).
- Live at `0e6acc4`, real APIs, isolated Gateway, throwaway plugin that steers on the 2nd tool start (`"Also run 'echo STEERED' before you answer."`):

| Agent | Allowed steer | Effect | Plugin disabled mid-run (config hot reload) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Codex, OpenAI | `{ steered: true, runId }` | native rollout has the injected guidance, then `echo STEERED` and output `STEERED` | `{ steered: false, reason: 'Plugin "steer-probe" is no longer loaded' }`; no injected item in the rollout |
| Built-in, OpenAI `gpt-5.6-luna` | `{ steered: true, runId }` | transcript has hidden `internal_system` guidance from `plugin:steer-probe`, then `echo STEERED` output | same rejection; no injected item in the transcript |

repository release. Compatible releases keep running Corepack on the
repository Node as before.

fix: recovery originals stay retirable after a doctor NOCOW rewrite (#169893)

* fix(doctor): keep recovery originals retirable across a NOCOW rewrite

Doctor's btrfs NOCOW repair copies every store file into a fresh directory, so
the inode and mtime recorded in the migration manifest no longer match the live
file. `update cleanup` then classifies a verified recovery original as
blocked/artifact-metadata-changed, and its destination-database check rejects
the rewritten database, permanently disabling a documented retirement path for
operators who followed the NOCOW guidance.

After a successful directory exchange the rewrite now re-records the relocated
identity of the recovery originals and destination databases it exchanged,
only after proving the copy still carries the recorded content (size and
sha256). Anything that cannot be proven keeps its original record and stays
protected, so no cleanup safeguard is weakened.

Fixes #169674

* fix(doctor): refresh NOCOW recovery identities only for the recorded generation

The earlier reconciliation refreshed whichever file occupied a recorded path, so
a valid database that replaced the recorded destination before the rewrite was
adopted and cleanup could then retire the original against the wrong generation.
Bind each refresh to the rewrite's pre-exchange dev/ino: an artifact must still
match its recorded identity and carry the recorded size and sha256, and a
destination must still be the generation whose migration was verified. Mismatches
stay protected and are reported, preserving PR #162771's destination binding.

Fixes the P1 review finding on #169893.

* fix(doctor): preserve exact recovery identity across NOCOW rewrites

Consolidate the verified rewrite identity handoff and preserve the pre-copy metadata check. Exercise actual cleanup and refusal for replaced destinations, originals, metadata, and changed bytes.

Describe the review design as current state, not as a delta

one reading,' 'one dispatch,' and an example still showing diffs pasted

Spec: record iterations 2-3 results and final frozen-config matrix

Hand reviewers the diff as a file, not a paste

Paste adoption stayed at 0/15 even as a Red Flag — and the controller's
reluctance is locally rational: pasting loads the diff into the (most
expensive) controller context permanently, while a reviewer self-fetch
costs a few cheap turns. The diff-file handoff is cheap for both sides:
the controller redirects git diff to /tmp without reading it, and the
reviewer gets the whole change in one Read call.

Reviewer skepticism covers the implementer's design rationales

Fourth planted-defect failure mode: the implementer's self-report said
'noted mild structural duplication; left unabstracted per YAGNI' and the
reviewer deferred to that framing, rating the duplication no finding at
all. The pre-judging keeps relocating — controller prompt, then reviewer
calibration, now the implementer's report. Rationales are claims; they
never downgrade severity.

Make diff-pasting non-optional for task reviewer dispatch

Adoption was 6/11 reviews on fractals and 0/17 on svelte when phrased
as guidance; reviewers without the diff re-derive it by hand, which is
the single largest remaining reviewer cost. Now a Red Flags Never entry
and a REQUIRED marker on the template placeholder.

reviewer rated it Minor (YAGNI) under the strict cannot-be-trusted
definition of Important, and the Minor-rolls-up rule meant no fix was
ever dispatched and the final review never saw the finding. Calibration
now names merge-blocking maintainability damage (verbatim duplication,
swallowed errors, assertion-free tests) as Important, and controllers
must paste accumulated Minor findings into the final review dispatch.

feat(brainstorm-server): gate every endpoint behind a per-session key

The companion server is reachable by any local browser tab (default loopback
bind) and by any host that can route to it (remote --host bind). It served
screens, files, and accepted event-injecting WebSocket connections with no
authentication, so a malicious browser tab or a direct remote client could read
brainstorm content or inject events that the agent reads as the user's input
(prompt injection into a live session).

Generate a per-session secret token, carry it in the served URL as ?key=, and
mirror it into an HttpOnly SameSite=Strict per-port cookie on first load so
same-origin subresources and the WebSocket handshake authenticate automatically.
Every HTTP request and WebSocket upgrade now requires a valid key (query or
cookie, constant-time compared); unauthenticated requests get a friendly 403
explaining they need the full URL. A secret authenticates the client uniformly
across loopback, tunnel, and remote binds and defeats DNS rebinding, which a
Host/Origin allowlist cannot.

Also guard handleMessage against a null JSON payload that crashed the process.

Probe per-user Git Bash and Scoop before falling back to PATH on Windows

Stock Windows 10/11 ships C:\Windows\System32\bash.exe (the WSL
launcher) as the first match for `where bash`. WSL's bash cannot
execute Windows-style script paths, so when Git Bash is installed
outside the two standard system locations -- specifically the
per-user "Only for me" Git for Windows installer
(%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Git) or a Scoop install
(%USERPROFILE%\scoop\apps\git\current\usr\bin) -- run-hook.cmd
silently fails: WSL prints "Windows Subsystem for Linux must be
updated", the script returns 0, and Superpowers' SessionStart
bootstrap is never injected. From the user's perspective skills
auto-trigger inconsistently or not at all, with no surfaced error.

Add explicit probes for both locations between the existing system-
wide Git for Windows checks and the `where bash` fallback. Also add
a comment to the fallback documenting the WSL-launcher trap so future
maintainers understand why the explicit probes must come first.

Pipe SessionStart hook printf through cat to absorb EPIPE on Windows

On Windows + Git Bash, the SessionStart hook prints a confusing
diagnostic at every startup ("printf: write error: Permission denied")
when Claude Code closes the hook's stdout pipe before the printf has
finished writing. The hook still runs to completion and context still
gets injected, but the diagnostic surfaces every session because
Git Bash's printf reports EPIPE as "Permission denied" (not "Broken
pipe" like Linux) and our `set -euo pipefail` lets that error escape.

Piping each printf through `cat` makes the external cat process the
recipient of any SIGPIPE / EPIPE. cat's failure does not propagate to
the parent bash under pipefail because cat is the last command in the
pipeline and exits cleanly when the pipe stays open long enough to
hold the data. On macOS/Linux the cat passthrough is transparent (no
behavior change, no measurable cost).

Verified:
- Existing tests/hooks/test-session-start.sh: 7/7 pass on macOS
- Manual run on Windows 11 + Git Bash 5.2 + Node 22 produces valid JSON,
  clean stderr, and exit 0
- JSON output is byte-identical to the unpatched hook

* Fix owner-PID false positive when owner runs as different user

ownerAlive() treated EPERM (permission denied) the same as ESRCH
(process not found), causing the server to self-terminate within 60s
whenever the owner process ran as a different user. This affected WSL
(owner is a Windows process), Tailscale SSH, and any cross-user
scenario.

The fix: `return e.code === 'EPERM'` — if we get permission denied,
the process is alive; we just can't signal it.

Tested on Linux via Tailscale SSH with a root-owned grandparent PID:
- Server survives past the 60s lifecycle check (EPERM = alive)
- Server still shuts down when owner genuinely dies (ESRCH = dead)

Fixes #879

* Fix owner-PID lifecycle monitoring for cross-platform reliability

Two bugs caused the brainstorm server to self-terminate within 60s:

1. ownerAlive() treated EPERM (permission denied) as "process dead".
   When the owner PID belongs to a different user (Tailscale SSH,
   system daemons), process.kill(pid, 0) throws EPERM — but the
   process IS alive. Fixed: return e.code === 'EPERM'.

2. On WSL, the grandparent PID resolves to a short-lived subprocess
   that exits before the first 60s lifecycle check. The PID is
   genuinely dead (ESRCH), so the EPERM fix alone doesn't help.
   Fixed: validate the owner PID at server startup — if it's already
   dead, it was a bad resolution, so disable monitoring and rely on
   the 30-minute idle timeout.

This also removes the Windows/MSYS2-specific OWNER_PID="" carve-out
from start-server.sh, since the server now handles invalid PIDs
generically at startup regardless of platform.

Tested on Linux (magic-kingdom) via Tailscale SSH:
- Root-owned owner PID (EPERM): server survives ✓
- Dead owner PID at startup (WSL sim): monitoring disabled, survives ✓
- Valid owner that dies: server shuts down within 60s ✓

Release v5.0.6: inline self-review, brainstorm server restructure, owner-PID fixes

Fix owner-PID lifecycle monitoring for cross-platform reliability

Two bugs caused the brainstorm server to self-terminate within 60s:

1. ownerAlive() treated EPERM (permission denied) as "process dead".
   When the owner PID belongs to a different user (Tailscale SSH,
   system daemons), process.kill(pid, 0) throws EPERM — but the
   process IS alive. Fixed: return e.code === 'EPERM'.

2. On WSL, the grandparent PID resolves to a short-lived subprocess
   that exits before the first 60s lifecycle check. The PID is
   genuinely dead (ESRCH), so the EPERM fix alone doesn't help.
   Fixed: validate the owner PID at server startup — if it's already
   dead, it was a bad resolution, so disable monitoring and rely on
   the 30-minute idle timeout.

This also removes the Windows/MSYS2-specific OWNER_PID="" carve-out
from start-server.sh, since the server now handles invalid PIDs
generically at startup regardless of platform.

Tested on Linux (magic-kingdom) via Tailscale SSH:
- Root-owned owner PID (EPERM): server survives ✓
- Dead owner PID at startup (WSL sim): monitoring disabled, survives ✓
- Valid owner that dies: server shuts down within 60s ✓

Fixes #879

Fix owner-PID false positive when owner runs as different user

ownerAlive() treated EPERM (permission denied) the same as ESRCH
(process not found), causing the server to self-terminate within 60s
whenever the owner process ran as a different user. This affected WSL
(owner is a Windows process), Tailscale SSH, and any cross-user
scenario.

The fix: `return e.code === 'EPERM'` — if we get permission denied,
the process is alive; we just can't signal it.

Tested on Linux via Tailscale SSH with a root-owned grandparent PID:
- Server survives past the 60s lifecycle check (EPERM = alive)
- Server still shuts down when owner genuinely dies (ESRCH = dead)
