Release v5.0.2: Subagent context isolation, zero-dep brainstorm server

Subagent Context Isolation:

All delegation skills (brainstorming, parallel agents, code review,
subagent-driven development, writing plans) now explicitly instruct the
dispatching agent to construct review context from scratch — never
forward session history to subagents.

This fixes a problem observed with Codex, where subagents inherited the
full parent session context including the dispatcher's internal
reasoning, prior conversation, and user-facing tone. Reviewers that
inherited this context behaved as if they were the lead developer rather
than a reviewer — they'd reject reasonable code for not matching
unstated preferences, demand rewrites beyond scope, and treat advisory
feedback as blocking. The fix is simple: the dispatcher crafts precisely
what each subagent needs (the spec, the code, the review criteria) and
nothing else. This keeps reviewers focused on the work product, not the
thought process that produced it, and also preserves the dispatcher's
own context window for coordination.

Zero-Dependency Brainstorm Server:

The brainstorm visual companion server has been rewritten from scratch
as a single zero-dependency Node.js file. The previous implementation
vendored Express, ws, chokidar, and 714 npm packages (84,000+ lines of
third-party code) — a supply chain surface area that was
disproportionate to what the server actually does.

The new server.js (~340 lines) implements everything with Node built-ins
only: RFC 6455 WebSocket protocol, HTTP server with template wrapping,
fs.watch with debounce, and lifecycle management.

731 files changed, 1,700 insertions, 85,000 deletions. The entire
vendored node_modules/ directory is gone.

Server Lifecycle Management:

The brainstorm server now automatically shuts down when no longer
needed, preventing orphaned processes. Owner process tracking captures
the harness PID at startup and checks every 60 seconds. 30-minute idle
timeout as fallback. The visual companion guide now instructs agents to
check .server-info before each write and restart if .server-stopped
exists.

fix: restore polyglot wrapper to fix Windows hook window spawning

Claude Code spawns hook commands with shell:true + windowsHide:true,
but on Windows the execution chain cmd.exe -> bash.exe causes Git
Bash (MSYS2) to allocate its own console window, bypassing the hide
flag. This creates visible terminal windows that steal focus on every
SessionStart event (startup, resume, clear, compact).

The fix:
- Rename session-start.sh to session-start (no extension) so Claude
  Code's .sh auto-detection regex doesn't fire and prepend "bash"
- Restore run-hook.cmd polyglot wrapper to control bash invocation
  on Windows (tries known Git Bash paths, then PATH, then exits
  silently if no bash found)
- On Unix, the polyglot's shell portion runs the script directly

This avoids Claude Code's broken .sh auto-prepend, gives us control
over how bash is invoked on Windows, and gracefully handles missing
bash instead of erroring.

fix: replace O(n^2) escape_for_json with parameter substitution

The character-by-character loop using ${input:$i:1} was O(n^2) in
bash due to substring copy overhead. On Windows Git Bash this took
60+ seconds, freezing terminal input even with async hooks.

to be dramatically faster on Windows Git Bash where the original

mode on Windows, freezing all keyboard input. The pure-bash
escape_for_json function is O(n^2) on Git Bash, taking 60+ seconds.

superpowers context. Multiple users confirmed this workaround.

- Read file-type filters as include and exclusion globs: rg -t/--type
  and the Grep tool's type include ripgrep 14.1's globs for the type,
  rg -T/--type-not exclude them, fd -e/--extension includes *.<ext>.

  filter and never credits, like --exclude-from.
- Treat a path pattern as a filter: the Glob tool's pattern must match
  the target below its root; a shell glob operand must match the target
  or a directory above it; a git pathspec matches the same way with its
  * also matching /. One operand that admits the target is enough.
- Extend "a search of the target itself gives nothing" to searches
  confined to the target's own file name: when every include, the Glob
  pattern, or every path pattern ends in that exact name, the stem never
  credits, and the closest-miss note says it was a lookup.

  as the read-only shell check already does; the old literal-prefix scope
  hid that src\core\*.ts reached the parser as srccore*.ts.
- Make an edit non-trivial when either text holds U+2028, U+2029 or
  U+0085, which end a JavaScript or C# line comment; the lexer splits
  lines only at \n and \r.

hooks: first operand after -- is still the sed script when no script option was given

Greptile P1: sedScriptParts stopped at -- and discarded the remaining
operands, so 'sed -- <script>' skipped script collection entirely. GNU sed
4.9 (verified): with no -e/--expression anywhere, the first operand after --
is the script and an s///e in it still executes.

The operands after -- are now collected as positionals, so the existing
first-positional-becomes-script rule applies. Operands after the script stay
file names (data). 2 regression tests pin both sides. Suite: 812/812.

hooks: block escaped sed exec fragments conservatively; decompose sed readers

Greptile P1 findings (both verified by running GNU sed against the hook):

1. Escaped replacements evade the check: GNU sed decodes \xHH, \oOOO, \dNNN,
   case operations and unknown escapes like \g before executing an s///e
   replacement or e operand. Scanning the raw text let \x67it decode to git.
   Decoding that surface faithfully is out of scope, so any backslash in an
   exec-bearing fragment now throws UnsupportedSedEscape and the hook blocks
   with an explicit reason — mirroring the existing env -S escape precedent
   instead of pretending to interpret sed. Escaped-newline continuations of an
   e operand are refused by the same check.

2. Continued commands went unchecked: the e operand reader stopped at every
   newline, but GNU sed joins escaped newlines into one operand. Now covered
   by the same conservative refusal.

Also decomposes the sed readers into sub-50-line helpers per the repository
function-size rule (AGENTS.md): readSedDelimited, readSedCommand,
readSedExecute, readSedLineOperand, assertSedLiteral.

5 regression tests pin the escape paths and the benign boundary (a backslash
in a non-executing script stays data). Suite: 810/810.

hooks: parse sed options through the whole argv — later -e scripts still execute

CodeRabbit security review (Major, CWE-693) correctly identified that GNU sed
collects -e/--expression scripts from any argv position: a script option after
positional operands is still executed, so stopping the option walk at the first
positional let an e-flagged script hide behind it.

Verified against GNU sed 4.9 before fixing:
- 'sed -e s/x/y/ - -e s/y/X/e' runs X (the later -e executes)
- with any script option present, every positional is a file operand

sedScriptParts now walks the full argv, collects scripts from all -e/
--expression positions, and only promotes the first positional to the script
when no script option was given. Unknown options after positionals still fall
back to the opaque default.

4 regression tests pin the reported bypass paths (suite: 805/805).

hooks: model GNU sed execution — script and file operands are data, e/s///e are shell receivers

Ported from the #3051 discussion (test intent, not the old scanner):

- A confidently-parsed sed invocation whose script contains no execution
  construct is a pure text transformation: the script operand and every file
  operand are data. This removes the specific false positives where file names
  or non-executing scripts merely containing 'git ...' were blocked.
- The GNU sed `e` command (bare or with operand) and the `s` command with the
  `e` flag run text through the shell. Their literal fragments (the s
  replacement, the e operand) and any piped/redirected source are scanned as
  real shell source, closing the `printf x | sed 's/x/git commit --no-verify/e'`
  gap reported on 2026-10-09.
- Anything the literal parser cannot confidently read (addresses it cannot
  consume, -f script files, -i suffix ambiguity, unknown options, expansion
  residue) falls back to today's opaque default. No behavior changes for
  unmodeled launchers.
- shell-scan.js is untouched and remains the canonical scanner.

fix(hooks): never run .sh hooks through the WSL bash launcher on Windows

plugin-hook-bootstrap (shell mode) and observe-runner probed a bare
`bash.exe`. On Windows that resolves to the first match on PATH, and
%SystemRoot%\System32 normally sits ahead of Git's bin directory, so the
pick was System32\bash.exe: the WSL launcher. The existing guard (require
a clean probe exit) only catches it when no distro is installed. With one
installed, the probe passes inside Linux, then the hook script is handed
over by a Windows path (C:\...) or a Git Bash path (/c/...), neither of
which exists in WSL. The hook exits 127 instead of running, and
observe-runner's continuous-learning observation fails on every call.

Resolve bash candidates on Windows to absolute paths from PATH, skipping
bash.exe in System32, SysWOW64, Sysnative, and the WindowsApps alias
directory, so a native bash later on PATH (Git's) is used. With none
available, the existing "no bash binary found" skip applies. An explicit
BASH override still wins, and other platforms keep bare names.

The shared resolver lives in scripts/lib/windows-bash.js with a
platform-independent test. A Windows integration test puts System32 ahead
of Git's bash and requires the .sh hook to actually run. Upstream's
bootstrap fails that scenario with exit 127 ("/bin/bash: C:Users...hook.sh:
No such file or directory"); this one prints the hook output.

fix: record skill runs under OpenCode and report unmeasured skills honestly

Under OpenCode the skill-health dashboard had no writer and no honest
fallback, so it reported every discovered skill as healthy (#2463).

Root cause: `post:skill:track` is only wired for Claude Code, where
`posttooluse-dispatcher.js` fans the event out to `skill-run-tracker.js`.
The OpenCode plugin re-implements the harness events instead of reusing that
dispatcher, so nothing ever wrote `skill-runs.jsonl` — and the tracker's
matcher only accepted the exact Claude Code tool name `Skill`, while OpenCode
calls the tool `skill`, so even wiring it would have dropped every event.
Commands that locate ECC through the inlined resolver in
`scripts/lib/resolve-ecc-root.js` also fell back to `~/.claude`, which does
not contain ECC, so they could not find their scripts.

Changes:

- `.opencode/plugins/ecc-hooks.ts`: dispatch `post:skill:track` from
  `tool.execute.after`. The tracker module is imported lazily and behind
  try/catch, matching the existing `changed-files-store` pattern: this file is
  OpenCode's startup entry point, so a static import failure would crash the
  session before any hook runs (#2530). The module is reused rather than
  reimplemented, keeping its identifier validation, length bounds and
  "never persist prompt text" guarantees.
- `scripts/hooks/skill-run-tracker.js`: match the tool name case-insensitively
  so `Skill` and `skill` are both accepted.
- `scripts/lib/skill-evolution/health.js`: split the summary into
  measured/healthy/declining/unmeasured instead of deriving `healthy = total -
  declining`, which turned "no telemetry" into "everything is fine" for every
  skill.
- `scripts/lib/skill-evolution/dashboard.js`: show the breakdown and warn
  explicitly when skills have no recorded runs, since absence of telemetry is
  not a health signal.

Under OpenCode the resolver also needs `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT`, which only the
plugin can supply: `shell.env` exports it when a root is found, without
replacing a root the user set or one an earlier plugin already put in
`output.env`.

Root discovery is per capability and probes required runtime files — never
optional content. Probing for `skills/continuous-learning-v2` (the
`workflow-quality` module) rejected supported modular installs that ship the
plugin and tracker without that optional module, disabling telemetry and the
root export for exactly those users.

Also fixes an incidental bug: the compiled plugin bundle is ESM, where
`__dirname` is undefined, so the ECC version lookup silently fell back to its
default. The module directory is now derived from `import.meta.url`.

Tests: `tests/opencode-plugin-hooks.test.js` covers the telemetry dispatch
(skill tool recorded, other tools ignored, minimal profile respected), a
modular install without the optional skills module, the root export and both
override paths; `tests/hooks/skill-run-tracker.test.js` covers the
case-insensitive matcher; `tests/lib/skill-evolution.test.js` and
`tests/lib/skill-dashboard.test.js` cover the unmeasured bucket, the warning
and the aged-out-coverage wording.

The existing harness cannot measure what it set out to measure. Every trap
hides its deciding fact in the repository, which agents reliably discover, and
trials run one-shot under "do not ask clarifying questions", so a fact-forcing
gate is evaluated with no user to answer it. Its scenarios also declare the
question the gate ought to raise, chosen by reading the gate's own taxonomy, so
the suite passes by construction and can never find a missing question.

- scenarios-intent/ keeps the deciding fact in intent.json, as a choice between
  plausible conventions the repository cannot settle, so an agent that does not
  ask can only guess and the ungated arm cannot sit at the ceiling.
- user-sim.js plays that user with a separate cheap model: it answers the
  question in front of it, never volunteers, and reports which fact ids it
  disclosed, so asking something and asking the deciding thing are told apart.
  An unparseable judge is a recorded failure, not a silent stonewall.
- session.js runs multi-turn sessions joined by --session-id and --resume, and
  tells every arm the user is reachable, so the comparison is symmetric and the
  gate's contribution is whether it makes the agent ask the deciding question.
- coverage.js classifies each trial from behaviour alone into working, lucky, or
  a follow-through, targeting, silence or coverage hole, and reports the
  questions the gate actually raised rather than asserting declared ones.
- run-intent.js refuses minus-target, which needs targets these scenarios
  deliberately lack, and checks every grader separates the start, the trap and
  the reference before a session is billed.

working trap looks like, so it must not make a scenario unusable.

fix(gateguard): report fresh-process failures and fail the gate on them

The previous fix stopped a throwing hook from aborting the cold replay by
recording it as an allow, matching the warm path. But coldSummary only counted
disagreements, so a failure on a step the worker also allowed was no
disagreement and left no trace: the report showed no failure, a run with no
measured step reported a cold latency of 0 ms because percentile of an empty
list is 0, and the exit status passed. Trading a crash for a clean-looking
success hid exactly the failure the crash had exposed.

coldSummary now counts errors and samples, and reports no latency when nothing
was measured rather than a 0 that reads as a fast hook. The report prints "no
valid sample" in place of a latency and adds a line for steps that failed in a
fresh process, beside the existing disagreement line. The exit check moves into
gateFails, which fails on cold errors as it already did on warm errors and cold
disagreements, and is exported with coldSummary so both can be tested.

The render test builds its report from summarize([]), the real summary shape,
so it keeps working as metrics are added.

fix(gateguard): a throwing hook no longer ends the fresh-process replay

measureColdLatency ran each step in a fresh process through execFileSync,
inside try/finally with no catch. A hook that threw made the child exit
non-zero, execFileSync threw, and the error left measureColdLatency and then
evaluate, so neither the report nor the requested SARIF was written for a run
that had hit a single bad step.

The probe now catches a throwing require or run itself and records it the way
workerMain does: the raw payload stands in for the result, so the step reads as
an allow, and the error is kept. Matching the warm path matters because
coldSummary counts every cold decision that differs from the warm one as a
disagreement; any other choice would have reported disagreements that do not
exist. A child that dies without writing parseable output is caught outside the
probe and recorded the same way with no latency, and coldSummary leaves
unmeasured steps out of the percentiles while still counting them.

The new tests run a hook that always throws through both passes. They fail
against the previous code, 2 of 17, and pass against this one.

fix(agent-payment-x402): release the session reservation when nothing was signed

payOnce reserved MAX_AMOUNT before awaiting confirmation but only released
it when confirmWithUser returned false. A prompt that threw (timeout, closed
window) or a challenge the payment policy rejected before signing kept the
reservation, so five such failures exhausted SESSION_CAP with zero payments.

Track per call whether a request carrying PAYMENT-SIGNATURE / X-PAYMENT was
actually sent, and release the reservation in a finally block unless it was.
A sent signed request may settle, so it stays counted even if the response
fails. The reservation still happens before any await, so concurrent calls
cannot overrun the cap. Mirrored in ja-JP and zh-CN.

fix(package): publish scripts/github-coordination.js for the /epic-* commands

`package.json` `files[]` enumerates each top-level `scripts/*.js` by hand, and
`scripts/github-coordination.js` was never added. npm therefore drops it from
the tarball while `scripts/lib/` still ships wholesale, so only the CLI entry

to run:

    node scripts/github-coordination.js <command> <issue> --repo <owner/repo>

so anyone who installs from npm -- including the documented
`npm i -g ecc-universal` path -- gets seven commands that cannot run:

    Error: Cannot find module '.../ecc-universal/scripts/github-coordination.js'

It works from a git clone, which is what masked it locally.

Add the missing `files[]` entry, the matching publish-surface allowlist entry in
`tests/scripts/npm-publish-surface.test.js` (CONTRIBUTING asks for both), and a
guard test that fails when any published command invokes a `scripts/*.js` that
the publish surface does not cover. The guard reproduces this exact bug: with
`package.json` reverted it fails naming only `github-coordination.js`.

fix(onboarding): an ending closes the install flag first, and deleting a compression parent ends nothing

Adversarial review findings on the explicit-end change:
- The install flag closes before the run ends. A failed config write used to end the run and tell
  every window (Skip setup gone) while the flag stayed set, so the next launch started a fresh run.
  Now the write raises first: the run stays open and the same Skip, Done or delete can be retried.
- Only the compression tip holds the live run. Deleting the parent keeps the tip, and ending the
  parent's stale copy ended the live run and sent onboarding.ended twice.
- onboarding.state returns "" for a run started before runs had ids, the value onboarding.start
  returns for it, so the window's re-check does not end a run the backend still has open.

fix(onboarding): the first-task page opens in the browser on a local backend, also on Windows

A local backend opens the page in the default browser with the open command;
a remote backend shows it with desktop_preview, named with its tool_call shape
({"action":"open","url":"<file>"}). The "How to work" list and every first-task
output line now follow that rule instead of always saying desktop_preview.

Windows command: cmd.exe /c start "" "<file>", with the full Windows path.
The terminal tool's Git Bash sets MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1, so argv reaches Windows
as written. Git's /usr/bin/start runs "$COMSPEC" //c start and relies on MSYS
turning //c into /c; with conversion off cmd gets a literal //c, starts an
interactive shell, prints its banner and exits 0 with nothing opened (Vesper
run 1). A single-slash /c needs no conversion. explorer.exe was not chosen
because it mis-handles forward-slash paths. A ~ or /c/ path is not converted
either, so the prompt asks for the C:/Users/... form.

New rule: the model says the page is open only after the open command (or
desktop_preview) succeeded; on Windows an exit 0 with a cmd banner is named
as a failure.

fix(onboarding): the look-around offer comes before the connectors card

feat(onboarding): the backend tells every window when a run ends (onboarding.ended)

onboarding.ended {run_id, stored_session_id, outcome} to every connected window. It is emitted from
one place, the active-to-ended edge in onboarding_record._transition, so done (first-task card
answered), skipped, replaced (a rerun from any window) and deleted all reach the window showing
the run, including one subscribed to another chat. A repeat end is not a second event. The event
goes out before the install-flag write, which can fail; the record already says the run ended.

Each run gets a run_id at start; onboarding.start and onboarding.state return it, so the desktop
matches the event by run and not by a runtime id that changes on every resume.

fix(desktop): a catalog link that launches Desktop opens the install dialog

A `hermes://plugin/install?catalog=` link that launches a closed Desktop
is delivered as soon as the renderer mounts its deep-link listener. That
is before the backend socket exists, so the lookup failed before anything
reached the backend, and no dialog appeared. On main the renderer fetched
the docs JSON instead, which needs no backend, so cold start worked there.

The lookup now waits for the active gateway to open, within the
renderer's existing cold-boot budget (`BACKEND_BOOT_WAIT_TIMEOUT_MS`,
180 s). The route lookup plus the RPC is also bounded as one call
(`LOOKUP_TIMEOUT_MS`), because the route step has no deadline of its own.
Past either bound the lookup reads as `unavailable`, so a startup link
always ends in the dialog or a visible error.

Live, dev Desktop from this branch, isolated home, link in argv:
- Before: link delivered 17:02:55, gateway active 17:03:00; at 50 s no
  install request, no dialog.
- After: link delivered 17:04:06, gateway active 17:04:10; the Install
  plugin dialog opened for hermes-memory-wiki at pin abec9e82.
- Desktop running (second-instance link): fish-audio opens the dialog;
  `plugins.catalog.lookup` sent once, no plugins.json fetch.
- Unknown name: "not in the Hermes plugin catalog" toast.

fix(desktop): the catalog lookup falls back only for a backend without the method

`lookupPluginCatalogEntry` fell back to the direct docs fetch on any
gateway error. Desktop's compatibility rule keeps a fallback narrow and
tied to an identified older runtime, so it now falls back only when the
backend answers "method not found" (`isMissingRpcMethod`). An unreachable
backend reads as `unavailable`: it could not run the install either.

`CatalogRequest` is typed to the one RPC it sends (method name, `{name}`
params, the reply shape), which removes the generic cast and the
`Record<string, unknown>` params. The tests use typed `vi.fn` fakes in
place of `as unknown as` casts (anti-slop: no net-new findings).

The gateway handler resolves the kill list once
(`resolved_removed_entries`) and matches the name and the repo against
it, in place of two `find_removed` calls that each re-read the in-tree
and live lists.
fix(desktop): a malformed catalog lookup reply reads as unavailable; the gateway validates names with the CLI's own rule

fix(desktop): catalog deep links ask the backend for the entry

hermes://plugin/install?catalog=<name> fetched /docs/api/plugins.json from
the renderer. The docs host answers that URL with a cross-origin 301 that
carries no Access-Control-Allow-Origin, so the browser rejects the redirect
and every link reported the catalog as unreachable.

The backend already reads the live catalog (cache, failure window, in-tree
fallback, kill list) and resolves catalog installs from it. A new
plugins.catalog.lookup {name} gateway method returns the entry from there,
and lookupPluginCatalogEntry calls it. A backend that predates the method
falls back to the old direct fetch, so nothing regresses on skew.

fix(update): a git exiting mid-scan no longer makes the index.lock owner unknowable

The Linux /proc scan in _held_open_proc reads each git's argv, then its
cwd and environ. A git anywhere on the machine (another repository) that
exits in between has dropped its fds and cwd, and the kernel refuses its
environ (EACCES once it is exiting or a zombie). The scan read that as a
hidden git that may be working in the checkout and answered None
("unknowable"), so _release_dead_index_lock kept the dead lock and the
launch-time repair printed "a running git holds the index after an
interrupted `hermes update`" and exited 1. Users hit it whenever any git
exits during the scan (IDE integrations, git maintenance, a build), and
the next launch retries; CI hit it as a flake of
test_update_recovery_closure.py (32 test files in parallel, each running
gits).

A process whose argv is now empty (it released its memory) or whose
/proc entry is gone has exited: skip it. A live process we still cannot
read (another user, non-dumpable) keeps the conservative None.

1 failure in 271 file runs, with the instrumented scan recording
UNK_CWD on a zombie `git add --all` from another test
(stat Z, environ PermissionError). Deterministic repro: a 0.2 s sleep
injected between the argv and cwd reads (scratch copy) plus unrelated
`git hash-object` gits that exit and are reaped lazily: base fails
14/21 file runs with the CI message, the fix 0/15.

test: start the job-teardown driver suspended so its tree is in the job

test_non_breakaway_child_killed_by_job_teardown failed on ~6% of Windows CI
runs ("child without breakaway must be killed by kill-on-close job teardown").

Mechanism: the test started the driver with a plain Popen and assigned the
RUNNING process to the kill-on-close job afterwards. On CI sys.executable is a
venv Scripts\python.exe redirector, which starts the real interpreter as its
own child; when that CreateProcess beat the test's AssignProcessToJobObject,
the real interpreter (the one that spawns the grandchild) was never in the
job, so the grandchild survived the teardown. The go-marker handshake only
ordered the grandchild spawn, not the redirector's child.

Fix: create the driver CREATE_SUSPENDED, assign it, then resume it
(update_lock.resume_suspended_child, the seam the updater's
bind_child_to_update_tree already uses), so nothing it starts can escape.
Also:
- assert IsProcessInJob on the grandchild before the teardown (in the job
  without breakaway, out of it with breakaway), so a setup escape fails as a
  precondition instead of reading as the #48820 product bug;
- watch the grandchild through a handle opened while it was alive and await
  the kill with WaitForSingleObject, instead of a 2 s sleep plus a pid probe a
  reused pid could fool;
- the driver publishes the grandchild pid with an atomic replace, so the
  reader never parses an empty file.

Repro: a 1 s delay between the driver's Popen and AssignProcessToJobObject
fails the old test on every run; the new test passes under the same delay.

Not a product defect: the updater already binds children suspended.

test: display-watch and stall-fallback tests wait for the background writer they race

Two main-run flakes, one shape: the test read state that a background thread was
still legitimately writing.

test_display_watch: the process-wide lease watcher thread runs the same
_poll_runtime_files pass every 0.5 s that the tests drive by hand. When its tick
lands between launcher.kill() and the test's own poll, it claims the transition
(updates the mark) and broadcasts only after its slow snapshot, so the test's
poll sees an unchanged mark and asserts on an empty event list (main run
37878861443). The fixture now wraps both poll passes in one lock; the thread
resolves them from server globals each tick, so a hand-driven poll returns only
after any claimed broadcast is out.

test_compression_stall_deterministic_fallback: the first attempt's fence-cancelled
worker re-arms the stall cooldown from its own thread after _compress_context
returns. Clearing before it lands let the second attempt run cooldown-skipped
(committing with no LLM call, calls == []) — main run 37727931904. The 0.4 s idle
window also bounded the deterministic rung's no-LLM compress pass, which a loaded
runner outran (main run 37621211515). Wait on the admission count (frees only when
the worker has returned) before the clear and before the final cooldown read, run
the second attempt once instead of a retry loop, idle 0.4 -> 2.0 s.

fix(mcp): a parked OAuth server no longer replays its dead refresh token on every new session

server without a session. Desktop/TUI backends re-run discovery on every
agent build while no MCP server is connected, and gateway cron runs it per
job, so each new session POSTed the same rejected refresh token to the
authorization server (plus PRM/ASM discovery and a 401'd MCP request).

and locked the user out of the Portal.

An auth-failure park now records a stat-only stamp of the server's token and
client files. Discovery skips the nudge while the stamp is unchanged and
nudges again as soon as a re-authorization (`hermes mcp login`, Desktop
re-auth) rewrites them. Explicit reconnects and the timed self-probe are
untouched, so a throttling authorization server is still retried every
_PARKED_RETRY_INTERVAL.

feat(plugins): fork a session's live context for background side questions (#170146)

Related: #169564 (Advisor, the first consumer)

## What Problem This Solves

Plugins that review or summarize an ongoing conversation in the background can only see what they rebuild themselves: a bounded excerpt sent through `api.runtime.subagent.complete`. That loses detail and costs a fresh, uncached prompt every time. In a real-API evaluation, an excerpt-based reviewer produced 2 false corrections in 5 runs (it misread polled background commands as extra launches), while a review that saw the session's full context was correct in all 5.

## Fix

Adds `api.runtime.subagent.forkSession({ sessionKey, message, signal?, timeoutMs? })`. It asks one question against an ephemeral fork of the session's current context and returns `{ text, usage }`. It works mid-run, at `agent_end`, and after the parent turn has finished.

- **Same prefix, warm cache.** The fork reuses the parent's exact request prefix, so the provider prompt cache hits:
  - Codex runtime: ephemeral `thread/fork` on the parent's own app-server client, replaying the parent's recorded developer instructions, private persona/skills context, tool surface and turn settings. The parent's last tool declarations are kept in a bounded in-memory LRU (32 MiB global) and restored into the fork request byte for byte. When the parent used a WebSocket continuation (`previous_response_id`), history comes from native Codex reconstruction; no response output is buffered or rebuilt.
  - Built-in runtime: the embedded runner records the exact request it sent at the model-call boundary (bounded, in memory, cleared with session cleanup) and replays it with one appended user message through the same stream function and payload hooks. Anthropic cache breakpoints and the OpenAI `prompt_cache_key` stay where they were. The parent's one-shot continuation `onPayload` callback is not replayed.
- **No tool execution.** Tool definitions stay byte-identical, but every call is denied:
  - dynamic and native Codex tools are denied at dispatch (this also fixes a fail-open path: the native hook relay dropped `PreToolUse` when no global hook was installed);
  - hosted tools: `tool_choice: "none"` on OpenAI and `{ type: "none" }` on Anthropic for every fork request; unsupported APIs fail before dispatch;
  - Codex native `web_search` stays disabled. Its `web.run` declaration is still sent (copied from the parent), so the cache prefix matches but nothing can execute it.
- **No side effects.** Nothing is written to the transcript, delivered, counted as a turn, or drained from queued next-turn context.
- **Authority.** Same background admission as `subagent.complete` (plugin lifetime, cancellation, revalidation after awaits), plus the conversation-access grant, `sessions.get` session visibility, and live Gateway caller authority. These are checked right before every physical send through the guarded-fetch request authority, including DNS/proxy setup, retries and redirects; native ChatGPT WebSocket and SSE sends check them through the existing Responses request lifecycle. Ordinary parent settlement and usage updates (including a briefly unmaterialized session row) do not revoke a fork. A session reset or deletion, a replaced Codex client or thread, withdrawn conversation access, or a retired plugin still revokes it.
- **Same network policy as the parent.** Built-in replay takes the current proxy, TLS and local-service settings (including the local-service reconciler) from the existing transport owner, not from the snapshot. Native ChatGPT forks open their own transient WebSocket and never change the parent's socket, continuation or SSE fallback state.
- **Supported APIs.** OpenAI Completions, OpenAI Responses (including native ChatGPT), Anthropic Messages, and Codex. APIs whose sends the fork cannot fence (for example Bedrock) fail closed before dispatch with `Session forks do not support provider API <api>`.
- **Runtimes.** CLI runtimes (for example `claude-cli`) have no prepared context to fork, so a fork fails closed before any CLI or provider I/O. Ordinary `/btw` on CLI is unchanged.
- **Concurrency.** Forks run on the same subagent lane as `subagent.complete` (`CommandLane.Subagent`), so `agents.defaults.subagents.maxConcurrent` caps both together.
- **Fails closed** with an actionable error when no parent request was prepared by this runtime (for example after a Gateway restart).
- Fixes forked-turn usage reporting on Codex (forks only emit `thread/tokenUsage/updated`) and admits forked requests through the private inference proxy.

Ordinary `/btw` is unchanged from `main`. An earlier revision rejected `/btw` when tools were present, and rejected CLI backends with `nativeToolMode: "none"` and no `sideQuestionToolMode`; both are restored, and CLI admission stays with `prepareCliRunContext` (this answers the review note about #70413). The provider-review continuation callback from #155214 is not replayed by forks.

## User Impact

None by default: no core feature calls `forkSession` yet. Plugins that opt in get full-context side questions at cached-input prices.

## Evidence

Live, real provider APIs, isolated Gateway at the PR head, a throwaway plugin that calls `forkSession` from its service scheduler on each `agent_end`: one fork immediately (parent still settling), then two forks 8 s later (summary, plus a "use web search now" bait). Each parent turn makes 3 tool calls.

| Runtime / provider | Parent last input | Fork at `agent_end`: cache read | Late fork: cache read | Search bait |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Codex, OpenAI (API key, WebSocket continuation) | ~19.7k | 19,642 | 19,967, cacheWrite 0 | `NO_SEARCH` |
| Built-in, OpenAI `gpt-5.6-luna` | — | 15,660 (input 566) | 15,660 (input 608) | `NO_SEARCH` |
| Built-in, Anthropic `claude-sonnet-5-5` | — | 19,595 (input 73) | 19,595 (input 73) | `NO_SEARCH` |

- Codex wire check: the fork's `additional_tools` item (51,233 bytes) has the same SHA-256 as the parent's, and `prompt_cache_key` matches. Before this fix, the late fork read 0 cached tokens because disabling `web_search` removed `web.run` from the `exec` catalog (10,831 bytes).

post-kill confirmation with a dedicated 10 s budget
(COMMAND_PROCESS_GROUP_EXIT_CONFIRMATION_MS). Polling still ends as soon as
the group is gone, so normal cleanup is unchanged; only a group that truly
survives SIGKILL now reports uncertain after 10 s instead of 300 ms. The
scoped-command settle, the runner's forced termination and the custody
settlement drop their private 300 ms loops; pre-kill identity checks, error
messages and Windows paths are unchanged, and the Linux adopted-zombie
reaper registration now outlives the new confirmation window.

No new configuration, schema, SDK, or migration contract is introduced beyond target main. There is no product UI change.

The capture owner retains whether a failed admission inserted a new row. Abandonment deletes only that owner’s unchanged, stopped, empty, never-accepted candidate through the existing SQLite worker. Speech advances its separate content revision and remains preserved.

feat(models): support endpoint-resolved custom model aliases (#170009)

Closes #170008. Builds on merged #169977.

## What Problem This Solves

Custom router aliases can return a concrete upstream model id even though OpenClaw used the requested route, causing a misleading “Model route changed” notice.

## User Impact

Operators can set `models.providers.<id>.models[].responseModelEquivalent: true` on a user-authored custom model row. The endpoint may select any response model for that alias, including endpoint-internal substitutions. The concrete served model and usage remain recorded; actual OpenClaw model/provider fallbacks and overrides still produce their notice.

Omitted or false preserves normal detection. Bundled/official provider policy cannot be overridden, including official catalog aliases such as `azure-openai-responses`. Plugin/catalog rows, agent `models.json` rows, and rows marked `metadataSource: "models-add"` cannot grant equivalence. No Doctor migration is needed for an optional key; existing stored data formats are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both terminal producers use the route classifier, which reads the captured authored source and existing policy/catalog ownership indexes. This implements the October 12, 2026 maintainer decision: boolean key, authored rows only, official policy authoritative. It includes the review-requested fix for official catalog aliases without broadening auth-policy ownership. Contributor commits by @xyrolle are preserved; main was merged without rebasing or force-pushing.

## Evidence

Real macOS proof used `pnpm openclaw --profile alias-route agent --local --json`, isolated state/config/agent directories, and a recording router forwarding to Ollama `qwen3:8b`. Every case returned `ALIAS_OK` and retained `responseModel: qwen3:8b` plus nonzero usage. No hosted model inference or operator Gateway was used.

| Authored custom row, true | Absent | No | 77.01 s |

| Official OpenAI row, true | Present | No | 99.46 s |

The custom opt-in and official catalog alias were rerun on final head `09df299b433a633dafefb28b228d12a9837abade`; the other rows retain valid proof from the initial head. The official alias's requested/effective provider and model stay identical, so its case tests the response-id decision directly.

The regression against the original permissive feature implementation had 6 expected failures; the catalog-alias regression had 2 expected failures. The final classifier suite passes all 30 cases. The 74 unchanged sibling/terminal cases also passed:

refactor(extensions): simplify plugin paths and lifecycle bookkeeping (#170511)

## What Problem This Solves

Consolidate duplicate extension paths and remove speculative lifecycle defenses in Codex, Memory Core, Microsoft Teams, Matrix, Reef, and Workboard. The candidate removes **522 net production lines** (tests, fixtures, generated files, declaration files, and documentation excluded; both new production modules included). This uses the campaign's honest 500–999-line fallback after the scoped growth/largest-first pass; it does not remove features to reach a quota.

Workboard's four card actions now share one discriminated action component, its draft controls share one renderer, and menu-only pass-through components are gone. Reef's worker and released-host adapters share one pure seven-command trust-transition policy while retaining their own atomic storage boundaries. Teams reuses its Graph/context/setup owners. Memory keeps normal parallel-query and sync-generation retirement draining, expressed with simpler active-completion tracking rather than nested borrower wrappers.

An adjacent Workboard defect is fixed: conditional Solid fragments could run a popover ref before the preceding trigger entered the document, positioning the details menu at the page origin. Listener/anchor setup now runs after the DOM commit. The regression fails against the unchanged implementation and passes with this repair.

No SDK export, config, protocol, dependency, database schema, durability, retention, or permission contract is changed. The protected standalone session-memory backend is untouched. No changelog edit.

User impact: Workboard details menus anchor to their trigger instead of the page origin. Other changes simplify internal implementation, with the best-effort timing and diagnostic compromises below; no migration or operator action is required.

## Best-effort tradeoffs accepted

- Codex diagnostic accessors throwing or mutable transport identities: [#163388](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/163388) adds synthetic throwing-accessor coverage, not an actual-use human report. Actual accessors are local reads and registration publishes frozen identities. Accessor programmer errors now surface; the diagnostic sink catch, disclosure allowlist, attempt isolation, and timeout/cleanup behavior remain.
- Offline Codex migration CAS conflicts: [#168479](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/168479) introduced retry loops without a human competing-writer report. Gateway ownership excludes live foreign writers. One atomic attempt plus existing persisted-result validation now retains the source sidecar and reports a warning on conflict; a later Doctor run can retry.
- Retired Codex legacy JSON rewritten during migration: [#104504](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/104504) added a synthetic locator-rewrite test; human [#104503](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/104503) concerns fingerprint overflow, whose fix remains. Legacy indexes are offline inputs, so a second locator/lifecycle read is removed. Initial containment/malformed-owner validation and canonical session ownership checks remain; unsupported concurrent legacy edits are picked up next run.
- Memory manager acquisition repeatedly retrying failed global retirement: [#144252](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/144252) has synthetic close failures, no human incident requiring recursive acquisition recovery. Acquisition now awaits the pending close once and reports its error; the retirement owner is retained and explicit close can retry.
- Abandoned, abort-ignoring memory diagnostic probes holding provider retirement indefinitely: [#113471](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/113471) and [#166973](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/166973) provide synthetic lifecycle proof, not a human abandoned-probe incident. Timed-out read-only diagnostics no longer retain a redundant inner borrower. Ordinary active searches, sync generations, healthy operations, and custom closable-provider draining remain protected.
- Teams simultaneous Gateway writers: [#88411](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/88411) introduced the persistence migration/file lock without a human multi-Gateway incident and did not test live tenant traffic. The Gateway is the sole database owner. Removed cross-process stale-lock/backoff machinery; local FIFO remains. Unsupported simultaneous processes may overwrite each other rather than coordinate.
- Workboard stale cache publication and an exact-expiry late join: [#165896](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/165896), [#165141](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/165141), and [#165698](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/165698) use synthetic performance/interleaving controls, not a human incident. One read may return an older projection/fallback; normal revision/age invalidation refreshes it next read. Measured caching, the 64-entry bound, and read authority remain.
- Workboard direct stop/start before asynchronous startup settles: [#146976](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/146976) forces unsupported lifecycle ordering in a test. The host service owner already awaits raw startup before stop. Removed plugin-local generation/startup handoff; supported host lifecycle is unchanged, unsupported direct reentry no longer has a second lifecycle owner.
- Reef failed owner-notice dispatch/ack retry timing: [#109160](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109160) pins injected failures and exponential timers, without a human report requiring that second scheduler. Durable pending notices now retry during ordinary successful 30-second reconciliation or restart. A failed acknowledgement may redispatch conservative stop-only guidance; durable resend reservation/cooldown prevents granting a second resend. The per-peer queue also makes the removed in-flight set redundant.
- Reef synchronous intermediate lease theft: [#109380](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/109380) and [#168340](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/168340) describe synthetic interleavings, not human concurrent-writer incidents. SDK callbacks commit synchronously and there is no await between acquisition and settlement. Unsupported reentrant callbacks/foreign writers are no longer checked at every intermediate step. Initial acquisition, final head-owner check, staged recovery, uncertain-commit witness, rollback, and retention ordering remain.
- Workboard fabricated native event targets and repeated widget predicates: renderer port [#168606](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/168606) added boilerplate without a human incident. JSX native bindings already guarantee `currentTarget` types, and the owning menu already excludes widgets. Fabricated direct handler calls may throw; real event dispatch, widget behavior, and untrusted `event.target` checks are unchanged.

fix(llm): strip leaked reasoning from self-hosted model output

Self-hosted reasoning models served through vLLM or llama.cpp without a
reasoning parser, or through Ollama without a thinking template, return
their chain of thought inside message content. The OpenAI-compatible
providers and the Ollama provider passed it through verbatim, so
LLMOutput.content and ReActAgent final answers began with the reasoning.

Models whose chat template prefills <think> in the generation prompt
(Spark-X2.5, Qwen3 thinking variants) only emit the closing tag, so the
content arrives as "...</think>answer" with no opening tag.

Add strip_reasoning() and apply it in the OpenAI, Astraflow, Atlas and
Ollama providers. A <think> that does not open the output is kept as a
literal, and unterminated reasoning is left unchanged.

fix(install): support invocation through POSIX sh (#3014)

* fix(install): make install.sh robust to sh/dash invocation

Two related portability fixes so `sh install.sh` behaves correctly
even though the script is written for bash:

- The cygpath detection used the bash-only `&>/dev/null` redirection.
  dash misparses `&>`, so `command -v cygpath &>/dev/null` always took
  the true branch and tried to run the nonexistent `cygpath` binary,
  failing with "cygpath: not found". Switched to the POSIX-portable
  `>/dev/null 2>&1` form.

- Some dash builds don't support `set -o pipefail`, so `sh install.sh`
  can fail immediately at that line before even reaching the cygpath
  check (or the `[[ ... ]]` symlink-resolution logic further down).
  Added a guard that re-execs the script under bash when the current
  shell lacks bash capabilities, so the rest of the bash-only syntax
  always runs under a real bash regardless of the invoking shell. The
  guard probes for the `[[` compound command directly (via
  `eval '[[ 1 == 1 ]]'`) rather than trusting the $BASH_VERSION
  environment variable, since that variable could be inherited or
  spoofed under a non-bash shell and cause the guard to be skipped.

fix(control-pane): settle the poll guard against the last settled request

The staleness guard compared a poll against the newest poll STARTED, and
only the failure path used it. Two orderings were wrong.

An older success settling after a newer one had no guard at all, so it
overwrote the newer counts, the canvas label and the announcement with
older data. Both paths now check the token.

An older failure settling while a newer poll was still in flight was
discarded, because a newer poll had merely started. The page then kept
the last successful counts and its no-steering message as if they were
current. Anchoring the guard to the newest poll that has SETTLED fixes
that: the older failure is still the newest thing to have settled, so it
lands, and the pending poll restores the view when it answers.

That single change covers both orderings, so the guard no longer needs
to know which path it is on. Each poll records itself as settled when it
finishes, whatever the outcome.

A poll also had no timeout, so a request that never answered left the
last steering guidance on screen indefinitely. Each poll now aborts
after ten seconds through an AbortController, and that abort is what
wakes the poll, so a timeout is reported as an outage instead of
silently leaving stale guidance.

The test harness can now hold a request open indefinitely and fire
pending timers on demand, so the timeout is exercised without waiting.
New assertions cover an older success losing to a newer one, an older
failure landing while a newer poll is in flight and then being
recovered by it, and a hung poll timing out into the offline state.
Removing the success guard, re-anchoring the guard to the last started
poll, and removing the timeout each fail one of those assertions, and
the unmutated file passes all of them.

fix(hooks): keep the arguments after env -S whole

GNU env -S splits only its own argument; the ones after it reach the command unchanged. Joining them into the split string let a quoted ';' inside a later argument read as a command separator, so env -S 'echo' '; psql -c "drop table users"' was denied. Each later argument is now escaped back into a single literal word, which still leaves env -S 'psql -c' 'drop table users' denied.

fix(skill-comply): stop a failed step supplying evidence downstream (#3109)

* fix(skill-comply): stop a failed step supplying evidence downstream

`_check_temporal_order` fell back to the raw classifier output whenever
the referenced step was absent from `resolved`. A step only enters
`resolved` once it passes, so "failed" and "not graded yet" were the
same thing to that lookup, and a dependant could pass on an event
belonging to a prerequisite that had failed its own ordering check.

With three steps C, A (before C) and B (after A) and events C@T0,
A@T1, B@T2, A fails and B passed on A's classified event: 2/3 instead
of 1/3. It compounds down a chain, so one failed prerequisite could
leave a five-step workflow reading 4/5.

The grader now tracks which steps have been graded at all. A referenced
step that was graded and is missing from `resolved` failed, and its
events are refused with a reason that says so. A step not graded yet is
a forward reference to a step declared later, and the fallback stays as
it was: that is what makes an out-of-order declaration work, and the
existing regression for it goes red if the fallback is removed instead.

`before_step` deliberately keeps the old fallback. The two fail in
opposite directions: an `after_step` fallback can only turn a failure
into a pass, a `before_step` one can only turn a pass into a failure,
so dropping it would relax a constraint because some other step failed.

* fix(skill-comply): revoke a pass that rested on a later-failing prerequisite

Review of #3109 found the mirror image of the case that PR fixes. `graded`
only catches a prerequisite that had already failed when its dependant was
graded. A step declared *before* its `after_step` is graded against the
classifier's raw events for a step that has not run yet — the fallback that
makes an out-of-order declaration work — and nothing revisited it once that
step went on to fail its own checks.

Add a pass after grading that demotes any detected step whose `after_step`
ended up failing, repeated to a fixed point: one demotion can invalidate
whatever depended on it, in either declaration order. Demotion only removes
passes, so it terminates. `compliance_rate` is computed from the demoted
results.

Also from review: build `graded` and the chain test's step list as new
objects rather than mutating (AGENTS.md immutability rule), and annotate the
injected mocks in the tests this PR owns.

fix(scripts): extract cross-platform openBrowser helper with structured launch result (#3180)

scripts/plan-canvas.js and scripts/control-pane.js both define their own
openBrowser helpers for launching the user's default browser. The two
implementations have diverged:

- plan-canvas.js dispatches across darwin/win32/linux but its
  try/spawn try/catch does not catch async child errors (ENOENT/EACCES
  on hosts without the launcher command). Returns a bare true/false.
- control-pane.js is darwin-only and silently returns early on
  Windows/Linux, so the two scripts behave inconsistently across
  platforms.

When the launcher command is missing (e.g. headless CI without xdg-open)
the JSON output still says 'browser: opened', lying to the agent.

Changes:
- scripts/lib/platform-launch.js: shared openBrowser helper that
  dispatches per platform, wires child 'error' so ENOENT/EACCES
  propagate, and returns {opened, reason} instead of a bare boolean.
- scripts/plan-canvas.js: drops its local helper, imports the shared
  one, and adds browserReason to its JSON output.
- scripts/control-pane.js: replaces its darwin-only branch with the
  shared helper and logs the structured reason on failure.
- tests/lib/platform-launch.test.js: 7 node:test cases covering
  opener-command selection, invalid-URL guard, structured-result
  shape, and a smoke run for the actual spawn.

Verification: node --test tests/lib/platform-launch.test.js → 7/7 pass.

fix(hooks): match the index case-insensitively, and isolate the pytest probe

Red-teaming the guard from 3c317470 found two more ways to get a repository's own
code executed. Both are demonstrated by a planted binary that appends to a witness
file, counted before and after.

Case folding. git matches index pathspecs case-sensitively even where
core.ignorecase is set, but APFS does not -- so a repository that commits
`.venv/bin/Python` gets `$venv/bin/python` opening and running that file while the
guard's lowercase query finds nothing in the index and reports it untracked. The
witness logged two invocations. It applies to `venv` and `env` as well, and to any
folding of the name. The query now uses a `:(icase)` pathspec; all nine
directory-by-spelling combinations are refused, and an untracked venv still runs.

Module shadowing. `python -c "import pytest"` puts the working directory first on
sys.path, so a repository that commits a `pytest.py` in its root has that file
imported, and executed, by a check whose only job is to answer whether pytest is
installed. The probe is now `python -I -c "import pytest"` on the virtualenv, uv
and poetry paths alike. Isolation does not hide a real pytest -- it lives in the
interpreter's own site-packages, confirmed against a venv holding pytest 9.1.1.

Still true, and not something this hook can fix: running the repository's declared
suite runs the repository's code. `pytest` imports conftest.py, and the Node arm
runs package.json scripts. That is what a pre-push verification hook is for. The
line this guard draws is narrower and worth keeping -- a capability probe, and the
choice of which interpreter to trust, should not be things the pushed repository
gets to decide.

fix(hooks): resolve the venv path before asking git whether it is tracked

The guard added in 9cdc40e6 was incomplete. `git ls-files` reports paths as they
are indexed and does not follow symlinks, so a repository that commits `.venv` as
a symlink to its own root alongside a tracked `bin/python` gets asked about
`.venv/bin/python` -- a path git has never heard of -- and the answer is
"untracked". The interpreter then runs. Measured on that shape: the planted
executable logged two invocations against 9cdc40e6 and none against this commit.

`repo_ships_interpreter` now resolves the bin directory with `cd -P`/`pwd -P`,
resolves the worktree root the same way, and asks git about the resolved path
relative to it. The three cases that matter all hold: a plainly committed venv is
still refused, the symlink shape is now refused, and a developer's own untracked
venv still resolves and runs.

`cd -P`/`pwd -P` rather than `realpath` or `readlink -f`, because neither is
portable to a stock macOS.

fix(hooks): name the remedy in the blank-override failure

The hook is global and this message blocks a push, so "ECC_PYTEST_CMD is set but
names no command" left the operator holding a refusal with no next step. It now
says to point the variable at a runner or unset it to fall back to discovery,
which is the same advice the no-pytest-found branch already gives from the other
direction.

fix(hooks): do not run a virtualenv interpreter the repository ships

This branch taught the hook to run `.venv/bin/python`, and that is a binary the
repository can supply. On main the Python arm only ever ran `pytest` from PATH --
the developer's own -- and on a machine without one it ran nothing at all, which
is exactly the machine this branch was written for. So the exposure is new, and
it arrived with the fix.

The hook is installed globally through core.hooksPath. Cloning a hostile
repository, committing nothing, and pushing it to your own fork is enough: the
pre-push hook finds the committed `.venv/bin/python`, runs it once to probe for
pytest and again to run the suite. Reproduced -- the planted executable logged
two invocations under the previous commit and none under this one.

A virtualenv is never committed. It is platform-specific binaries and every
Python project gitignores it, so `git ls-files --error-unmatch` separates the
two cases exactly: a developer's own venv is untracked and still resolves, a
tracked one is skipped with the reason printed. An absolute $VIRTUAL_ENV outside
the worktree reads as untracked, as it should.

Not addressed here, and worth a maintainer's view: `uv run` and `poetry run`
resolve from the repository's own lockfile, so they carry the same shape of
trust in a form this check cannot see. They are gated behind a lockfile being
present, and changing their semantics is a larger decision than this fix.

fix(hooks): a blank ECC_PYTEST_CMD is an override, and say when one is in use

`[[ -n "${ECC_PYTEST_CMD:-}" ]]` asked whether the variable had a value, not
whether it was set, so `ECC_PYTEST_CMD=` fell through to virtualenv discovery
while `ECC_PYTEST_CMD="   "` failed the push. Two spellings of the same mistake,
two behaviours. Falling through is the wrong one: an override that evaluated to
nothing -- a command substitution that found no pytest, say -- then silently ran
a different runner than the operator named, which is exactly the substitution
this resolver refuses to make anywhere else. Both now fail closed.

`${ECC_PYTEST_CMD+set}` rather than `[[ -v ECC_PYTEST_CMD ]]`, because `-v` is
bash 4.2 and a stock macOS /bin/bash is 3.2, where it is not a false but a
syntax error. The hook runs under whatever `env bash` resolves to.

The override is still not probed -- probing runs the operator's command, and a
wrapper that ignores `--version` executes the whole suite and is then rejected
for not printing a version. What the gate can honestly do about a stale override
is refuse to be quiet about it, so a push that uses one now says so, every time,
and says the hook has not checked that it is pytest. A bypass that announces
itself is not the silent gate this resolver exists to prevent.

The fixture env is built from nothing instead of inheriting process.env with two
keys blanked. Blanking is no longer neutral: a blanked ECC_PYTEST_CMD is now an
override, and every one of these tests would have taken that branch.

fix(hooks): stop probing the pytest override, and stop failing on exit 5

Three defects, found by reviewing this branch against a running pytest rather
than by reading it.

Exit 5 is not a failure. pytest reserves it for NO_TESTS_COLLECTED, and
`|| fail "pytest failed"` collapsed it into a blocked push. The `|| fail`
predates this branch, but this branch is what makes it reachable: a repository
whose pyproject.toml only configures ruff or black, with pytest in its venv and
no test files, used to hit the "pytest is not installed" skip and now gets
gated. $VIRTUAL_ENV is the first candidate, so merely having a venv activated in
the pushing shell drags any requirements.txt repository into this path, and the
hook is installed globally. Reproduced with pytest 9.1.1. Exit 5 is now
non-blocking but loud -- a bad rootdir, testpaths or an unimportable conftest
also collects nothing, and swallowing that silently would reopen the hole this
resolver exists to close. Other non-zero codes now carry the code, because 1
(tests failed) and 4 (usage error) call for different responses.

The ECC_PYTEST_CMD probe ran the operator's command. Validating the override
with `--version` assumed it would answer like pytest. A wrapper that sets an
environment variable and execs pytest ignores the flag and runs the whole suite,
so the probe executed the tests, then rejected the command for not printing a
version, then blocked the push -- with the suite green. That is worse than the
silent gate the probe was added to close, so the override is taken as given
again: it is a deliberate setting, the hook cannot inspect it without running
it, and pointing it at something that is not pytest is the operator's call.
`is_pytest` still guards the PATH candidate, which this script composes itself,
where `pytest --version` is harmless. An empty override still fails closed.

The tests inherited the ambient environment. `runHermeticPythonPrePush` passed
process.env through, so an exported ECC_PYTEST_CMD or an activated virtualenv
resolved a pytest the fixture never created and the venv test failed for anyone
who runs the suite that way. Both variables are now neutralised in the base env.

Coverage: the gate had no test proving it blocks. Changing the run line to
`|| true` left all three previous tests green. Seven now cover a spaced venv
path, a red suite, exit 5, an override invoked exactly once with no probe, an
empty override, and the PATH candidate in both directions.

test(hooks): build the pre-push python fixture env without mutation

AGENTS.md makes immutability mandatory and the helper built `env` by assigning
into it. Rather than reassigning a `let` through spreads, the two stub paths are
now resolved before the object exists, so `env` is a single `const` built in one
expression with the conditional keys spread in. Nothing to mutate and nothing to
rebind.

fix(hooks): keep venv paths intact and check every pytest candidate

Two holes in the resolver this branch added, both found in review.

A virtualenv path may contain spaces. `resolve_pytest` returned one string and
the caller expanded it unquoted, so `/home/me/my env/bin/python -m pytest` split
into `/home/me/my` and `env/bin/python`. The probe that accepted the candidate
was correctly quoted, so the hook reported the venv as usable and then failed to
run anything in it -- rejecting the push for a reason with nothing to do with
the code being pushed. It now builds an argv array and runs `"${PYTEST_CMD[@]}"`.

The resolver's contract is that every candidate is confirmed to be pytest, and
two of them were not. `ECC_PYTEST_CMD` was returned unchecked, so
`ECC_PYTEST_CMD=true` made the hook run `true -q`, exit 0 and report a Python
project verified by nothing. The PATH branch used `command -v pytest`, which
proves only that a file of that name exists. Both now go through `is_pytest`,
which runs `--version` and requires the output to name pytest -- `--version`
alone is not evidence, since `true --version` also exits 0.

A bad `ECC_PYTEST_CMD` fails the push rather than falling through to the next
candidate. An operator who set it asked for that command, and silently running
a different one hides the misconfiguration -- which is the same silent-gate
failure this branch exists to remove, one level along.

Three regression tests cover the three paths: a venv whose directory name
contains a space, an override that is not pytest, and an override that is.

fix(hooks): pre-push skipped every Python project that uses a virtualenv

The Python block gates on `command -v pytest`, so it only runs when pytest is
on PATH. Installing a project's tools into a virtualenv is the norm rather
than the exception, so in practice the hook printed

    [ECC pre-push] Python project detected but pytest is not installed. Skipping.

while standing in a directory with `.venv/bin/pytest` in it, and pushed.

The failure mode is worse than not having the hook. A skip line reads like a
pass: the push succeeds, the output looks healthy, and nothing indicates the
gate declined to gate. A repository can sit behind it for months believing
its tests run on every push. Found on a project with 893 tests, none of which
the hook had ever executed.

`resolve_pytest` now looks, in order, at `ECC_PYTEST_CMD`, `$VIRTUAL_ENV`,
`.venv`, `venv`, `env`, `uv run` when a `uv.lock` is present, `poetry run`
when a `poetry.lock` is, and finally PATH. Each candidate is confirmed by
importing pytest rather than by the path existing, so a half-built venv falls
through to the next one instead of failing the push.

Two deliberate choices:

The log line names the command it resolved -- `Running: .venv/bin/python -m
pytest -q` -- so which interpreter ran is visible in the push output rather
than inferred. When nothing resolves, the message says where it looked and
names `ECC_PYTEST_CMD`, instead of asserting pytest is not installed when it
may well be.

`uv run` passes `--no-sync` so the hook cannot mutate the developer's
environment on its way to running the tests.

Behaviour change worth flagging for the release note: on any Python project
with a working virtualenv this hook now actually runs the suite, and will
block a push whose tests fail. That is the intent, but it is new behaviour
for every such repository, and `ECC_SKIP_PREPUSH=1` remains the escape.

Verified on two real repositories: a uv/venv Python project (resolves
`.venv/bin/python -m pytest`, 893 tests, exits 0; exits 1 when the suite
fails) and a Node project (unchanged, still runs lint/typecheck/test/build).

(category M), so `re.findall(r'\w+', 'রহিম')` gives ['রহ', 'ম']. Say
that precisely, note where `\w` is ASCII-only (JavaScript, re.ASCII), and
point at [ঀ-৿] or \p{Bengali} instead.

feat(free-tier): connectors and managed tools use a connectors-only guest token

A free-tier guest who only uses connectors or managed tools no longer meets
the free-inference browser challenge. The connectors-side resolver
(resolve_nous_access_token: tool gateway, NAS connector routes, account
reads) serves whichever guest token is live (an inference one covers it) and
otherwise mints with purpose "connectors" (hermes-portal#1516), which NAS
never challenges. An inference token is minted, inside run_with_challenge,
only when the free model is called.

The connectors-only token is stored in providers.nous.connectors_token, next
to the existing inference slot, so auth.json written by current releases
loads unchanged. Which slot a token fills is read from its JWT scope claim,
so a NAS that predates #1516 (it ignores purpose and returns an inference
token, or answers 428) keeps working through today's challenge path.

Two non-chat paths no longer mint inference for a guest behind its back:
the auth keepalive skips a guest (its tokens are minted on demand, matching
the start-time guard), and the Nous model catalog and pricing reads run as

old_string anchors mid-line -- normal when replacing an expression
rather than a whole statement -- old_string never captured whatever
precedes it on that line, so old_indent comes out empty. The existing
check, _leading_whitespace(line).startswith(old_indent), is then
vacuously true for every line ("".startswith("") == True), so every
line in new_string gets the file's indentation prepended on top of
whatever indentation it already carries, and the tool still reports
success: true. Confirmed via source and reproduced directly against
_reindent_replacement/_apply_replacements (a mid-line anchor with a
genuine old/file indent mismatch mangles every line without this fix,
and leaves them untouched with it).

whenever that is False, before old_indent is ever computed or trusted.

indentation is unaffected -- match_starts_at_line_start is still True
there, so the existing re-anchoring logic (including relative-nesting
preservation across multi-line replacements) runs exactly as before;

fix(kanban): respawn guards compare mixed int/ISO times by value

  indefinitely, and a 90-day-old ISO PR comment kept `active_pr` on.

SQL range still returns every text stamp (TEXT > INTEGER), and the decision
is made on its `_to_epoch` value. One policy for an unreadable time: it is
dropped (never guards, never lifts); the only exception is a PR comment,
which counts as "just posted" so the duplicate-PR guard fails closed. The
post-success requeue check likewise no longer treats an old ISO event as
a re-queue.

spares a run, an old ISO start times out and goes stale, and the
unreadable-start / dead-worker cases are kept.

Code health blocks new wall-clock sleeps in tests (HX013), adds a shared wait_until helper (#136644)

* feat(code-health): HX013 blocks new wall-clock sleeps in tests

A fixed time.sleep()/asyncio.sleep() is a bet that the code under test finishes
in time; on a loaded runner it loses and the test flakes. Main has ~1,470 of
them in tests/ and nothing stopped new ones (HX rules exclude tests).

HX013 runs only on test paths (Rule.include) and flags time/asyncio/anyio/trio
sleeps with a delay that is not a literal 0, plus a fresh threading.Event().wait(x).
Existing sleeps are grandfathered by the ratchet's base-relative compare; moved
code keeps its debt; '# health: allow HX013 -- <why>' waives a deliberate delay.

The fix text points at tests/waiting.py (wait_until / async_wait_until), a shared
poll-with-deadline helper replacing the ~60 private copies across the suite.

* fix(code-health): HX013 passes the interval of a poll under a deadline

The frozen replay (PRs merged 2026-10-08..09) hit three private poll helpers
(while not done and monotonic() < end: sleep(x)): that is the compliant shape the
fix text recommends, not a fixed delay. A while loop that reads a clock and can
end on a non-clock condition now exempts its sleep; a loop that only waits out
the clock, or polls with no deadline, still counts. tests/waiting.py needs no
waiver any more; tests/AGENTS.md names the rule and the helper.

* fix(code-health): HX013 passes a round-bounded poll loop

The second frozen window (2026-10-06..07) hit 'for _ in range(200): await
asyncio.sleep(0.01); if idle: return', a poll bounded by its round count: load
stretches it but cannot make it return early. A for-range loop whose body can
leave on a non-clock condition now exempts its sleep; a range loop of fixed
delays, or a poll over arbitrary items, still counts.

* fix(code-health): HX013 exempts only a real poll's own interval

Review fixes for the HX013 poll-loop exemption, plus a file split:

- Split: the HX013 checker moves to scripts/code_health/py_rules_sleep.py,
  and the AST helpers it shares with py_rules (Ctx, _FUNCS, _dotted,
  _call_name, _deferred_parts, _eager) move to a leaf module py_ast.py.
  py_rules.py drops from 1,034 to 877 lines (928 on main); CHECKERS still
  registers HX013.
- Clock-only conditions: only a test operand that reads something other
  than the clock counts as a condition. Combined clock checks
  (`monotonic() < a and monotonic() < b`), `not`/constant operands, and
  locals assigned only from clock arithmetic (`now < end`) no longer
  exempt the sleep. `and`/`or`/`not` follow their logic, so `while not
  done() or monotonic() < end` still waits out the clock.
- Loop ownership: a `break` ends only the loop whose body holds it (a
  nested loop's break does not count for the outer loop; one in the
  nested loop's `else:` does). Nested defs, lambdas and classes are
  skipped. A sleep in a loop's `else:`, `while` test or `for` iterable is
  not that loop's interval.
- Retry polls: a `try` body's return/break counts as conditional when the
  body calls something that can raise (`try: return probe() except
  OSError: sleep`). A body that only sleeps still counts as a fixed delay.

On origin/main this flags 2 more grandfathered sleeps and exempts 12 retry
polls the old rule missed, so the count goes from 923 to 913.

fix(gateway): offer an admitted completion again when its turn cannot confirm the owner

Admission marks a durable completion delivered before the receiving turn resolves its session. When the owner compressed in between and the turn's ownership read then failed, the turn dropped the event while the row read delivered, so nothing would deliver the result again.

A turn that cannot confirm the owner now returns the rows admitted with its event to pending and puts them back on the completion queue, so the next delivery re-runs the pre-flight against the compressed session. Verdicts that mean a user boundary (/new, /resume, a user-ended session) still drop the event, and a row past the delivery budget converges to dropped, as on the other delivery paths.

fix: signed reasoning replays after resume on Anthropic and Bedrock Converse

What users saw
- Anthropic (last-turn-only Claude models, e.g. Sonnet 4.5): after `chat --resume`
  or on the next gateway/TUI turn, the previous answer's signed thinking block was

- bedrock_adapter + transports/bedrock: Converse turns record the model that produced them (a private

  them back, they replay verbatim with signatures. Other models keep the per-model

fix(release): staging checks each metadata row's commit and tag, not stamp-only fields

rc.10-v0.21.7's "Stage verified stable candidate artifacts" job failed with

  ValueError: Built package provenance does not match the release

assemble() ran stamp_matches() on each metadata row. stamp_matches() is the
check for an install-stamp.json and requires baseVersion, but a metadata row
is what record() writes (platform, arch, tag, commit, identity, version, ...)
and never carries baseVersion. So every bundled stable release failed here
once all packages were built. record() already verified each package's own
stamp (including baseVersion) when it wrote the row.

The row check is now what the row actually contains: commit and tag. The
staged-candidate fixture wrote a baseVersion into its rows, which is how the
mismatch stayed hidden; it now writes exactly the keys record() does. With
the corrected fixture, main's code fails 8 tests with the production error.
