fix(browser): browser_exec's private-URL route reaches local Chromium on its own daemon

The salvaged route declined the provider in browser_use_cli, but the
managed-Chromium resolver still asked _get_session_info for the plain
cache key, and with a cloud provider configured that key builds a CLOUD
session — the private-URL call still created a Browser Use cloud browser.

- the sidecar call uses the `::local` cache key, so _get_session_info
  builds local Chromium (the same key browser_navigate's sidecar uses);
- it runs under its own harness daemon (BU_NAME `_local_<name>`): the
  daemon reads BU_CDP_* once at spawn, so reusing the cloud route's
  daemon would relay the private URL to the cloud browser;
- a follow-up call with no URL literal stays on the route the previous
  call took, like browser_navigate's _last_session_key.

fix: compute each URL's routing verdict once, not once per decision

Review caught that `_hybrid_routes_locally` resolves DNS (`_url_is_private` ->
`socket.getaddrinfo`) and is not memoised, so evaluating it separately for the
pre-flight and again for the backend choice lets a host whose answer changes
between the two lookups split them: the first lookup looks private, which
relaxes the private-address floor, and the second looks public, which clears
`force_local_sidecar` — so the call executes against the CLOUD provider with the
private URL in it. That is the leak this change exists to prevent.

`_code_url_verdict(code)` now makes ONE pass over the URL literals and returns
`_CodeUrlVerdict(blocked, local_sidecar)`; `browser_exec` consumes the returned
verdict instead of re-deriving it, so both decisions rest on the same captured
evidence. This is the discipline `browser_navigate` already applies — it derives
its safety relaxation from the session key (`_is_local_sidecar_key`) rather than
re-running the predicate. `_blocked_url_in_code` is gone rather than kept as a
wrapper: a caller that recomputed the route after it would reintroduce exactly
this bug.

Tests: `test_rebinding_host_cannot_split_verdict_from_route` stubs
`socket.getaddrinfo` to answer private then public, counts predicate evaluations
and asserts both that they are one per URL and that the call never reaches the
cloud provider — RED against the previous commit ("evaluated 2 times"), green
after. `test_public_then_private_answer_is_refused_not_leaked` pins the other
direction, where the safety check sees the private answer and refuses (the
over-block is the safe side). No live DNS in either. 10 existing cases moved to
the renamed helper. Full browser suite: 68 files, 830 passed, 0 failed.

fix: browser_exec honours hybrid routing for private/LAN URLs

With a cloud browser provider configured (the picker's `nous`, or any
browserbase/browser-use key), `browser.auto_local_for_private_urls` is on by
default and `browser_navigate` routes private/loopback/LAN URLs to a LOCAL
Chromium sidecar so the cloud provider never sees them. `browser_exec`'s
pre-flight URL scan did not consult that decision, so *every* LAN URL was
refused with "Blocked: URL targets a private or internal address" — and in
Browser Use mode (`browser.backend` unset, the default) `browser_exec` is the
only browser tool, so the documented hybrid workflow was unreachable.

Relaxing the pre-flight alone would have been wrong: the exec call resolves ONE
CDP endpoint for the whole code blob (`_resolve_backend_cdp`), so an allowed
private URL would then have been executed against the configured cloud browser
— exactly the leak the guard exists to prevent. Verdict and route now move
together:

* Extract `_hybrid_routes_locally(url)` in browser_tool as the single source of
  truth for the predicate; `_navigation_session_key` reads it too, so the
  navigate and exec paths cannot drift apart.
* `evaluate_url_safety(url, *, auto_local=False)` forwards the relaxation to
  `_url_policy_error` (the cloud-metadata floor stays unconditional).
* `_blocked_url_in_code` passes `auto_local=_hybrid_routes_locally(url)`, the
  same verdict the navigation path reaches for itself.
* `browser_exec` computes `local_sidecar` from the URLs in the code and threads
  it through `_route_backend` → `_resolve_backend_cdp(force_local_sidecar=...)`,
  which declines the cloud provider so the local engine serves the call. One
  endpoint per call means a mixed call runs wholly local — the safe direction.

Scope is deliberately narrow: no cloud provider, a CDP override, or Camofox all
leave `_hybrid_routes_locally` False, so those paths are byte-for-byte unchanged.
The two operator overrides (BU_CDP_*/`browser.cdp_url`) still outrank it.

Tests: 9 new cases in tests/tools/test_browser_use_cli.py covering the URL
verdict (LAN, loopback, public, IMDS still blocked, hybrid off, no provider) and
the endpoint the verdict depends on (LAN-only and mixed calls must never reach
the provider; public-only still must). Full browser suite: 663 passed.

rest of the process, but `hermes chat --resume` (or a gateway restart)

fingerprints) and is loaded once per session_id. Still keyed by

Every model reasons and intends that reasoning to be replayed, but the
chat-completions wire echoed reasoning_content only to DeepSeek/Kimi/MiMo/

- Reactive recovery: a 4xx unknown-field rejection that NAMES a reasoning
  key this request carried is recorded per (provider, host, model) and the

- Gemini thought_signature survives on Gemini hosts/providers even when the

- Vendor keep-reasoning flags (docs-only): GLM thinking.clear_thinking=false,

fix(acp): bind cancellation to the interrupted root activity

Cancelling during the prompt's initial whenIdle() wait could retain its
slot indefinitely. If a child delivered a result while the aborted root
was unwinding, Agent.whenIdle() followed the replacement driver and waited
for the newly autonomous summary. The earlier child-wait recheck could
not help because settlement had not yet reached that child wait.

This is an inherited latent issue: the pre-PR ACP bridge also awaited the
same replacement-following whenIdle() after cancellation. Existing
continuable spawn children could expose it; the unified asynchronous fork
default makes the ordering possible for fork delegations as well.

Give the existing InflightPrompt one cancellation-completion promise,
replacing the local cancellation wake-up and its listener. The private
admission AbortSignal is the cancellation flag instead of duplicated
boolean state. The exact root's emitted status identifies the interrupted
activity's retirement and synchronously adopts that output queue. Later
root work and later output cannot replace the first captured completion.

Record whether cancellation began at public idle. Maintenance has that
public status too, so its next running transition establishes release of
work behind maintenance; the ordinary whenIdle promise provides a
fallback when no transition occurs or plugin disposal detaches observers.
Both observations settle the same promise. Settlement races that promise
against initial idle and child waits, then waits only for the interrupted
activity/output on the cancellation path. No future work is re-cancelled,
child admission remains open, and session close keeps its separate full
quiescence and descendant teardown.

fix(cron): avoid repair alerts before fresh-run verification (#170073)

Closes #170014

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes unsuccessful-repair alerts being sent when a cron run started before the owner-conversation repair had finished and therefore could not verify its changes.

## User Impact

Owned automations keep running during repair, but failures from runs started before repair settlement no longer trigger the unsuccessful-repair alert. A fresh failing run still alerts once, and an unobserved or stuck repair is bounded by the existing agent timeout. The failure counter and ten-failure auto-disable backstop are unchanged; success still clears the incident silently.

Upgrade behavior: older stored incidents containing only `repair.atMs` keep today's request-based escalation. New incidents store additive JSON timestamps; no database schema migration or new configuration key is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Following the [maintainer decision](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/170014#issuecomment-6128665736), cron observes the repair's correlated terminal lifecycle result, rather than treating acceptance as completion. The repair now owns a detached async continuation: the initiating cron run cannot cancel its observer when that run's scope retires. The same observer records settlement for both successful and failed repair turns; loss of observation through timeout or Gateway shutdown stays unconfirmed and uses the persisted deadline. The scheduler compares the failed run's start time with settlement. Existing lifecycle and notification-cycle fences prevent stale writes.

The repair brief asks the owner turn to describe what it changed, not claim that the automation is fixed. No admission hold, transient-retry policy change, side-effect replay change, or auto-disable change is included.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes.

## Evidence

- Focused checks: 83 tests in four requested and executed files passed in 67.52 seconds: `src/gateway/server.cron.test.ts`, `src/gateway/server-cron-notifications.test.ts`, `src/cron/service.failure-repair.test.ts`, and `src/cron/service/failure-alerts.persistence.test.ts`, using the canonical `scripts/test-projects.mts` entrypoint. fix: preserve node Git metadata across workspace updates (#170338)

## What Problem This Solves

Accepted Gateway workspace updates replaced a node checkout's Git metadata. A later turn lost its origin, node-created commits, branches, and detached HEAD. Keep the existing atomic workspace replacement. Preserve incoming Git objects, discard the staging checkout's other metadata, then copy the node's authoritative Git metadata before the swap. The original checkout remains available for rollback. Reuse the existing cancellation check at replacement. This adds a copy of local Git metadata during full accepted replacements; no speedup is claimed.

Net production LOC: +12 (+13/-1), one production file. No protocol, lifecycle, schema, or configuration changes.

## Evidence

The old merge-copy candidate rewound packed refs in two direct Git probes. The actual transfer regression also failed twice at the retained branch tip (21.73 s / 21.70 s). The test covers node commits, detached HEAD, packed refs, unshallowed history, and node-selected origin/refspec across a real accepted transfer. `pnpm test src/gateway/worker-environments/node-workspace-transfer-retention.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 6 passed in 67.68 s; focused repeat passed in 22.26 s. Direct Git probes also verify a Gateway-only object survives the metadata replacement. Final cross-machine replays passed twice: the agent used the reachable origin, switched branch, committed on the node, detached HEAD and initialized a real submodule. Independent checks after reconciliation verified the exact node HEAD, detached state, origin, committed file and submodule Git root; a second turn verified them again. Gateway HEAD stays at the source commit while file changes reconcile; the node commit remains node-local.

Release-note context: node workspaces preserve local Git history and metadata across accepted Gateway file updates.

fix(skills): background reviews save only repeatable procedures (#170277)

## What Problem This Solves

The background skill review saves too much. On a busy Gateway it changed skills after almost every review run (20 review edits on one day), mostly one-off details from a single request (one preorder, one menu, one museum's holiday hours) plus routing and formatting tweaks. Its routing advice ("patch a skill that covers the task", "merge into one umbrella skill") pushed these into a few catch-all skills that grew to about 55 KB each. The agent then reads that bulk on every matching task.

## User Impact

- Background reviews change a skill only for a repeatable procedure: a class of task the user will ask for again, where the next run would go wrong or redo work without the change.
- Facts true of only one request stay in the conversation.
- A review makes at most one change. Each skill covers one class of task, so an unrelated lesson gets its own focused skill instead of a new branch in a catch-all.
- Most reviews now change nothing, so there are fewer Learned notices.
- `/learn` (user-requested) is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The review prompt (`buildSkillExperienceReviewPrompt`) is the owner of what a background review saves. The change replaces its trigger and routing sentences with one explicit bar, in the concise, positive style of well-crafted agent skills: state the target (a small set of sharp, repeatable procedures), the evidence that qualifies, the at-most-one-change limit, and "replace stale lines rather than appending". Authoring standards and the do-not-capture list are unchanged. No code judge or cap was added; the model still decides. Docs in `docs/tools/self-learning.md` describe the new bar.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes (`git log origin/main --author=pash@openai.com --author=sjf@openai.com` on the touched files is empty).

- **Isolation:** each run used an isolated copy of the state, with the session transcript cut at the moment the original review ran and Workshop skills restored to their pre-review versions. No user messages were replayed, and no channels were configured.
- **Credentials:** the OpenAI key came from an exec SecretRef, never from the environment or arguments.

fix(auth): invalidate persisted profiles on explicit refresh (#170201)

## What Problem This Solves

`models.authRefresh` can acknowledge success while republishing a removed credential from its warmed persisted-row cache. A persisted change without an in-process write receipt does not invalidate that cache, so rebuilding the prepared runtime alone does not honor the explicit refresh request.

Clear auth snapshots, persisted-row caches, and derived materializations through the existing auth snapshot owner before rebuilding and publishing the selected agent's credentials. Ordinary in-process mutation refreshes keep their existing receipt-driven behavior. The registered-RPC regression removes a synthetic local credential without a Gateway receipt, then requires refresh to remove it from auth status while preserving the shared profile and rejecting a read-only caller.

The RPC remains `operator.admin` only. The router's current-operator check immediately before handler invocation, request/agent validation, and existing credential-publication authority checks remain intact. No security check is removed. Accepted bookkeeping cost: an explicit refresh clears process-wide auth caches, so unaffected agents may rebuild their snapshots on their next access. The fault-injection test does not establish support for concurrent external database writers.

## Evidence

Existing isolated Codex P0–P2 review is scoped-clean. Formatting, type-aware lint, and normal commit hooks passed when the candidate was created. `pnpm test src/gateway/server-methods/models-auth-refresh.integration.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` passed 2/2 on validation composition `8d087040fefe` (216.05 seconds in Vitest; 237.41 seconds including orchestration). Reverting only the production fix with the same test blob produced the expected 1 failure/1 pass: the removed local credential remained visible after explicit refresh. That control took 226.15 seconds in Vitest and 320.42 seconds including orchestration. The validation checkout was restored to the exact composition, clean, with no surviving test processes.

The same composition passed build, production and test types, lint, source-contract and boundary checks, T1/dialect ratchets, Madge, Knip, and the SDK report in [CI run 38298120555](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/38298120555). The standalone head `e9dcb44c4679` preserves both tested source blobs; the auth owners, refresh helper, credential runtime, RPC authorization/dispatch, direct test helpers, package manifest, and lockfile also match the validation composition. These are CI's split static checks, not a separate `check:changed` invocation. Exact standalone-head [CI run 38302005065](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/38302005065) then completed successfully: 38 successful jobs, 26 skipped, zero failures, including all applicable production/test type, lint, source-contract, architecture, Knip and ratchet gates.

Supplemental coverage limitation: the untouched OAuth authority-chain sibling stopped before Vitest at the managed Gateway artifact-separation guard (zero tests); no bypass or retry was attempted. Ordinary PR CI does not run `test/oauth-refresh-authority-chain.e2e.test.ts`. Its supported CI coverage is the release workflow's `validate_repo_e2e_gateway` job with repository E2E enabled and no live-suite filter: a full build followed by four dynamically selected `pnpm test:e2e:gateway` shards. That mapping is source evidence, not a passing sibling result. The direct registered-RPC tests cover credential publication and rejection of a read-only caller for this change.

A new file staged on the Gateway during a worker turn is missing from the node on the next turn.

The local reconciliation owner includes the trusted Gateway index before both unchanged and changed result acceptance. fix(skills): make background review channel notices opt-in (#170025)

## What Problem This Solves

Background skill reviews post a "💾 Learned: …" message to the chat that triggered them. On busy channel conversations (Telegram topics, Discord) these messages arrive often and add noise to the conversation.

## User Impact

- New setting `skills.workshop.autonomous.channelNotices` (boolean, default `false`).
- Default: channels get no Learned message. The session, including a channel session opened in the web UI, gets the **Learned** row in the Control UI chat, with skill chips and **Undo**.
- `channelNotices: true`: channels get the notice with its Undo button as before. As on `main`, the transcript copy of that channel message is unmarked, so the Control UI shows it as plain text, not the Learned row. Slack still never gets a channel message, but its sessions now get the Control UI row instead of nothing.
- Saying "undo" in the conversation works in both modes, because the next turn gets the exact revert call. `/learn undo <id>` is unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Owner decision: the notice is clean in the web UI and noisy in channels, so channel delivery becomes opt-in. `postWorkshopChangeNotice` sends to the channel only when `channelNotices` is on, the channel is deliverable and not Slack. In every other case it writes the existing transcript row (`deliveryMirror` kind `skill-workshop-change`), which the Control UI already renders. The system-event wording no longer claims the user was told, because with notices off channel users do not see the row.

Update behavior: the new key is optional and needs no migration. Existing configs keep working; channel notices stop until the operator sets the key. None of the notice work is in a release yet.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes (`git log origin/main --author=pash@openai.com --author=sjf@openai.com` on the touched files is empty).

## Evidence

- Focused tests pass (8 files): `review-outcome`, `config`, `commands-learn`, `review-undo`, `experience-review`, `server-methods/skills-workshop`, `schema.help.quality`, `config.plugin-validation`.
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:test:src`, `config:docs:check`, `config:schema:check`, oxlint, oxfmt and `git diff --check` pass.
- Smoke against isolated state, using the real config validator, session store, `postWorkshopChangeNotice`, transcript reader and system-event queue, with network guards:
  - the validator accepts `channelNotices: true` and rejects `"yes"`;
  - **off (default)**, Telegram session: one assistant transcript row with `deliveryMirror.kind=skill-workshop-change` (the Control UI **Learned** row), one undo system event, no network attempts;
  - **on**, Telegram session: the channel send path ran (`Outbound not configured for channel: telegram`, because the smoke has no Telegram account), no transcript-only row, one undo system event.
- Upgrade compatibility (real `validateConfigObject` + `resolveSkillWorkshopConfig`): configs written before this change stay valid and resolve to notices off: no `skills` key, `{autonomous:{mode:"auto"},maxSkillBytes:60000}` (keeps 60000), and `{autonomous:{mode:"off"}}`. `channelNotices: true` resolves on. No stored data changes: transcript rows keep the existing `skill-workshop-change` marker, and no migration is needed.
- Not caused by this PR: `src/gateway/gateway-workshop-learning.e2e.test.ts` fails the same way locally with this PR's files reverted to merge base `3302551873b` (the review makes no change, so no notice appears). `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-composer-disabled-banner.test.ts` (TS2322) is outside this diff.
- Telegram Test Server proof (`telegram-e2e-userbot`, Convex lease, real QA user in a DM, `--source-gateway` on this head). Each run sends a turn, then a scenario command makes real Workshop changes under a `skill-workshop-review:<uuid>` run id and calls the real `postWorkshopChangeNotice` in the test Gateway's state:
  - **Off (default):** after the trigger, no SUT message, edit or Learned notice for about 82 s. The session transcript has the assistant row with `openclawDeliveryMirror.kind=skill-workshop-change` (the Control UI Learned row).
  - **On** (`skills.workshop.autonomous.channelNotices: true`): Telegram shows "💾 Learned: updated deploy-staging (tightened the rollback step); created release-notes (drafting release notes)…" with an **Undo** button (`tgcmd:/learn undo <reviewId>`). Pressing it removes the button and replies "↩️ Undid the skill change: restored deploy-staging; archived release-notes." Verified afterward: the rollback step is restored, `release-notes` is archived, and the change feed shows `user restore` and `user archive` under `skill-workshop-undo`.

fix(workers): retry admission after unrelated placement changes (#170085)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes session lifecycle admission failing with `Worker placement inventory changed` when another session claims, releases, or reconciles a worker. Concurrent testing reproduced the rejection, including three rejected turns in a 180-turn soak.

## User Impact

An unrelated placement change during admission is retried once automatically. Changes to the admitting session's placement, repeated inventory invalidation, and lost database authority still reject admission. No configuration, schema, or worker protocol changes are required; update the Gateway.

## Why This Change Was Made

Maintenance must retain a global inventory because it protects other sessions from pruning. Keep that guard and record the session IDs that invalidated its observation. At the lifecycle write boundary, rebuild preparation once when those IDs exclude both the prior and resulting session IDs. Never retry removals or an acknowledged commit.

Production LOC: **+30 net** across five production files; eight changed files total. The small increase records invalidation ownership and bounds recovery, with no sleeps, timeouts, new generations, or persistent state. Removed an unused preparation argument and a one-use authority wrapper. No latency improvement is claimed.

The deterministic fixture commits real placement changes after a real database-worker inventory read and after capture, before admission.

The existing integration suite includes worker compilation and Gateway maintenance fixtures; no new boot fixture or real timer was added. Controls verify that a same-session change and a second invalidation still fail without writing the target session.
- Targeted type-aware Oxlint, formatting, and `git diff --check` passed. Independent Codex P0/P1 review was scoped-clean.
- Final [CI run 38292616527](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/38292616527) passed on `aaa4b6438e4d43683dad835b208fb77fdd94b76c` (953 s elapsed), including static checks, changed-code tests, and the wrapper closure. fix: compact ChatGPT sessions before large context jumps (#169755)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: ChatGPT sign-in sessions wait too long to compact, so a large next message or tool result can push the request beyond the model window and force slower client-side compaction.

## User Impact

ChatGPT V2 compaction starts at the earlier of the existing reserve-based budget and 90% of the effective context window. A 500,000-token window with a 20,000-token reserve starts at 450,000 instead of 480,000 tokens. API-key, proxy, manual `/compact`, and overflow-recovery behavior are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The request boundary in `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/chatgpt-v2-compaction.ts:118` previously returned whenever the outgoing request fit the reserve-based budget. The new soft trigger uses the same measured/projected request pressure without changing the hard context cap or checkpoint coverage. If V2 is unavailable while the request still fits, normal inference continues; a failed V2 attempt is not retried in that run. Client-side fallback still starts only at its existing budget boundary or the physical hard cap.

A single pending suffix can still jump past the physical window before a safe boundary. V2 must send the entire outgoing request, and its append-only checkpoint covers that whole prefix; partially compacting it here would incorrectly cover pending content. The existing client fallback remains for that case and is documented.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes. No storage or configuration schema changes.

## Evidence

- Regression fails on the original boundary: a settled 465,674-token window followed by a large tool output calls the client fallback. It passes with the earlier boundary, one tool execution, one replay of the tool output, and a durable checkpoint after session reopening.
- V2 boundary suite: 20 passing tests, including below-threshold behavior, reserve-first small windows, soft-zone pending tools, failed V2 suppression, unchanged over-budget fallback, and checkpoint coverage.
- Existing preemptive-compaction suites: 39 passing tests. Public Responses payload policy: 8 passing tests, including its unchanged 70% threshold.
- Core typecheck, affected agent test typecheck, scoped Oxlint/Oxfmt, and whitespace checks pass. Both runtime builds pass. The 67 targeted tests and core/test typechecks also pass on the merged head with matching dependencies.

### Isolated ChatGPT sign-in, account-reported 500,000-token window

| Observation | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compaction route | Client fallback; no V2 dispatch | One earlier V2; no client fallback |
| Trigger evidence | Prior request 466,264 input tokens; projected next request 558,535, above the 500,000 hard cap | V2 request 447,346 actual input tokens; the soft trigger uses estimated request pressure |
| Compaction lifecycle time | 30.643 s | 22.443 s (22.398 s transport) |
| First normal request after compaction | 71,620 input tokens | 16,071 input tokens |
| Normal request after all final tool results | 71,620 input tokens | 90,272 input tokens |
| Recall, before / after Gateway restart | 3/3 / 3/3 | 3/3 / 3/3 |
| Restart replay | Same client summary and three tool-output hashes, each once | Same opaque checkpoint and six post-checkpoint tool-output hashes, each once |

Both Gateways are stopped and the original configuration is restored. No credentials, message bodies, or encrypted checkpoint bytes are included in the transport capture.

This is a two-way door: reverting restores the old threshold without a storage migration. The blast radius is automatic V2 compaction on the native ChatGPT sign-in route; other compaction owners and thresholds are untouched.

fix(gateguard): detect dd by command word, not by text match

Review on #2829 found the regex fix widened a false positive: matching
`\bdd\s+if=` against the whole flattened line gated `echo dd if=/dev/zero`
and `grep dd if=/dev/zero file`, neither of which runs dd. That class was
already present before — `echo dd if=x` matched the old arm too — but the
boundary fix extended it to the slash and dot spellings, so the arm now
decides on text position rather than on what is being executed.

dd moves to isDestructiveDd(tokens), next to isDestructiveRm and
isDestructiveGit, and DESTRUCTIVE_SQL_DD goes back to SQL only. The
per-segment loop already tokenizes every executable body, so the check runs
where the command word is known.

This resolves four things the text match could not:

  dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sda    was allowed  -> denied  (the reported bug)
  sudo dd if=/dev/zero           was allowed  -> denied
  dd of=/dev/sda if=/dev/zero    was allowed  -> denied  (operands are order-free)
  echo dd if=x                   was denied   -> allowed (pre-existing false positive)

Leading sudo/doas/env, their flags, and VAR=value assignment prefixes are
skipped so a wrapped invocation still resolves to dd; flags are only skipped
once a wrapper has been seen, so the scan cannot walk into an unrelated
command's arguments.

Tests: 6 fail on upstream main, 155 pass with this change.

Refs #2642

fix(gateguard): deny dd whose input path is not word-initial

DESTRUCTIVE_SQL_DD shared one trailing \b across every alternation arm.
`dd\s+if=` ends in `=`, and a \b after a non-word character only holds when
the NEXT character is a word character, so the arm matched `dd if=x` and
missed every path starting with `/`, `.` or a quote:

  dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sda    allowed
  dd if=./disk.img of=/dev/sdb   allowed
  dd if="/dev/zero" of=/dev/sda  allowed

The word-boundary suffix now applies only to the arms that end in a word
character. The split is what keeps the widening bounded: dropping the
trailing \b outright would let `truncate` match `truncated`, and dropping the
leading \b would let `dd if=` match inside `add if=`. Both are covered.

This is the half of #2642 that survived the structural findGitSubcommand()
parser, which already handles `git checkout -- .`.

Not addressed here: `dd of=/dev/sda if=/dev/zero` with the operands reversed
is still allowed, before and after, because the pattern requires `if=`
immediately after `dd`. That is a different defect from the boundary bug and
widening a P0 gate's pattern shape is a maintainer call.

fix(block-no-verify): bound the flag scan to the enclosing quote/heredoc line

The scanner locked onto a `git commit` literal that sat inside a quoted
string of an OUTER command (a python heredoc's string, a VAR="..."
assignment, a printf JSON payload), then hasNoVerifyFlag() re-tokenized from
that inner offset with a fresh quote state. When quote parity flipped, the
"segment" ran past the enclosing string and picked up an unrelated later
`bash -n` / `sed -n` / `grep -n` as `commit -n`. Two legitimate commands were
blocked this way in one working session.

The first attempt at this PR (d5c428c) fixed the false positive by SKIPPING
`git` tokens judged to be in "data" context. That was the wrong lever: data
becomes executable the moment it is piped to a shell (`echo '...' | bash`,
`bash <<< '...'`, `cat <<EOF | bash`), and no regex list of shell invocations
is complete (`bash --noprofile -c` slipped). Three independent reviewers
(codex, Greptile, CodeRabbit) demonstrated executing bypasses; that commit is
squashed away here and none of its behaviour survives.

This version keeps every `git` candidate visible and keeps main's blocking
surface intact. A single O(n) preprocessing pass (buildScanBoundaries)
records, for each enclosed character, the closing quote or the current
heredoc-body line end. Subcommand discovery and flag tokenization are capped
at that boundary, so tokens after the enclosing data can never leak into a
candidate's argument list. Also: comment detection is a single mask pass
instead of a repeated prefix scan; heredoc parsing accepts quoted hyphenated
delimiters and CRLF terminators and preserves the `<<` vs `<<-` tab
distinction; quote-assembled words (`g''it`) are recognized.

Verified (all payloads run through the hook as JSON on stdin):

  on main AND here (CRLF heredoc trailer: 0 on main, 2 here);
- green-list, 16 leak-class false positives -> exit 2 on main, 0 here;
- tests/hooks/block-no-verify.test.js 84/84 (main's 25 retained verbatim,
  d5c428c's 8 removed, 59 table-driven red/green cases added);
  tests/hooks/cursor-block-no-verify.test.js 14/14;
- 204,807-byte command with 8,905 non-command `git` literals: 8.5 ms.

feat(install): require an explicit hook decision at the apply layer

The guided installer asks how ECC hooks should run, but that consent
lived only in the wizard path. Running install-apply directly with a
profile that includes hooks-runtime still materialized the hook runtime
with no disclosure and no decision.

Gate the apply layer instead, so every entry point is covered:

  the hook runtime, and refuse to apply until the caller decides

uninstall operate on already-recorded state and stay unchanged.

The documentation surface test scanned the hook's raw source with two
regexes. That had two holes, both confirmed against the shipped parser:

fix(suggest-compact): don't quote a percentage against an assumed window

The context signal always rendered "N% of <window> window", including when
the window size was the assumed 200k default rather than a detected value.
On a 1M session whose transcript carries no [1m] marker, that produced
lines like:

  [StrategicCompact] Context ~194k tokens (97% of 200k window)

while actual usage was ~19%. The user compacts on a false alarm, loses
context, and the resulting quality drop reads as a model regression.

The gap is structural: the context threshold defaults to 80% of the
window (160k on 200k), so the signal fires precisely in the 160k-200k
band where the size cannot be determined — above 200k the observed-tokens
fallback correctly infers 1M, and below 160k nothing fires.

Model id alone cannot close this. A tier may ship both a 200k and a 1M
variant under one id, so neither the known-family table nor a new entry
can distinguish them, and the transcript records no window field.

So stop asserting what isn't known: resolveContextWindow() now reports
whether the size was detected (env override, [1m] marker, known family,
or observed tokens > 200k) or assumed, and the hook omits the percentage
and window label when it was assumed. The token count, threshold, and
firing behaviour are unchanged.

resolveContextWindowTokens() keeps its existing signature and semantics.

fix(hooks): treat HTTP 404 MCP probes as reachable

The mcp-health-check preflight probes HTTP MCP servers with a bare GET.
Some Streamable HTTP servers route only POST /mcp and answer a bare GET
with 404 (Paper Desktop 0.5.3 is one). The probe scored that as down and
blocked every tool call for the server indefinitely, since the 30s
backoff just re-probes and re-fails.

A routed HTTP response of any status proves the endpoint is reachable,
which is all this preflight claims to check -- 400/401/403/405/406 are
already treated this way for the same reason. Add 404 to the set and let
the real MCP client validate the endpoint.

200 on POST /mcp); it fails on the current code and passes with the fix.

fix: probe POST-only Streamable HTTP MCP servers before marking them dead

The preflight probe in mcp-health-check only ever sent a bare GET to the
server URL. Some Streamable HTTP MCP servers route POST exclusively and
answer any GET with 404 — api.telnyx.com/v2/mcp is one — so the probe
failed permanently against a perfectly healthy server.

404 is not in HEALTHY_HTTP_CODES, so every probe failed, the backoff
compounded to the 10-minute ceiling, and the hook blocked every tool call
for that server before it left the machine while `claude mcp list` still
reported it Connected.

Replay a failed GET as a real JSON-RPC initialize POST and accept that as
proof of life. Whitelisting 404 was the alternative, but it would mask
genuine outages on every other server.

Adds a regression test with a POST-only server that 404s all GETs and
validates the initialize body; it fails without this change.

fix(continuous-learning-v2): emit loadable frontmatter from evolve --generate

Artifacts written by `evolve --generate` are inert: Claude Code (and every
spec-compliant Agent Skills client) injects only `name` + `description` at

fix(config-protection): protect ignore files and current config spellings

The hook blocks edits to linter/formatter configs so an agent fixes the code
instead of weakening the checks. It did not cover the cheapest way to weaken
them: adding one path to an ignore file. Measured against the hook, with the
file already on disk:

  .eslintignore        -> allow
  .prettierignore      -> allow
  .stylelintignore     -> allow
  .markdownlintignore  -> allow

Nor did it cover the current config names — only the legacy `.stylelintrc*`
and `.markdownlint.json` spellings were listed, so a project using the
documented `stylelint.config.js`, `.markdownlint.jsonc` or markdownlint-cli2
had no protection at all.

First-time creation stays allowed by the existing existence check, so
scaffolding a fresh ignore file is unaffected.

fix(config-protection): protect shared/base linter configs, not just entry points

`PROTECTED_FILES` matches exact basenames, so it only ever guarded a tool's
canonical entry point. Real repos split flat config across files — a shared
`eslint.config.base.mjs` holding the ignore list and rule severities, imported
by per-workspace `eslint.config.mjs` files, is the common monorepo shape.

That meant the hook protected the leaves and left the trunk wide open:

    eslint.config.base.mjs        <- ignore list + rule severities   UNPROTECTED
    frontend/eslint.config.mjs    <- imports the base                protected
    backend/eslint.config.mjs     <- imports the base                protected

An agent blocked from touching the two leaves could silently rewrite every rule
severity in the file they both import. Hit in practice: two edits to
`eslint.config.js` were correctly blocked, then an edit to
`eslint.config.base.mjs` in the same repo went through unchallenged.

Adds `PROTECTED_PATTERNS` alongside the existing Set, covering
`<tool>.config.<qualifier>.<ext>` and `.<tool>rc.<qualifier>.<ext>` for the
linters and formatters already listed. Case-insensitive, for the same reason
the Set lookup is (#2543).

Deliberately NOT matched: `vite.config.ts`, `vitest.config.ts`,
`jest.config.js`, `playwright.config.ts`, `tsconfig.json`. This hook exists to
stop a LINTER config being weakened in place of fixing the code; editing a
bundler or test-runner config is ordinary work, and sweeping those in would
make the hook obstructive. A second test pins that boundary so a future
widening of the patterns cannot quietly cross it.

The exact-name Set is untouched, so nothing previously protected becomes
unprotected, and first-time creation stays allowed (the bootstrap path).

Tests: 11 pass. The new regression test was verified failing against the
unpatched hook first; the boundary test passes either way by design and is
there as the control.

feat: thin Pi adapter mounting ECC's canonical skills and commands (#2759)

* feat: add thin Pi adapter mounting ECC's canonical skills and commands

Adds first-class Pi (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent) support as a thin
adapter layer, following the maintainer review on #2352. ECC's canonical
assets stay the single source of truth: nothing is copied or generated
under .pi/.

The `pi` manifest in package.json points Pi directly at `skills/` and
`commands/`. No transformation is needed — ECC's SKILL.md files already
follow the Agent Skills standard Pi implements, and ECC's command
frontmatter is already Pi's prompt-template format.

.pi/extensions/index.ts is the only adapter logic. It:

- uses Pi's documented `pi.on(...)` lifecycle, not an undocumented event bus
- resolves hook scripts from the installed package via `__dirname`, never
  `process.cwd()`, so global installs work from any project directory
- runs hooks with `execFile(process.execPath, [...])` and no shell, so paths
  containing spaces or shell metacharacters are safe
- invokes hooks through ECC's own `run-with-flags.js`, so `ECC_HOOK_PROFILE`
  and `ECC_DISABLED_HOOKS` keep gating hooks under Pi
- runs hooks in the user's project directory so project detection stays
  correct, while resolving the scripts themselves package-relative
- injects the SessionStart hook's `additionalContext` into the system prompt
  on the next `before_agent_start`
- isolates hook failures behind a timeout and an output limit
- registers `/ecc-doctor` for install diagnostics

Registers `.pi` in the platform-configs install module and adds a Pi row to
the harness adapter compliance matrix.

Verified against Pi 0.84.1: a global `pi install` exposes 285 skills and 94
commands resolved from `skills/` and `commands/`, plus `/ecc-doctor`, with
no generated copies.

Scope deliberately excludes subagents, chains, approval gates, todos,
profiles, and MCP; ECC works in Pi without any companion package.

* fix: address review findings on the Pi adapter

Bot review on #2759 surfaced two real runtime defects and several
hardening gaps.

Runtime fixes:

- Attach an `error` listener to the hook child's stdin. `stdin.end()`
  writes asynchronously, so a hook that exits, short-circuits, or is
  killed by the timeout before reading the payload raises EPIPE as an
  `error` event that the surrounding try/catch cannot see. Unhandled,
  that event would terminate the Pi session and break the isolation
  guarantee the adapter documents.
- Clear `pendingContext` at the top of the `session_start` handler. Pi
  can start a new session (/new, /resume, /fork) before
  `before_agent_start` consumes the previous value; if the newer hook
  then failed, the next agent start received context describing a
  different session's project state.
- Replace `require.resolve` companion detection with a read of Pi's own
  `packages` list, honoring `PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR`. Pi installs packages
  under its config directory, which is not on Node's module resolution
  path from the extension, so the previous check reported every
  companion as missing no matter what was installed.

Compliance matrix: remove internal semicolons and a trailing period from
the Pi record's list entries. The renderer joins entries with "; ", so
those characters split one entry into several in the rendered cell.

Tests: run profile gating against the temp skeleton instead of the real
checkout so it cannot leave marker artifacts behind; count files under
.pi/ by walking disk rather than git, so untracked copies cannot bypass
the regression guard; allow negated phrasing in the README heuristic;
pin the adapter's real parser guards with source assertions so the local
mirrors cannot silently diverge; add coverage for EPIPE isolation, stale
context clearing, and companion detection.

* docs: point users at existing companion Pi packages instead of bundling them

Every capability listed as out of scope is already provided by a maintained
community Pi package: pi-subagents, @juicesharp/rpiv-ask-user-question,
@juicesharp/rpiv-todo, and pi-mcp-adapter for MCP.

Pi supports pulling other pi packages in via dependencies plus
bundledDependencies, but this adapter deliberately does not. Bundling would
ship third-party code that executes with full user permissions in every ECC
install, turn optional capabilities into mandatory ones, and add four
fast-moving pins to maintain.

Instead /ecc-doctor now prints the exact `pi install npm:<name>` command for
each companion it does not find, so adopting one stays a deliberate user
choice.

Also corrects the MCP claim: Pi core has no MCP surface by design, but the
community pi-mcp-adapter package adds one. This adapter neither installs nor
verifies it, and ECC's MCP reference configs are not known to be compatible.

* docs: ECC's MCP configs work in Pi through pi-mcp-adapter, verbatim

Tested rather than assumed. The community pi-mcp-adapter package reads the
standard mcpServers format from .mcp.json and ~/.config/mcp/mcp.json, which
is exactly the format ECC already uses in .mcp.json and
mcp-configs/mcp-servers.json.

Verified against pi-mcp-adapter 2.21.2 in an isolated PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR:
copying mcp-configs/mcp-servers.json to a project's .mcp.json registers Pi's
`mcp` tool and `/mcp` command with all 35 ECC servers discovered, coexisting
with this adapter's /ecc-doctor. No translation layer and no ECC change are
needed, so this stops being a limitation and becomes documentation.

Recorded caveats: the adapter's first run against a new config performs
initialization that blocks in non-interactive mode, and only discovery was
verified, not live tool invocation.

ECC still neither installs nor depends on the package.

* feat: inject ECC's canonical engineering rules into Pi's system prompt

ECC's rules were the one durable asset the adapter did not deliver: skills
and commands reached Pi in full, but the 122 rule files that carry ECC's
coding style, testing, security, git workflow, and code-review standards
did not, so ECC in Pi was a library of skills rather than a set of
enforced standards.

Rules are read at runtime from the canonical rules/common/ directory of
the installed package and appended to the system prompt inside an
<ecc-engineering-rules> block. Nothing is copied or generated under .pi/,
which keeps the single-source-of-truth constraint this PR exists to
satisfy. Injection reuses the before_agent_start path already built for
session context, so no new lifecycle mapping is introduced.

Rules are re-applied every turn because they are standing policy, while
the session context stays one-shot and is consumed on first use.

agents.md, hooks.md, and performance.md are excluded: they describe Claude
Code primitives Pi does not have (Task/TodoWrite delegation, Claude hook
event types, thinking-budget toggles), so injecting them would point the
model at tools that are not there. A test asserts they stay excluded, and
a leakage test asserts none of those primitives appear in the injected
text. Language-specific rules under rules/<language>/ are out of scope for
this first adapter.

Injection is bounded by MAX_RULES_BYTES and can be disabled with
ECC_PI_RULES, following ECC's existing off-switch convention. /ecc-doctor
reports the state and injected size.

Measured on this repo: 7 files, 12,361 characters, roughly 3k tokens.

Also replaces a Function() call in the test helper with direct arithmetic,
and repins a stale assertion that pinned one spelling of the context
handoff rather than the guarantee (read before clear, clear before return).

* fix: /ecc-doctor misreported filtered packages and partial rule installs

Two reporting defects in /ecc-doctor, the command whose whole job is telling
a user what is actually installed.

Pi's settings accept a `packages` entry in two shapes: the bare source string
("npm:pi-subagents") and an object carrying that source alongside resource
filters ({ source: "npm:pi-subagents", skills: [] }). normalizePiPackageName
only recognized the string, so a user who narrowed which resources a companion
contributes was told the companion was not installed, along with an install
command for something already present. The source type still decides whether a
name is comparable, so an object wrapping a git source or a path stays
unrecognized exactly as before.

loadPortableRules drops rule files it cannot read, drops empty ones, and stops
at MAX_RULES_BYTES, but describeRulesStatus reported PORTABLE_RULE_FILES.length
regardless. A partial install that loaded 3 of 7 files reported "7 rule file(s)"
to the one command a user runs to find a partial install. The loaded count is
now tracked next to the cache and reported as a ratio, with the shortfall named.

Also reconciles the Notes bullet in .pi/README.md, which still called MCP out of
scope after the MCP section landed documenting that ECC's configs load in Pi
through pi-mcp-adapter.

Both defects were reported by CodeRabbit and verified against Pi's own
packages.md before fixing. Adapter tests go from 24 to 26; the two source
contracts that pinned the previous spellings now pin the new guards, so the
object-form unwrapping and the loaded-count reporting cannot be silently
reverted.

fix(continuous-learning-v2): warn when the observer never survives a hook invocation (#2489) (#2606)

* fix(continuous-learning-v2): warn when the observer never survives a hook invocation (#2489)

The observer is lazy-started from a hook process that exits immediately
afterwards. start-observer.sh's liveness check runs inside that still-living
process tree, so it always sees a healthy observer and prints "Observer
started (PID: N)". On native Windows (Git Bash/MSYS2) the reap happens later,
when the hook's Job Object closes, so no self-check placed in
start-observer.sh can ever observe the failure.

The next hook invocation is the only place the death is visible, and
_CHECK_OBSERVER_RUNNING already found it there -- then discarded it, deleting
the stale PID file and restarting silently, once per tool call, forever. Users
were left with an observer-start.log full of success lines and an observer
that never completed a single analysis cycle.

Record the "well-formed PID that is no longer alive" case, count consecutive
non-survivals in ${PROJECT_DIR}/.observer-nosurvive-count, and log one
explanatory warning when the streak reaches ECC_OBSERVER_NOSURVIVE_WARN_AFTER
(default 3). Warning fires on equality so a persistent failure logs once per
streak rather than once per tool call; finding the observer alive resets the
streak. The Windows-specific explanation is gated on uname so Linux/macOS
users are pointed at observer.log instead of a wrong diagnosis.

Counting happens in the caller, not inside _CHECK_OBSERVER_RUNNING, because
that function is invoked once per PID file and again under the start lock.

The PowerShell backgrounding rewrite is deliberately not included: it cannot
be exercised on a non-Windows machine, and untested process-spawning code is
a worse outcome than an accurate diagnostic.

* docs(continuous-learning-v2): state observer platform support and the new warn threshold

The observer's Windows limitation was only discoverable by hitting it. Record
it next to observer.enabled, where it is read before the flag is set, and
document ECC_OBSERVER_NOSURVIVE_WARN_AFTER so the knob added alongside the
warning does not repeat the undocumented-env-var problem tracked in #2573.

zh-TW is intentionally left alone: translation parity is not enforced here and
the repo rejects blind translation imports without translator review.

* fix(continuous-learning-v2): serialize the non-survival streak under the lazy-start lock

observe.sh runs on every tool call, so the streak read-modify-write could race
between concurrent invocations -- losing an increment or logging the warning
twice. That is the same class of bug the signal counter hit in #2296, and this
repo's rule is to never fall back to an unlocked read-modify-write.

Rather than add a second lock, move the increment into _START_OBSERVER_LOGGED.
All three of its call sites already run inside the lazy-start lock
(flock / lockfile / mkdir), so the update is serialized with no new machinery.
Counting at the restart instead of at detection also means N racing hooks
record one death rather than N.

The reset stays in the caller: it is an idempotent unlink, not a
read-modify-write, so it needs no lock.

Adds a regression case pinning the increment inside _START_OBSERVER_LOGGED and
asserting all three call sites remain locked.

* fix(continuous-learning-v2): harden the non-survival threshold and warning output

Three review findings on the #2489 diagnostic:

- An all-zero threshold silently disabled it. `00` passes a digits-only check
  but compares as zero, and the streak only grows, so the warning could never
  fire. Normalize with base-10 arithmetic and fall back to the default for
  anything below 1. Base 10 is forced explicitly because a leading zero would
  otherwise be read as octal, and `08` is an arithmetic error that would abort
  the hook under `set -e`. The same normalization now guards the streak read.

- An unwritable log silently swallowed the diagnostic. Build the message once
  and fall back to stderr when the append fails. This cannot spam: the block
  runs once per streak, not once per tool call. The counter write keeps its
  `|| true` -- observe.sh runs on every tool call and the repo rule is that
  hooks exit 0 on non-critical errors, so a full disk must not break tool use.

- The live-PID test fixture used process.pid, which is 1 in a container and is
  deliberately rejected by _CHECK_OBSERVER_RUNNING; the reset case would then
  fail for the wrong reason. Use a spawned child and clean it up.

Adds a regression case for the all-zero threshold. Verified on bash 3.2 (the
macOS CI runner shell) as well as bash 5.

* fix(continuous-learning-v2): warn only on a persisted streak increment

If the counter write fails, the file stays below the threshold, so every later
hook invocation rereads it, re-increments in memory, hits the equality check
and warns again -- turning the once-per-streak diagnostic into once-per-tool-
call spam. That is worse in exactly the case the stderr fallback added in the
previous commit was meant to cover, since a disk that cannot take the log
usually cannot take the counter either.

Gate the warning on the write succeeding. The write stays non-fatal: it runs
as an `if` condition, so `set -e` is satisfied and an unwritable counter costs
a delayed diagnostic rather than a broken tool call.

Tests: an unwritable counter must stay silent across repeated invocations while
the hook still exits 0, and a leading-zero threshold ("08") must be read as
decimal -- "00" alone did not exercise the base-10 conversion, since it is zero
either way.

fix(skills): add a session boundary to the buyer example, tighten the ATA check

Two findings from the bot review.

The reusable payment client had no authorization boundary. The policy
validates one challenge at a time, so it cannot see a session total and
cannot ask a human anything — a long-lived wrapped client could pay
repeatedly, to any recipient, past any intended budget. This also
contradicted the skill's own Spending Controls section, which promises
per-session budgets and allowlisted recipients.

Adds an allowlist of recipients to the policy, and routes every paid call
through a boundary that asks for confirmation once and holds a session
ledger. Settlement responses carry no amount, so the ledger reserves the
per-call cap — a deliberate over-estimate that can stop early, never late.
The payment-enabled client stays private behind it.

The Solana recipient check was too loose. Scanning an owner's token
accounts proves only that some account exists for the mint; the exact-SVM
client targets the canonical ATA specifically, so an auxiliary account
would pass while settlement still fails. Now derives the ATA with
findAssociatedTokenPda and checks that exact address. Also corrects the
provisioning advice: a bare transfer does not create the account, only one
that includes the create instruction does.

fix(hooks): context-monitor noise — loop-detection false positives + per-call cost-warning spam (#2486)

* fix(hooks): context-monitor noise — loop-detection false positives and per-call cost-warning spam

Two independent noise sources in the PostToolUse context monitor injected
agent-facing warnings on nearly every tool call:

1. LOOP WARNING false positives. hashToolCall() hashed only the first 160
   chars of a Bash command, so distinct long commands sharing a prefix
   (heredocs, long one-liners) collided and consecutive DIFFERENT calls
   looked like a stuck loop. Additionally LOOP_THRESHOLD=3 against a
   5-entry ring buffer fired on legitimate repetition (retries, polling).
   Fix: hash the full command (digest truncated, not the input — same
   treatment the Edit/Write branch already got), and require all 5 of the
   last 5 calls to be identical before warning.

2. COST NOTICE spam. run() deduped warnings on exact message text, but the
   cost figure embedded in the text moves on nearly every call, so once a
   session crossed $5 a 'new' COST NOTICE was injected per tool call for
   the rest of the session. Context warnings had the same defect via the
   remaining-% figure. Fix: dedupe on a stable per-tier key
   (cost:notice/warning/critical, context:warning/critical, scope) so each
   tier fires exactly once and re-fires only on genuine escalation. The
   existing ECC_CONTEXT_MONITOR_COST_WARNINGS opt-out is unchanged.

Tests: loop threshold updated (5-of-5 fires, 4-of-5 does not), long
shared-prefix Bash hash regression, and a run()-level tier-dedupe test
(notice fires once, silent on cost tick, re-emits on escalation).

fix(memory-vault): compare dev only when both stats report one (#2637)

ecc memory writes and --body-file reads fail on Windows. sameFileIdentity()
compares the dev field of a path-based stat against a handle-based fstat, and
libuv 1.49.0 through 1.50.x resolve path-based stat() and lstat() on Windows
through GetFileInformationByName, which leaves the volume serial unset while
fstat() reports it. The comparison never matches, so the TOCTOU guard rejects
every operation.

Keep the inode strict and compare dev only when both sides report one. POSIX
always reports a non-zero dev, so the original strict behaviour is preserved
there.

Request the guard's stats as BigInt. On the affected libuv versions dev is 0,
which leaves the inode as the only identity signal, and Windows file IDs run
past Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER where two distinct files can collapse to the same
number-valued inode.

Fixes #2626

fix(lib): reject invalid token counts and document the Fable/Mythos tier

`estimateCost` used `inputTokens` and `outputTokens` without validation.
A negative count yielded a negative cost, and a non-finite one yielded
NaN. That matters here specifically because this module backs the
cost-aware-llm-pipeline budget skill: `NaN > budget` is false, so a
corrupt token count silently passes the budget check it exists to
enforce. It now throws a RangeError naming the offending field.

The unknown-model fallback to sonnet rates deliberately stays fail-open:
that degrades an estimate, whereas these inputs corrupt one.

Separately, the estimator prices Fable and Mythos at $10/$50 per million
tokens, but all three pricing tables (the skill and its ja-JP and zh-CN
translations) listed only Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus, so a reader could not
budget for two supported model families. Added the missing row to each.

16 of the new assertions fail against the previous behaviour (23 passed,
16 failed) and all pass with the guard (39 passed).

fix(hooks): never format installed plugin and marketplace clones (#2667)

The Stop hook formats every JS/TS file edited during a response, grouped by the project root each file happens to sit in. That includes trees under .claude/plugins, which are third-party checkouts we only read.

Formatting them writes to code the user does not own. It also does real damage when a repo's committed code has drifted from its own formatter config: the rewrite is not a no-op but a wholesale reformat, so an unrelated bugfix ends up carrying hundreds of untouched lines. I hit this contributing to this repo — a 162-line fix arrived as a 478-line diff, most of it reformatted code the change never went near.

Skips both the user-level install root and a project-local one, mirroring the lookup in scripts/harness-audit.js. Paths are resolved before the prefix comparison, and a sibling such as .claude/plugins-backup does not match. The user own .claude config outside plugins is still formatted.

Adds 7 tests for the predicate, plus an end-to-end check that a clone file listed in the accumulator is left byte-identical. Suite 16 to 23.

fix(hooks): catch the bypass short flag anywhere in a cluster (#2668)

isCommitNoVerifyShortFlag anchored on the first character, so it only recognised the flag when it led the cluster. fix(continuous-learning): /evolve never produces skill or agent candidates (#2664)

* fix(continuous-learning): cluster instincts by keyword overlap in /evolve

`cmd_evolve` grouped instincts by exact string equality of the whole
normalized trigger sentence. Triggers are free-form sentences, so every
instinct landed in its own bucket and `skill_candidates` was always empty.
`agent_candidates` is derived from `skill_candidates`, so agents never
generated either — `/evolve --generate` could only ever emit commands.

Measured on a 42-instinct project: 42 instincts produced 42 unique cluster
keys, largest cluster size 1.

Group on keyword overlap instead. Jaccard is the wrong metric here — trigger
keyword sets average ~7 words, so even clearly related pairs top out around
0.33 — so this uses the overlap coefficient (shared / smaller set) at 0.5,
plus a floor of 2 shared keywords so one incidental word cannot pull
unrelated instincts together. The same 42 instincts now yield 4 clusters.

Also unify the command/agent slug used by the preview and the writer. The
preview called `.replace('a ', '')`, which strips "a " anywhere in the
string, mangling "extracting data from Reddit" into
`/extracting-datfrom-R` while `--generate` wrote `extracting-data-from.md`.
Both paths now share `_evolved_command_name()` / `_evolved_agent_name()`.

Adds tests/scripts/instinct-cli-evolve.test.js, which fails on the previous
implementation (0 clusters instead of 1; preview name `extracting-datfrom-R`)
and covers the negative cases so unrelated triggers still stay apart.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(continuous-learning): correct clustering metric name in docstring

The docstring said "Jaccard" while the implementation uses the overlap
coefficient, which is the point of the change.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(continuous-learning): generate every evolve candidate and cut slugs on word boundaries

_generate_evolved() wrote only skill_candidates[:5], workflow_instincts[:5]
and agent_candidates[:3]. On a project with 36 command candidates that meant
5 files and no warning, so the output read as complete while 86% of the
candidates were dropped.

Generation is now unbounded by default and takes a --limit N flag for callers
that want a cap. A cap that truncates says so:

  Note: writing 3 of 36 command candidates (--limit 3); 33 skipped.

The analysis preview keeps showing five per kind but now names the remainder
("... and 31 more command candidates not shown") instead of presenting a
sample as the whole set.

Slugs were also cut with a hard slice, which split words mid-token and
produced /investigating-comple, /learning-about-compl and
/researching-mechanis. _truncate_slug() retreats to the last separator that
fits, and keeps the full head when the cut already lands on one, so
"analyzing large text files" stays /analyzing-large-text rather than losing
a word. A first word longer than the limit still falls back to a hard cut
because no boundary is available.

Shorter slugs collide more easily, and a collision used to mean one file
silently overwriting another. _assign_unique_slugs() suffixes duplicates
(-2, -3) and is called by both the preview and the writer over the same
ordered list, so advertised names and written names cannot drift apart.

Skill directory naming moved to _evolved_skill_name(); it previously used its
own inline slug expression, so it was the one truncation the shared helper
did not cover.

Adds tests/scripts/instinct-cli-evolve-generate.test.js: 7 cases covering
word-boundary cuts, the separator-aligned cut, unbounded generation, --limit
reporting, collision dedup, preview remainder and preview/writer agreement.
Six of the seven fail against the previous implementation.

The auto-update command's inline ECC_ROOT resolver delegates to
resolveEccRoot() with the default probe (scripts/lib/utils.js). A
hooks-runtime-only install copies scripts/lib/ into ~/.claude, so the
partial install satisfies the probe and shadows the full plugin root

root that actually contains the script the command runs. Applied to
the command doc and its ja-JP/zh-CN translations, with regression
tests for both the resolver behavior and the embedded snippets.

fix(mcp): accept reserved _meta field in tools/call params (#2670)

* fix(mcp): accept reserved _meta field in tools/call params

The memory MCP server rejected any tools/call whose params contained a key
other than name/arguments, returning -32602 "Unknown or missing memory tool."

MCP clients (e.g. Claude Code) attach the spec-reserved `_meta` field
(such as progressToken) to request params, so every tool call from a
compliant client failed and the entire memory MCP surface was unreachable —
even though initialize/tools-list and the `ecc memory` CLI kept working.

Per the MCP base protocol, `_meta` is reserved for request metadata and
must be accepted. Add it to the params key allowlist.

fix(hooks): dedupe transcript usage by message.id in cost-tracker (~2.5-3x inflation) (#2483)

Claude Code writes one transcript JSONL line per content block, so a
single API response (one message.id) spans multiple assistant lines that
each repeat the same message.usage. sumUsageFromTranscript summed every
line, inflating token totals and estimated_cost_usd roughly 2.5-3x.

Verified on a real session: 704 assistant lines but only 286 unique
message.ids (2.46 lines/response on average); line-summing reported
$866.52 while the deduped total is $332.62. Usage payloads are identical
across lines of the same id (0/286 varied), so counting once per id is
equivalent to taking the last line per id.

Fix: collect usage into a Map keyed by message.id (last line wins) and
sum unique entries. Lines without a message.id (older transcript shapes)
keep the previous per-line behavior via a synthetic key, so existing
tests and old transcripts are unaffected.

Adds a regression test: a response split into 3 content-block lines with
the same message.id is counted exactly once.

Note: rows already written to ~/.claude/metrics/costs.jsonl by the old
code carry inflated token counts and estimates (except rows whose cost
came from the harness-cost cache, where cost is authoritative but token
counts are still inflated). Downstream consumers may want to annotate
history; this change intentionally does not rewrite the raw log.

compiler cannot build them (Ubuntu 20.04's g++ 9 rejects -std=gnu++20)
failed the whole install and lost the TUI and web UI builds as well, with
"a source update could not be finished automatically" on every launch.

("desktop dependencies failed", the line the hand-off scripts match), and

fix(release): treat any missing stable baseline as no upgrade arm

A release that skipped bundles never writes the stable baseline pointer,
so its absence is normal at any point, not only before the first bundle
release. Drop the final-tag scan. A 404 on the default pointer now always
plans no upgrade arm. A supplied baseline-manifest that does not exist
still blocks, because that is a bad input.

test(install/macos): poll app quit through the run loop

NSRunningApplication.terminated changes only when the run loop runs.
JXA delay() does not run it, so the check stayed false after the app
quit and the leg failed when the setup app had launched Hermes. Spin
the run loop while waiting. The quit stays the normal one.

fix(pm): use the pinned mirror when the upstream host does not resolve

A macOS release leg could not resolve ffmpeg.martin-riedl.de, and PM
stopped there. A name lookup failure is not a retry case, but the R2
mirror is a different host and the pinned SHA256 still checks the bytes.
Let that failure fall through to the mirror.

fix(release): let the first bundle release pass without an upgrade baseline

No stable release has shipped signed packages yet. Every final tag so far
skipped bundles or predates the claim pipeline. So
releases/stable/release-candidates.json does not exist, and the three
"Pin actual OLD and NEW signed packages" jobs refused with "No published
stable package baseline".

transitions now treats a 404 as a first release only when no final stable
tag records a candidate manifest and no baseline-manifest input was given.
It still validates the receipt, emits empty matrices and baseline=none.
The packaged upgrade arms skip on that output. The gate accepts their skip
only when their own planner succeeded with baseline=none, so a missing
baseline after a real bundle release still blocks.

fix(pm): re-seed the uv cache when an update ships a new lock

uv_cache_dir() wrote a bare ".seeded" marker after the first seed and
never compared against the payload again, so an updated install never
received the new payload's wheels. Enabling a plugin re-resolves without
--offline, so uv fetched the new pins from PyPI instead; for
cryptography 50.0.1 on Windows ARM64, which has no wheel on PyPI, that
is an sdist Rust build.

The marker now records the running uv.lock's digest, so the first call
under a new lock merges the new payload into the existing cache.

fix(pm): finish a partial uv cache seed instead of marking it complete

uv_cache_dir() copies a sealed payload's uv-cache into the machine cache and
writes .seeded only after a clean copy. The retry after a failed or killed
copy skipped every top-level entry that already existed, so the copy that had
created archive-v0/ but not finished it was recorded as complete. uv then
fails on the unfinished bucket, e.g. "The wheel is invalid: Missing
.dist-info directory".

The retry now merges into the existing tree (dirs_exist_ok) and copies each
file that is missing or whose size differs from the payload's, leaving
finished files alone.

fix(local-models): recommend nothing when no model reaches the speed floor

When no resident model cleared 20 tok/s, the resolver still recommended the
fastest one (fastest-resident). A "32 GB" machine without a discrete GPU reads
31.5 GB, where only the 27B fits, at a predicted 13 tok/s, so CPU-only and
integrated-GPU machines were steered to a slow dense model. Those machines now
get no recommendation, and every fitting model stays one click away in Browse.
The no-recommendation copy now says the model must run at full speed, the user
guide states the rule, and the unused fastest-resident tooltip string is gone
from every locale.

fix(local-models): size a Windows integrated GPU from what Windows lets it allocate

With no nvidia-smi answer and no discrete engine device, probe_budget budgeted
all of RAM as unified memory. Windows caps an integrated GPU at its GPU memory
(DXGI dedicated plus shared, Task Manager's figure): an Arc B390 on a 31.5 GB
machine gets 18 GB, yet Local Models showed 31.5 GB and priced the 27B as
fitting. The pool is now capped at that figure, read through DXGI for the
adapter the engine named, else the only non-NVIDIA adapter when a Vulkan or HIP
engine will run the model. The CPU engine keeps the RAM budget, whether the
user chose it or it is the only build for the machine (a Snapdragon). The
engine's own number would overshoot: ggml-vulkan sums every heap of an
integrated GPU, host-visible ones included. The DXGI reader is a cached host
fact in hermes_platform. The cap only lowers the pool; CPU-only machines,
other platforms and a failed DXGI read keep the RAM figure.

fix(desktop): offer local setup only for the recommended model

The composer's "This could run on your computer" card took the recommended
catalog row, else the first row marked `fits`. A row fits when any build runs,
including one spilled to system RAM, so a GTX 1080 with 16 GB of RAM was
offered the 27B, which the resolver never recommends there. The card now names
the recommended model, and a machine without one gets no card.

ci(desktop): re-smoke an already-built package without rebuilding it

The native smoke only ran inside desktop-bundled-release, and it checked out
its test scripts at the same commit as the artifact it fetched. Changing a
test therefore meant a new commit, and a new commit meant a full signed
build (about an hour per platform) just to rerun the smoke.

Add workflow_dispatch: `sha` picks the staged artifact to fetch, and the
scripts come from the ref the dispatch runs on. Release callers are

test(desktop): the MSIX plugin smoke runs with a user's environment, not the CI driver's

The smoke's CLI inherited the driver's HERMES_HOME / HERMES_RUNTIME_DIR /
HERMES_PYTHON, so PM built the plugin's environment on the driver's own
Python under C:\a\_temp\setup-pm and never touched the packaged
interpreter: the bug could not show. Clear HERMES_*/UV_*/PYTHON* and the
driver's tool dirs from PATH in the basic-user batch, and fail if the

fix(pm): MSIX plugin installs build on a writable copy of the bundled Python (#135236)

Enabling a plugin with Python dependencies, and `hermes pm install`, failed
in the packaged Windows app: uv lock/sync/pip check exit 101 with "Unable to
create process using ...\venv\Scripts\python.exe".

uv queries a venv by running its Scripts\python.exe. That redirector lives
outside the package and CreateProcess's the interpreter named by
pyvenv.cfg `home`. 6a031bf1b3f moved generations onto the packaged
interpreter, so `home` names a file under WindowsApps that a process without
package identity may not start (exit 101 is the redirector's
RC_CREATE_PROCESS). Restore the verified writable copy of the pinned Python
in the user store as the build interpreter for sealed Windows payloads.

venv_command (also from 6a031bf1b3f) stays: Hermes still enters those venvs
on the packaged interpreter, so its own children keep package access to the
bundled git, rg and PM worker.

test(desktop): the Windows MSIX smoke installs a plugin with Python deps as a basic user

The installed-package smoke only chatted, so nothing exercised PM building
a dependency generation inside the package. After the chat it now installs
a local plugin that declares a Python dependency through the package's CLI
execution alias with --enable --yes-deps and requires `plugins list` to show
it enabled.

It runs under a Safer NORMALUSER token at medium integrity: GitHub runners
are administrators, and Administrators can start files in a package
directory without package identity, which a normal user cannot. A probe
that the token is refused the packaged python.exe keeps the check honest.

fix(tests): the test runner kills detached processes a test leaves behind

`_kill_tree` SIGKILLs the per-file pytest process group, which misses any
child that left the group with `start_new_session=True` (an auto-started
`gateway run`, a setsid server). Those are reparented to init and run
forever: one host accumulated 215 orphan gateways (~52 GB RSS, up to 21 h
old), and every `hermes update` listed each as "another Hermes home — left
alone".

After every attempt the runner now SIGKILLs any process whose environment
still points into that attempt's unique temp root (PYTEST_DEBUG_TEMPROOT /
TMPDIR, or a HOME / HERMES_HOME a fixture created under it). The root is
unique per attempt, so the match names only that attempt's processes.
Linux-only (/proc); the process-group kill stays the fallback elsewhere.

Pull requests and pushes to main no longer run any E2E suite: ci.yaml's detect gate
forces every e2e* lane off unless the run is a stable-release run (inputs.release) or a

live-providers drops its nightly schedule and keeps the release-tag push + dispatch.

Why: a one-row change to left_core_migration.py held a PR for 40 minutes on the

the release gate already runs all of them strictly.

fix(gateway): a service definition is written only by the home it pins

Two homes can resolve to one gateway service name: `<root>/profiles/<name>`
and `~/.hermes/profiles/<name>` both take `hermes-gateway-<name>`
(`ai.hermes.gateway-<name>` on launchd). Every gateway boot, start and
restart calls `refresh_systemd_unit_if_needed` / `refresh_launchd_plist_if_needed`,

therefore repointed the real install's unit at the scratch directory; the
real gateway failed on its next restart (200/CHDIR once the scratch dir was

  refuses a write from any other home; `refuse_foreign_home_install()`
  gates `gateway install` for a home outside the platform-default tree.
- Writers refuse a definition pinned to another home: the systemd and
  launchd refreshes (boot/start/restart) and both installers, `--force`
  included. The system-scope check runs on the caller's own home, before
  `systemd_unit_is_current` adopts the unit's home into os.environ (else
  the check compares the unit with itself); a sudo-stripped caller with no
  HERMES_HOME still acts for the unit's pinned home, as before.
- `gateway install` refuses a HERMES_HOME outside the account's Hermes
  tree that owns no bare service name and has no service installed yet: a
  service registered for a scratch home outlives the run.
- New `gateway install --force-unit-path` overrides both refusals (an
  explicit repoint of the definition at this home).
- Refused installs exit 1, so `gateway install` no longer goes on to start
  the other home's service; the setup wizard reports the refusal and
  continues, as ensure_gateway_service already did.
- Existing tests whose sandbox HERMES_HOME is a tmp dir opt in to the

fix(s6): read the supervised pid from s6-svstat -o, not the status line

Inside the official image, `hermes gateway stop` (and `--all`) never wrote
the planned-stop marker. The gateway classified the s6-svc -d SIGTERM as an
unexpected signal, exited 1, persisted gateway_state=running (so boot
reconciliation restarted it) and left no clean-shutdown marker.

S6ServiceManager._supervised_pid parsed the human s6-svstat line with
`\(pid (\d+)\)`. s6 2.15.0.0 (s6-overlay 3.2.3.0, pinned since the s6
adoption) prints `up (pid N pgid N) Ss`, so the regex never matched and
stop() skipped the marker silently. The unit tests that came with the
marker (5cf6e28a2f) faked a `up (pid N) ...` line real s6 never prints.

Query machine-readable fields instead: a small _svstat_fields helper runs
`s6-svstat -o <fields>`; _supervised_pid reads `-o pid` (-1 when down ->
None, never raises) and is_running reads `-o up` == "true" (replacing an
"up " substring check that only matched by accident). The stop() marker
write is unchanged.

Tests replay real s6 2.15 output in both legacy and -o modes: up/down,
nonzero rc, garbage, short output, missing binary, timeout, marker-write
failure still stopping, and is_running on the down line containing
"normally up".

Adds tests/docker/test_s6_gateway_planned_stop.py: in the real image, bring
gateway-default up, run the gateway stop verb, and assert s6 records exit 0,
gateway_state.json persists stopped, and the log carries the planned-stop
line instead of the unexpected-signal one.
