fix(approvals): treat webhook platforms as notifier-blind in _presence

The TurnRunner lane registers a gateway notify callback for every inbound
turn with no platform branch (run_turn_runner._run_conversation_with_approval),
so on webhook/msgraph_webhook the 'no notifier' discriminator can never fire:
is_ask stays True, the adapter renders no send_exec_approval surface, the
inbound lane is POST -> 202 with no reader, and the turn blocks in
_await_gateway_decision for the full approval timeout before failing closed
— the residual stall of #100532 that the notifier derivation missed.

A registered notifier only means 'someone can answer' on api_server, whose
turn paths choose whether to register one. Add _NOTIFIER_BLIND_APPROVAL_PLATFORMS
({webhook, msgraph_webhook}) and drop is_ask there regardless of registration;
api_server keeps the notifier test. New tests drive the gate with a registered
notifier on both platforms (the suite previously had no
HERMES_SESSION_PLATFORM=webhook case at all).

fix(approvals): resolve an unattended turn from unattended_mode when no notifier is registered

start_gateway() sets HERMES_EXEC_ASK=1 process-wide, so an api_server/webhook
turn inside a gateway still reads as 'ask' in _presence() even though
_is_gateway_approval_context() already excluded the platform. The unattended
branch then never runs: a smart ESCALATE (or any manual-mode dangerous
command) falls through to the interactive transport, and on a session with no
gateway notify callback — non-streaming /v1/chat/completions, webhook,
msgraph_webhook — the card parks as pending_approval that no client can ever
answer, while approvals.unattended_mode is never consulted (#100532).

Drop is_ask for unattended-platform sessions without a registered notify
callback, so the unattended branch resolves instantly from
approvals.unattended_mode before the guardian call runs. /v1/runs and
streaming chat completions register their callback and keep the ask path.

fix(timeout): end an idle demand the transport abandons

An aborted read can stay pending forever: undici drops the error when the
abort lands on an in-flight response-body read (observed on the coverage
lane's Node v24.13.0), and the stalled body of
`llm-retry/tests/transport-recovery.spec.ts` then never settles. The idle
watchdog delegated termination to the iterator observing its signal, so the
request outlived its own deadline and the agent stayed `running` until
Vitest's 90s budget; awaiting the abandoned request generator's `return()`
queued behind that demand and would have re-hung the settled outcome.

`idleWatchdog.next` now races its demand against its own deadline and
rejects with the watchdog's TimeoutReason, so the deadline — not the
transport — decides when an outstanding demand ends. Both adapters that
consume the watchdog stop awaiting the abandoned generator's drain; the
abort they already issue owns socket and SDK teardown.

Evidence: instrumented stress harness at ~1s idle on Node v24.13.0 hung 4/160
iterations before this change (each with the abort delivered at ~1002ms and
the underlying read never settling) and 0/160 after; Node v24.19.0 never
hung. The new case in transport-recovery.spec.ts pins the behavior
deterministically: it fails (times out) with the watchdog change alone and
with no product change at all.

Root build scripts, the desktop bundle and the dev:web watcher pass the

fix(build): reject Node processes without TypeScript type stripping

fix(windows): diagnose and repair ACL failures in one run

The script made the caller choose a mode, so one sandbox failure cost two
approvals: one to diagnose and one to repair. It now has no modes. A single run
adds the signed-in user's full-control allow ACE to the directories on the chain
that lack effective WRITE_DAC or WRITE_OWNER, removes explicit package allow ACEs
at their sources, ancestor first, and verifies every change by re-reading it.

A directory the caller cannot provision also has its subtree checked for explicit
package allow ACEs in that same run: the sandbox reports its provisioning failure
on the workspace root while the conflicting entry often sits deeper, and the walk
is bounded and reports truncation. The authorized root itself may be granted and
restored, so a workspace root can repair and roll itself back.

Recovery artifacts shrink to one record and one script per modified object; the
unused icacls save file and the duplicated command file are gone. The skill, its
README paragraphs and the script tests follow the single command: the former
-Fix, -GrantFullControl and -Compact switches are rejected.

fix(windows): verify ACL repairs against the object's own entries

Comparing whole DACL strings and whole icacls listings reported a successful
package-ACE removal as a collateral change: listing order, inherited entries
and the object's own entries were treated as one value. The package allow
filter also matched the rendered ACE row instead of the ACE's SID, so -Fix
could never verify a removal.

Compare the object's own ACEs and its inheritance protection instead, save and
restore own ACEs only so a parent that changes during the repair cannot make a
correct restore fail, and let -GrantFullControl accept the authorized root
itself so a caller can repair its own workspace root.

perf(javascript): reuse semantic member-mutation lookups (#2941)

The semantic member-mutation collector revisits the same nodes while it closes
alias chains, and each visit re-derived results that cannot change within the
phase:

- resolveSemanticBindingState re-walked the scope chain for the same identifier
  node. Definition collection completes before this phase, and addBinding is
  reachable only from it, so a scope's bindings no longer change.
- directInitializerPosition, directMutationPosition and
  referenceInitializerPosition are pure functions of a node and the analysis
  parent map, but were recomputed for every mutation and initializer.
- markValue re-encoded the same capture tuple with JSON.stringify and built a
  fresh long key for every Set/Map lookup, so each lookup re-hashed the whole
  key. The capture key is now cached per binding, origin and owner, and the
  lifetime key is derived from it.

On pdfjs-dist 5.3.93 wasm/openjpeg_nowasm_fallback.js (462316 bytes, sha256
53c228428a8861035a34738966af263fc9d4cee6df25a0ad942af947469a0bd9) the semantic
phase takes 177.8 s instead of 272.9 s in-process, with a byte-identical
semantic IR. With --max-heap-mb 3072 and the default heap the base revision
exhausts the worker; with the default 300 s per-source deadline raised, the
completed CLI run takes 240.6 s instead of 396.7 s and its output is identical
apart from volatile identifiers.

fix(sqlite): keep triggers whose declaration spells the table in another case (#2807)

* fix(sqlite): keep triggers whose declaration spells the table in another case

SQLite stores a trigger's target in sqlite_schema.tbl_name exactly as
written in CREATE TRIGGER and resolves it by ASCII case folding, while an
index stores the table's own name. The selected_table scope filtered
tbl_name with COLLATE BINARY, so a trigger declared ON users for table
Users was omitted while the schema still reported complete. Match
dependents with COLLATE NOCASE, and report each trigger's table as the
stored table or view name so the selected-table contract still holds.

* fix(sqlite): refuse an inexact table before the case-folded schema scan

With the NOCASE expansion, a selection such as users for table Users
expanded the stored table's declarations before readRows reported the
missing exact name, so large trigger definitions could surface as an
output-limit failure instead of the selection error. Check the exact
table name against PRAGMA table_list first and share the selection
failure with readRows.

* fix(sqlite): fold dependent names only for a row-selectable table

An exact view, virtual or possible shadow table passed the exact-name
guard, so the NOCASE scan could still expand a differently cased trigger
past the reply budget before readRows refused the selection. Fold case
only when the selection is an ordinary table that is not a possible
shadow table, and keep the exact filter otherwise so every refused
selection fails as it did before the case-folding change.

* fix(sqlite): resolve trigger tables without folding unrelated names

The stored-name lookup case-folded every PRAGMA table_list name up front,
so a selected-table inspection of a tiny table paid for large unrelated
identifiers. A selected-table scan only returns the selected table's
dependents, so report the selected name directly; other scopes use an
exact stored name when one matches and fold the stored names once, only
when a trigger spells its target differently.

* perf(sqlite): fold each table name once when matching shadow parents

The extracted shadow-parent helper folded the table name inside the find
callback, once per unresolved virtual table, and the selected table was
checked both before and during the schema scan. Fold the name once per
call as before, and reuse the selected table's result in the scan.

fix(native/windows): share FILE_SHARE_DELETE so owned objects can be marked delete-pending (#2445)

* fix(native/windows): share FILE_SHARE_DELETE so owned objects can be marked delete-pending

The Windows native authority self-test (`binding.call("inspect", [])`) fails
closed on stock Windows x64 with a non-admin user:

    Delete owned object by handle failed (Win32 5): Access is denied.

Reproduced deterministically (15/15 failures) on Windows 11 x64, Node 22.22.2,
non-elevated account. Because `inspect` is a hard gate, every provider-backed
operation is rejected and the whole native authority is unusable.

Root cause: Windows requires that every handle currently open on an object
grants FILE_SHARE_DELETE before that object can be marked delete-pending via
SetFileInformationByHandle(FileDispositionInfo).

`createRelative()` creates the runtime object with FILE_SHARE_READ only, and the
returned handle is retained for the lifetime of the runtime
(`Runtime::directory`). `closeRuntime()` later needs to mark that same object
delete-pending, but the retained handle never shared DELETE, so the transition
is denied (Win32 5).

The child handles opened by `closeRuntime()` for recursive cleanup have the same
defect: they request DELETE access while sharing only FILE_SHARE_READ, so the
subsequent `dispose()` call on those very handles is denied too.

Fix: add FILE_SHARE_DELETE to both share masks, keeping FILE_SHARE_READ and
deliberately not adding FILE_SHARE_WRITE, so the existing write-exclusion
behaviour of the retained leases is preserved while the delete-pending
transition the cleanup path depends on becomes possible.

Verified end-to-end after the change: `inspect` passes, the full runtime

fix(apple): report a recognized connector that cannot name its owner (#2484)

* fix(apple): report a connector that cannot name its owner as an omission

A connector is recognized by class name and then dropped by an early
`continue` when its owner cannot be resolved. Nothing recorded the drop, so
connection coverage derived `complete` with `examined: 0` and `omitted: 0`
for a connector that was present, recognized and discarded.

Both producers of that coverage contract are affected and are changed
together, because they share the facet and the reason value:

- the keyed-archive parser records the drop as `unresolvedConnections` and
  reports it through the `connections:<path>` facet, the document
  `connection_count` and the graph omission total;
- the NIBArchive projection in the artifact adapter recorded nothing at all,
  and the projected dictionary carried no trace of the dropped connector for
  a downstream consumer to find. Its count is taken where the connector is
  discarded and plumbed through the same per-document omission channel that
  already carries incomplete hierarchies, so the reason follows the cause.

An unresolved source cannot be represented as a connection at all, because
connection identity requires a non-empty source; that is unlike an unresolved
destination, which the graph already retains as an unresolved edge.
`connection_limit_reached` stays reserved for connections dropped by the hard
cap and `serialized_view_hierarchy_incomplete` for hierarchy omissions.

`connection_count` also includes the unresolved connectors. That field already
counts connectors the parser recognized but could not emit, because
connections dropped by the hard cap are counted there too, so unresolved
connectors follow the existing rule rather than a new one.

Verified with 98 focused Interface Builder and catalog tests, check:fast and
verify:test-discovery on macOS arm64, and through the public CLI: a rooted
archive holding one ownerless UIRuntimeOutletConnection reported complete with
examined 0 and omitted 0 before this change and reports partial with the reason
connection_unresolved and omitted 1 after it.

The document summary was left unchanged, so the same recognized connector
counted as one in a keyed archive and zero in a NIBArchive. The dictionary
parser only sees connectors that were projected, so the omission recorded
where the connector was dropped is added to the matching document here.

The facet reason was overwritten unconditionally, so a NIBArchive holding both
a connection dropped by the limit and an ownerless connector reported
connection_unresolved and lost the cause a higher limit could recover. The
existing reason is kept when the graph already named one, which is the

feat(ghidra): decode Swift String literals in function dossiers (#2049)

* feat(ghidra): decode Swift String literals in function dossiers

Swift passes a String as two words. Small literals keep their UTF-8 bytes
inside those words, and immortal large literals keep a count plus a pointer
to their bytes biased by 32. Ghidra creates no data reference for either, so
analyze_function reported no strings for Swift code.

On AArch64 programs that contain Swift metadata, the Ghidra bridge now runs
constant propagation over the function and decodes register pairs where
Swift consumes a String: consecutive argument registers at calls and tail
calls, x0 and x1 at returns, and both registers of one STP. Large literals
must resolve to terminated bytes inside one initialized block that is not
executable. A pair whose registers both come from conditional selects is
skipped, because Ghidra forks each select without correlating the
condition and could otherwise pair words from different cases.

Decoded values are a derivation from the ABI layout rather than observed
references, so they appear in a new optional swift_string_literals field
with their source instruction, registers and raw words, and in a matching
inspect_analysis_view facet. referenced_strings is unchanged.

Refs #2030

* fix(ghidra): bound Swift literal reads and compare decoded strings

Large immortal literals are measured against the remaining heap before
allocation, and a failed fit stays visible as a limitation. The canonical
empty string is kept. Small and large literals now require matching
address nullability, and function comparison treats decoded literals as
string evidence without equating a missing record to an empty one.

* fix(ghidra): budget Swift literal decoding and tighten use sites

Large literals now draw on one heap budget per dossier, measured once
before decoding, instead of a separate check per literal. A literal that
does not fit is listed in a new swift_string_literal_omissions field
with its address, byte length and reason, so consumers read omissions
from structured data rather than from limitation text.

strings_names comparison checks referenced strings and names first and
reports a change there even when Swift literal coverage differs; it
returns unknown only when those facts match and literal coverage is
absent on one side or partial.

A computed jump counts as a tail call only when it has no resolved
target inside the function, so jump tables no longer qualify, and a
return requires a RETURN p-code operation, so traps no longer qualify.

Decoded literals keep control characters, which Swift strings may
contain and JSON escapes. The Swift verifier builds the literal fixture
for arm64 on any Mac host and now also covers the empty string and a
literal containing a tab.

* fix(ghidra): charge escaped JSON and follow copied selects

The Swift literal budget now charges the worst case per UTF-8 byte: UTF-16
text, six escaped JSON characters held in Gson's growing buffer and in the
returned String, and the UTF-8 bytes written to the socket. Literals made
of control characters can no longer exceed the reserved heap.

A jump counts as a tail call only when every resolved target lies outside
the function. The conditional select check follows register copies back
to their definition, so selects copied into argument registers are
recognized like selects written there directly.

strings_names reports a change when both dossiers decoded different
literals at the same use site, even when either side has omissions; it
returns unknown only when no such use site disagrees.

* fix(ghidra): bound literal records and trace selects across branches

Every Swift literal record now pays a fixed cost against the dossier
budget in addition to its text, so many empty or small literals are
bounded as well. The first record that does not fit is kept as an
omission and decoding stops there, which keeps the omission record
itself bounded; omissions now describe small or large literals.

The conditional select check searches every predecessor path for the
reaching definitions, following register copies, so selects made
before a branch into the use block are recognized.

A dossier records Swift literals and their omissions together. Coverage
reads omissions first, and strings_names compares every use site that
neither side omitted: a decoded literal is known where it was recorded,
and an absence is known only in a dossier whose decoding examined every
use site.

* fix(ghidra): stop every flow at the literal budget and route omissions

Ending one flow from the evaluator leaves other queued flows running, so
the budget now records a shared stop that every flow checks before it
examines another instruction. A record that exceeds the budget is routed
by that capacity result rather than by whether text was decoded, so a
small literal over budget becomes an omission instead of a literal.

When coverage is partial, the per site comparison keeps each literal's
representation as well as its value, matching the full strings_names
projection.

fix(windows): preserve caller affinity only within one processor group (#2202)

* fix(windows): preserve caller affinity only within one processor group

`spawnProcess` read the caller's affinity mask and applied it to the
suspended child unconditionally. A mask names processors relative to one
processor group, and Windows assigns each new process to a group of its
own choosing, so on hosts with more than 64 logical processors the child
is often placed in another group. `SetProcessAffinityMask` then rejects
the mask with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER (87) and the spawn fails, making
every owned provider process start intermittently on such hosts.

Affinity is a nicety, not an authority or isolation control, so it is now
applied only when the caller and the suspended child both occupy the same
single processor group. A child placed in another group keeps that group's
default affinity and the spawn proceeds. Job Object membership,
kill-on-owner-close policy, owner normalization and priority preservation
are unchanged, and the mask failure remains fatal within a shared group,
where it is not expected.

Single-group hosts, including every host with 64 or fewer logical
processors, are unaffected: `GetProcessGroupAffinity` reports one group
for both processes and the same mask is applied as before.

The optional process-boundary fixture gains an `affinity` observation,
and the native verification lane asserts that an owned spawn succeeds and
that the child's mask matches the caller's whenever both share a single
group.

Fixes #2181

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(windows): refuse to widen a pinned caller's affinity across groups

Addresses review feedback on the first commit.

An unconstrained caller loses nothing when Windows places an owned child
in another processor group, so that spawn proceeds with the group's
default. A caller deliberately pinned to fewer processors than its group
holds is a different case: silently accepting the default would hand the
provider tree the whole group, which `docs/installation.md` tells
operators to rely on affinity to prevent. Such a spawn now fails naming
the constraint instead. `GetProcessAffinityMask` already reports the
group's active set, which distinguishes the two without another query.

Selecting the caller's group at creation through
PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_GROUP_AFFINITY was tried first and rejected:
`CreateProcessW` fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER on a host with a
single processor group, both alongside PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST and
on its own, so it cannot carry the ordinary path.

The boundary fixture's affinity observation now reports a process id's
own mask rather than its own, because a separate probe process is
assigned its own group and cannot stand in for the process that spawns
the child. Masks and the group's active set cross as fixed-width
hexadecimal strings: a mask can set bits above the safe-integer range,
where `JSON.parse` would round two different masks to one value.

The verification lane asserts the mask is inherited exactly when caller
and child share a group, and otherwise that the caller was unconstrained.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* docs(windows): record what owned-process affinity does not preserve

A mask covering its group's whole active set does not distinguish a
caller the system placed in that group from one that selected the group
deliberately, so an owned child can still be placed elsewhere with its
processor count bounded and its group placement lost. Treating that case
as constrained instead is not available: on a multi-group host an
ordinary process is assigned a group by the system and its mask is that
group's active set, so refusing it would fail every owned spawn there.

fix(artifacts): bound archive decompression by source size (#2144)

* fix(artifacts): bound archive decompression by source size

A ZIP/APK/IPA/MSIX member is attacker-controlled and can expand far
beyond the archive that carries it. Inventory hashed every member to EOF
and extraction wrote every member with no ceiling, so a ~2 MiB archive
could drive ~30 s of CPU during inventory and ~150 s plus 2 GiB of disk
writes during extraction.

A fixed per-entry byte cap is the wrong shape: it rejects legitimately
large members inside large packages. The ceiling instead scales with the
archive's own size (500x, with a 256 MiB floor), so large packages keep a
proportionally large budget while a small archive cannot amplify into
unbounded work. The cumulative declared size is charged from the central
directory before any entry is decompressed, and zip.js already verifies
streamed output against each declaration, so the check is exact and
covers both inventory and extraction through the shared reader.

fix(javascript): bound value evaluation through nested closure aliases (#1941)

* fix(javascript): bound value evaluation through nested closure aliases

A closure that aliases a binding from its enclosing scope evaluates that
binding once live and once at its own capture point. The capture cannot
order a binding declared in another function, so it fell back to a second
live evaluation. Only primitive results were kept, so every level of
nesting doubled the work: 20 nested closures over a non-constant value
took about 14 s, and a 443 KB generated wrapper reached the 300 s
analysis timeout.

Keep a live binding value when no caller could change it: no alias cycle
closes on or above the binding and the expression depth budget was not
reached. Bindings on a cycle are still re-evaluated, so their values and
reasons are unchanged.

Found while building a source-owned reproduction for #1847; that report's
worker heap exhaustion is a separate, already closed defect.

* fix(javascript): keep the expression depth budget for retained values

Reusing a retained composite value from any depth let a chain of wrappers
(s1 = {x: s0}, s2 = {x: s1}, ...) nest past the expression depth budget:
300 wrappers produced a 299-level value where the budget stops at 86, the
serialized IR grew quadratically, and 3,000 wrappers overflowed the stack
in JSON.stringify.

Record the expression depth at which each caller-independent value was
derived and reuse it only at that depth or shallower. A deeper reader
derives the value again and reaches the budget exactly as before. Closure
aliases read their outer binding at one depth on both paths, so nested
closures stay linear.

fix(reference): report sloppy scripts, PHP, C# and enclosing Git facts (#1770)

* fix(reference): report sloppy scripts, PHP, C# and enclosing Git facts

Importing the source/ subtree of a legacy PHP and C# checkout produced
four wrong or missing facts:

- Babel's unambiguous mode parses a module first and keeps its
  strict-mode recovery errors after falling back to a script, so a valid
  sloppy-mode `delete messages;` was reported as a parse failure and the
  semantic IR marked the file as parser-recovered. Parsing now goes
  through one owner that re-parses such a script as a script.
- .php and .cs files had no language; they are now detected as PHP and
  C# (detection only, no parsing).
- A root without its own .git was reported as having no version
  control even inside a checkout. The adapter now resolves the nearest
  enclosing repository, as Git does, and reports `none` only when no
  ancestor has one.
- The CLI recorded importer_version as null although the package
  version is known.

* fix(reference): keep module strictness and classify C# and PHP as source

Review follow-up. `.mjs` and `.mts` files are modules by extension, but
the script fallback re-parsed them in sloppy mode and erased real
strict-mode errors. The parser boundary now owns the extension rule,
parses explicit modules as modules and applies the fallback only when
the mode is ambiguous; the require-binding analysis uses the same rule.

`.cs` and `.php` received a language but stayed classified as unknown,
so source-to-bundle comparison dropped them. Both are now source
extensions, like the other detected languages.

* fix(reference): honor package module scope and keep unknown-mode strict errors

Review follow-up. A `.js` file under a package.json with `"type":
"module"` is an ES module, but it went through the script fallback that
erases strict-mode errors. The import now reads each in-inventory
package.json and parses `.js` files in a module scope as modules. Other
`.js` and `.ts` sources keep an unknown mode, because bundlers treat them
as modules without that field: they are no longer forced to script, and
errors that only the module parse reports are kept as an entry limitation.

* fix(reference): bound package scopes and keep application parsing unchanged

Review follow-up.
- `.cjs` files parse as scripts, so module-only strict errors no longer
  become limitations on CommonJS trees. `.cts` keeps an unknown mode
  because TypeScript compiles ES import syntax there.
- An unreadable or linked package.json now bounds the module scope with
  an unknown type instead of letting an outer `"type": "module"` apply.
- The application pipeline parses as on main again. Its module-only
  strict errors keep a source partial; package-mode handling stays in the
  reference importer.

* refactor(reference): keep unmarked module modes unknown instead of resolving package scope

Review follow-up. Resolving Node package scope for `.js` kept pulling in
more of Node's lookup semantics (require bindings, excluded or
directory-named manifests). Only extensions now select a mode: `.mjs`
and `.mts` parse as modules and `.cjs` as scripts. Every other source
keeps an unknown mode, so module-only strict errors stay visible as an
entry limitation instead of being dropped or asserted. This matches the
require-binding analysis, which also treats unmarked paths as unknown.

fix(apple): preflight XML plist nesting before keyed archive decoding (#2161)

* fix(apple): preflight XML plist nesting before keyed archive decoding

inspect_keyed_archive documented a 128-level nesting limit, but the XML
plist path reached recursive decoding before any depth check: plist and
the prototype-key traversal in parseXmlPropertyList recurse once per
nesting level, so a ~75 KiB, 3000-level XML plist exhausted the call
stack and reported Maximum call stack size exceeded instead of the
bounded-resource limit that shallower over-limit documents (129, 200)
already produced. The CLI classified both as truncated, so no crash or
classification bypass was involved; the diagnostic was the defect.

Reject excessive nesting in parseXmlPropertyList before any recursive
pass, using the projection's own limit (MAX_PLIST_DEPTH) so the error is
identical to the one projectPlistValue raises: callers keep the
limit/truncated classification with no error-handler translation. Depth
counts values the way the projection does - container members nest one
level deeper, dictionary keys name members rather than nesting, and a
self-closing element is the value at its own level - so the guard
rejects exactly the documents the projection rejected, at the same
boundary, and every in-limit document decodes unchanged. The guard sits
at the shared decoder boundary, so Interface Builder, app Info.plist
resolution and native inspect_plist gain the same deterministic limit;
the binary plist path keeps its existing expansion preflight.

Binary plist behavior, ordinary XML decode, __proto__ omission counting,
and archive digest/Evidence provenance are unchanged. OpenStep
autodetection is untouched by this guard, as the existing Interface
Builder preflight also scopes its depth check to XML.

Regression coverage: decoder unit tests at and just past the limit for
dictionary and array nesting with self-closing and opaque markup,
module tests through decodeKeyedArchiveBytes including a valid
NSKeyedArchiver XML envelope at the limit, a production-boundary test
through inspectBundleKeyedArchive, and the compiled public CLI
reporting code truncated / reason limit for a 3000-level plist.

Reuse the iterative XML decoder document for depth preflight and prototype-key lookup. Bound recursive plist wrappers alongside dictionaries and arrays without interpreting markup inside attributes or DOCTYPE declarations as values.

hardened ZIP reader and reports build facts as observations:

  the exact input, and a target with no libapp.so reports not-detected
  with complete coverage.

The scanner is streaming with explicit pending-magic and rescan
bookkeeping, so chunk boundaries cannot double-count or drop sections, and
magic-free streams never accumulate. No engine, no external lookups: the
hash-to-SDK mapping stays with external datasets by design.

* fix(flutter): address the Codex review findings

Eight findings, all applied:

- P1: SnapshotHashScanner keeps candidates in a Set (no quadratic
  Array.includes) with a 64-distinct-hash cap, so a hostile payload of
  magic+hash records cannot stall the scan or bloat the response.
- P1: projectStringPool stops admitting new distinct entries once each
  category reaches twice its projection bound and reports
  collectionCapped; allocation and sorting now track the response, not
  the payload.
- P2: ZIP reader rejections during entry iteration or entry streaming
  map into the typed error algebra (cancellation vs input refusal)
  instead of escaping as unhandled exceptions in both operations.
- P2: magic_valid now marks coverage only for the *Data symbols; a
  complete four-symbol image with valid data magics reports complete
  coverage (the instruction symbols intentionally lack the magic).
- P2: the MCP server closes the Flutter provider during shutdown, so a
  retained snapshot root is retried and reported, not leaked.
- P2: LabeledStringScanner commits matches only when a printable run is
  delimiter-terminated; the carry grows to 600 bytes so a 500-character
  toolchain line survives any chunk boundary untruncated.
- P2: both Flutter tool effects declare writesFilesystem: true; the
  owned APK snapshot and extracted libapp.so are temporary writes.
- P2: the verify lane asserts every ABI agrees on exactly one snapshot
  hash instead of discarding the computed set.

* fix(flutter): address the second Codex review round

Nine findings on the first-round fixes:

- P1: identify_flutter_build enforces a cumulative extraction budget
  (768 MiB) across every library entry, not just per library, so an APK
  with many ABIs cannot stream an unbounded total.
- P1: a single NUL-free printable run stops materializing at 1024 bytes
  and marks the pool capped, so an adversarial one-run section cannot
  allocate unbounded strings.
- P1: ELF cString bounds the NUL-terminator scan to the name maximum
  plus one, so malformed symbol tables cannot scan the whole image per
  entry.
- P2: mapReaderFailure distinguishes ArtifactReaderFailure texts —
  budget/limit rejections map to resource constraints, integrity
  failures (CRC/overlap/signature) to their own input refusal — instead
  of collapsing all reader failures into one message.
- P2: the labeled-string carry is cleared when a delimiter commits a
  run, so consecutive toolchain lines are never concatenated.
- P2: string-pool counts are renamed *_count_at_least and documented as
  lower bounds, because capped collection discards values beyond twice
  the projection bound.
- P2: inspect_dart_aot marks hash disagreements, non-pair source counts,
  and candidate-cap saturation as partial coverage.
- P2: only valid lowercase-hex hash records count as snapshot sources;
  complete magic records with non-hex fields do not inflate agreement.
- P2: the per-entry size refusal in inspect_dart_aot moves after ABI
  selection, so an oversized unselected ABI no longer refuses a small
  request.

* fix(flutter): address the third Codex review round

Five findings:

- P2: the owned snapshot revalidates the source after the copy (size,
  mtime, inode), so an in-place replacement or swap mid-copy refuses
  the observation instead of publishing mixed bytes.
- P2: a failed ZipArtifactReader close retains the snapshot root for
  close() retry instead of silently swallowing the descriptor leak,
  in both operations.
- P2: snapshot headers are parsed within their symbol bounds and a
  symbol smaller than the 16-byte header reports magic_valid false,
  so trailing-image bytes can no longer fake a valid data section.
- P2: the verify lane counts provider.close() cleanup failures as
  lane failures instead of certifying a run with retained roots.
- P2: LabeledStringScanner reports toolchain_capped when further
  distinct matching lines are observed past the 4-line projection;
  identify marks such results partial with a naming limitation.

* fix(flutter): address rounds three and four of the Codex review

Round three (one missed finding) plus round four (five findings):

- P2: the GNU build-id note descriptor size is decoded from all four
  bytes of the little-endian field, rejecting nonzero high bytes
  instead of masking them to 16 bits.
- P1: the Flutter MCP handlers route through createContractToolHandler
  and the session's analysisAdmission, so close_binary and snapshot
  operations drain in-flight Flutter calls instead of racing them.
- P2: the owned-snapshot copy is a streamed, abort-checked write (no
  copyFile), so cancellation stops the write promptly while the
  source-identity revalidation (size, mtime, inode) still guards
  against mid-copy replacement.
- P2: identify marks any snapshot_hash_sources value other than exactly
  two as partial, matching the inspection path's pair requirement.
- P2: the verify lane refuses to run without --apk (exit 2) instead of
  printing a false-green pass, and the engine check requires every
  libapp-carrying ABI to have a present libflutter with a valid hex
  build-id rather than filtering missing engines away vacuously.

* fix(flutter): address the fifth Codex review round

Six findings plus the upstream duplication baseline:

- P2: the flutter-provider kind reports available in the capability
  inventory, so binary_session no longer lists always-registered
  Flutter tools as provider_missing.
- P2: printable runs that exceed the 1024-byte cap are discarded at
  their delimiter instead of emitting their truncated prefix as a
  fabricated observation.
- P2: ELF symbols must fit inside the file-backed portion of their
  PT_LOAD segment (p_filesz), so addresses in gaps or BSS are refused
  instead of accepting unrelated bytes.
- P2: the build-id carry spans the complete 80-byte maximum note
  (16-byte header + 64-byte descriptor) so chunk-boundary splits
  cannot drop the first byte.
- P2: the labeled-string carry is sized for the toolchain pattern's
  true 605-byte maximum, not the previous 600.
- P2: the AOT completeness predicate requires exactly two sources and
  one candidate unconditionally, so zero-source images with valid data
  magics report partial instead of complete.

to a dedicated FlutterTestFixtures module, eliminating cross-file test
duplication; jscpd now passes at 2.50% while main sits at 2.52%.

* fix(flutter): address the sixth Codex review round

Five findings:

- P2: snapshot-hash scanning is bounded to the exported data symbols'
  byte ranges, so decoy or stale magic/hash sequences elsewhere in the
  image cannot inflate source counts or contribute candidates.
- P2: labeled-string runs longer than the carry bound are rejected
  instead of truncated, preventing a regex prefix from being published
  as a verbatim source string.
- P2: the AOT image reread checks cancellation between file reads and
  before the synchronous parsing stage, so a cancelled caller cannot
  receive a success from a completed 256 MiB read.
- P2: the verify lane requires exactly two snapshot sources per ABI,
  matching the provider's pair requirement, instead of accepting any
  count >= 2.
- P2: ELF section and program header entry sizes are validated against
  the class-defined minimum widths before walking either table, so
  undersized entries cannot cause field reads to cross into
  neighboring bytes.

* fix(flutter): address the seventh Codex review round

Six findings:

- P2: data-symbol ranges are deduplicated by offset and size, so aliased
  symbols mapping to the same bytes are scanned once and the result
  marks partial coverage with a limitation naming the shared range.
- P2: openEntrySafely forwards return/throw to the underlying Readable's
  iterator, so an early for-await exit closes the ZIP entry stream and
  releases its producer instead of leaking a backpressured pipe.
- P2: inspect_dart_aot now reports snapshot_hash_candidates and
  snapshot_hash_sources alongside snapshot_hash, so a null hash from
  conflicting evidence is distinguishable from missing hash data.
- P2: overlong printable runs only set toolchain_capped when they begin
  with a recognized label prefix (Dart VM version: or Android (); other

  headers are absent (e_shnum 0, ET_DYN), so stripped Flutter libraries
  with exported snapshot symbols are no longer refused; the dynamic
  table is bounded by DT_STRSZ, DT_SYMENT, and the image end.

* fix(flutter): address the eighth Codex review round

Five findings:

- P2: each data-symbol range gets a fresh SnapshotHashScanner so the
  carry from one noncontiguous slice cannot fabricate a record spanning
  into the next; results are aggregated after scanning.
- P2: dynsym name lookups are bounded to the linked string table —
  st_name offsets outside the table and terminators beyond it are
  rejected instead of reading unrelated payload bytes as symbol names,
  in both the section-header and PT_DYNAMIC paths.
- P2: identify_flutter_build routes its reader.entries and reader.open
  calls through the same collectEntriesSafely and openEntrySafely
  wrappers as inspect_dart_aot, so malformed ZIPs surface as input
  refusals instead of AnalysisProtocolError.
- P2: mapReaderFailure recognizes ArtifactReaderFailure texts carrying

* fix(flutter): harden streaming, sizes, and cancellation after self-review

Four issues found in a systematic self-audit across all bug classes
from eight Codex rounds:

- createReadStream in both the digest function and the owned-snapshot
  copy now receives the AbortSignal directly, so cancellation aborts
  the filesystem read at the source instead of waiting for the next
  chunk to arrive on a slow filesystem.
- The owned snapshot enforces a 2 GiB APK-level size cap before any
  copy I/O, so a path pointing at an enormous file is refused before
  disk usage grows.
- identify_flutter_build preflights the sum of declared entry sizes
  against the 768 MiB cumulative budget, refusing before any ZIP
  extraction when the declared total already exceeds it.
- The LabeledStringScanner triple result() call is collapsed to a
  single invocation (the previous code called result() three times in
  the emission, relying on end() being idempotent).

test(ghidra): require pending multi-HI16 coverage in the real MIPS relocatable lane (#1974)

* test(ghidra): require pending multi-HI16 coverage in the real MIPS relocatable lane

Post-merge review on #1950: the relocation oracle exposes coverage.multiple_hi16, but the real-Ghidra lane never required it, and Clang's C output never produces a LO16 that resolves several pending HI16s. Ghidra's loader could therefore mishandle that stream while the lane still passed, although most GCC-built kernel modules checked contain it.

The relocatable fixture adds an assembly block with two lui %hi(rea_mips_rel_carry); LLVM's relocation sort then leaves one HI16 pending until a later LO16 that resolves it together with another HI16, including the carry. The lane now requires multiple_hi16: false on the previous fixture, true for all three variants (LE, BE, soft-float module) on real Ghidra 12.1.4.

* test(ghidra): make the MIPS multi-HI16 fixture independent of relocation sorting

Review on #1974: the block used two %lo of rea_mips_rel_carry, a symbol with other %lo uses, so the relocation stream depended on the assembler's HI16/LO16 sort. Clang 21 happened to leave a HI16 pending; Clang 17 (per review) and GNU as 2.45 (checked here: HI@4 LO@8 HI@0 LO@10) pair each HI16 with its own LO16, so multiple_hi16 stays false and the lane fails.

Use a dedicated symbol with two %hi and exactly one %lo. Any assembler that orders each HI16 before a matching LO16 must then emit both HI16s ahead of that single LO16: Clang 21 gives HI@0 HI@4 LO@8, GNU as 2.45 gives HI@4 HI@0 LO@8. The real-Ghidra lane passes for LE, BE and the soft-float module variant with multiple_hi16 true.

fix(native): accept universal binaries with LIB64 x86_64 slices (#1982)

* fix(native): apply printed lipo capability bits to CPU subtypes

lipo -detailed_info prints a slice's capability byte separately from its
symbolic subtype: CPU_SUBTYPE_LIB64 for x86_64 and ppc64, and other bits
as hex. Only the arm64e pointer-auth form was applied, so a LIB64 x86_64
slice normalized to subtype 3 while its FAT entry carries 0x80000003,
and slice validation rejected the universal binary as an integrity
mismatch. Fold the printed capability byte into the subtype code.

* fix(native): leave lipo CPU subtypes unknown without capability bits

The lipo shipped with macOS 26 prints an empty capabilities line for
x86_64 slices whose FAT capability byte is 0x80 as well as 0x00, so a
symbolic subtype alone does not identify the slice's CPU subtype. The
parser assumed no capability bits and still reported subtype 3 for
LIB64 slices, which made universal applications such as Sublime Text
fail slice validation. Report the subtype code as unknown when lipo
prints no capability byte, as arm64e already does; slice validation
then relies on the remaining physical facts.

* test(native): cover printed and blank lipo capability bits

Fold CPU_SUBTYPE_LIB64 and hex capability bytes into x86_64 subtype
codes, and keep the code unknown for the blank capabilities line that
macOS 26 lipo prints.

* test(native): match a LIB64 x86_64 slice with blank lipo capabilities

Read a universal image whose x86_64 FAT entry carries 0x80000003 while
lipo reports CPU_SUBTYPE_X86_ALL with a blank capabilities line, as
macOS 26 lipo does, and expect both slices instead of an integrity
failure.

* fix(native): compare named lipo subtype bits without capability bytes

A blank capabilities line leaves the subtype code unknown, and slice
matching then skipped the subtype entirely. A FAT entry whose named
subtype differs, such as CPU_SUBTYPE_ARM64_V8 recorded by lipo as
CPU_SUBTYPE_ARM64_ALL, was accepted. Keep comparing the complete
subtype when lipo printed its capability byte, and otherwise compare
the subtype bits its record names.

* test(native): share LIB64 slice reader setup

Read the LIB64 universal fixture through one helper that takes the
x86_64 subtype lipo reports, so further cases reuse the same image and
lipo record. The existing expectation is unchanged.

* test(native): reject a blank-capability lipo subtype naming other bits

With the capabilities line blank, a lipo record naming
CPU_SUBTYPE_X86_64_H for the x86_64 LIB64 slice still disagrees with
the FAT entry's subtype bits and fails slice validation.

owners — remainingInspectionTime, the snapshot default, the containment seed/
compare sites, and the registration inspection seed/compare sites — so the
budget stays bounded while the monotonic inspection timers are in flight.

fix: reuse provider connections across Responses turns (#169802)

## What Problem This Solves

Responses turns close reusable provider connections when the terminal SSE event arrives before HTTP EOF, forcing another TCP/TLS handshake on the next turn.

## User Impact

Finished responses remain immediate while the connection gets a bounded opportunity to return to the provider pool. This avoids repeated connection setup, especially on higher-latency links.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the response body's original reader across terminal delivery. Decoder cancellation only stops decoding; a detached drain discards at most 64 KiB for at most 250 ms, and caller cancellation or Gateway shutdown cancels it. A zero-prefetch forwarding stream keeps ownership on one reader without Node/DOM stream conversion or type assertions. Trailing SSE content never becomes assistant output or tool calls.

The focused command took 73.69 s; file durations were 2.39 s for disposal bounds/cancellation, 5.09 s for five-turn socket reuse, 28.75 s for capture (including its existing production 10-second idle deadline), and 3.74 s for fetch-guard release.

fix(ai): accept canonical OpenAI compaction windows (#169771)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes valid OpenAI `/responses/compact` responses falling back to client compaction when the returned window retains fewer user messages or includes assistant messages.

## User Impact

API-key sessions can save and reuse the provider's returned context window, including retained assistant text, across subsequent requests and Gateway restarts. Existing size, transcript-redaction, route, and next-request-budget checks remain in place. No checkpoint format or schema changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The endpoint client required the output to retain every input user message, while the shared window validator rejected assistant roles and `output_text`. Both restrictions conflict with the [documented canonical window](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/compaction).

A live follow-through also exposed a second failure: retained assistant IDs referred to reasoning items absorbed by the checkpoint. Replaying those IDs produced HTTP 400 (“message was provided without its required reasoning item”). The window reader now omits those IDs from the decoded replay copy, without changing stored JSON, content, order, phase, or the opaque checkpoint. Endpoint errors identify the failed rule instead of blaming every failure on the trailing item.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes.

## Evidence

- Before: the retained production trace had two input user messages and an HTTP 200 output of `[message, compaction]` (451,393 input tokens), but the client rejected it. Three focused regressions fail on the original owners; a fourth fails on dangling assistant IDs after accepting the window.
- After: 51 focused endpoint, replay, and session-owner tests pass. Coverage includes fewer retained users, assistant `output_text`, reload/replay, no trailing checkpoint, empty encrypted content, duplicate checkpoints, bounded JSON, redaction, and next-request budget rejection.
- Core and selected package-test TypeScript checks, scoped type-aware lint, formatting, and the build pass.
- Live API-key proof used isolated Gateway state and small sessions. Secrets were read through a 0600 file in a 0700 directory and deleted; all proof Gateways were stopped.

| Live preflight case | Context before compaction | Returned items | Next request | Recall | Restart |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| GPT-5.4 mini | 43,856 tokens | 6 retained messages + checkpoint | 23,659 tokens | 3/3 | Pass |
| Second OpenAI API-key model | 43,204 tokens | 2 retained users + checkpoint initially | 23,738 tokens | 3/3 | Pass |

The same small, text-heavy mini scenario also proves the assistant-ID repair independently: before the replay repair, a second compaction returned HTTP 400; afterward, the second compaction returns HTTP 200 (38,233 input tokens), and a normal request accepts the retained assistant window (48,197 input tokens). Its restart recall is also 3/3. The text-heavy window does not shrink enough for a tiny context budget; the preflight cases above use ordinary read-tool results as the reducible history rather than claiming that acceptance guarantees a smaller window.

Total observed proof usage, including failed/setup attempts: 1,096,906 input tokens and 7,756 output tokens (below the 2M input-token cap).

Revert is a two-way door: it restores the old rejection behavior without a data migration. Blast radius is the explicit OpenAI compact-window validator/replay path; native xAI retained-prefix restrictions are unchanged.

perf(sessions): reuse transcript admission and projection facts (#169523)

## What Problem This Solves

Transcript context, search, and rebuild paths repeat reads of facts already owned by the Gateway. The bundled memory visibility loader also enters the synchronous session-store path.

## User Impact

No configuration or storage-format change. Bundled memory visibility loads the complete cross-session view through the existing worker. The public synchronous loader remains compatible, emits a bounded deprecation warning, and is scheduled for removal in the next SDK major; its replacement is `loadCombinedSessionStoreForGatewayAsync`.

## Design

Use committed admission receipts for transcript bounds, return the completed search snapshot with projection readiness, and stop recounting/rechecking acknowledged rebuild work. Final publication retains source validation and bounded append catch-up. SQL projections that avoid materializing large payloads remain in SQL.

Removed checks and accepted edges:

- Admission identity/role/generation reread: direct SQLite edits outside the Gateway owner are unsupported; the admission receipt supplies committed bounds. Store/session/user-role validation and effect-boundary authority remain.
- Search connection revision reread: an append racing a completed search appears on the next search.
- Rebuild claim source/clean-index rereads: stale prepared work can temporarily dirty a derived index before final publication rejects it.
- Rebuild chunk recount/classification reread: acknowledged chunks are authoritative; final source validation remains.

Native-incognito paths remain for the separate incognito-removal migration. Deprecated public synchronous contracts and explicit offline maintenance remain honestly classified. Follow-up target/caller cutovers are being shipped separately; this PR does not claim the entire lane is at zero.

## What Problem This Solves

Ordinary session writes invalidated the target-inventory memo even for per-agent stores, whose topology depends on paths and registered database ownership. A warmed turn repeatedly sent discovery and reader-cleanup requests that executed no SQL.

## Design and Impact

Keep the existing Gateway-owned inventory memo across row writes only for per-agent stores. Every fixed-store selection retains row-write invalidation because its visibility can depend on session rows. Registry receipts, configuration keys and physical file identity still invalidate reusable topology. No new cache, worker command, schema, SDK or update behavior is introduced.

Removed check and accepted edge case: an ordinary per-agent activity write no longer invalidates topology; that write cannot introduce a store owner. Registry/configuration changes and physical replacement remain covered by their existing invalidation. Current authorization at real effects is unchanged.

Shared SQL harness, alternating M1/C1/M2/C2, base `c832c45aff53c2cb060ca10b0c3ab6668cd1b4e1` and final candidate `e4b4c650a59d5eb080d68c7b5058e8f744e450be`. All four isolated fixtures completed the 13 turns, child session, cron, compaction and shutdown with exact statement/request census reconciliation. Under RELAXED TESTING v6 one pair was required; the second pair resolved timing ambiguity. Both sides used the same supported 120-second handshake timeout after an initial baseline failed before its first turn. The original harness was not edited.

Values are median [min–max] across the two runs. Each warmed measurement is the total over ten warmed turns divided by ten.

Context candidates are recorded before returning; workspace-dependent maintenance still follows acceptance. The old conflict suffix and assistant delta are removed.

fix(agents): prevent next-turn failures after native compaction (#169583)

Related: #168164

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes the next user turn failing with `Session transcript projection is rebuilding` after provider-native compaction and foreground preemption of session maintenance.

## User Impact

The next embedded turn waits for the session's pending transcript projection before reading its saved history. Cancellation remains respected, and detached in-memory transcripts do not wait on unrelated durable state. No configuration, schema, or persisted-format changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

The session lane already waits for deferred maintenance, but that work can settle before its independently scheduled transcript projection does. Bounded history hydration then fails closed instead of serving the next turn. Join the existing projection owner at the same pre-global-lane checkpoint; do not retry inference or weaken the history guard.

The fail-closed projection guard dates to `7d71d7cf6b3` (#108851), later extracted by `5621979a469`; the missing foreground barrier predates the native-default change. #168164 (`77e2261b573a`) made the API-key compaction path part of the default behavior. This patch does not change the provider's compaction policy.

The accompanying request-shape investigation found **no covered-history replay bug** in the reported token growth. Original captures show zero input items before each replayed checkpoint. The mini-model requests had 6, 9, and 8 input items: one checkpoint followed by 5, 8, and 7 later items, respectively. Instructions and tools are still sent, and the model produced new reasoning/tool calls after the inline checkpoint. The docs now explain why token totals alone cannot establish replay duplication.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes.

## Evidence

### Before

Captured on `16d913005f9`, public OpenAI Responses API, API-key authentication, `gpt-5.4-mini`, 50,000-token local context and 22,000-token inline threshold. Two synthetic file reads followed immediately by recall:

```text
2026-10-12T08:59:10.261+05:30 [agent/embedded] context-engine compaction failed errorMessage="Session maintenance yielded to a foreground turn"
2026-10-12T08:59:16.125+05:30 [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=main durationMs=98 error="Session transcript projection is rebuilding: f126b9b2-109e-4efc-8ff5-d3e1f471ff8c" errorName=SessionTranscriptProjectionUnavailableError taskKind=turn sessionKey=agent:main:v2b-b-gpt-5.4-mini-1791775686 runId=511762d8-1d3f-4bf4-8ac3-4c740679cc52
```

Recall CLI exited 1 before inference. Inline-request input grew through 23,318 / 25,799 / 40,603 / 52,261 tokens; explicit compaction consumed 55,953 input tokens.

### After

One new isolated live campaign with the same API-key model, limits and synthetic two-file/recall flow reproduced the maintenance-preemption condition, but recall completed:

```text
2026-10-12T09:16:43.495+05:30 [agent/embedded] context-engine compaction failed errorMessage="Session maintenance yielded to a foreground turn"
2026-10-12T09:16:49.874+05:30 Vault code 7291-HERON, courier Isadora, city Hobart.
2026-10-12T09:16:49.876+05:30 [agents/agent-command] [agent] run 53ceae27-6416-4eb2-a68f-c90bd3942337 ended with stopReason=stop
```

Both CLI turns exited 0; recall preserved all 3 planted facts. Explicit compaction consumed 55,074 input tokens; the next user request consumed 18,422 and contained exactly `[compaction, message:user, message:developer]`, with no pre-checkpoint items. The isolated Gateway was stopped and its 0600 credential file deleted.

### Regression and checks

- New regression fails before the patch with `SessionTranscriptProjectionUnavailableError: Session transcript projection is rebuilding: foreground-projection`; it passes after the patch using a real SQLite projection rebuild and bounded hydration.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run-orchestrator.projection.test.ts`: 8 passed. Test execution 27.67 s; wrapper wall time 47.59 s. The added case took 3.633 s in that run.
- `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:test:src`: passed.
- Repository `oxfmt`, focused `oxlint`, and `git diff --check`: passed.
- One `pnpm build` with the runtime-only declaration-skip flag and shared build cache: exited 0. It reported the existing advisory Control UI chat-boot request count (38 vs 35); this patch does not change UI code.

**Merge risk:** two-way door; reverting restores the previous timing behavior. The blast radius is embedded durable-session startup while a transcript projection rebuild is pending. No schema or storage-format changes, no provider request changes, and no ChatGPT V2 changes.

fix: show provider request time for model connection checks (#169554)

Closes #169066

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes slow, misleading **Test connection** results that count model/credential preparation and internal agent-session work as provider latency.

## User Impact

Connection checks make a fresh request without creating an agent session. Each credential shows a labeled **Request round-trip**; the ambiguous aggregate header timing is gone. Empty or thinking-only responses fail the format check, timeouts remain timeouts, and provider diagnostics remain useful and secret-redacted.

## Why This Change Was Made

The original probe in [40181af](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/40181af) exercised a real provider request through an embedded agent. [#117494](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/117494) added the structured internal session required by that runtime. Connectivity checks can now use the existing isolated-completion owner instead of paying for that agent-session lifecycle.

The deliberately isolated, read-only direct-credential generation from [#125816](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/125816) stays intact. Every credential still uses raw OpenClaw transport, preserving [#121500](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/121500). OAuth refresh remains with its normal persistent owner, including the historical-peer fencing and settlement from [#168957](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/168957); no new cooldown/quota writes are introduced. Known configured models no longer trigger unnecessary catalog preparation.

Checked Sarah's [#159246](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/159246): its Agents API restricted-session contract and runtime defaults are unchanged. No overlap with Pash's changes.

## Evidence

- Command/target/resource regressions: **38 passed**. Includes direct and stored credentials, immutable API-key auth state, expired OAuth refreshing once into the real shared store with owner/peer fences and peer settlement, and valid OAuth causing no credential/state write.
- Isolated-completion suite: **50 passed**; Gateway probe suite: **13 passed**.
- Models view: **38 passed**; i18n verification passed; Models browser E2E: **7 passed**.
- Discriminating negative control: removing the output/timeout/diagnostic fixes makes empty and thinking-only responses incorrectly report `ok`, aborted timeout output report `unknown`, and provider-detail assertions fail.
- Mock-export gate passes after six justified isolation annotations and removal of six retired baseline entries.

### Paired timing comparison

Real Gateway and Control UI button clicks against the same synthetic HTTP provider with a 250 ms response delay. Baseline `cbba7e2e2ef` versus candidate `994f04547a9`; five alternating measured samples per row, excluding one warmup per lane. These are local stub measurements, not live-provider speed claims.

| Scenario | Median full probe RPC, before → after | Median displayed credential duration, before → request-only after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Successful response | 2,103 → 738 ms | 1,532 → 256 ms |
| HTTP 401 | 1,073 → 389 ms | 929 → 256 ms |

The stub's median HTTP duration was 251–253 ms. Each success made one HTTP request; the old 401 path made two, while the new isolated check made one. Full probe time still includes setup; it is not shown as provider request time.

feat(agents): compact ChatGPT sign-in sessions server-side (remote compaction V2) (#168401)

Closes #168088. Related: #168164.

## What Problem This Solves

With ChatGPT sign-in, every automatic compaction in OpenClaw ran a client-side summary: separate summarization requests with 0 cached tokens, and a lossy text summary in place of the conversation. Codex compacts the same route server-side ("remote compaction V2"): the next normal model request carries a trailing `{"type":"compaction_trigger"}` item, and the provider returns one opaque `compaction` item that stands in for the history.

## Fix

- **Request:** automatic compaction on the ChatGPT route (preflight before a turn, and mid-turn between tool rounds) sends V2 as the next normal request, through the same attempt pipeline and native ChatGPT stream, with `compaction_trigger` appended last. Tools, instructions, parameters, cache key and the full input prefix are the turn's own, so the compaction request reads the warm prompt cache.
- **Result:** exactly one non-empty `compaction` item is accepted, only after a successful terminal response and never after an abort. Collection resets for each provider attempt.
- **Checkpoint:** real user messages are retained newest-first within 64k tokens, plus the item, matching Codex `compact_remote_v2.rs`. Users retained from an earlier window stay eligible, so repeated compactions keep them.
- **Fallback:** every fallback to client compaction logs a WARN with its reason. Overflow recovery, `/compact <focus>` and manual `/compact` stay client-side; manual V2 needs session-writer ownership work and is a follow-up.
- **Fixed during live testing** (each with a regression that fails on the defect):
  1. V2 never ran: the compact request was checked before the async provider adapter dispatched it.
  2. V2 ran only in the managed client; real ChatGPT turns use the native stream. V2 now runs there.
  3. Replay normalization dropped the checkpoint turn as an empty failed turn, so the next request grew back to full history. It now keeps successful compaction checkpoints; error turns and suppression markers are still dropped.

## User Impact

ChatGPT sign-in sessions compact server-side with no extra summarization requests. Compaction reads 87–100% of its input from cache, and later turns stay at about 14–22k input tokens instead of about 91k. `params.responsesCompactEndpoint: false` turns it off.

## Evidence

Live, real ChatGPT OAuth login, `openai/gpt-6-astra`, isolated Gateway, synthetic corpus, three facts seeded before compaction. The host was loaded, so wall times are upper bounds.

| Compaction | Compaction input / cached / output | Wall | Input before → after | Next user turn input / cached | Recall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Preflight | 90,999 / 73,856 / 885 | 20.2 s | 90,999 → 22,308 | 22,439 / 22,144 | 3/3 |
| Mid-turn, first | 91,075 / 82,560 / 575 | 12.3 s | 91,075 → 13,904 | 14,121 / 12,928 | 3/3 |
| Mid-turn, second | 76,486 / 58,880 / 716 | 17.4 s | 76,486 → 14,476 | 14,709 / 14,336 | 3/3 |

Request parity, compaction request vs the preceding normal turn:

| Compaction | Tools | Instruction chars | Input prefix | Cached vs previous input |
|---|---|---|---|---:|
| Preflight | 6 → 6 | 35,857 → 35,857 | 26/26 items identical | 89.3% |
| Mid-turn, first | 6 → 6 | 35,855 → 35,855 | 26/26 items identical | 99.8% |
| Mid-turn, second | 6 → 6 | 35,855 → 35,855 | 39/39 items identical | 86.7% |

The tool schemas, instructions, parameters and cache-key hashes were identical in all three. The final head sent exactly 3 `compaction_trigger` requests, all HTTP 200, and no client-summary requests.

**Client comparison (same route, before this change):** one client compaction of a 117.9k-token session took two summary calls (9,777 input, 0 cached, 961 output, 24.4 s). The next turn read 33,967 input with 12,800 cached. Trigger points were not matched to the V2 runs, so this is a reference, not a head-to-head benchmark.

**Tests:** fetch-boundary regressions across the managed and native ChatGPT streams cover:
- request parity;
- failed, cancelled and incomplete terminal responses;
- aborts;
- duplicate or empty items;
- multilingual retention;
- two consecutive persisted compactions;
- the async-dispatch case and replay normalization through the real `SessionManager`.

Negative controls fail on each defect. tsgo core/src/packages pass; `check-changed` passes.


## Release-landing follow-ups (2026.10.2)

- **ClawSweeper P2 fix (budget anchor), commit e9021240:** V2 used to price the outgoing request with the conservative preflight estimator. That estimator counts unchanged instructions twice, because measured usage already includes them. The V2 boundary now uses the same accounting as the mid-turn precheck it replaces:
  - The shared code is `resolveProjectedRequestPressure`, split out of `checkMidTurnPrecheck`.
  - The stream guard's request observation now returns the matching measured predecessor. The foreground request is observed before V2 decides, so both price the same anchor. A checkpoint request is then observed again as its own request.
  - Requests with no anchor keep the conservative estimate.

fix(ui): new session shows "runner isn't ready" while the page loads (#169402)

Related: #158903

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: the new-session page replaces its place controls with "The selected runner isn't ready yet. Try again in a moment." on every page load and reconnect, even when no worker is configured and the session will run locally.

## User Impact

User impact: the new-session composer shows its normal controls at once. The runner text appears only when the Gateway requires a worker profile. No configuration, protocol or schema change.

## Why This Change Was Made

The page asked the Gateway for the session placement policy with its own `agents.list` call, and blocked the controls and Send until the reply arrived. It repeated that call on every load, reconnect and node topology event.

The app already loads the agent roster once per connection, and the page already needs it. The roster request now sets the existing `includeSessionPlacement` flag, and the page reads the policy from the roster. The page's own request, its ready flag and its reset points are removed.

Behavior that stays the same:

- A Gateway with `cloudWorkers.requiredProfile` still shows the required-worker indicator and still waits for that profile before Send.
- Send stays blocked until the roster has loaded, with the existing "Refreshing agent defaults…" reason.
- Starting a required session still revalidates the policy with a fresh read.

One visible difference on a required-worker Gateway: during a cold page load, the normal place controls show until the roster reply arrives, then the required-worker indicator replaces them. Send is blocked during that time.

## Evidence

Same mocked Gateway in both captures: the reply that carries the placement policy is held.

Before (`main` at 9a733c62d8e):

![Before: runner text replaces the place controls](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1ac96ff5-8ba6-4a07-b5df-bccede1931df)

After (this branch):

![After: normal place controls while the reply is held](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/851ccc58-80f4-431f-8cd2-38be66cc7e29)

Checks run locally on the branch head:

- UI unit tests for `ui/src/pages/new-session`, `ui/src/components`, `ui/src/lib/agents`, `ui/src/lib/sessions` and `ui/src/pages/chat`: 13,358 passed.
- Control UI e2e, all new-session, placement, worker-inference and command-palette files (61 files): 322 passed.
- `check:changed`: types, lint, i18n and ratchets pass.

Gaps:

- The `check:changed` dead-export scan fails locally on files this PR does not touch (for example `src/agents/context.ts`, `ui/src/pages/systems/systems-page.tsx`). I did not check whether `main` has the same result.
- No run against a real Gateway with `cloudWorkers.requiredProfile` set. The required-worker path is covered by the mocked unit and e2e tests only.
- Three unit tests of stale-reply fencing in `required-placement.test.ts` are removed. That guard now belongs to the agent roster store, which has its own tests (`ui/src/lib/agents/index.test.ts`).

## Merge Danger

Two-way door: a revert restores the previous behavior fully. It writes no state and changes no published contract.

Blast radius: the new-session page and the command palette's new-session draft. If it is wrong, a Gateway with a required worker profile could show local place controls or the wrong Send state; the Gateway still enforces the required worker when the session starts.

fix(anthropic): guide Claude CLI to registered OpenClaw tools (#153032)

* fix(anthropic): name bundled OpenClaw tools the way Claude Code registers them

Claude Code registers every bundled OpenClaw tool through the `openclaw` MCP
server as `mcp__openclaw__<name>` and, once the MCP catalog is large, defers
those tools behind ToolSearch. The shared system prompt and the stranded-reply
retry prompt refer to the delivery tool by its short OpenClaw id
(`message(action=send)`), so a fresh Claude session calls a tool literally
named `message`, gets `No such tool available: message`, searches
`select:message`, finds nothing, and the reply strands. In a
`visibleReplies: "message_tool"` group the user then only sees
"I generated a reply but could not deliver it to this chat. Please try again."

Observed on one claude-cli gateway over nine days: 22 of 116 Claude sessions
began with that bare `message` call; the sessions that never guessed the
prefixed name produced every stranded-reply diagnostic in that period. A
keyword ToolSearch ("send message to telegram conversation channel") returned
`SendMessage`, `PushNotification` and unrelated MCP tools but never
`mcp__openclaw__message`; only an exact `select:mcp__openclaw__message` did.

- Add a backend-owned `transformSystemPrompt` for `claude-cli` that appends an
  "OpenClaw tool names in Claude Code" section after the cache-stable prefix:
  short names map 1:1 onto `mcp__openclaw__<name>`, a missing tool is loaded
  with `select:mcp__openclaw__<name>`, and native `SendMessage` /
  `PushNotification` are not OpenClaw delivery.
- Mention the MCP registration in the stranded-reply retry prompt, which is
  the exact prompt after which the model was observed searching
  `select:message`.
- Share the `mcp__openclaw__` prefix from `cli-constants.ts`.
- Document the overlay in the CLI backends and groups guides.

Related: openclaw/openclaw#147006 (zero `mcp__openclaw__*` tools seen by a
Claude CLI request, same `No such tool available: message` trace) and
openclaw/openclaw#139599 (message_tool_only replies dropped when the model
skips the message tool).

fix(sessions): keep transcript backlog traversal moving when the writer revision is unknown (#169467)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: after auto-compaction, a run can wait forever for its session's transcript projection to rebuild. The rebuild never comes, so the run never starts its retry. Every later message for that session queues behind the hung run and is never answered or saved. Nothing is logged.

Observed on a long-running Gateway (about 2,480 sessions in one agent database): a Telegram topic compacted mid-turn, then silently dropped the next two messages. 45 minutes later `sessions.describe` still reported `hasActiveRun: true`, and `needs_rebuild = 1` was set on that session only.

## Root Cause

`maintainSessionTranscriptIndexStatus` stores the sibling write revision in its TEMP cursor, with `-1` for "unknown". On entry it reset the whole traversal (cursor, pending inventory) whenever the stored value was `-1`. While the revision stays unknown, every call therefore stores `-1` again and the next call resets again. Each call scans the same first 128 sessions, the traversal never reaches its end, and `readTranscriptIndexBacklog` loops without bound. The reconcile stays registered, so `waitForPreparedSessionTranscriptProjection` keeps polling for a session past the first batch.

A `diagnostics.cpuProfile` of the affected Gateway showed exactly that: the hung run in `waitForPreparedSessionTranscriptProjection`'s poll, and the reconcile owner repeatedly running `drainTranscriptIndexStatus` → status `preflight` publications. The stuck session sorted at position 605 of 2,482.

## Why This Change Was Made

An unknown sibling revision only means the clean receipt cannot be trusted. `isSessionTranscriptIndexStatusClean` already refuses an unknown revision, and the end-of-traversal check already restarts the cursor when the stored revision differs from the current one. The entry reset on `-1` adds nothing except the livelock, so it is removed. A schema change still resets the cursor and pending inventory.

With the revision unknown, a traversal now reaches its end; `drainTranscriptIndexStatus` sees `completedTraversals` advance and ends the pass with the late dirty session in `sessionIds`.

The deployed build where this happened produced the unknown revision through the writer census that #168859 removed. Current `main` can still return an unknown revision (closed or suspended database, or a file database with no admission record), so the reset path is still reachable.

## User Impact

User impact: a session past the first 128 in its agent database no longer hangs after compaction while the writer revision is unknown, and follow-up messages for it are no longer held behind that run.

## Evidence

- New regression in `session-transcript-index-status.test.ts`: 300 sessions, the last one dirty, sibling revision reported as unknown. It fails on `main` ("Backlog traversal never reached the late dirty session") and passes with this change.
- `src/config/sessions/session-transcript-{reconcile,index,projection}*.test.ts`: 17 files, 262 tests pass.
- `check:changed`: all lanes pass except "typecheck core tests", which fails only in the `ui` shard on `main`'s current MCP App test-type errors (fix in #169439); the `src` test shard is clean.

Not covered:

- No end-to-end reproduction through a real Gateway; the test reports the revision as unknown through a module mock, because current `main` has no natural way to hold it unknown in a unit test.
