* fix(ghidra): model soft-float MIPS as a prototype for every typed callable

Review feedback on #1949: rewriting storage per Function left external
functions and indirect calls through typed function pointers on Ghidra's
hard-float o32 prototype, which still read $f12/$f14/$f0 while the session
reported success. A negative control confirms it: without the change,
`(*rea_mips_soft_callback)(8.5f, 9.5f, sel)` decompiles to
`(*rea_mips_soft_callback)(in_f12, in_f14, sel)`.

ReaGhidraMipsSoftFloat.java now derives a `__rea_soft_float` prototype from
the program's own default o32 model (encoded, float pentries and
float-consuming rules removed, so byte-order-specific aggregate rules and the
hidden struct-return pointer are kept), installs it as a specification
extension, and assigns it with dynamic storage to every non-thunk function,
external function and function-pointer definition whose formal types use
float or double. Thunks follow their targets. Float types are kept
everywhere, so the integer-retype fallback is removed. The script fails
without writing its report if the derived prototype or any reassigned
function still uses an FPU register.

The policy becomes `o32-soft-float-prototype-v1` with a

fix(install): describe automatic setup and guard truncated downloads (#1902)

* fix(install): describe automatic setup and guard truncated downloads

The help text said the installer only installs the CLI and that
`rea setup` must be run separately, but the installer starts
`rea setup` interactively whenever a terminal is available. Describe
that behaviour and the --no-setup/--no-prompt opt-out.

Wrap the installer body in `main` and call it on the last line, so a
truncated `curl | bash` download fails to parse instead of executing a
partial script. Behaviour is otherwise unchanged.

Add an installer scenario that runs a copy truncated right after the
npm install line and requires that it prints nothing and never invokes
npm; it fails against the previous script.

Validation: bash -n, shellcheck 0.10.0, installScript boundary tests.

* fix(install): require the closing token before running main

Wrapping the installer in main() kept a truncated download from running
a partial body, but the last line was a bare `main "$@"`. If the piped
download stopped right after `main` (or `main `), bash saw a complete
command at EOF and ran main with no positional parameters. Under the
documented `curl ... | bash -s -- --dry-run` (or --version / --no-setup)
path that silently dropped the caller's flags, so a dry run could resolve
the latest release, run npm, and start setup.

The call now sits in a brace group:

  {
    main "$@"
    exit $?
  }

Bash does not run the group until it has read the closing brace, so
every truncation inside it is a syntax error and nothing executes; a
truncation before the group leaves only function definitions. A comment
in install.sh records why the bare call is not enough.

Validation: a new boundary test pipes install.sh to `bash -s --
--dry-run` truncated at every byte offset from the end of main() to EOF
and asserts that npm and the rea binary are never invoked; offsets
inside the group must exit non-zero with a bash parse error and no
stdout, offsets before it must print nothing, and the complete group
must finish the dry run. Reproduced the original bug by cutting the old
script after `main`: the dry run invoked npm install. `bash -n` and
shellcheck 0.11.0 are clean.

* fix(install): wrap the whole script in the truncation guard

The previous guard only wrapped the final `main "$@"` invocation, so the
preamble streamed on the `curl ... | bash` path before any incomplete
compound command was open. A download cut off right after the bytes
`set` reached EOF with a complete, argument-less `set`, which prints every
shell variable, so inherited tokens could reach stdout.

The brace group now opens on line 2, directly after the shebang, and
closes on the last line, enclosing `set -euo pipefail`, the constants, the
functions and the final `main "$@"` / `exit $?`. Bash must therefore read
the whole file before running anything; any earlier cut is a syntax error
at EOF. `set -euo pipefail` still applies inside the group (checked
manually for `false`, an unbound variable, and a failing function body),
and shellcheck 0.11.0 and `bash -n` are clean.

The truncation test now pipes every prefix of install.sh, from byte 0 to
EOF (about 6,100 cuts, run 16 at a time with a minimal environment that
includes a sentinel variable), into `bash -s -- --dry-run`. Before the
group opens it must exit quietly; inside the group it must fail with a
syntax error; in every case stdout stays empty and neither npm nor rea is
invoked. Only the complete script performs the dry run.

fix(apple): bound binary plist expansion before decoding keyed archives (#1515)

plist.parseBinary, which recurses on every object reference and copies
shared containers. A 484-byte archive of forty nested [next, next] arrays
grew the process past 4 GB until it died with no result, which would also

and was reported as an artifact too large to process.

now runs first, with an 8x keyed-archive decode budget. Over-budget depth
or expansion is a limit; a reference cycle is a malformed archive. Its

accepted archives stay accepted. Interface Builder behavior is unchanged.

chore(ci): run Barnacle auto-response in the shared ClawSweeper listener (#169355)

## What Problem This Solves

Every issue and pull request event in this repository starts separate Actions runs for `ClawSweeper Dispatch` and `Auto response`, even when both jobs skip. ClawSweeper's own comments and labels are ordinary events, so on 2026-10-11 `Auto response` alone started 19,837 runs in 24 hours; about 70% of them were triggered by `clawsweeper[bot]` and ended `skipped`.

## User Impact

No user-visible change. Barnacle replies, labels and moderation behave as before. The repository creates roughly 20,000 fewer Actions runs per day, which also frees hosted-runner queue slots and API quota.

## Why This Change Was Made

GitHub creates one run per subscribing workflow before it evaluates job `if:` conditions, and it has no actor filter at trigger level. `ClawSweeper Dispatch` already subscribes to every event `Auto response` handles, so the Barnacle job now lives in that file as a second job:

- It keeps its exact original event set (issue opened/edited/labeled, comment created, PR opened/edited/synchronize/reopened/labeled/unlabeled) through an explicit admission clause, so it never runs on push, review, reopen/unlabel of issues or `ready_for_review`.
- It keeps its author-association, bot-comment, empty-edit and ClawSweeper-label exclusions, credentials, trusted base checkout and its own per-item concurrency group. Job-level concurrency means a superseded dispatch cannot cancel it, and the reverse.
- The check name stays `auto-response`, so `watch-pr-ci` still excludes it.
- The listener file keeps its path because ClawSweeper's direct queue intake verifies the OIDC `workflow_ref` of `.github/workflows/clawsweeper-dispatch.yml`.

`Security Review` also listens to comment events, but folding it in would change its publisher run identity, which `scripts/pr-lib/merge-prior-ci-security.mjs` verifies, and it is owned by secops. It is left unchanged here.

## Evidence

- Run counts before the change, 24 h ending 2026-10-11 18:00 UTC: `ClawSweeper Dispatch` 30,723, `Auto response` 19,837. Every `Auto response` event type is a subset of the dispatch triggers, so the expected saving is the full `Auto response` volume.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/ancillary-workflow-concurrency.test.ts test/scripts/clawsweeper-dispatch.test.ts test/scripts/ci-workflow-guards.test.ts test/scripts/watch-pr-ci.test.ts`: 4 files, 452 passed. The existing Barnacle admission cases now run against the shared listener, and a new case proves the job stays off push, `ready_for_review` and issue reopen/unlabel events that the listener now receives.
- `node --import tsx scripts/check-workflows.mts` (actionlint, zizmor): passed.
- Limit: `pull_request_target` and comment workflows run from `main`, so the live run reduction is only observable after merge. I will compare hourly `ClawSweeper Dispatch` and `Auto response` run counts for the first hours after merge.

Supersedes #162080, carrying @mcooks-cmd's fix forward on current main. Thank you to @mcooks-cmd for identifying and fixing the retained native-module identity problem; their branch is left intact.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a long-lived Gateway's model-catalog worker retains another native ESM plugin graph whenever the same workspace's plugin context changes.

## User Impact

An unchanged installed native ESM entry now evaluates once per workspace during a catalog worker's lifetime. Registration remains generation-owned, workspaces remain isolated, and lazy imports—including imports from compiled TypeScript helpers—continue after the originating generation retires. New installed paths/workspaces still add resident modules; installed source replacements are picked up on worker restart. CommonJS and explicit recovery behavior are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Current main already caches each workspace's current plugin context, but replacing that context still gives unchanged installed code a new capture URL that Node cannot unload. The loader now owns one retained capture/compiler/module record per installed entry and workspace, with separate live generation owners. A single registration guard rejects calls through another generation's replaced API handle. Cleanup has one owner, including failed compiled evaluations.

This ports the fix onto main's newer source custody, digest validation, native recovery, Node/Bun selection, and admission reuse. The new identity module, instance-method monkey-patching, parallel retention maps, duplicate API-facade guard, separate worker fixture, both oversized retention test additions, and all knip/wrapper/test-inventory changes were eliminated.

## Evidence

Fresh real-worker comparison against main `34292e09ea88e45a4b0013470ce4ddc6c71aa3ca`, using the same generated installed `type: module` plugin, an initial catalog and **20 context changes**:

| Measurement | Main | Candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Entry evaluations | 1 → 21 | 1 → 1 |
| Distinct capture URLs | 21 | 1 |
| Array buffers, first → last | 5,269,381 → 89,208,672 B | 5,269,386 → 5,063,679 B |
| Array-buffer growth | +83,939,291 B | −205,707 B |
| JS heap, first → last | 111,752,168 → 103,941,920 B | 114,025,592 → 108,785,304 B |

The regression fails on main and passes on the candidate. The fixture retains a 4 MiB typed array; the leak is visible in external/array-buffer memory, not an increasing sampled JS heap. These are generated-fixture measurements, not a replay of acpx/codex/slack.

fix(cron): keep delivered results in the destination conversation (#168996)

## What Problem This Solves

When an automation delivers to another conversation, that conversation can receive the message without the result becoming available to its next model turn. Transcript-only mirrors and creator-awareness notes provide competing accounts of the same result.

## Why This Change Was Made

Make the resolved destination own the conversation result for agent, command, and script jobs. Send the already prepared channel/account/recipient/thread without resolving it again against the execution session. After confirmed delivery, commit through the canonical background-result writer, behind active turns and with occurrence idempotency. A conversation-write failure cannot undo confirmed delivery. If execution already owns the destination, retain its existing final reply instead of appending another.

Remove recipient mirrors and creator-awareness notes. Normalize intentional silence before either sending or writing.

## User Impact

- **Upgrade:** results delivered to another chat now belong to that destination's model-visible history, not the creator's. Creatorless jobs gain destination context. Existing stored jobs require no migration or configuration change.
- `none` and `webhook` do not create automatic conversation results.
- A destination bound to another agent still receives the notification, but neither agent gets an invented conversation entry. The previous job-agent-local mirror/awareness write is removed; the run records a delivery warning instead.
- Native-only output without an honest text projection still sends and records a warning, rather than blocking delivery or inventing transcript text.
- Two accepted regressions versus main: a job's message-tool send to a chat other than its delivery target no longer leaves a model-visible note there ([#168683](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/168683)); delivery-failure awareness notes in the recipient chat are removed ([#168684](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/168684)).

fix(models): allow API-key setup while the Gateway runs (#168588)

Related: #168135, #168108, #168471

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes API-key setup from the CLI when a running Gateway owns local state.

## User Impact

Users can run `openclaw models auth paste-api-key --provider <id>` without stopping the Gateway. The Gateway saves the key and refreshes its model catalog. Offline behavior is unchanged. An explicit, non-empty `--profile-id` still requires offline use.

## Why This Change Was Made

#168135 correctly stopped CLI processes from writing credentials around a live Gateway. It also kept CLI flows offline where the existing Gateway APIs could not preserve their behavior. Manual API-key setup already uses the same credential writer as `models.authSetApiKey`, so that subset can use the owner instead of refusing.

This change uses the canonical `local-state-owner.ts` route, as in #168108 and #168471. It binds the request to the discovered local owner and port, sends `expectedOwnerId`, requires `operator.admin`, rechecks ownership before dispatch, and never retries a possibly accepted write locally. API-key input is collected only after owner selection. The RPC checks the expected owner at credential and config writes; calls without that field retain their existing behavior. Owner-bound requests preserve the CLI's agent-selection rules.

Update behavior: an older Gateway that lacks `models-auth-set-api-key-owner-v1` is refused before the API-key request; update and restart it, or stop it and retry offline.

No request/response schema, new RPC method, config option, database schema, or paired-device fallback is added.

### Command-to-RPC mapping

| CLI command or option | Existing RPC | Result in this change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `paste-api-key --provider <id> [--agent <id>]` | `models.authSetApiKey` | Delegate provider, key, and agent; print saved profile and any application warning. |
| `paste-api-key --profile-id <id>` | No profile-id field in `models.authSetApiKey` | Refuse this option with offline guidance. |
| `paste-token [--expires-in <duration>]` | No equivalent API-key write | Stay offline: token type and expiry must not become an API key. |
| `login`, including API-key plugin methods | `models.authLogin` and `wizard.*` | Stay offline: CLI method/profile/default/force semantics are not an exact manual-key mapping. |
| `login-github-copilot` | `models.authLogin` and `wizard.*` | Stay offline; device flow is outside this change. |
| `add` / `setup-token` | No exact generic mapping | Stay offline; these can run local provider CLI or import flows. |
| `list` | `models.authStatus` | Stay offline: the status projection lacks the CLI list's state-path, cooldown, disabled-state, and recovery fields. |
| `logout <profileId> [--yes]` | `models.authLogout` | Deferred; retain current offline behavior. |
| `order get` | `models.authStatus` | Deferred; retain the existing owner-aware read. |
| `order set <profileIds...>` | `models.authOrderSet` | Stay offline: the RPC requires the full profile order; the CLI allows partial lists. |
| `order clear` | `models.authOrderSet` | Deferred; retain offline reset behavior. |
| `activate <profileId>` | No exact test-and-activate mapping | Stay offline. |

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: the generic-help login-gate browser test can time out waiting for the login screen while its own startup barrier is held.

No user-visible change. This repairs a Control UI test fixture without changing Gateway authentication, login behavior, timeouts, or assertions.

## Why This Change Was Made

The startup regression added in 9a98e2e9226 holds the emitted Chat JavaScript chunk before waiting for the lazy login screen. That barrier can also prevent the login screen from becoming available, so the test never reaches the release.

Hold the existing route-only Chat stylesheet set instead. The test still observes `startupPending === true`, starts the no-error fixture before startup completes, and retains every collapsed-help and reveal assertion.

No overlap with designated maintainer changes was found in the changed file's history.

- Unchanged #168588 head `b61c1f05efbb1db980722db07e9feacf922afe0b`: the requested direct login-gate command passed twice (25/25 each).
- Clean main `ab6c07f595e963ec86b93c11c90ac8d7ebf470b6`: passed twice (25/25 each).
- Clean main `95dcdf93588b82b7c6f929d01089bfece6f933a1`: failed twice (24 passed, the same generic-help `.login-gate` 30-second timeout each time).
- Focused old JavaScript-barrier negative control: reproduced the same timeout. Captured state showed `startupPending: true`, a stopped Gateway with `AUTH_TOKEN_MISSING`, and the connecting splash instead of the login screen.
- Focused stylesheet-barrier case: passed.
- Original-race negative control: temporarily removing the existing startup wait still fails with `Missing mounted login gate` using the repaired barrier; the wait was restored before final proof.
- Final direct browser run of `login-gate.e2e.test.ts` and `initial-connect-splash.e2e.test.ts`: **38/38 passed**.

refactor(sessions): add inactive memory backend to session actor (#169124)

## What Problem This Solves

Native incognito sessions still use a separate SQLite owner, so the session actor cannot serve them without main-thread database work.

## User Impact

No production behavior changes in this first Phase E step. Production acquisition still declines native incognito; a regression exercises `acquireSessionInputActor` and proves it cannot create a memory owner. The native owner remains authoritative until the complete consumer cutover.

## Why This Change Was Made

Extract the shared actor lifetime, phase dispatch, and receipt construction from the durable transport. Add a pure-memory backend behind that same contract, with canonical transcript bytes, pending-input custody, completion and Goal receipts, bounded context, and per-session command ordering. Pure policies are shared with the durable implementation and their old copies are removed. Memory acquisition opens neither SQLite nor a database worker.

Caller release drains accepted commands and retains the session; close invalidates handles and removes state. The following PRs add storage operations and migrate consumers while remaining inactive. The final PR selects memory for every incognito flow and deletes the native and pinned-worker owners together. There is no parallel production writer during this sequence.

Accepted edges: process exit loses incognito data by design; transport work already handed off may finish during close, with existing teardown at the effect. No revocation generations or new fencing are introduced. No ordinary runtime check is removed in this inactive backend step; native identity/currentness machinery is removed with its owner in the final cutover. Transcript overwrite predicates and custody checks remain because they protect real user data. Talk voice-call metadata retains its separately selected durable owner.

* fix(agents): keep inter-session provenance in replayed history

#167938 freezes a user turn's first model-facing text as a projection and
replays it as history. For inter-session input (e.g. a sessions_send
follow-up) the stored transcript text carries the "[Inter-session message]
sourceSession=... sourceTool=..." safety envelope, while the active request

the routed body. Capturing the body as the projection meant that once the

came from another session rather than its user.

the replacement request-local so history replays the stored,
provenance-annotated text. Comparing the full stored text (not the body's
prefix) also covers forwarded bodies that carry their own envelope. Other

durable projection but the stored user record is left unchanged.

fix: agents can resume their own conversation after CI and failed one-shot automations are never silent (#169102)

* fix(cron): let agents resume their own conversation later and never drop a failed one-shot silently

A Team session told to "finish and land" a PR published it, saw CI still
running, promised to continue, and never came back. It first tried an `at`
job targeting its own `session:<key>` with a `systemEvent` payload; the
validator rejected it with a message that called the target "isolated" and
talked about scripts, and the gateway misclassified it as internal_error.
The agent then improvised an isolated script that called `automations wake`,
which automation runs are not allowed to do. That one-shot failed once, was
disabled, and never alerted because failure alerts wait for 2 consecutive
failures and the owner-conversation repair skipped disabled jobs.

The supported shape already existed: an `at` + `agentTurn` job with
`sessionTarget: "session:<key>"` runs a turn inside that conversation with its
history and worktree. Nothing told the model so.

- Validator rejections name the target used and the exact fix; CLI add/edit
  delegate to the same owner; the gateway classifies them as invalid input.
- The automations tool description documents the resume-this-conversation
  recipe, that `current` is detached, that `wake` has no delay, and that
  script runs only get self-scoped automations.
- github_publish says how to schedule the continuation when the automations
  tool can add jobs.
- A one-shot that fails terminally now notifies on that failure: owned jobs
  get a repair turn in the owner conversation with a terminal brief (do the
  work, add a corrected job, stay silent, or ask), falling back to the normal
  failure alert if that turn cannot start; unowned jobs get the normal alert.
  Recurring-job thresholds are unchanged.

Live model eval (gpt-6.1-sol, high effort, real tool descriptions and
validator text, canned tool results, 20 trials each): schedule-after-publish
0/20 -> 20/20, recover-from-rejection 0/20 -> 20/20, terminal repair brief

fix(workers): enforce heap limits under process-wide flags (#166581)

## Problem

A process-wide Node heap flag overrides `Worker.resourceLimits`, allowing catalog and storage workers to inherit the Gateway's much larger heap budget. Clearing a worker's argv or environment cannot fix V8's process-wide precedence. Removing the Gateway's heap budget would reduce main-isolate capacity and leave operator-supplied flags unfixed.

## Change

Clear V8's old-space and total-heap overrides after the main isolate initializes, at the shared worker construction owner. The main isolate keeps its configured budget; new workers use their resource limits. This covers CLI, direct service and library entrypoints without changing early CLI recovery. Explicit V8 flag-freezing/abort-on-contradictory modes preserve their existing behavior and warn rather than aborting natively. No new configuration or raised catalog budget.

Thanks to @valkyriweb for the V8 reset mechanism and @xydigitLybnnnn for the managed-service diagnosis and comparative measurements. Fixes #157575. Fixes #157630. Supersedes #158201.

## Size and validation

- Six changed files; +1 production TypeScript line under the source-directory filter, +18 runtime lines including the packaged JavaScript helper. No changelog changes.
- Secretless AWS, Node 24.21.0 and 26.11.1: argv, NODE_OPTIONS, underscore, total-heap and percentage flags preserve the main ceiling and restore a 128 MiB worker budget (224/176 MiB total V8 ceiling instead of 1120/1072 MiB). These are heap ceilings, not RSS measurements.
- Final head: heap regression 7/7 (5.79 s wall), launcher 130 passed / 2 platform skips (344.49 s cold, including the runtime build), worker lifecycle 6/6 (33.43 s), extracted wrapper 17/17 (25.97 s).
- Final type-aware lint, formatting, export-name collision guard, core types, SDK surface and full build pass (283.23 s). Every candidate Knip finding was independently reproduced on clean main 6e06137f85ef.
- Independent correctness review and diff cleanup completed. The runtime and packaging regressions found during validation were repaired and retested.

## Inherited CI disposition

Broad CI remains red and is not represented as green. The exact untouched-main Node 24.19 replay reproduces node/paired-worker terminal failures and the steering acceptance/cleanup failure. Unchanged mock-export/import-boundary, nested-runner resolution and duplicate-code failures are separately qualified. The SQLite verifier carries no heap flags, so the added reset effect is not executed there; its baseline replay passes, without claiming that a passing replay fixes the intermittent terminal-status failure. Scoped proof and full build pass on the candidate.

Native merge admission could not settle its mergeability projection despite REST reporting the exact head mergeable. The authorized head-pinned REST fallback is used with the inherited-failure evidence retained by the maintainer.

Low-priority follow-ups from review: the diagnostic V8 exit-on-contradictory-flags mode is not handled by the current guard, and the warning can name the blocking flag and recovery action more explicitly. No security, user-data-loss or money-risk finding was identified.

refactor(agents): simplify runtime publication bookkeeping (#168981)

## What Problem This Solves

Agent runtime bookkeeping repeatedly restarted otherwise valid work when configuration, plugin, or catalog metadata changed during an asynchronous operation. This maintainer-requested simplification removes that speculative retry machinery.

## User Impact

Normal model selection, tool execution, credential checks, FIFO scheduling, and shutdown settlement remain. A request racing a reload may fail visibly and be retried by the caller; passive metadata may remain at its captured version until the next refresh. No configuration, protocol, SDK, schema, durability, retention, or permission contract changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Prepared runtime acquisition and remote catalog adoption now take one preparation path rather than repeatedly rebinding and rebuilding. Admission still handles the concrete drain, retirement, and failed-activation recovery stages. Cache publication keeps its final currentness check; tool and credential effects keep their authority checks. Steering and Tool Search retain their actual owner, FIFO, and settlement contracts without comparing unrelated metadata.

Production: **519 net lines removed**. Tests that exclusively required the removed synthetic interleavings were removed with them. Open-parent borrowing, pending-auth cancellation, explicit MCP acquisition config, and queued-tool implementation checks remain. No new lint suppressions, timeouts, retries, or skips were added.

Scope proof also caught two nearby correctness issues: an earlier MCP reload could overwrite a new caller's explicit configuration, and snapshot reconciliation could prepend a separator to a later text block. Both are fixed with their existing boundary tests. Bootstrap fixtures now test the no-clobber fallback already shipped by the pinned fs-safe version; no dependency or storage policy changed.

## Best-effort tradeoffs accepted

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes OAuth model-catalog refresh failing before contacting the provider when other agent databases exist, including empty historical databases.

## User Impact

Shared OAuth credentials can refresh during catalog discovery without requiring users to delete other agents or sign in again. Historical copies remain fenced during rotation and are settled afterward. No schema, stored format, or authentication-policy changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Historical-peer updates entered the host-only database executor from the catalog Worker. They now use that Worker's existing native auth-write scope, retaining the captured database path and file identity, existing-only opening, transactional credential comparisons, and committed publication. The same path handles fencing and settlement. Pre-request failures still roll claims back; failures after provider I/O remain terminal because a rotating token might already be consumed.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes.

## Evidence

- Three real catalog-Worker integration cases pass: shared OAuth with empty agent databases; an exact historical copy fenced during a held token exchange and removed after successful rotation; and rollback of earlier claims when a later peer already owns the generation.
- All three fail against unmodified `origin/main` (`390f0f0acb98c577d5ccf71cd04201a6c4083c7b`) with the same built-runtime prerequisite: `Failed to fence every historical OAuth refresh peer. | Agent admission requires its host owner.` No refresh HTTP call is made.
- The registered-runtime prerequisite and worker regression pass together (8 tests). The clean-shard prerequisite omission found by hosted CI is corrected and covered by the runner-selection test.
- Existing candidate-store, peer-settlement, store-update, and catalog-retirement tests pass (31 tests across four files).
- Isolated bundled xAI Gateway proof used only synthetic credentials and an operator-configured CONNECT/TLS stub with an ephemeral CA. Main, configured-peer, and historical-peer credentials were simultaneously pending-fenced during the held exchange. One refresh succeeded; both catalog requests used the rotated bearer; `models.list` published **Synthetic Grok catalog** with `xai:proof` marked `ready`. Historical rows were removed after settlement and an unrelated generation was unchanged.
  [Inspectable synthetic Gateway trace and settlement evidence](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/168957#issuecomment-6106538675).
- `pnpm build`, targeted Oxlint, the agents-root test typecheck, database-worker/dialect ratchets, line-cap/max-lines ratchets, assertion-safety, and `git diff --check` pass. The final Codex review reported no actionable defects.

Merge danger: two-way door; reverting restores the old execution path without changing stored formats. Blast radius is refresh-managed OAuth used by catalog discovery, including shared credentials and historical agent copies.

fix(ci): flag SKILL.md frontmatter defects in validate-skills (#1669)

* fix(ci): flag SKILL.md frontmatter defects in validate-skills

Issue #1663 reported two SKILL.md frontmatter defects (missing `name:`
on skill-stocktake; literal block-scalar `description: |-` on
openclaw-persona-forge) that PR #1664 addresses at the data level.

This change is complementary: it extends `scripts/ci/validate-skills.js`
to catch the same class of defect statically going forward, so the
frontmatter-vs-renderer problems do not silently reappear as new skills
land.

## Checks added
- Frontmatter must declare a `name:` field.
- Frontmatter `description:` must not use a literal block scalar
  (`|` / `|-` / `|+`) — these preserve internal newlines and break
  flat-table renderers keyed off `description`. Folded (`>`) and inline
  strings are accepted.

## Behavior
- Frontmatter findings default to WARN (exit 0) so this PR does not
  break CI while the two known offenders are still on main. Pass
  `--strict` or set `CI_STRICT_SKILLS=1` to promote them to ERROR
  (exit 1). Structural findings (missing / empty SKILL.md) remain
  errors as before.
- Today against main, the validator reports exactly two warnings —
  the same two files called out in #1663 — and exits 0. When #1664
  lands, the validator reports zero warnings, at which point strict
  mode can be enabled in CI.

## Parser notes
- Bespoke frontmatter parser mirrors the style of `validate-agents.js`
  (tolerant of UTF-8 BOM and CRLF; no new npm dependency).
- Block-scalar continuation lines are skipped so keys inside a block
  scalar are not mistaken for top-level keys.
- Hidden directories (`.something/`) under skills/ are now skipped.

## Tests
Adds five focused tests to `tests/ci/validators.test.js`:
- warns when frontmatter is missing `name` (default mode)
- errors when frontmatter is missing `name` (--strict mode)
- warns on literal block-scalar description (|-)
- accepts folded (>) and inline descriptions under --strict
- skips hidden directories under skills/

## Docs
Adds two bullets to the `Skill Checklist` in CONTRIBUTING.md covering
the two rules now surfaced by the validator.

Refs #1663. Complements (does not compete with) #1664.

fix(hooks): resolve MCP health-check spawn ENOENT on Windows (#1456)

* fix(hooks): resolve MCP health-check spawn ENOENT on Windows

On Windows, commands like 'npx' are batch files (npx.cmd) that require
shell expansion to resolve via PATH. Without shell: true, Node.js
spawn() fails with ENOENT.

However, absolute paths (e.g. C:\Program Files\nodejs\node.exe) must
NOT use shell mode because cmd.exe misparses paths containing spaces.

Fix: enable shell mode only for non-absolute commands on Windows, using
path.isAbsolute() to distinguish. This matches how attemptReconnect()
already handles the shell option.

Fixes #1455

* fix(hooks): harden Windows shell spawn — validate command for metacharacters

Addresses bot review feedback on PR #1456:

- Add UNSAFE_SHELL_CHARS regex to guard against shell injection when
  needsShell=true: cmd.exe operators (&, |, <, >, ^, %, !, (), ;,
  whitespace) are rejected before shell mode is enabled
- Add typeof command === 'string' check so path.isAbsolute() cannot
  throw on malformed non-string command values
- Rename test to 'via PATH resolution' (not Windows-only; runs all platforms)
- Fix misleading test comment: 'node' resolves via PATH like npx.cmd but
  does not itself use .cmd; comment now accurately reflects the intent

* fix(hooks): kill full process tree on Windows when shell mode is used

When needsShell=true, the spawned child is cmd.exe. Calling child.kill()
only terminates the shell, leaving the real server process orphaned.

Use taskkill /PID <pid> /T /F on Windows+shell to kill the entire
process tree rooted at cmd.exe. Fall back to SIGTERM+SIGKILL on all
other platforms or when shell mode is not active.

* fix(hooks): fall back to child.kill() when taskkill fails

Windows taskkill can fail if it's not on PATH, the process already
exited, or permissions are denied. Previously the failure was silently
ignored and no kill signal reached the child.

Now: capture the spawnSync result and fall back to child.kill('SIGKILL')
on any taskkill error or non-zero status. This still may leak a
detached server process but at least guarantees the cmd.exe shell is
signaled.

fix(observe): skip Windows AppInstallerPythonRedirector.exe in resolve_python_cmd (#1511)

On Windows 10/11 without Python installed from the Microsoft Store, the
"App Execution Alias" stubs at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps\python.exe
and python3.exe are symlinks to AppInstallerPythonRedirector.exe. These
stubs neither launch Python nor honor `-c`; calls print a bare "Python "
line and exit, silently breaking every JSON-parsing step in observe.sh.

Net effect: observations.jsonl is never written, CLV2 appears installed
correctly, and the only residual artifact is `.last-purge`.

  2. Teaches `resolve_python_cmd` to skip stub candidates and fall
     through to the next real interpreter (typically C:\...\Python3xx\python.exe).
  3. Exports the stub-aware CLV2_PYTHON_CMD before sourcing
     detect-project.sh, which already honors an already-set value,
     so the shared helper does not re-resolve and re-select the stub.

POSIX-compatible. No behavior change on macOS / Linux / WSL where no
such stub exists.

The SessionStart hook injects the most recent *-session.tmp as
additionalContext labelled only with 'Previous session summary:'.

but it can stop amplifying it. Wrap the injected summary in an
explicit HISTORICAL REFERENCE ONLY preamble with a STALE-BY-DEFAULT

treats everything inside as frozen reference material.

silently split the same project into multiple project_id records:

   bash, so project_name was garbled whenever CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR was
   passed as a native Windows path. Normalize backslashes to forward
   slashes before calling basename.

fix(agent): a credit-limited 402 retries once with the affordable output cap instead of failing as billing

OpenRouter answers a request whose max_tokens exceeds the remaining balance with
"402 ... You requested up to 65536 tokens, but can only afford 56272". The account has
credit; only the cap was too large. The main loop classified it as terminal billing and
failed the turn (or rotated off a credential that still had credit), so a request that
needed a few hundred tokens was dropped (#49769).

recover_after_classification now retries once with the output cap lowered to the affordable
budget before pool rotation, reusing the auxiliary client's _affordable_max_tokens_from_error
parse (same 64-token margin and 512-token floor) and the existing one-shot
_ephemeral_max_output_tokens seam. A second credit-limited 402 on the same call, or a body
with no parseable budget, keeps today's billing handling. Classification is unchanged.

fix(pm): give text that leaves PM the ordinary spelling of store paths

Store now spells its root \\?\C:\... on Windows so PM's own file calls
under it pass MAX_PATH. That spelling must not escape: the same folder
spelled two ways hashes and compares differently, and children such as
cmd.exe, gpg or uv refuse or record the prefix (uv would write it into
pyvenv.cfg).

native() now converts store-derived paths where their text leaves PM:
- process argv and cwd: uv via PythonEnvironment._run (its one exit),
  binary version probes, npm self-install, the PortableGit extractor,
  gpg provenance checks, the plugin-eviction interpreter probe;
- environment values: compose_env (PATH and package env diffs), the
  activation PATH dirs, HERMES_RUNTIME_DIR;
- hashed identities: the PM runtime inputs and isolated-environment
  identity, so existing records still match and nothing rebuilds;
- API results callers execute or compare: installed_package,
  uv_launcher, verified_tools entries;
- user-facing verification messages.

Facts records already store {STORE}-templated env, so no absolute path
reaches them. Tests pin that identities are spelling-independent and that
records, composed env and uv invocations from a verbatim root carry no
prefix (both fail on e8c97320ac).

test(pm): live Windows proof for PM with LongPathsEnabled=0 (#130242)

fix(pm): give Store a long-path root on Windows

Windows cuts plain file calls at 260 characters when LongPathsEnabled
is 0, which is the default. PM's copy, walk, digest, rename and delete
calls under the store then fail or silently skip files (#130242).

Store now spells its root in the extended-length form (\\?\C:\...).
Every path built from it with entry() or / inherits that spelling, so
the file calls beneath the root no longer hit the limit. Relative
paths, and so digests, are unchanged. On POSIX the root is untouched.

native() returns the ordinary spelling for text that leaves PM's own
file calls (argv, environment values, hashed identities, records and
messages). The call sites adopt it in follow-up commits.

- plugins remove / rm / uninstall, dashboard_remove_user_plugin and the

uninstallable plugin cannot strand. The message gives the

fix(gateway): never replay a written spool row whose file cannot be deleted

When a spooled row was written but its file could not be deleted, the OSError aborted the drain: the files after it were left for later, so the live row landed ahead of them, and because the file stayed, the next live write replayed and wrote the same row again, once per write. The boot pass had the same repeat. _remove_replayed now logs the failure, remembers the path so neither replay pass in this process touches it again, and lets replay go on with the later files. A restart still writes that row once more, since nothing on disk marks it; the log says to delete the file. Live rows are not held back for this: an unwritable spool directory stays fail-open.

Review finding by Greptile.

fix(gateway): quarantine only rows sqlite cannot bind

is_row_rejection treated every sqlite3.InterfaceError as a bad row, but SessionDB retries InterfaceError('no more rows available') as WAL contention and re-raises it once its patience runs out, so a valid row could be moved out of replay for good. Among sqlite errors only a 'binding parameter' message now counts; OverflowError does too. _bindable_text also passed ints outside sqlite's 64-bit range, which raise OverflowError even for a TEXT column and stalled the session the same way a dict did; they are now stored as text.

fix(gateway): stop one malformed spooled row from stalling its session

transcript_append_kwargs passed tool_call_id, tool_name, role, reasoning and platform_message_id to sqlite as they were, so a spooled dict or list in one of them failed to bind on every replay. With live writes now waiting behind a failing spool, that one row stopped the whole session persisting, across restarts too. Those fields are now made bindable, and a row the database still rejects on its own values is moved to *.json.bad and logged once instead of holding the session back, both at boot and in the live drain.

Also from the same review: the live drain and the restart pass share one sort key (_spool_sort_key), so a string or NaN ts no longer raises in the live drain; boot recovery returns the sessions it held back and the store marks them under its lock (mark_spooled_drop_sessions) instead of handing out its set; _recover_pending_flushes moves out of gateway/run.py as shutdown_flush.recover_gateway_pending; the transcript_append_kwargs import sits outside the try; blocked_sessions is required; the agent-history reason is a constant; the recovery tests share one store fixture and compare replayed rows with the live writer's.

Review findings by @kshitijk4poor.

fix(gateway): keep the spool replay error classifiable when it blocks a live write

Gating the live write on a pending spool raised a generic RuntimeError, hiding the replay's real failure from the FTS-rebuild, replaced-database and compression handlers, so a repairable FTS fault became a permanent stall. _drain_spooled_drops now returns the replay's own exception, the caller raises it, and after a successful FTS rebuild the loop drains the older spool again before writing the live row.

Found in independent review.

fix(gateway): replay the pending spool before boot resume turns and queued inbound

Boot recovery ran in main() only after runner.start() returned, by which point start() had already run the auto-resume turns and drained the inbound queued during startup. Those turns write live transcript rows, and a fresh store does not know which sessions have spooled rows, so the previous run's spool landed after them. _start_finish_wiring now runs _recover_pending_flushes just before _schedule_resume_pending_sessions(), and failures log at WARNING instead of being swallowed silently.

Review finding by @dokterdok.

fix(gateway): keep live transcript rows queued while older spool files fail to drain

The live writer replayed a session's spool before each write but ignored a failed replay and wrote the new row anyway, so a second failure (boot hold-back, then the pre-write drain) gave the live row a lower row id than the older spooled rows. _drain_spooled_drops now reports files left on disk, and the write takes the existing retry path instead, leaving the row queued in memory behind them.

Review finding by @ehz0ah.

fix(gateway): order shutdown slot heads before same-second overflow

Treat an absent sequence as -1 during restart sorting, before the overflow tail starting at zero. This also repairs ordering for existing spool files, without requiring a new writer format. Frozen-clock adversarial-filename regression reproduces B,A,C before the fix and A,B,C afterwards. Review finding by @keeltrace.

fix(gateway): bound decoded payload memory during restart recovery

fix(gateway): drain boot-held-back spool files before the session's next live write

The live writer drains the spool only for sessions in SessionStore._spooled_drop_sessions, which only this process's own spooling filled, so the session's next live row landed ahead of the held-back files until the next restart.

recover_pending_to_db now adds the sessions it held back to a caller-supplied set, and _recover_pending_flushes passes the store's own drain set (exposed as spooled_drop_sessions()), so the next live write replays them first.

Found in review by @BearHuddleston.

fix(gateway): catch only read and decode errors when ordering spool files

fix(gateway): stop a session's spool replay after the first failed append

Ordering the spool files fixes the happy path only. If append_message
fails partway through — the DB is still unhealthy, which is the situation
that produced the spool in the first place — the loop logs the failure,
keeps that file for a later retry, and then carries on and writes the
messages that come after it.

Those later messages land now; the failed one lands on some future start.
Because SessionDB orders a conversation by AUTOINCREMENT id, the retried
message then gets a HIGHER row id than the messages it originally
preceded, and the inversion this pass just prevented is written to disk
anyway — this time permanently, since both files are gone.

files are kept for the next attempt (the DB is likely still unhealthy)."
Apply it here too.

The block is per-session rather than global. Replay order is only defined
within a session, and this function drains every session's spool in one
pass, so a single unhealthy session must not strand the others' messages
on disk. Non-transcript pending payloads are unaffected.

fix(gateway): replay cap-dropped transcript spool files in drop order on restart

recover_pending_to_db walks sorted(flush_dir.glob("*.json")) to replay
spool files left behind by a restart. Spool files are named
pending-<uuid4>.json by _write_payload, so that sort is effectively
random: a transcript recovered after a crash comes back scrambled.

The damage is permanent rather than cosmetic. SessionDB restores a
conversation with "ORDER BY id" — AUTOINCREMENT insertion order, never
timestamp — precisely so a non-monotonic clock cannot sort an assistant
tool_calls row after its tool response, "breaking tool-call/response
adjacency and triggering an HTTP 400 on replay". Replaying the spool in
filename order writes exactly that inversion into the row ids, so the
session errors out on the next turn.

The payloads already carry the ordering fields: spool_dropped_transcript_
message stamps every one with "ts" and a monotonic "seq". The sibling
consumer of the same spool in this file, drain_transcript_spool, already
sorts on them via sorted(entries, key=lambda e: e[:3]); only the restart
path ignored them. Order on (ts, seq, filename) so the live drain and the
cross-restart drain agree.

Ordering by the payload rather than by a new file-naming scheme also
recovers spool files that were written before this change, which are the
ones an affected user already has on disk.

Payloads that cannot be parsed keep their previous treatment: they sort
last, are handed back unparsed, and are re-read inside the loop so the
existing handler reports and preserves them unchanged.

fix(fallback): log when provider-alias collapse degrades to lowercase (reviewer)

The lazy import in _normalize_provider_id is wrapped in a broad except that
silently returns value.lower(), disabling alias collapse with no signal. A
future import cycle/refactor could regress the same-backend dedup invisibly.

fix(agent): collapse provider aliases in the fallback-chain dedup

`_entry_identity` compared the fallback entry's provider id as a raw,
lowercased string. A provider reachable under two ids — the canonical
models.dev id (`opencode`) and a legacy rename alias (`opencode-zen`) —
was therefore kept as two separate slots in the fallback chain. That shifts
the chain by one slot and lets an alias slip past the same-backend skip,
so a turn can hit the alias slot, recover from a re-seeded rate-limit pool
against it, and exhaust retries without ever reaching the real paid
fallback.

Normalize the provider id (lazy `normalize_provider` import to avoid
cycles) before computing the entry identity, so aliases collapse onto the
canonical id for dedup. The returned chain still carries each entry's
original provider id — only the identity used for dedup is normalized.

* feat(platform): app declarations list every place an app may be installed

An app block's location may now be one path or an ordered list. A list
item is a path, where a `*` segment stands for a versioned folder and the
highest version is tried first, or a mapping naming a location kind:
command (PATH), uninstall_registry (InstallLocation plus a file, Windows),
app_bundle (/Applications, ~/Applications), flatpak (app id) and snap.
The directories behind each kind live in known_dirs.

Each kind's OS, key, presence and locator are one LOCATION_KINDS entry in
resolver/app.py. The declaration parser validates against that table, so
a new kind is one entry instead of three coordinated edits in two modules.

With requires.min_version, availability reads the version of every
present copy and returns the first that qualifies, so an old copy found
first does not hide a newer one; if none qualifies it reports the highest
readable version. A Linux block may omit a version source (Linux has
none) and is then gated on presence only; Windows and macOS blocks still
need one, and a Linux-only declaration cannot set a minimum.

clients reject a list location, so it follows a release that ships this.

fix(desktop): ship the SSH relaunch marker gate on stdin, not in the ssh command

assertRemoteInstallUpdateClear inlined the ~7.5 KB marker gate program with
`python3 -c`, making the ssh command ~8.1 KB. ssh.exec rides the POSIX
ControlMaster mux socket, where ssh writes the session request and only then
hands our stdio descriptors over with sendmsg(SCM_RIGHTS); a request that still
fills the socket buffer - 8 KB for a unix-stream socket on macOS - leaves no
room for that descriptor message, so the pass fails with EMSGSIZE:

    mm_send_fd: sendmsg(0): Message too long
    mux_client_request_session: send fds failed

ssh exits 255 and the fail-closed gate reads it as "Could not prove that the
remote Hermes install is clear for SSH startup." on every attempt, so no remote
host connects while nothing is wrong on the remote. The window depends on the
client's socket buffer and the command's exact length, which is why a shorter
probe to the same host can still answer.

Hand the program to `python3 -` on stdin instead. Python compiles the whole
program before running it and the gate never reads stdin, so argv keeps the same
`<marker> [payload] [hermes...]` positions while the command stays a few dozen
bytes however the judge grows.

fix(dashboard): don't 500 file listings on dangling symlinks or vanished entries

The dashboard file browser's listing route built entries via a bare
comprehension over os.scandir, calling _managed_file_entry() per entry.
That helper raises HTTP 500 ("Could not stat path") on any OSError from
resolved.stat(), so a single dangling symlink (or an entry removed
between readdir and stat) aborted the whole directory listing with a 500
— e.g. a broken ~/.claude link or Steam's recreated linux32/steam made
the entire Files page unusable (#47154).

Whole-class fix, consolidated from the open contributor PRs:

- _managed_file_entry() classifies a symlink whose target is definitively
  missing (FileNotFoundError) before the resolved-target boundary check
  and returns a `broken_link: true` placeholder entry instead of 500ing.
  The placeholder is only emitted for entries inside the managed root
  even when the missing target resolves outside it. Permission and other
  OSErrors still surface as 403/500 as before.
- Symlink stat results are captured in one snapshot (no second stat), so
  a target disappearing mid-listing cannot flip a result into a 500.
- New skip_missing flag lets the listing scan skip an entry that
  vanished between readdir and stat (returns None); the write-result
  caller stays strict.
- The listing loop appends placeholders and skips vanished entries, so
  one dead entry never loses its siblings. The sibling fs_list route
  already tolerated ENOENT; /api/files now agrees.

Reading/downloading a broken link directly still returns 404; 403
boundary and sensitive-path behavior are unchanged.

fix(tools): a task's own patch keeps its full-file write baseline

A deployment reported that write_file -> read_file (full) -> patch ->
write_file refuses the last write with stale_write_blocked and "exists
but this task has not seen its full current content", in 50 of 50 trials.
No other writer took part. When the model does not reread before the turn
ends, the refusal surfaces as the "File-mutation verifier: N file edit(s)
FAILED" footer.

Mechanism. The write_file baseline is an exact file version: (st_dev,
st_ino, st_size, st_mtime_ns, st_ctime_ns, sha256)
(tools/file_tools_read_tracking.py _file_version, _mark_full_write_baseline,
_has_full_write_baseline). write_file_tool marks a fresh baseline from the
bytes it wrote. patch_tool only ran _note_edited and
_reset_patch_failures, so the task's own patch changed the version and
left the baseline it held stale. _stale_overwrite_blocker then treated the
task like an external writer.

Invariant: after a task's own successful patch, the task may replace the
file whole exactly when it held a current full baseline for the bytes the
patch read and the bytes the patch wrote are what is on disk.

Lineage. a8af57fcd2 added the guard. dddefaefae counted paged, extracted
and post-compaction reads. e636aedebf kept a baseline across narrower
rereads of unchanged bytes and bound it to the sha256. That is the change
that made this sequence refuse (its parent lets the write through). Own
patches are the missing case of e636aedebf's principle that unchanged
knowledge survives.

Shape:
- Under the per-path locks, before the patch reads, patch_tool records
  the sha256 of each path whose baseline still matches disk
  (_known_full_content_sha256).
- read_file_raw and patch_replace report the sha256 of the exact bytes
  they read, BOM included. Each file write records (path, read sha256,
  written sha256) in PatchResult._writes for replace, V4A Update and V4A
  Add.
- _carry_full_write_baselines marks the baseline only when the read
  sha256 equals the known one (or the patch created the file). The mark
  goes through _mark_full_write_baseline with the written sha256 as
  expected_sha256. A writer that lands before the patch reads leaves a read
  sha256 the task never knew. One that lands after the patch writes fails
  the expected-sha check. Neither case gets a baseline. Several operations
  on one file in one V4A patch chain in order.
- A blind patch (no baseline, or a partial view) is noted per task in
  blind_patches. While disk still holds exactly those bytes, the refusal
  says "Your patch changed this file after a partial view. Read the
  current file in full before a whole-file overwrite, or continue with
  targeted patches." Sibling, external and never-read refusals keep their
  wording.

Remote backends: the baseline logic already stats the host path. On a
sandbox backend (non-LocalEnvironment env, verified with the
remote-binary-guard transport double), read_file records no baseline,
and _stale_overwrite_blocker lets the write through because the host path
does not exist. The carry hashes the same host path, so it records
nothing there. Paths the backend rewrites (translated mounts) do not match
the resolved host path and are skipped. Behaviour on those backends is
byte-identical to before.

Hint contradiction: after three failed replace patches, option (3) said
"use write_file to replace the entire file", which is the call the guard
refuses after a patch. It now says "re-read the file in full, then use
write_file to replace it".

Out of scope: enforcing recovery from a stale_write_blocked refusal
before a turn ends. The stale_write_blocked receipt and the file-mutation
footer are unchanged.

  ancestor of the holder (psutil). A holder with no PTY ancestor — a plain

The matched sessions are popped under the registry lock and closed outside
it (a close can wait out the helper SIGHUP grace and the lock serializes
every new chat), still before the spawn so the lease is released first —
the close discipline main's teardown series adopted, carried from #131179.

fix(dashboard): release the PTY a rotated attach token strands

fix: a ZIP stage no longer fsyncs a journal rewrite per file

`record_staged` rewrote and fsynced the whole swap journal once per entry:
124 durable writes for this repo's 123 top-level entries, ~8.6 ms each on
ext4/NVMe, ~1 s of a ~1.8 s stage (review K132361 P3, efficiency).

The write that has to happen is the one that makes a directory's staging
id durable before copytree fills it: a kill mid-fill must leave a partial
tree that recovery can prove is the update's and delete. A file entry is
already fully copied when its hook runs, so nothing waits on its record.
Its id now rides the next directory's write, or the last entry's, which
still lands inside `_stage_entries` before anything else runs. The journal
format, the reader and the whole-record temp+fsync+replace are unchanged.
Real 123-entry stage of this repo's tree: 124 -> 31 durable writes,
median 1859 -> 979 ms. All 93 top-level files copy in ~5 ms, under one
fsync, so a crash window that leaves a copy unrecorded (it is kept aside
and reported, never deleted) gets no materially wider.

now uses that reader with the same `--no-replace-objects` git, and keeps

When the host update-restart record cannot be written, the arm falls back
to the invoking profile's fleet_restart_pending marker, which only that
profile reads. The fallback counted profiles with list_profile_names(),
which suppresses enumeration errors and returns ['default'], so an
unreadable profiles dir read as a single-profile install: the commit point
moved the tree while the other profiles saw no debt (review S2 residual).

The fallback is now one stdlib-only function,
update_host_obligation.arm_host_obligation, used by both the commit point
(update_cmd_fleet._write_fleet_restart_pending_marker) and the historical
updater's takeover (_update_takeover._arm_fleet_obligation), which had its
own copy with no profile check and no warning (kshitijk4poor P2). It
settles the debt with the marker only when a COMPLETE roster proves no
named profile exists; any error listing the roster or reading an entry's
identity/tombstone is unknown, so the arm returns False and says so. The
commit point refuses before the move; the takeover (tree already moved)
keeps the warning. The marker name has one definition.

fix: the host restart record has one durable writer that also syncs its directory

_write_record and replace_bytes were two copies of the same
mkstemp/fsync/replace writer, and neither fsynced the state dir after the

back to "nothing owed". _write_record now encodes and calls replace_bytes,
which fsyncs the parent dir after the rename on POSIX (Windows opens no
directory handle; NTFS journals the rename) (kshitijk4poor P3).

fix: a completed restart never deletes the unkeyed restart debt another install armed

release's unkeyed host-update-restart.json. An installation still on that
release writes the unkeyed record; install B's completion judged only B's
own keyed record, yet deleted A's debt too (mixed-version schedule
B arm -> A arm -> B complete). Discharge now removes exactly the record
this install's readers judged (_owed_path): its own record whenever it
has one; the unkeyed one only when it was the record judged (this install
armed none), so an upgrade's own interrupted debt stays dischargeable
(review S3 residual).

fix: ZIP recovery deletes a backup temp only on the identity the swap journaled

b9ae435d78e let recovery delete <entry>.hermes-update-old.<gen>.tmp when its
bytes were a prefix of the live file. That is a necessary property of a
killed backup copy, not proof: a file created there after the journal (a
prefix, a full copy, or an empty file) was deleted and the journal retired.

The swap now journals each backup temp's identity (dev:ino:type: its size
and mtime move while it fills) the moment _copy_file_exclusive creates it,
before its first byte; the journal's new "temps" map is keyed by the temp's
file name. Recovery deletes a temp only when that recorded identity matches,
and still requires the prefix: FAT, where this copy path runs, hands a
recreated name its old inode. Anything else is kept aside and reported, as
before. The committed journal drops the map: every temp is a backup by then.
A journal without the map (an older writer) vouches for no temp.

Two Hermes installations of one OS user (a second checkout, a ZIP install)
shared the single host-update-restart.json in the host state dir. Install

checkout the module runs from (host-update-restart-<key>.json): every
profile of one install still shares one record, each install owes and
clears its own. The key comes from __file__ and hashlib only, so the N-1

fix: an unwritable host restart record refuses the move on a multi-profile install

When the host update-restart record could not be written,
_write_fleet_restart_pending_marker fell back to the invoking profile's

reads only its own home, so it saw "no restart owed" for a tree the commit

refuses with the user's bytes intact; a non-git install proceeds. The swap
refuses (and rolls back) when a backup path exists that staging did not

The equal-blob branch now asks `_modes_git_wrote`: the target keeps the pre blob
under another mode and the entry already has that mode. The worktree shows it

fix: a build command that starts outside the update job is put in it instead of refused

On native Windows Store Python the job-joining launcher is a packaged interpreter: it joins
the update job, but a program it starts outside its package (the managed node) is created
with desktop-app breakaway and leaves every job that permits breakaway, which the update
job does for restarted gateways. The F54 gate then refused every Node build of the update
(`the command would start outside the update job`) although no writer had escaped (F80).

The launcher keeps the command suspended and, when IsProcessInJob says it is outside the
update job, assigns it there and re-checks; the command runs only once it is in, and its own
descendants stay in the command's tree job, which permits no breakaway. A command Windows
will not add to the job is still killed before its first instruction and refused (D2/F54).
The Windows live cell that asserted refusal for the escaped-but-bindable topology now asserts
the build completes inside the job; a new control with a one-process job limit keeps the
genuine refusal.

fix(update): ZIP recovery deletes only the entries its journal proves it made

The ZIP swap journal named entries by path only: recovery took any
<entry>.hermes-update-old for the swap's backup and any entry at a
journaled name for the one the swap installed. A suffix a user created
after the kill was installed over the live file (whose bytes were lost),
and a file that replaced an installed entry was deleted.

The journal now carries provenance: each entry records its staging copy's
identity as that copy comes into existence (a directory before it is
filled; the journal is rewritten per entry) and, at the swapping phase,
the live entry's identity, which its backup keeps (hardlink or rename).
Identity is the entry's own lstat dev:ino:type, plus size and mtime for a
non-directory (a recreated file often reuses the inode). The run's random
gen tags its no-hardlink backup temps (<old>.<gen>.tmp) so recovery owns
those by name. Recovery deletes only what it can prove is its own; any
other entry is renamed aside (.hermes-update-kept) and reported, never
deleted; restoring a backup needs no proof because it destroys nothing.
A dst that is still the recorded live entry is left alone (nothing moved).

compatibility path.

fix(workspace): keep the default Workspace path language-neutral

The first-use directory name and its stored title came from the Client's
startup language, so one product decision carried two incompatible
requirements: a path addressed by shell commands, tool arguments, @path
references, and session logs, and a label a reader reads.

The controller now owns the fixed `default-workspace` directory name and
the registry titles the Workspace after that same segment, so
`workspace.initializeDefault` takes no request at all —
WorkspaceInitializeDefaultRequest and its name validation are gone, and
the registry resolver returns a path instead of a path and title. No
language reaches the Host.

Browser consumers label a Workspace through the new
`workspaceDisplayTitle`: a title still equal to the automatic one reads
as the localized default name from the `common` namespace, every other
title reads verbatim. The Workspace browser resolves it once at the store
read, so rows, hover card, search meta, and the rename and delete dialogs
inherit it; the hero picker and the Conversation chip resolve it too.
Confirming a rename stores the text on screen, which is what stops a row
following the language.

fix(plugin-manager): bound pnpm runs so a silent child cannot hold the profile lock (#4982)

* fix(plugin-manager): bound pnpm runs so a silent child cannot hold the profile lock

A pnpm child that prints its completion line and then never exits holds the
profile write lock until the host is restarted, so every other session and host
on that profile fails after its own lock timeout (issue #4981). execa resolves
its promise only once the piped stdio has ended, so a run now completes on the
process's own exit and drains the pipes under a bound instead of awaiting their
end.

A service run whose captured output stays silent for idleTimeoutMs is
terminated, reports timedOut alongside its exit status, and is not retried on
the next registry; a run with inherited descriptors captures nothing and is
left unbounded for its operator.

* test(plugin-manager): type the mocked child and await the drain descendants

The inherited-descriptor fixture no longer needs its legacy `as unknown` cast,
because the mocked child is typed for the fields the operations read; the
retired baseline entry is pruned (verify-no-unknown-casts).

The drain specs wait for the killed descendant to exit before removing its
directory: Windows refuses to delete a directory a live process still holds.

* test(plugin-manager): stop the drain descendant deterministically

The descendant that holds the pipes now ends on a stop file the teardown
writes, and on its own after a minute, so the fixture leaves no process behind
when a kill cannot be delivered. Windows stops it through taskkill, and the
spec waits for the exit before removing the directory it ran in.

* test(plugin-manager): run the drain descendant from its own script file

Windows cannot carry a nested `-e` script through another spawn argument: the
descendant failed to start there, so the fixture asserted on a process that was
already gone. The descendant now runs from a script file the fixture writes.

* test(plugin-manager): cover the bounded drain everywhere and stage the real descendant on POSIX

Windows does not stage a descendant that keeps the inherited pipes open past
the direct child's exit, so the real-process cases run on POSIX only. The
mocked child now models execa's own completion rule — its promise settles only
once both pipes end — which covers the bounded drain on every platform and
still fails without the raw-exit race.

* test(plugin-manager): cover the drain failure path without a child process

An output consumer failure that the bounded drain cuts short is staged with the
mocked child as well, so the per-file coverage gate also holds where the
real-process cases are skipped.

* fix(plugin-manager): terminate the whole tree of a stalled run

A lifecycle script is a child of pnpm, so signalling pnpm alone left an
approved postinstall writing into the profile after the operation reported a
timeout and released the lock. A stalled run now stops its process group (or
Windows process tree) and waits for it to disappear before the caller restores
the files. The cut tail's close is told apart from a reading failure by where it
happened, so a failure from before the cut still surfaces.

* docs(plugin-manager): regenerate the config catalog after the rebase

The English catalog gains `idleTimeoutMs` from the regenerator, and the Chinese
counterpart carries the same interface line so the pair stays consistent.

* fix(plugin-manager): terminate a run's tree through execa, keeping exit cleanup

Spawning a service run with `detached` made execa skip the handler that kills
the child when the manager exits, so a crashed manager left the pnpm tree
running in the profile. `killDescendants` spawns the run as its own process
group while keeping that cleanup, and it addresses the tree on every kill path,
including cancellation. The module now only decides the probe target and waits
for quiescence.

The fatal recovery dialog showed the last eight lines of the error and

packaged installation never surfaces. Two field failures were diagnosed
from screenshots of those eight lines: a Host killed by an uncaught

Every reportFatal caller now names its source (host, web-boot, renderer,
main). Before the first dialog opens, the shell writes
crash-<time>-<source>.log under app.getPath('logs') with the source, the
startup or running phase, application and runtime versions, the complete
inspected error with its properties and cause chain, and the primary
window's recent error-level console output (a 64 KiB tail captured from
webContents 'console-message'). The dialog names the file on its own line,
independent of whether the error was shortened and in the listener-conflict
variant too; the wait is bounded to one second and a failed write shows the
dialog without a path. Startup keeps the ten newest reports. Buttons and

fix(release): pin vendor dependencies for dsh 0.1.5

fix(desktop): drop connection-level headers and bundle cache headers when forwarding to the Host

forwardWebRequest relayed transfer-encoding, connection, keep-alive, and
the other hop-by-hop headers from the Host's response into the dsh-app://
response, describing a Node fetch connection that Chromium never saw. It
also relayed the Host's `cache-control: public, max-age=31536000,
immutable` on plugin bundles whose revision changes on every launch, so
each start wrote another unreusable copy into the renderer's disk cache.

The forwarder now strips the connection-level header set alongside the
encoding headers it already removed and marks /plugins/ responses
no-store. Whether either header contributed to the observed batch load
failure is unverified; both are corrections in their own right.

feat(client-modules): recover from a failed batch script and record import errors

One application batch is a single classic script that registers every
package in sequence, requested exactly once during boot. A transient
failure of that one <script> request failed every row in the batch and,
through arriveGraphRow's dependency wait, every row that injects or
requests them; the boot audit then listed each as "import failed (see
console for the import error)" with the real error only in the renderer
console.

Arrival now distinguishes the two failure kinds. A transport failure
(script error event, nothing executed) is retried once on the same URL and
the retry is shared by every row waiting on that batch. A script that
loaded without registering a row is never re-executed, because register()
rejects duplicates and a replay would stop at the first package the
original run did register. Either way each still-missing row then loads its
own one-resource combo URL, which the Host serves for every package. A batch
URL that failed is remembered so later rows skip straight to their
fallback; a one-resource URL is not, so it stays retryable on the next
import as before. Dependency failures are wrapped with the consumer and
dependency names so a cascade reads as a chain.

The module system records the last import() or prefetch() failure per
graph row at the outer operation, so factory execution errors are captured
as well as arrival errors, and clears it on success or invalidation.
assertEntriesActive takes the module system and reports that text per
fiberless entry.
docs(ip-geolocation): refresh the module dependency graph
fix(ip-geolocation): align the package with the current release

feat(app-boot): treat uncaught exceptions as fatal through installFailLoud

The Desktop Host and every other profile launcher installed a fail-loud
handler for unhandled rejections only. A synchronous throw from a stream
'data' listener fell through to Node's default uncaught-exception path: it
printed and exited without the surface's release hook, and the label and
format differed from every other fatal diagnostic.

installFailLoud now registers the same report for 'uncaughtException' with
the label `fatal uncaught exception`, shares the exit latch and release
timeout with rejections, and never resumes the process. The diagnostic is
util.inspect(err, { depth: 4 }) instead of err.stack so enumerable
properties (a node:fs error's code, syscall, and path) and the cause chain
reach stderr; the `fatal load failure` label for rejections is unchanged
because the Web profile expected-output e2e tests match it.

fix(subprocess-local): contain spill file failures instead of killing the host

OutputCollector.spillAll ran openSync/writeSync inside the stream 'data'
listener with no containment. When the private per-process spill directory
had been removed by a temporary-file cleaner, the first overflowing chunk
threw ENOENT from Pipe.onStreamRead, became an uncaught exception in the
Desktop Host, and the Electron shell reported it as a fatal failure.

Spilling is best-effort by contract (spillPath is optional; a failed final
close already withholds it). Every filesystem failure while opening or
appending the spill file now discards the spill, reports once through the
owner's logger, and leaves in-memory collection untouched. Spill inputs move
into one SpillOptions object with the reporter, so tail-only collectors no
longer pass an empty directory; prepareManagedProcessBinding is the explicit
resolve step for the directory and reporter defaults, and the runtime and
SSH helper supply their plugin loggers.

Tests cover ENOENT on open (removed directory), ENOTDIR on open, and ENOSPC
on append after the file exists, asserting the tail stays byte-exact, the
spill file is withdrawn, and the reporter fires once.

fix(desktop): report Windows extraction failures with 7-Zip evidence

The installer showed "Failed to decompress files" and discarded 7-Zip's
error output, so a failure such as security software quarantining an
extracted file could not be told apart from a full disk or a broken
download.

- InstallerExtract returns negated Win32 errors for launch failures so
  they no longer collide with 7-Zip exit codes; 7-Zip writes UTF-8 errors.
- window-frame.dll composes a report (result, archive, destination,
  Windows version, full 7-Zip output), saves it under the updater cache
  directory, and presents a task dialog with the first error line, a
  collapsible bounded excerpt, and a Copy error details button. Silent
  installs keep only the report; a missing task dialog falls back to a
  message box.
- Unsigned Windows builds name their installer *-unsigned.exe so a
  shared file cannot pass for a release artifact; version discovery
  still counts them.
