fix(update): cleanup ignores original-state update captures (#168177)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `openclaw update cleanup` never lists or retires original-state update captures, so `<state>.update-captures/` keeps one capture per update (about 1 GB each on a real install, 23 GB after 24 updates) with no supported way to reclaim it.

## User Impact

User impact: `openclaw update cleanup --dry-run` now lists every entry in `<state>.update-captures/` with its logical bytes, outcome, and reason, and the summary adds an `Update captures:` total. `--yes` (or interactive confirmation) removes only candidate captures. The command, flags, and JSON shape stay the same; capture entries add `kind: "update-capture"`. Nothing is removed automatically.

## Why This Change Was Made

Captures use the same release rule as other recovery originals: a later update must have succeeded. Attribution comes only from the capture's run id in update history:

- `candidate`: a sealed capture (`superseded-update-capture`) or an unsealed capture (`unsealed-update-capture`) from a finished update, including an already-current skipped run, when a later update succeeded.
- `protected`: the latest successful update and anything after it (`awaiting-later-completed-update`), running or rollback-pending runs (`unfinished-update-run`, `pending-update-recovery`), a sealed baseline from a failed update that is neither restored nor repaired forward (`unresolved-failed-update`), and anything without the capture marker or a matching run (`unmanifested-update-capture`), including standalone Doctor captures.

Removal uses the existing state-write check, SQLite maintenance lock, re-inventory after consent, and directory identity check. The capture marker is deleted last so an interrupted removal stays attributable. Cleanup also finds captures retained beside the former default state directory, and each inventory uses one shared database snapshot.

[Maintainer scope approval](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/168177#issuecomment-6093879932) covers explicit retirement of attributed unsealed captures and their nested generations. Nothing is deleted automatically; no schema or persisted-state format changes.

Update behavior: updater and Doctor entry points do not call the combined capture inventory or retirement operation. Those are reached only by `update cleanup`. A published 2026.9.8 driver cell was not run; the real native-update sequence below exercises the existing capture producer and the final candidate.

## Evidence

- **Real native updates, final head:** installed `7008414e344`, updated to `901a02fcaa2`, then updated to final `2dca26db4995f88ec5d0d709daee42a2fd371372`. Both managed updates finished `status: ok`, exit 0, with the Gateway answering readiness afterward. These runs created the real capture markers, manifests, and payloads; no synthetic capture data was substituted.
  - Final candidate `update cleanup --dry-run --json`: older capture candidate, **3,754,843 bytes**; latest capture protected, **4,107,471 bytes**, reason `awaiting-later-completed-update`.
  - After stopping only the isolated profile, `update cleanup --yes --json`: `status: complete`, **3,754,843 bytes removed**, one `update-capture-retired`.
  - Follow-up dry-run: only the latest protected capture remains. Canonical history still reads both succeeded update runs, and the existing Gateway settings and linked/bundled plugin configuration remain readable.
- **Regression tests:** all four final-head cleanup tests pass (dry-run and retirement for current and pre-migration capture roots). They cover latest, failed-baseline, unfinished, unmarked, and unattributed protection. The original two command regressions fail on `origin/main`, which returns no capture entries. Related cleanup suites passed.
- **Larger synthetic fixture:** 24 captures totaling 24,895,021,926 logical bytes. The previously installed CLI reports zero artifacts; the candidate removes 22 eligible captures / 22,733,763,357 bytes, preserving the latest and unresolved failed capture.
- Final-head CI passes, including production/test types, lint, and import-cycle checks. Final code review reports no actionable regressions.

Merge danger: one-way when cleanup is confirmed: a revert cannot recover deleted captures. No schema or automatic retention change. Blast radius: operators who run `openclaw update cleanup --yes` or confirm interactive cleanup; a misclassification could delete an update capture. Captures remain protected without a later successful update, while their run is unfinished, or while sealed recovery remains unresolved.

fix(gateway): avoid blocking stops on native skills watcher cleanup (#168273)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes Gateway stops spending 10–38 seconds retiring skills watchers one at a time on macOS.

## User Impact

Process-owning Gateway stops no longer wait for individual native watcher shutdowns. In-process restarts, hosted stops, and embedded Gateways still fully retire their watchers before continuing.

The installed updater cannot change the old Gateway's shutdown behavior. Once the candidate Gateway is running, later stops and updates use this fix. There are no configuration, schema, or stored-state changes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Stopping each FSEvents stream synchronously blocks the JavaScript thread on a native round trip. A Gateway that owns its process can instead fence skills observation immediately and let process exit release the native resources together. Detached subscriptions remain owned so an explicit later close can still retire them.

The stop decision stays with the existing process-exit owner. No overlap with protected maintainer changes.

## Evidence

- Retained macOS reproduction: closing 20 native watchers took 11.5 seconds, with the event loop blocked for the entire close.
- The regression exercises the real early-runtime unsubscribe path with real fs-safe subscriptions. It covers an exiting Gateway, late callbacks after detachment, explicit later retirement, and a Gateway that stays in-process.
- The original implementation fails the exiting-Gateway assertion by retiring all 32 subscriptions instead of zero.
- Real macOS CLI `gateway run` → `skills.status` → SIGTERM, with 20 extra skill roots and 293 reported skills: `restart.close.skills-watcher` fell from **514.9 ms to 0.4 ms**. Both processes exited cleanly without reaching the shutdown deadline.
- Total SIGTERM-to-exit time was 2.588 s before and 11.311 s after; the candidate spent 7.58 s in plugin metadata retirement under host contention. This demonstrates removal of the skills-watcher bottleneck, not an overall shutdown speedup.
- The native comparison used the runtime change at `adfd008c553f`; the final adjustment only narrows an internal export and fixes optional-promise handling in the regression test.
- All 16 focused startup/watcher tests passed on the final head (67.19 s wall time for the two-file command); core and core-test type checks passed.
- [Final-head CI is green](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/38032671854). The plugin-activation test initially reported `settled` instead of `worker`; rerunning that job on the unchanged head passed.

Two-way door: reverting restores the previous shutdown behavior. The blast radius is skills watcher cleanup during Gateway shutdown; normal skills discovery and refresh are unchanged.

fix(opencode-go): show every listed Go model and identify model-list requests (#168286)

## What Problem This Solves

Signed-in OpenCode Go accounts didn't see every model their account serves. The plugin kept only listed IDs that also appear in `models.opencode.ai` metadata. Four models listed by `/zen/go/v1/models` and served by Go (`deepseek-flash`, `glm-5.1`, `omen-alpha`, `minimax-m2.5`; each returns 200 for a direct request) were missing from the picker, and `opencode-go/<id>` failed with "Unknown model".

The Go model-list request also went out with the generic `undici` User-Agent. OpenCode asks clients to identify themselves with their own user agent (https://opencode.ai/docs/go/).

## User Impact

- Signed in to OpenCode Go: every model the account lists now appears and runs, even when OpenCode's public metadata doesn't describe it yet. Those models use Go's OpenAI-compatible route with default limits until metadata arrives.
- Models that upstream metadata marks deprecated stay hidden, as documented. Known case: `kimi-k2.6` is marked deprecated in metadata but is still on OpenCode's Go docs list and still served. It remains hidden from the picker, and `opencode-go/kimi-k2.6` keeps working as an explicit ref.
- Go model-list requests now send `openclaw/<version>`, the same User-Agent inference already sends.

## Why This Change Was Made

- `extensions/opencode-go/provider-catalog.ts`: Go owns its listing projection. Listed IDs with upstream metadata keep the existing enrichment and lifecycle. Listed chat IDs without metadata (the shared non-chat classifier still drops embeddings and similar rows) get the provider's default route `openai-completions` at `https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1`. Metadata never chooses the route for these IDs, so rejected metadata (for example an off-origin base URL) still can't redirect inference.
- `createUpstreamProviderCatalog` gains an optional `projectRows`. It defaults to the existing `projectProviderCatalogSnapshotRows`, so OpenCode Zen is unchanged. Model-list and starter-model requests now carry the provider's attribution headers from `resolveProviderRequestHeaders`, the same owner inference uses. That owner has a policy for Go only, so Zen requests are unchanged.
- Docs: Go catalog behavior, and the SDK helper description.

No schema, config, or protocol changes.

## Evidence

- Regression: `extensions/opencode-go/index.test.ts` "lists every advertised chat model…" (listed ID without metadata appears on the Go route; deprecated row hidden; embedding row dropped; model-list request sends `openclaw/…`) and the updated rejected-metadata case. Both fail on `origin/main` and pass on this branch.
- Live, real Go account, isolated profile, loopback Gateway, outgoing requests recorded by a loopback MITM proxy (credentials never recorded):
  - Base (`origin/main`): sign-in with the Gateway running → 31 Go rows appear about 2 s later, no restart. 29 of 31 first turns reply `OK`, on openai-completions, anthropic-messages and openai-responses. The two `muse-spark-*-contributor` models are refused by OpenCode until the workspace allows paid endpoints that train on request data (an account Privacy setting). Inference requests carry `User-Agent: openclaw/<version>` and `x-opencode-session` equal to the OpenClaw session id. The model-list request carried `User-Agent: undici`.
  - New-model simulation on base: a throwaway build with `qwen3.8-max` removed from the Go manifest, the recommended list and a local catalog.openclaw.ai v2 copy. The model still appeared from live listing + upstream metadata, and its first turn replied `OK` over anthropic-messages.
  - This branch: sign-in with the Gateway running → 35 Go rows (the 31 above plus `deepseek-flash`, `glm-5.1`, `omen-alpha`, `minimax-m2.5`) within about 1 s, no restart. First turns on those four and a `glm-5.3-flash` control all reply `OK` over `/zen/go/v1/chat/completions` with `x-opencode-session`. The model-list request now carries `User-Agent: openclaw/2026.9.9`.
- `node scripts/check-changed.mjs`: all stages green except `typecheck extensions`, which I fixed in the last commit and reran (`pnpm tsgo:extensions` passes).
- `pnpm exec oxlint --type-aware` on changed files: clean except two `no-redundant-type-constituents` errors on `ProviderRuntimeModel` in `extensions/opencode-go/provider-catalog.ts` (`resolveOpencodeGoModel` / `normalizeOpencodeGoResolvedModel`, unchanged lines). The unmodified file reports the same two errors on this base, so they aren't introduced here.

## Known follow-up (not in this PR)

OpenCode Zen with the same key: `/zen/v1/models` lists 3 IDs without upstream metadata (`jev-1.13-free`, `test`, `jev-1.13`). Zen free-tier models are refused outside OpenCode's own client (403 `FreeTierError`: "OpenCode's free tier can only be used from within OpenCode"). Zen keeps its current projection until those rows get their own filtering decision. Zen has no attribution policy, so its requests keep their current User-Agent.

fix(cron): manual runs lose tool access after the starting turn ends (#168037)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: manually started automations lose tool access after the chat turn or tool invocation that started them finishes, failing with `operator execution authority is no longer active` or `operator tool invocation authority expired`.

Reported as P0 by @obviyus after repeated automation permission failures. This PR fixes the reproduced manual-run lifetime failure; it does not claim every cron permission error has the same cause.

## User Impact

User impact: accepted manual runs can keep using their scheduled tools and deliver their results after the initiating request ends, just like timer-fired runs. Existing jobs need no recreation, permission expansion, new configuration, or migration.

Real revocation, missing saved accounts, job cancellation, and stored tool restrictions remain enforced. A separate missing repository-workspace binding is not repaired here.

A manual run no longer carries the caller's identity or request scope once it is accepted; it runs like a timer-fired run. A job that only worked when an admin started it by hand now behaves the same way it does on its schedule.

Revoking the caller's device after the run starts does not stop the accepted run, the same as for timer-fired runs. Revocation before the run starts still rejects it.

## Why This Change Was Made

The manual command queue preserves its submitting async context. Although it already detached root-work admission and transcript writes, it retained both operator-tool authority and the request-scope client. Those temporary authorities could expire while the accepted cron was still running.

After guarded activation finishes, hand execution and finalization to the existing scheduler-owned Gateway context outside the initiating operator-tool scope. Keep preparation and activation under the original commit guards; the stored job and its run receipt still own permissions, cancellation, and delivery. Direct manual, stream, and on-exit execution converge on this boundary. Do not broadly weaken the generic scheduler or authorization checks.

## Evidence

- Before: isolated reproduction through the real `cron.run` handler, queue, and GitHub-status tool fails with the exact inactive-authority error; an invocation-scope case fails with expired authority; timer control passes. Model execution and the GitHub response are synthetic.
- After: **36/36** focused manual-run, cancellation, queued-caller revocation, FIFO, and transcript-delivery cases pass. **28/28** regression/stored-policy/requester-provenance cases pass (three overlap the first group).
- **7/7** real isolated-agent account-policy/history cases pass, including a manually queued job after invocation closure: its removed saved account is still rejected, model execution stays at zero, and error history is recorded.
- **Authority chain, 4/4** (`src/cron/isolated-agent/run.manual-tool-authority.test.ts`). An admin creates the job through the real `cron.add` handler and starts it through the real `cron.run` handler. The request then ends before the job's tool call. From there the run uses the real queue, the scheduler runner, `runCronIsolatedAgentTurn`, the job's stored `toolsAllow`, real tool construction with the embedded runner's allowlist filter, and the real `cron.list` handler. Only the model is controlled.
  - (a) A job allowed to use `automations` reaches the real `cron.list` handler once. It receives the job's restricted caller-scoped inventory, not the admin's view. With the `ops-run.ts` change reverted, this case fails with `operator execution authority is no longer active`.
  - (b) A job whose stored `toolsAllow` is `["read"]` is never offered `automations`, even though the request that started it had `operator.admin`, and the handler is never called. Without the allowlist filter, this case fails.
  - (c) Disabling or removing the job after preparation, before the tool runs, cancels the run. The pending tool call is rejected as aborted and the handler is never called. Without the run abort signal, this case fails.
- After the change, `src/cron/service/run-receipt-settlement.test.ts` expects manual execution to be scheduler-owned, the same as stream, on-exit and startup runs (17/17).
- The failure in `src/gateway/server-plugin-reload.recovery.test.ts` is not from this PR. It fails 9/111 on the PR head, on the PR head with the fix reverted, and on clean `main` (`89c0368fe52` and `1f307d61d0f`).
- Test cost, one worker: `pnpm test src/cron/service/ops.operator-lifetime.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 3 cases, **15.31 s** command wall / 12.41 s Vitest. `pnpm test src/cron/isolated-agent/run.account-policy.test.ts --maxWorkers=1` — 7 cases, **44.60 s** wall / 42.90 s Vitest including cold compiled-worker preparation; the added negative case takes **309 ms**. Hosted CI seconds are pending.

New approach:
- post-edit-accumulator.js (PostToolUse/Edit): lightweight hook that
  records each edited JS/TS path to a session-scoped temp file in
  os.tmpdir(). No formatters, no tsc — exits in microseconds.
- stop-format-typecheck.js (Stop): reads the accumulator once per
  response, groups files by project root and runs the formatter in
  one batched invocation per root, then groups .ts/.tsx files by
  tsconfig dir and runs tsc once per tsconfig. Clears the accumulator
  immediately on read so repeated Stop calls don't double-process.

fix: filter session-start injection by cwd/project to prevent cross-project contamination (#1054)

* fix: filter session-start injection by cwd/project to prevent cross-project contamination

The SessionStart hook previously selected the most recent session file
purely by timestamp, ignoring the current working directory. This caused
Claude to receive a previous project's session context when switching
between projects, leading to incorrect file reads and project analysis.

session-end.js already writes **Project:** and **Worktree:** header
fields into each session file. This commit adds selectMatchingSession()
which uses those fields with the following priority:

1. Exact worktree (cwd) match — most recent
2. Same project name match — most recent
3. Fallback to overall most recent (preserves backward compatibility)

No new dependencies. Gracefully falls back to original behavior when
no matching session exists.

* fix: address review feedback — eliminate duplicate I/O, add null guards, improve docstrings

- Return { session, content, matchReason } from selectMatchingSession()
  to avoid reading the same file twice (coderabbitai, greptile P2)
- Add empty array guard: return null when sessions.length === 0 (coderabbitai)
- Stop mutating input objects — no more session._matchReason (coderabbitai)
- Add null check on result before accessing properties (coderabbitai)
- Only log "selected" after confirming content is readable (cubic-dev-ai P3)
- Add full JSDoc with @param/@returns (docstring coverage)

* fix: track fallback session object to prevent session/content mismatch

When sessions[0] is unreadable, fallbackContent came from a later
session (e.g. sessions[1]) while the returned session object still
pointed to sessions[0]. This caused misleading logs and injected
content from the wrong session — the exact problem this PR fixes.

Now tracks fallbackSession alongside fallbackContent so the returned
pair is always consistent.

Addresses greptile-apps P1 review feedback.

* fix: normalize worktree paths to handle symlinks and case differences

On macOS /var is a symlink to /private/var, and on Windows paths may
differ in casing (C:\repo vs c:\repo). Use fs.realpathSync() to
resolve both sides before comparison so worktree matching is reliable
across symlinked and case-insensitive filesystems.

cwd is normalized once outside the loop to avoid repeated syscalls.

Addresses coderabbitai Major review feedback.

fix: the planned-stop consumer takes the pause lock only for a pause on disk and drops settled receipts

consume_planned_stop_marker_for_self took .hermes-update-paused-gateways.lock
on every platform for every stop (up to 2 s when busy), creating the lock
file in the root home, and on a busy lock fell back to keeping the request
and writing a .accepted receipt that nothing ever removed. The lock only
protects the checkpoint into a Windows update pause record; with no record
or claim of this checkout on disk (every non-Windows host, or a pause
recovery/the updater already retired) there is nothing to checkpoint.

The consumer now holds the lock only when a pause is on disk. The
checkpoint hook re-checks after the request was read, so a pause that
appeared after the first look (an update writes its record before its
request) is still checkpointed under the lock. With no pause on disk, the
consumer removes the .accepted receipt and an expired stamped request an
earlier drain left: their debt is settled. While any pause is on disk both
stay (never earlier).

test_a_busy_pause_mutex_never_turns_a_planned_stop_into_an_unplanned_one
now puts a pause record on disk first: without one, keeping the request on
a busy lock was the leftover this fixes; with one, its assertions (planned,
request retained, no block) are unchanged.

fix: a second stop signal never deletes a stamped accepted stop request

When the gateway's home refuses a new .accepted receipt, mark_stop_accepted
stamps the kept request itself with accepted=true; that stamp is then the
only durable trace that this draining incarnation accepted the update's
stop. _read_live_pid_marker unlinked every expired marker, so a second
signal past the request TTL (another Ctrl+C / SIGTERM, which calls the
consumer again) or a planned-stop watcher probe in the same home deleted
it, and recovery then retired the restart debt of a gateway that was still
draining.

An expired stamped request still matches nobody (no PID-reuse grief), but
the TTL cleanup no longer unlinks it.

fix: the stash and churn steps bind the paused gateways' tree gate before writing files

Round 6 bound the branch switch, the upstream syncs, the pull and the rollback.
Other steps that run while the Windows pause holds the gateways still rewrote
tracked files unbound:
- `git stash push` and its cleanup `reset --hard`;
- `git stash apply` and the reset after a conflict;
- the rejected-restore `reset --hard` + `clean`;
- the lockfile-churn `checkout -- <locks>` and the line-ending `checkout`.

If one of them was interrupted mid-write, the gate judged the torn file only
against whatever refs a fetch had left. A restore after the pull had no
baseline at the moved HEAD at all. Either way the paused set was admitted.

Each step now runs inside `_checkout_move`. `paths=` binds the files it
rewrites in place, and `revert=True` binds every tracked change it finds,
because it puts them back to HEAD. A restore binds its stash commit. The gate
counts those paths as writable. A restore that applied its tracked changes in
full reports `whole`, so the tree it changed by design retires its baseline
instead of holding the set.

Removed the "already up to date" switch-back `checkout <current_branch>`. It
only ran when no checkout had left current_branch: in-place and release
updates never switch, and a parked switch is excluded. It was a no-op that
nothing gated. Helpers take a `checkout_move` binder (`_moves_for(token)`);
test doubles of `_prepare_git_command` accept its new keyword.

fix: the paused gateways' tree gate judges a moved HEAD against the commit it reached

`git checkout <existing branch>` can exit 0 and move HEAD while leaving a file
unwritten ("unable to unlink old ..."): HEAD and the index name the new commit,
the file keeps the old bytes. `tree_is_whole` only judged baselines at an
unmoved HEAD, so that torn tree was admitted and the paused gateways started
on it.

`_checkout_move` now judges every move the moment git returns: the paths
between the commit it started from and the one HEAD reached that are changed
and were not already there byte for byte (`update_pause_record.torn_by_move`)
are recorded on the baseline as `landed[<head>]`. The gate holds while any of
those paths is still changed. Judging at return time, not at resume, keeps a
later dependency sync or stash restore that rewrites an upstream-changed file
(package-lock.json) from holding the set. A recorded move the updater died
before judging is judged at resume time against what the pause saw.

A step's own baseline is retired only when its move landed whole (it was
retired on any HEAD move before). The moved-HEAD gate reuses tracked_changes
and the dirty digests the record already carries.

fix: every checkout-writing update step binds the paused gateways' tree gate first

Only the principal pull recorded its target (mark_move) before git wrote the
tree. The first branch switch in _prepare_checkout_for_update (and its
`checkout -B` fallback), a fork's early and late upstream sync, and the
post-pull syntax rollback wrote the tree unrecorded: a torn switch or sync at
an unmoved HEAD was judged against whatever refs a later fetch left, and a
failed second move (upstream sync after a successful pull) had no baseline at
its starting HEAD at all, so the gate admitted the torn tree.

All of them now run inside _checkout_move(token, *targets). Before git runs it
persists the resolved target(s): on the pause's own baseline when the step
starts from the pause HEAD (it knows the edits already there), otherwise on a
new baseline taken at the step's starting HEAD with its dirty digests. A
record that cannot be written raises, so the step does not run. Once git
returns, a per-step baseline is retired if HEAD moved or the tree is exactly as
the step found it, so a clean refusal never holds the set. The upstream sync
takes the context as `checkout_move`; the pull's move is extracted to
_move_checkout_to so _pull_updates does not nest deeper.

fix: post-update relaunch verification polls every target in one loop

Retiring each paused runtime on its own readiness made the wait serial: every
profile and unmapped entry ran its own 2 s confirmation window (plus a 6 s
per-target floor past the deadline), so 3 profiles took 6 s and 5 took 10 s
where the fleet-wide wait had taken one window. All targets now share one poll:
one fleet process scan per tick, each target credited only on its own hits for
a whole confirmation window, and a PID one target vouched for is never credited
to another. Measured with readiness stubbed to succeed: N=1/3/5 went from
2.0/6.0/10.0 s to 2.0 s flat (N=10 also 2.0 s).

The reconciliation tests' liveness stub moves to the probe the verifier now
polls (_live_gateway_pids); their assertions are unchanged.

fix: startup gateway recovery prints to stderr, never the command's stdout

update_pause_record.recover() resumes paused gateways ahead of every hermes
command and prints its own notices to stderr, but the Windows resume path it
calls printed deferral/restart notices to stdout, corrupting the output of
unrelated commands (--json ones included). A recovering resume now routes its
stdout to stderr.

fix: a failed service pause keeps its record on typed rollback failures

_pause_windows_gateways_for_update decided whether to abandon the durable pause
record by searching the error text for "rollback failures"; rewording that
message would delete the record while gateways are still stopped. The service
pause now raises ServicePauseFailed carrying rollback_failures, and the record
is abandoned only when that list is empty. Any other exception keeps the record.

fix: a paused unmapped gateway keeps the home discovery proved

Discovery owns an unmapped gateway whose environment is unreadable when the
exact-birth spawn ledger names its home, but the pause snapshot re-read only
the environment and wrote `home: null`. The readiness predicate read that as a
pre-home record and let another home's gateway with the same selectorless argv
retire the debt.

The snapshot, discovery and readiness now share one resolver
(update_fleet_scope.gateway_pid_home: environment, else ledger witness). A home
that no longer proves refuses the pause before any stop, and only an entry with
no `home` key (an older updater's token) keeps argv-only matching; a recorded
empty home is never matched.

fix: the psutil-less identity test judges with one creation-time probe

update_lock caches this process's creation time (_OWN_CT). Warmed by an earlier
test through psutil, it differed from the stdlib probe identity() uses with
psutil hidden by that probe's resolution (macOS `ps -o lstart`: 1 s), so the
test failed in a full-file run and passed alone. It now starts from an empty
cache, so both sides use the same probe.

fix: drop update_pause_record.orphaned_record, which only tests called

Its callers (the record test helper and the hostile-host pause cell) now read
orphans() directly, the same survey recovery and adoption use.

fix: startup recovery keeps the Windows resume's progress lines off the command's stdout

recover() runs before unrelated commands (anything printing --json, the
serve/dashboard processes Desktop reads over a pipe). Its own notices already go
to stderr, but the Windows resume helpers it calls print with bare print(),
which landed in that command's stdout. The resume now runs with sys.stdout
pointed at stderr. The record tests' resume stand-ins report on the real stdout
(sys.__stdout__) accordingly; no assertion changed.

fix: a recovering launch pays an unready gateway relaunch once per backoff window

update_pause_record.recover() runs before every command but `update` and
`gateway run` (chat, doctor, config, the serve/dashboard processes Desktop
spawns). Its Windows resume waits out the relaunch readiness budget for each
profile/unmapped gateway; one that never became ready was handed back unowned
"so the next launch retries at once", so every following command stalled
~30 s again (measured: 31 s on each of three consecutive launches).

Profile and unmapped entries now get the stored backoff SCM services already
have (service_retry): an attempted entry the resume left owed gets
relaunch_retry {attempts, next_at} (60 s doubling, capped at 1 h); a launch
inside the window holds it owed beside the draining entries without relaunching
it. The debt itself is never dropped, a tree-gate deferral does not count as
an attempt, and `hermes update` (merge_into does not carry the backoff) still
retries at once.

fix: unreadable or unwritable accepted-stop evidence keeps a draining gateway owed

The pause record's second evidence reader (_names_request) turned a refused or
malformed planned-stop marker / accepted receipt into False, i.e. "this update
never asked it to stop". Past the request's TTL recovery then dropped the live,
still-draining gateway (drop_never_stopped) and durably retired its debt.
Now only an absent file or a valid one naming something else is "not asked";
refused/malformed is unknown: the entry stays owed (held as draining while its
process lives), and unknown is never resolved into stop_sent, so the next pass
judges it again.

The consumer's receipt (mark_stop_accepted) swallowed its own write failure, so
an accepted stop could leave no durable trace at all. When the home refuses the
new receipt file it now stamps the kept request in place ("accepted", opened r+,
never created); a torn stamp reads malformed, hence unknown, hence owed. An
expired request nobody accepted still expires.

fix: same-HEAD gateway admission is judged on the move the update recorded

The unmoved-HEAD tree gate decided which paths the failed move could have
written from the CURRENT FETCH_HEAD and remote refs, so a later fetch whose
target no longer touched a half-written file turned the gate from hold to
resume on unchanged partial bytes. And a path dirty at pause was exempt by name
alone, so an autostashed edit let different half-written bytes through.

_pull_updates now records the resolved move target on the pause's own baseline
before git writes (mark_move; a failure aborts the move), and the gate diffs
HEAD against that recorded target. The pause also stores each dirty path's
digest, so only the same bytes count as "seen at pause". A pause with no
recorded move, or a record from before these fields, keeps the fetched-refs
and pathname behaviour.

fix: an accepted planned stop stays owed for the whole drain

When both the producer's mark_stop_sent and the consumer's checkpoint into the
pause record were refused (busy mutex, Windows replace refusal), the consumer
still accepted the stop and left only the 60-second request marker. An updater
that died meanwhile left recovery to drop the still-draining gateway as never
asked once that TTL passed, losing its restart.

that target first. An unseen change now counts only on a path that differs
between HEAD and a commit in FETCH_HEAD or refs/remotes. When git cannot say or

  (refuses when that pause's owner is live).

The set of gateways/services `hermes update` stops on Windows lived only in the
updater's memory plus an atexit resume, so a killed updater (console closed,

fix: a group kill of the build's caller no longer kills the custodian of its detached writers

The POSIX build launcher (_REAP_TREE) holds the checkout-lock fd for node's tree because node
marks the donated fd close-on-exec. It stayed in the caller's process group, so the
completion child's interruption path (`os.killpg(group, SIGKILL)`) killed it along with node,
while a lifecycle descendant that started its own session survived without custody: a
contender acquired the checkout while that writer kept writing (review E).

The launcher now leaves the caller's group and starts node back in it (`process_group=`):
every group kill still reaches node and what it starts in that group, but the custodian
outlives it, kills and reaps the rest of the tree (subreaper / recorded tree, as on a normal
return) and only then exits and releases the fd. A launcher that already leads its group
(a caller gave it a session) cannot leave it and keeps the old topology.

recovery was refused until the daemon exited (review F1, helix4u's report).

The custody config for local mutators now carries `-c core.hooksPath=<os.devnull>` next to
the fsmonitor/credential suppression: internal updater mutations never run repository hooks.

mutators still hold the fd (test_lock_fd_reaches_local_mutators_only stays green).

fix(update): a macOS fetch dies with its killed update owner (review R3)

The updater's fetch runs without the checkout lock fd (m3: its network half and any
credential daemon must never hold the checkout). On Linux PR_SET_PDEATHSIG ends it when the
owner dies; macOS has no parent-death signal, so a killed `hermes update` left the fetch
rewriting refs (and holding live `*.lock` ref files) under the next lock owner. The docstring
pointed at a NOT_COVERED note that does not exist.

Where no parent-death signal can be armed, run_git now runs an fd-less ref writer (`fetch`)
under a stdlib watchdog: its stdin is a pipe only the owner writes; a byte means the fetch is
done, EOF without one means the owner died, and it SIGKILLs the fetch, as the death signal
would. It holds no lock fd and runs in its own session. A watchdog that cannot start is logged
and the fetch runs as before. Readers and ls-remote write nothing and stay as they were;
promisor lazy fetches add content-addressed objects only and are not watched.

fix(update): A7 marker mutex, one incarnation rule, delegate-aware release, checkout custody

R3 / A7 rule 1: every marker decision-and-mutation (reclaim of a dead claim,
adopt + delegate append, release, ownership hand-over) now runs while holding
the kernel lock on the never-deleted sidecar `<marker>.lock` (POSIX flock;
Windows: the file opened share-none, the same lock the PowerShell hand-off
takes), bounded to 10 s. Only the exclusive first publish stays lock-free

our creation time; a no-ct claim naming our pid is a previous incarnation
(dead) — in Python (`update_lock.incarnation_live`, exported for the pause
record) and in marker.rs (no more 2 s self tolerance; Electron's v1 own-pid
pre-write is reclaimed and republished as v2; the exit-2 heal requires our

The owner removes its claim regardless of delegate lines unless a LIVE
delegate other than itself exists, which then inherits the claim (rewritten
with the delegate as owner, started_at and run lines kept). A delegate drops
its line while the owner lives, else deletes. This is the native Windows

fix(bootstrap-installer): marker claim, parse and liveness follow the LP-LOCK r2 contract

feat(desktop): publish a build version without rewriting the manifests

Packaging a build for a test feed or a colleague required bumping the
version in 295 manifests plus the lockfile first, because the version a
build publishes was only ever read from the checkout. Those edits cannot
be committed, so every such build left the working tree dirty, and the
`<version>.<date>.<sequence>` convention behind them lived only in the
operator's memory.

The version a build publishes is now an input. `--release-id` names it,
`--release-id auto` numbers it after the builds already published to the
destination bucket (falling back to local artifacts, since a fresh CI
checkout has none), and it reaches electron-builder through
extraMetadata, the update feed, and the upload validation as one value.
The manifests keep the product version, aligned with the dsh npm
package, and a release still publishes exactly that.

Validation goes through `semver` itself, because `electron-updater`
compares feed versions with `semver.gt` against the installed
`app.getVersion()`: a build version must outrank the product version it
extends, which holds for `0.1.6-alpha.2.20260921.1` over
`0.1.6-alpha.2` and cannot hold on a stable version, where a fourth
release number is not a version at all.

Two things a build could not previously answer for itself:

- Artifacts now carry the commit they were packaged from and whether
  that checkout was dirty, so a build handed to a colleague is traceable
  without a tag.
- A production upload tags that commit as `desktop-v<version>` once the
  artifacts are public, and reports what to run by hand rather than
  failing an upload that already completed. Test and local builds are
  deliberately left untagged.

A toolchain step now probes tar and the Windows installer compiler
before the first build step, so a host that cannot finish the sequence
says so in seconds rather than minutes.

feat(desktop): opt-in Windows uninstall data removal

The Windows uninstaller keeps every user file by default and adds a custom
page with unchecked options for desktop browser data and update caches, the
desktop plugin profile, and the complete Harness home. Selecting the whole
home requires a native warning that names the actual folder and the CLI

refactor(client): let chrome rows own the macOS window drag

The macOS window's draggable area was a hand-written band: a 52px strip, deepened
to 76px by a marker the Conversation header had to keep in step with its own
height. It drifted from the layout — blank runs inside a chrome row did not drag,
and a control a few pixels away dragged the window instead.

Chrome rows now mark their own element (`data-window-drag`) and the shell declares
the surface once (`html[data-platform='darwin'] [data-window-drag]`), so a row's own
box is its draggable geometry and no fixed band has to match any row's height. The
frame band, its 52/76 figures, the marker, and the per-sheet drag rules are gone;
interactive controls and overlays portal beside `#root` where one rule subtracts
them.

Recollection becomes one shell watcher (`window-drag/recall.ts`): Electron rebuilds
the window's drag rects only when a computed app-region value changes
(electron#32341), so the watcher measures every marked row each frame while the
surface moves, sets `data-window-drag-recall` for the frames whose geometry changed,
and clears it on the frame that finds the geometry settled. The right panel's
hand-written pulse is deleted with it.

Coverage is a contract with executable parts. `window-drag/regions.ts` publishes the
composition rule and the interactive selector that both the sheet and its spec
compare against; the ui-theme gate asserts the package tree declares drag in exactly
two places and pairs every row's mark with its sheet, selector, and authored height;
and the browser lane boots the shipped composition in Chromium with the darwin
marker to assert per-row geometry, a content body under a marked head row, a
covering overlay, and the watcher's pulse. The plugin manager's detail views mark
the head row they share rather than the pane they render in, so their text and form
labels stay content.

Both real machines agree: the macOS matrix ran on a real `hiddenInset` window with
HID-level pointer input and window-frame readback, and the Windows matrix on a
Windows 11 ARM64 VM — chrome rows drag, content and the covering overlay do not,
and the controls keep their clicks.

feat(client): compose session row actions from slot lists

A Session row's "..." menu and its hover buttons become two list slots the
WorkspaceBrowser entry declares, `sidebar.workspaces.session.menu.item` and
`sidebar.workspaces.session.row.action`. The shipped actions register from
apply the way a client plugin does: pin (menu 100, button 200), rename (200),
fork (300), archive (menu 400, button 100). An entry receives only the row
identity, reads the pin and archive sets through Set hooks its own face
injects, decides its own visibility, renders `MenuItemButton` or one icon
button, and dismisses the menu through the slot-level `useMenuOpenState`
hook bound from the row's render occurrence.

Each action's behavior lives in its injected callbacks. `UiWorkspace` gains
`pinSession` and `unpinSession`; the pin write into the saved orders happens
there, through the viewing-store instance the apply creates and hands the
browser's registration as its handle (the ui-layout pattern), reading the
memberships current at completion. The rename dialog and the row-action
notice are `shell.overlay` entries fed by apply-closure observables through
the faces' `hooks`; the archived notice switches the archived filter
directly. WorkspaceBrowser threads no action callbacks, renders no toast,
and hosts no rename dialog; its title double-click raises the same rename
request.

In ui-primitives, `MenuItemButton` is the plain `role="menuitem"` row for
menus whose rows are components: it shares a data row's markup and styling
and needs no shared state, because `Menu` decides the keyboard walk from the
DOM and now runs the post-selection focus return once on the list's click
bubble for every row kind. `Menu` accepts such rows as `children` beside
`items`, which becomes optional together with `onSelect`; `separatorBefore`
lets a row start a group with the same hairline a separator entry draws. The
context-based `MenuAction` goes away with its extension group.

fix(process): stop failing captures on tokens macOS cannot expose (#1057)

* fix(process): stop failing captures on tokens macOS cannot expose

On a busy macOS 26 host the residual process sweep fails every capture:
KERN_PROCARGS2 omits the environment of Apple platform binaries for any
caller and fails with EINVAL for processes owned by another account, so an
unrelated process created after the capture baseline escalates to a hard
cleanup failure with cleanup_incomplete.

Report environment withholding distinctly from the Darwin token reader by
reading the platform-binary flag through csops, carry the effective uid in
the process table, and re-read unresolved tokens with a bounded retry plus a
final liveness confirmation so transient exec and exit states settle.

fix(javascript): bound semantic node projection for resource safety (#966)

* fix(javascript): bound semantic node projection for resource safety

analyze_javascript_application exhausted the heap or failed serialization on
ordinary inputs. A small extracted tree crashed outright, and a larger
application tree failed at both the default heap and an 8 GB heap.

Cause: the semantic projection emits one node per AST expression, call site,
binding and property slot, with no ceiling. A five-file tree already yields on
the order of 170,000 nodes, and the whole result is serialized after the object
graph is built and validated. Result ceilings were deliberately removed upstream,
so nothing bounded this growth.

Apply two resource-safety ceilings and report them through the graph's own
coverage contract rather than dropping data silently:

- SEMANTIC_GRAPH_NODE_CEILING bounds retained nodes per tree (100,000, roughly
  300 MB serialized, below V8's 512 MB string limit).
- SEMANTIC_GRAPH_FILE_NODE_CEILING bounds each source file (20,000) so one
  bundled library cannot starve the application's own modules.

Exhausting either marks coverage truncated with a partial status and records the
ceiling in coverage.limits. A small application stays complete and untruncated.

Verified: a previously-crashing application tree now returns Evidence in under a
minute, while a small tree stays complete. Existing tests and check:fast pass.

feat(native): observe function and Objective-C method calls under LLDB

Add observe_native_calls (CLI: observe-native-calls <path> <input-json>). It
launches the active Mach-O as an owned process under `lldb --batch`, stops at
caller-selected functions or Objective-C methods, records each entry and
auto-continues:

- thread, image, symbol, load and file address;
- raw integer argument registers and optional caller frames;
- for methods, the selector read from _cmd and the receiver's dynamic class,
  from LLDB's runtime reader without running target code.

on exit, max_events or duration_ms; REA then kills the process and confirms
that it is gone. The result also carries exit status, bounded stdout/stderr,
breakpoint resolution with partial coverage for unresolved requests, and
limitations. A target LLDB may not debug fails with a debugger-attach-denied
reason and remediation.

feat(artifacts): trace Mach-O dylib resolution in bundles

Add trace_dylib_resolution (CLI trace-dylib-resolution) to the artifact
family. For the active Mach-O, or every executable in the active .app
(the main app, XPC services, extensions, login items, helpers), it
reports which file each dylib load reaches and how.

A pure TypeScript reader decodes FAT and Mach-O load commands:
LC_LOAD/WEAK/REEXPORT/LAZY/UPWARD_DYLIB, including the newer
dylib_use_command encoding with weak, re-export, upward and delayed-init
flags, plus LC_ID_DYLIB, LC_RPATH, LC_DYLD_ENVIRONMENT and code-signature
presence. Malformed tables are reported with the failing command instead
of being guessed.

Resolution follows dyld:
- @executable_path comes from each process root;
- @loader_path comes from the loading image, or from the owner of the
  LC_RPATH entry being expanded;
- @rpath searches the loader's rpaths first, then up the load chain;
- dependencies load dependents-first in load-command order, once per
  process, and a matching install name reuses an already loaded image;
- symlinks are followed inside the analyzed root, and escapes stop.

Every candidate path is reported with its outcome. Each edge resolves to
resolved, conditional (an outside-root candidate such as /usr/lib/swift
precedes), unresolved, or undetermined. Absolute and shared-cache system
paths are never checked against the host. Derived findings cover
unresolved required or weak loads, absent earlier @rpath candidates (with
library validation left unknown), and LC_DYLD_ENVIRONMENT.

fix(browser): classify CSP host sources by their own origin (#707)

* fix(browser): classify CSP host sources by their own origin

A Content-Security-Policy host-source without a scheme (for example
`cdn.example.com` or `*.trusted.test`) was resolved with
`new URL(token, baseUrl)`, so it became a page-relative path and was
reported as the observed page's own origin. Third-party script, style, and
connect sources were therefore misreported as approved origins, and a bare
`*` wildcard collapsed to the page origin as well.

Resolve host-sources per CSP3 \u00a72.3.1: a scheme-less source inherits the
protected resource's scheme, wildcard host/port sources stay classified as a
set of origins, and non-host tokens remain `other`. Keyword and scheme
sources are unchanged.

Adds boundary coverage for scheme-less host sources, wildcards, and scheme
inheritance against the approved-origin set.

fix(agents): deprecated models show the generic "couldn't generate a response" error (#168187)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: chat replies with the generic "⚠️ Agent couldn't generate a response. Please try again." when the selected model has been deprecated (for example OpenCode over ACP reporting `Internal error: Model exo-free has been deprecated.`), so the user retries a model that can never answer.

## User Impact

User impact: a turn on a deprecated model now ends with the existing model-unavailable message, "⚠️ This model was not found. Choose another model in the Control UI or run `openclaw configure`.", which points to choosing another model.

## Why This Change Was Made

The model-unavailable classifier only recognized retired models and deprecations that also said "upgrade/transition to", so a bare "Model X has been deprecated" fell through to the generic incomplete-turn text. It now also recognizes a message that names the model itself as deprecated (`model [id] is|was|has been deprecated`). It stays narrow: deprecated parameters, fields, or names ("The model parameter `max_tokens` is deprecated", "The `model` field is deprecated") and scheduled-removal warnings ("... is deprecated and will be removed on ...") are not matched. No new user text; it reuses the existing `model_not_found` class and copy.

Merge danger: low. One extra pattern in the shared model-not-found classifier. A matching error now classifies as `model_not_found` instead of falling through, which also makes it eligible for configured model fallback, the same as other unavailable-model errors.

## Evidence

- Regression `src/agents/live-model-errors.test.ts` (positive: the exact OpenCode message, an OpenAI-style "has been deprecated, learn more", "This model is deprecated."; negative: deprecated parameter/field/name and a will-be-removed warning). Fails on `origin/main` (`Internal error: Model exo-free has been deprecated.: expected false to be true`), passes with the fix. `pnpm test src/agents/live-model-errors.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`: 2 tests, about 3 ms test time.
- Real run: isolated profile, loopback Gateway, `plugins.entries.acpx.config.nativeAgents.opencode=true`, local signed-in `opencode` 1.18.32, one `openclaw agent` turn per session ("Reply with exactly: OK"):

| Build | Model | Reply |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `origin/main` | `acp-opencode/opencode/exo-free` | `⚠️ Agent couldn't generate a response. Please try again.` (meta.error `Internal error: Model exo-free has been deprecated.`) |
| this branch | `acp-opencode/opencode/exo-free` | ``⚠️ This model was not found. Choose another model in the Control UI or run `openclaw configure`.`` |
| `origin/main` | `acp-opencode/opencode/big-pickle` | `OK` |
| this branch | `acp-opencode/opencode/big-pickle` | `OK` |

- `pnpm exec oxlint --type-aware` on changed files: clean. `node scripts/check-changed.mjs`: passed.

test(whatsapp): expect carried overflow in long styled chunks

The WhatsApp delivery-recovery test for long bold replies has been red on
main since #167958 (69bfe7b645c8). That change taught the shared
render-aware Markdown chunker to carry the overflow of a re-split chunk
into the next source window instead of sending it as its own tiny
message. A 340-character bold reply at textChunkLimit 160 now arrives as
*x158* / *x158* / *x24* instead of *x158* / *xx* / *x158* / *xx* / *x20*;
the old expectation encoded exactly the orphan-chunk artifact #167958
removed.

Update the expectation to the intended contract: every chunk keeps its
style markers and stays within the limit, the content is exact, only the
first chunk quotes the reply target, and each part reports one receipt.
Reverting only render-aware-chunking.ts to 69bfe7b645c8^ restores the
old output, which pins the cause. Main's scoped CI never selected this
suite for the markdown-core change, so the red surfaced only when a later
PR widened changed-test selection.

fix(agents): ChatGPT-listed models fail on the default Codex runtime before any request (#168033)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a model that the signed-in ChatGPT account lists (and that the model picker shows as available) fails on the default Codex runtime with `No route-compatible authentication source is configured for openai.` (or `... requires an OpenAI API key profile`) before any request is sent, when OpenClaw has no static ChatGPT route for that model id.

## User Impact

User impact: models your ChatGPT account offers, including newly launched ones that OpenClaw does not know yet, now run on the default Codex runtime with your ChatGPT sign-in, matching what the picker shows. Known models, API-key-only users, and the `openclaw` runtime keep their current behavior.

Behavior note: a user signed in to ChatGPT **and** holding an OpenAI API key, choosing a model id that OpenClaw does not know and that the catalog lists on both the Platform and ChatGPT rows, now prefers the subscription. This matches the picker and the `openclaw` runtime.

## Why This Change Was Made

The picker and the run read different catalogs. The picker reads the published catalog, which includes the account's live ChatGPT rows. A Codex-owned run planned auth from its native placeholder model, whose api/baseUrl describe only the Platform route, so the account-only route was never considered and auth planning failed closed.

A native-owned (Codex) foreground run now takes its observed routes from the published catalog captured at Gateway admission, which is the catalog the picker read, and auth planning chooses among those routes. The OpenClaw runtime path is unchanged. The native placeholder model is still not materialized for native-owned runs. The only SDK type change is an optional `observedRoutes` input on `prepareAgentRuntimeAuth`.

Known gaps (unchanged from today, not regressions):
- Direct CLI runs with no Gateway have no admission-captured catalog and keep today's behavior.
- A model that appears after admission fails closed with today's error until the next turn admits a fresh catalog.
- Codex isolated/utility completions still plan from the first catalog entry's route; follow-up.

Merge danger: low to moderate. The change is confined to native-owned foreground auth planning, which is the path every Codex turn takes. The controls below cover known models, dual-credential users, API-key-only users, and the `openclaw` runtime.

## Evidence

**Regression (QA-lab runtime e2e, real Gateway child + fake Codex app-server + loopback ChatGPT/Platform catalog fixture):** `test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/codex-account-model-route.product-proof.e2e.test.ts`. Profiles are seeded like a fresh sign-in (no explicit auth order). Each case refreshes `models.list`, asserts the model is available, patches the session model, sends a chat turn, and waits for `ok`. It then asserts that the app-server received `turn/start` for that model with the expected login, and that the route errors never appear in Gateway logs.

| Case | `origin/main` | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ChatGPT-only: account-only id, Platform-only manifest id listed by the account, `gpt-6-sol` (default runtime) | ❌ `No route-compatible authentication source is configured for openai.` | ✅ Codex `turn/start`, login `chatgptAuthTokens` |
| Control: ChatGPT + API key, `gpt-6-sol` | ✅ `chatgptAuthTokens` | ✅ `chatgptAuthTokens` |
| Control: API key only, `gpt-6-sol` | ✅ `apiKey` | ✅ `apiKey` |

Command: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs --config test/vitest/vitest.e2e.config.ts test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/codex-account-model-route.product-proof.e2e.test.ts`. It was rerun green after merging current `main`. The file has 3 tests and about 85 s of test time; wall clock was 100–560 s depending on host load. It runs in the e2e tier, not the unit lane.

**Real account (device-code ChatGPT sign-in, isolated profile, loopback Gateway built from this branch):**

test(qa-lab): quota-reset e2e fails when chat.history races agent database creation (#168106)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: `test/e2e/qa-lab/runtime/quota-reset.e2e.test.ts` fails on `main` (8 of 9 cases) with `GatewayClientRequestError: Session access facts are unavailable; retry after session storage is ready.` (`UNAVAILABLE` on `chat.history`, `retryable: true`, `retryAfterMs: 250`). CI only runs this suite when its files change, so `main` CI stays green.

## User Impact

No user-visible change. The quota-reset e2e suite is green again, so PRs that touch it (for example #168033) are not blocked by a failure that is already on `main`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The failure is a gap in the test fixture, not a product bug. Each fixture boots a fresh Gateway with no agent database yet (startup logs `registeredDatabaseCount=0`). The first agent write creates `agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite` shortly after the Gateway reports ready. The fixture's first `turn()` calls `chat.history` for a session that doesn't exist yet. When that read lands in the creation window, it fails like this:

- `chat.history` prepares negative-read facts for the absent row (`src/gateway/server-methods/chat-history-session-read.ts:178-186`). That captures the agent store as missing (`src/gateway/session-sharing-preparation.ts:324-338`).
- Creating the store publishes an agent-database registry change. `assertRegistryPublication` then sees the path go from missing to a real file (`src/gateway/session-sharing-preparation.ts:197-210`, `441-456`) and invalidates the facts.
- The handler sends back the documented retryable refusal (`chat-history-session-read.ts:335-339`, `chat-history-recovery.ts:37-50`).

This refusal is intentional. A store that appears mid-read could hold the row the read just reported as absent. ## What Problem This Solves

Passing tests that mirror the implementation can miss broken provider requests, recovery, and persisted state. Recent compaction work shipped five such mistakes that unit tests did not catch: a side request sent a different tool set and input from the warm turn (0 cached tokens), a paid result was discarded after a local check, a fallback was logged only at DEBUG, a rejected replay looped because its marker was never persisted, and a default reached auth modes it did not support.

- Root `AGENTS.md`: the testing rule becomes a short instruction with a triggered link. The link fires before changing provider requests, fallbacks, recovery, or defaults, not only when writing tests. "Stable conversation context" adds one rule: a side request that reuses a conversation shares the turn's request preparation or carries no cache identity.
- `docs/help/testing/writing-tests.md`: one compact section, "Prove behavior at the owning boundary". It covers behavior, red/green slices, final request parity, paid work, durable recovery, default reach, and measured claims.
- Testing, test-audit, PR-maintainer, and review-flow docs link to that section instead of repeating checklists.

## User Impact

Guidance only. No runtime changes, no new test framework, and no deletion of existing tests. Existing test-value and cost limits stay.

- `pnpm format:docs:check`: clean (1,326 files). `pnpm docs:check-mdx`: passed (1,340 files). `pnpm docs:check-links`: 14,944 internal links, 0 broken. `git diff --check`: clean.

fix(anthropic): Claude models fail with a missing API key after an earlier Claude CLI sign-in (#168074)

Related: #167963

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Claude models that Claude CLI sign-in did not add fail with "No API key found for provider anthropic" for anyone who signed in to Claude CLI on a release since native Claude CLI login (#129052), because those configs predate the `anthropic/*` runtime entry that #167963 now writes at sign-in. Sign-in also still added deprecated catalog models such as `claude-opus-4-8` to fresh configs.

## User Impact

User impact: after `openclaw update` (or `openclaw doctor --fix`), an earlier Claude CLI sign-in routes every Claude model through Claude Code, the same as a fresh sign-in. Fresh sign-ins no longer add deprecated catalog models; an existing entry for one, such as `claude-opus-4-8`, is kept.

Configs with an Anthropic credential, an API default model with a Claude CLI fallback, a provider-level Anthropic runtime, or an existing `anthropic/*` entry are left unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Anthropic plugin now owns a Doctor config repair (`doctorContract.configRepair`). It adds `agents.defaults.models["anthropic/*"] = { agentRuntime: { id: "claude-cli" } }` only when all of these hold:

- the default model is an `anthropic/...` ref whose entry pins `claude-cli` (what sign-in writes);
- no `anthropic/*` entry exists, whatever runtime it names;
- no `models.providers.anthropic.agentRuntime` (the wildcard would outrank it);
- no Anthropic credential is visible to config repair: an `anthropic` auth profile, a provider `apiKey` other than the retired `anthropic:claude-cli` marker, or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`/`ANTHROPIC_OAUTH_TOKEN` in the environment or config `env`.

Specific model entries keep winning over the wildcard, so entries that name a runtime are unaffected. Runtime reads only the canonical entry; there is no new compatibility reader. The change is reported as a Doctor change (`openclaw doctor` lists it, `--fix` writes it).

Sign-in seeding filters catalog rows with `status: "deprecated"`. Route probing and the setup picker still see every row.

## Update Behavior

The installed updater cannot be patched, so the repair keys only on config that shipped Claude CLI sign-ins already wrote. During `openclaw update`, the candidate's own Doctor runs twice: once as `doctor --fix` in the candidate rehearsal on a private state snapshot (`candidate-doctor`), then as `doctor --repair --non-interactive` in a fresh process after the package swap (`openclaw doctor`). The second run writes the repair through Doctor's normal backed-up config write (`openclaw.json.bak` ring plus `openclaw.json.pre-update`), so update rollback restores the earlier config. The update result lists the change under the Doctor migration notes. Gateway startup does not apply it to a valid config. After a manual package replacement, run `openclaw doctor --fix`.

## Evidence

- Regression tests fail at the parent commit and pass here:
  - `extensions/anthropic/cli-migration.test.ts`: `registered cli sign-in seeds no deprecated Claude CLI catalog rows` fails at the parent (`expected { …(12) } to not have property "anthropic/claude-opus-4-8"`). Its second case shows an existing `claude-opus-4-8` default and entry survive sign-in. Three existing seeding expectations drop `claude-opus-4-8`.
  - `extensions/anthropic/doctor-contract-api.test.ts`: covers the repair, idempotency, both kinds of existing wildcard, an API default with a Claude CLI fallback, a non-Anthropic default, auth profile, provider API key, config env key, process env key, provider-level runtime, and the retired provider marker. At the parent the module does not exist.
- Published-driver × candidate cells: Docker `bare` image, published `openclaw@2026.9.9` from npm, sign-in through the published `openclaw onboard --non-interactive --auth-choice anthropic-cli` with a stub `claude` that only answers `claude auth status`. Then `openclaw update --tag file:<candidate tgz> --no-restart --yes --json` to a package built by `scripts/package-openclaw-for-docker.mjs` from this head:

  | Cell | Config before update | `update` | `anthropic/*` after | Other model entries | Post-update `doctor` / `config validate` |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | A | 2026.9.9 sign-in: 11 seeded rows pinned `claude-cli`, default `anthropic/claude-opus-5-5`, no wildcard | `status: ok`, `2026.9.9 (bcfc888)` → `(587456f)`; result notes `Doctor migration: agents.defaults.models["anthropic/*"]: added the claude-cli runtime …` | `{ agentRuntime: { id: "claude-cli" } }` | unchanged (only `anthropic/*` differs); `.bak`, `.bak.1` and `.pre-update` have no wildcard | exit 0, no further Anthropic finding / `Config valid` |
  | B | A plus `"anthropic/*": { agentRuntime: { id: "openclaw" } }` | `status: ok` | still `openclaw` | unchanged | exit 0 / `Config valid` |
  | C | A plus an `anthropic:default` API-key auth profile | `status: ok` | absent | unchanged | exit 0 / `Config valid` |

  Replaying the candidate Doctor on a copy of cell A's pre-update config: `openclaw doctor --non-interactive` lists the `agents.defaults.models["anthropic/*"]` change and leaves the file unchanged. `openclaw doctor --fix --non-interactive` writes `{ agentRuntime: { id: "claude-cli" } }` and rotates `openclaw.json.bak`. The same replays leave cells B and C unchanged.
- `pnpm exec oxlint --type-aware` on the changed files: clean. `node scripts/check-changed.mjs` passed every lane, including the doctor contract declaration and closure guard tests and the extension typechecks, except the dead-export scan. That scan flags only untouched files (`extensions/telegram/src/sequential-key.ts`, `src/auto-reply/reply/model-selection.ts`). With `OPENCLAW_CHECK_CHANGED_SKIP_DEADCODE=1` it exits 0.

## Merge Danger

One-way door: `openclaw update` and `doctor --fix` write `anthropic/*` into existing configs. A revert stops new writes but does not remove entries already written; the pre-update backup still has the earlier config. Blast radius: Claude CLI users with no Anthropic credential visible to config repair. Claude IDs without a specific runtime-pinned entry move from a failing API route to Claude Code. A user whose only Anthropic API key lives in the auth store, with no config auth profile or env var, and who sets a Claude CLI-pinned default model, would also see unpinned Claude IDs move to Claude Code. That is the routing a fresh Claude CLI sign-in now produces.

feat(discord): show per-tool glyphs on progress draft tool rows (#168032)

## What Problem This Solves

Discord progress drafts show tool-log rows without a per-tool glyph (`• Exec: running`), while Telegram shows `🛠️ Exec: running` since #167392. Discord already marks the 🧠 reasoning and 💬 commentary lanes, so its tool rows were the only unmarked lane.

## User Impact

Discord tool-log rows in progress drafts now start with the tool's text glyph (`🛠️ Exec`, `📖 Read`, `🩹 Apply Patch`). The 🧠 / 💬 lanes, plan rows, approval rows, and plain status rows are unchanged. No config changes. Slack and other channels keep plain rows.

## Why This Change Was Made

#167392 added the core opt-in (`toolIcons?: boolean` on `createChannelProgressDraftCompositor`, glyph table in `src/channels/progress-tool-glyphs.ts`) and left Discord as a follow-up. This PR sets `toolIcons: true` on every Discord compositor so all Discord paths render the same:

- live draft preview (`message-handler.draft-preview.ts`)
- retained progress continuation after handoff (`message-handler.progress-continuation.ts`)
- retained-card `edit` action rendering a progress snapshot (`runtime.messaging.messages.ts`)

No Discord-specific glyph code. Rows that already carry an explicit `icon` keep it.

## Tests

- `message-handler.draft-preview.rest.test.ts`: new regression through the real draft preview and Discord REST client: `🧠 _Planning the check_` / `💬 Looking at the workspace` / `🛠️ Exec: running` / `📖 Read: running`. Fails on main with `• Exec: running` / `• Read: running`.
- `message-bodies.test.ts`: a retained row's explicit icon (`🧪 Read`) wins over the tool glyph.
- `message-handler.process.draft-final.test.ts`: existing expectations updated to the glyph rows.

## Bounded cost

- One static `Record` lookup per core-built tool row on Discord (core opt-in from #167392).
- No new config keys, protocol fields, network calls, or extra Discord sends/edits; the draft text gains one glyph and a space per tool row, inside the existing per-message length bounds.
- Production: +3 lines. Tests: +65/−5. Docs: +3/−3. No extra Discord sends or edits in the runs above beyond the existing progress-draft cadence.

## Evidence

Isolated gateway (`HOME`/`OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`/`OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` under `/tmp`) with the real bundled Discord plugin against QA Lab's Crabline Discord provider server, `streaming.mode: "progress"`, `progress.toolProgress: true`. Rows below are the Discord REST bodies the plugin sent, from the Crabline provider recorder (`artifacts/crabline/discord-provider-server.jsonl`).

**Live model `openai/gpt-6-astra`** (`qa suite --provider-mode live-frontier --model openai/gpt-6-astra --channel-driver crabline --channel discord`), prompt asked for one exec then one read:

```
POST  "Working\n\n🛠️ Exec: running\n🛠️ Exec: running"
PATCH "Working\n\n🛠️ Exec: running\n🛠️ Exec"
PATCH "…\n\n🛠️ Exec\n🛠️ Exec\n🛠️ Exec: running"
PATCH "…\n\n🛠️ Exec\n🛠️ Exec\n🛠️ Exec\n📖 Read from glyph-proof.txt"
POST  final reply (separate message)
```

**Scripted model (`mock-openai`)**, commentary + one exec:

```
POST  "Working\n\n💬 SLACK-QA-COMMENTARY-200C8C6D"
PATCH "Working\n\n💬 SLACK-QA-COMMENTARY-200C8C6D\n🛠️ Exec: running"
PATCH "Working\n\n💬 SLACK-QA-COMMENTARY-200C8C6D\n🛠️ Exec"
```

fix(anthropic): Claude models fail with a missing API key after Claude CLI sign-in unless sign-in seeded them (#167963)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: after Claude CLI sign-in (`openclaw models auth login --provider anthropic --method cli`), any `anthropic/<id>` that sign-in did not seed fails with `No API key found for provider "anthropic" … missing-provider-auth`. This affects Claude models published after sign-in and IDs typed with `--model`, `/model` or `models set`, such as `anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5`.

## User Impact

User impact: Claude-CLI-only users can type or pick any Claude model and it runs through Claude Code. The model picker still lists only models the Claude CLI catalog serves, so `claude-mythos-5` (direct API only) stays hidden. Users with an Anthropic API key and no Claude CLI sign-in keep the API route. Exact model entries that name another runtime still win. A session pinned to an Anthropic API-key account keeps that account's models, including `claude-mythos-5`, in its picker.

Existing installs that signed in on an affected build get the new routing only after they rerun `openclaw models auth login --provider anthropic --method cli`. This PR adds no Doctor migration.

User-authored `provider/*` wildcards for other CLI backends behave exactly as on `main`. For example, `google/*` → `google-gemini-cli` keeps the same picker rows, and its typed IDs run as before. The picker gate is keyed on the `anthropic/*` → `claude-cli` entry that sign-in writes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Since #129052, Claude CLI sign-in persists no OpenClaw auth profile. At run time, `resolveCliRuntimeExecutionProvider` (src/agents/model-runtime-aliases.ts) found no runtime policy for unseeded IDs and no `claude-cli` profile it could alias. The turn then fell to the embedded Anthropic API path. An instrumented isolated Gateway on 58ba7ede092 showed `policy=undefined … viaAuthProfile=undefined` and then `useCliExecution=false`.

- Sign-in (`extensions/anthropic/cli-migration.ts`) now also writes the existing, documented provider wildcard `agents.defaults.models["anthropic/*"] = { agentRuntime: { id: "claude-cli" } }`. It does not overwrite a wildcard that already names another runtime.
- Catalog decisions (`src/agents/model-catalog-cli-wildcard.ts`, used by `model-catalog-decisions.ts`) mark a row unavailable, with no "sign in" reason, when all of these hold: native Claude CLI credentials supplied the availability (`evidence: "runtime"`), the row reaches `claude-cli` only through that sign-in wildcard, the Claude CLI catalog does not list it (bundled manifest plus published catalog), and it is not a configured row. Availability from a selected or pinned API account is never narrowed. Run-time routing is unchanged, so typed IDs still run.

Production change: 3 lines in cli-migration.ts, 15 net lines in model-catalog-decisions.ts and a new 58-line module (about 45 code lines). No config keys, schema or SDK surface change.

Provenance (f8b06fbb69b, #166037): prepared catalog decisions keep saved account, model and runtime choices and their provenance. `createCliRuntimeModelAuthEvaluator` returns a pinned non-native account's own provider-auth result, and `evaluateNative` keeps host results for selected accounts. The wildcard gate now only narrows availability that came from native Claude CLI credentials, so a saved account choice keeps the models that account can use.

Real proofs used the machine's existing native `claude` login, OpenClaw's real sign-in flow, isolated profiles and a loopback Gateway:

- Before, on `main` 58ba7ede092: `models set anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5` plus one turn failed with `missing-provider-auth`, and the instrumentation showed no CLI route.

- After: `models set anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5` plus a turn returned `OK` through `claude-cli`.
- API-key control: on a profile with `paste-api-key` (key piped on stdin) and no Claude CLI sign-in, an `anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5` turn returned `OK` with `runner=embedded` and `winnerProvider=anthropic`. Mythos stays listed for API users, as on `main`.

  - `extensions/anthropic/cli-migration.test.ts`, including the registered non-interactive sign-in entry: 4 failures without the fix, 40/40 pass with it.
  - `src/agents/model-catalog-decisions.test.ts`: the Claude CLI wildcard test fails without the gate (`expected true to be false`). With the gate, it covers a listed row, an API-only row (unavailable, no reason), an exact pinned row, a configured typed row, an exact override to `openclaw`, and an unchanged `google/*` → `google-gemini-cli` row even when that backend lists its own rows.

chore(qa): Telegram E2E runs can create and delete their own forum topic (#168012)

## What Problem This Solves

Telegram forum-topic proofs could not run on the Test Server unless someone had already prepared a forum, because the harness only created run-owned forums for private production accounts.

## User Impact

No product change. Maintainers and agents can pass `--create-forum` with a `--scenario` to the Telegram E2E runner: it creates a run-owned forum supergroup and topic under the leased QA user, sends the scenario's messages to that topic, and deletes the forum before the lease is released, including after a failed or interrupted run.

## Why This Change Was Made

- One forum owner in the user driver now serves both environments, and each command family keeps its own guard: `prepare-forum`/`cleanup-forum` run only on Telegram's Test Server with the leased QA user, while `prepare-private-forum`/`cleanup-private-forum` stay production-only for operator-owned accounts. Only the production family creates the one-use invite link that its local-app participants need.
- The runner prepares the forum through the existing readiness path, which then checks the new chat as a selected forum target: bot membership, privacy and tester write access. Forum cleanup is chained ahead of the credential release, the same way run-owned groups are cleaned up. `summary.json` records the forum and topic ids with the setup and cleanup result under `testForum`.
- The recovery helper's `cleanup-group` is now `cleanup`: it cleans a retained run-owned forum and group before releasing the lease.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes.

Live Test Server run with a Convex lease and the mock provider (no live model), on unused ports:

| 22:44:57 | Run starts; readiness creates the forum supergroup and topic 3, then verifies it as the selected forum target |
| +0.6 s | QA user message `@<sut> Please answer with OPENCLAW_E2E_OK only.` lands with `topicType: messageTopicForum`, `topicId: 3` |

fix(openai): ChatGPT-only model list offers unlisted pro models that fail (#167975)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: for a user signed in with only a ChatGPT account, the default model list offers `openai/gpt-5.4-pro` and `openai/gpt-5.5-pro` even though that account's model listing doesn't include them, so choosing either one fails.

## User Impact

ChatGPT-only users stop seeing these two models in the default model view (TUI and the Gateway `models.list` default view). Models the account lists stay, and so do hidden rows the account is entitled to, such as `gpt-5.5`. A user who also has an OpenAI API key still sees both pro models.

## Why This Change Was Made

- A successful ChatGPT account listing now records every model id it returned, hidden rows included, as private `listedModelIds` on the ready provider outcome. The public `providerOutcomes` projection still carries only provider, profile and status.
- The picker's availability check uses that list. A model served both by an API key and by ChatGPT, but missing from the account's listing, can't be used through the ChatGPT account. It stays available only if a usable non-subscription credential exists.
- The list applies only to the credential that made it. The check reads the ready outcome whose `profileId` matches the selected ChatGPT profile; another account's listing never narrows or widens it, and a profile with no ready listing of its own keeps today's behavior.
- When the model is unavailable, no reason code is attached, so the UI and `/models` show a neutral "Unavailable" instead of "Sign-in needed" or "add a key". The user is signed in; this account just doesn't have the model.
- This change covers the picker only. If someone types an unlisted id by hand, the request can still reach OpenAI and fail with OpenAI's own error.
- To stay within the line-cap ratchet, two pieces moved: the runtime credential overlay now lives in `model-auth-availability.runtime-overlay.ts`, and the ready-outcome builder now lives in `extensions/openai/model-service-tiers.ts`. Neither move changes behavior.

## Evidence

Real ChatGPT account (device-code sign-in), isolated profile, loopback Gateway. Same profile, main build `d0fc39e` vs this branch `f53ad9c`:

| Gateway `models.list` view=default, provider openai | main | branch |
|---|---|---|
| ChatGPT-only | 11 rows: 8 listed + `gpt-5.4-pro`, `gpt-5.5`, `gpt-5.5-pro` | 9 rows: 8 listed + `gpt-5.5` |
| ChatGPT + OpenAI API key (control) | n/a | `gpt-5.4-pro`, `gpt-5.5-pro` present and available |

`openclaw models list --provider openai --plain` (configured view) showed the same 8 listed rows on both builds; that view was never affected.
