fix(shared): a hidden Desktop window no longer drops its own healthy gateway socket

The gateway.ping heartbeat failed the transport when the newest inbound
frame was older than the 45 s deadline. A hidden or minimized Chromium
window runs the 15 s heartbeat interval once a minute (intensive wake-up
throttling), so at every tick the previous ping's pong is ~60 s old even
though the backend answered it within milliseconds. Every idle hidden
window closed a healthy socket, redialed, and the renderer recorded
hermes.desktop.friction kind=backend_disconnect detail=network for it.

Judge silence only when the newest ping we sent is still unanswered
(lastPingAt > lastLivenessAt). A dead transport still fails one tick
after its first unanswered ping, throttled or not; an answered one is
never dropped for timer spacing. This also covers the suspended-process
shape (OS sleep, WebView freezer, SIGSTOP): the pre-suspend ping was
answered, so the first tick after resume pings instead of failing.

fix(compression): a keyless pinned route clears the main credential

A pinned stall-fallback route with no api_key (a local server) now has the
route fields cleared before it is applied, so the call carries that route's
own credential (no-key-required) and never the main api_key.

fix(compression): a stall-fallback pin replaces the main route, never merges over it

After the aux summary fell back to the main model, the main provider, base_url and
api_key were written into the call and a stall-fallback pin overrode only the fields
it set. A fallback_chain entry without base_url/api_key kept the main host (the
fallback was never reached), or sent the main provider's API key to the fallback's
host. The pin now replaces the whole route; the main route applies only when no pin.

fix(compression): name the main model when aux summary falls back

`_fallback_to_main_for_compression` clears `summary_model` to mean "use the
main model". But `call_llm(task="compression", ...)` resolves an unspecified
route from `auxiliary.compression`, i.e. the model that just failed. The
fallback therefore re-calls the failing auxiliary model; since
`_summary_model_fallen_back` is already set, no second fallback is allowed,
`_generate_summary` returns None, and with
`compression.abort_on_summary_failure` the whole compression is skipped.

Observed with an auxiliary model whose weekly quota was exhausted: two
identical 429s, `failure_class=summary_generation_aborted`,
`fallback_used=false`, and a session that kept growing uncompressed.

Add `_apply_summary_route()` as the single place that pins the summary wire
route, and use it from both compression entry points (`_generate_summary`
and `_micro_summarize_one`, which had the same defect).

Three existing tests asserted the buggy contract (`assert "model" not in
kwargs`, commented "no model kwarg -> call_llm uses main"); they now assert
the main model is named explicitly.

Salvaged from #88247 (slimmed: docstring, 2 invariant tests; dropped the redundant
_last_summary_auth_failure reset — a main-model success already clears terminal flags).
Fixes #123362.

fix(memory): punctuation-only old_text never selects an entry; consolidate tests

The typography-folded fallback in _substring_matches rejected a needle only when
it was quotes/dashes at the ends (needle.strip("'-")), so old_text="\u201c \u2014"
(curly quote, space, em dash) folded to "' -" and matched any entry containing
`" -`, deleting it via single or batch remove. The fallback now requires at least
one alphanumeric character; exact-entry and byte-substring priority are unchanged.

Tests: the PR's four new tests are folded into two invariants (layout/typography
match + punctuation-only rejection; self-correcting failure copy + #90468 alias).

fix(memory): stop false drift refusals; refused writes name the exact fix

Fleet telemetry (14d, v0.21.5) shows the builtin store returning
success=False on 34-47% of add/replace/remove calls. Live `hermes chat -q`
runs against origin/main reproduced the dominant causes:

- Drift guard refused every replace/remove/batch on a file whose only
  difference from the tool's own layout was whitespace (blank lines
  around the delimiter, an empty entry). Parsing only strips whitespace,
  so flushing such a file loses nothing; the round-trip signal could not
  protect any content and turned the store read-only until hand-fixed
  (#107270). The guard now fires only on the signal that can actually
  lose foreign text: one entry larger than the whole store's limit.
- An over-budget add/replace/batch said "would exceed the limit" but not
  by how much, so models retried with consolidations that were still too
  big. Every over-budget message now states the exact chars to free and
  points at the one-batch fix.
- An old_text that matched nothing (paraphrased, stale after a concurrent
  write, or several entries glued with the delimiter) returned no hint on
  the batch path. Zero-match errors now carry `closest_entries` (top word
  overlap) on both paths, and flag a delimiter-spanning old_text.
- A batch replace missing its own `content` now says to set it on the
  operation object.

Fixes #107270. Same diagnosis as #107278 (@KoNit-K) and #61612 (@webtecnica),
which normalized the round-trip comparison instead of dropping it.

fix: tolerant memory entry matching for quote/whitespace normalization

Background-review (and human /memory) replaces re-emit entry text with
different quote characters (straight ' vs stored ") or re-wrapped lines, so
byte-exact old_text substring matching wrongly reported 'No entry matched'
and the staged consolidation write failed to apply. Fall back to a
quote/whitespace-normalized match only when no exact match exists, preserving
today's unambiguous behavior. Adds regression tests for the quote-style
replace and for unrelated old_text still being rejected.

fix(memory): treat serialized-empty content as unset for the new_text alias

PR #86642 documented the single-op coalescing as
`content = content or new_text`, but the implementation only fell back
when content was None. Runtimes that materialize an omitted optional
string field as "" (some providers fill optional schema fields rather
than omitting them) bypassed the alias, and replace/add calls carrying a
genuine new_text failed with 'content is required for replace action.'
(#90468).

Treat content == "" like None on the single-op alias path, matching the
coalescing the batch ops already use (op.get('content') or
op.get('new_text')). A non-empty content still wins when both are set.

ensure_aiohttp flattened every PM failure into the non-retryable
whatsapp_aiohttp_missing. That covered PM's post-install
"sms installed; restart Hermes to activate it" (sync succeeded, process
could not adopt the generation), a busy dependency lock and a failed
download. With WhatsApp as the only platform the gateway exited 78 and
systemd's RestartPreventExitStatus=78 kept it down.

install here (lazy installs disabled, or a foreign interpreter not on the
install's selected or older generation), when aiohttp is present but
broken, or when it is still absent after a successful install. A plain
shadowing aiohttp.py (no __path__) is reported as an incomplete install
instead of escaping as AttributeError.

fix(whatsapp): install a missing aiohttp through PM and name every failed connect

A gateway whose dependency environment lacks aiohttp (a sealed env from
`hermes update` with a partial messaging extra, #126358) spawned the bridge,
then every /health poll raised ModuleNotFoundError inside
`_poll_bridge_health`'s blanket except. connect() returned False with no
fatal code, so the reconnect watcher retried forever while the bridge
answered /health 200, and telemetry counted each attempt as error_class
"other".

  extra that is exactly aiohttp) before starting the bridge, the same
  lazy-install path Slack/Teams use. When PM cannot install it (lazy
  installs disabled, foreign interpreter, install failure) or aiohttp is a
  half-removed namespace shell (#71308), it fails with the named,
  non-retryable `whatsapp_aiohttp_missing` and never spawns the bridge.
- The bridge-died / "did not start in 15s" paths set a retryable fatal code
  (`whatsapp_bridge_exited` / `whatsapp_bridge_timeout`), so reconnect
  status and connect telemetry name the cause instead of "other".
- Folds the salvaged test file into test_whatsapp_connect.py as two
  invariant tests.

fix(whatsapp): name a missing aiohttp in the bridge preflight (salvage of #126557)

A sealed env built by `hermes update` can ship a partial messaging extra
without aiohttp. check_whatsapp_requirements only verified Node.js, so
connect() spawned the bridge and every health poll raised
ModuleNotFoundError — swallowed by `except Exception: continue` — and
the gateway looped forever on the misleading "Bridge HTTP server did not
start in 15s" (#126358).

Add _aiohttp_available() and wire it into _preflight() as a named,
non-retryable whatsapp_aiohttp_missing fatal error with install guidance,
so the failure surfaces before any bridge process is spawned.

fix(skills): a revoked GITHUB_TOKEN no longer blocks hub installs; fall through to gh auth / anonymous and name it (#98725)

GitHubAuth resolved the .env PAT first and latched it for the process; GitHub's
401 Bad credentials was returned to callers as a plain miss, so every
GitHub-backed install failed even when `gh auth login` worked or the repo was
public, and the CLI blamed a "stale index entry".

fix(pm): record a partial pm update as failed in the pm receipt

Follow-up to the salvaged per-package pin isolation (#125400). Once a
failing pin no longer aborts the run, the surviving pins still run the
venv sync, whose receipt finalizes `ok` as latest.json. `hermes pm
status` and the desktop sync card read latest.json, so a run that left a
package on its old pin and exited 1 was recorded as a clean success.

Write a kind=update `failed` receipt after the sync, with one failed step
per pin, whenever any pin failed (also when every pin failed, which
previously wrote no receipt at all). Trim the tests to the two
invariants and assert the receipt in the mixed case.

test(pm): cover per-package pin isolation in _apply_pins

Three regression tests: a failing pin reports and does not block the
healthy ones (pinned row reaches the lockfile, broken row keeps its old
version), a run where every pin fails leaves the lockfile byte-identical,
and a clean run keeps exit 0 with no failure summary.

fix(pm): isolate per-package pin failures instead of aborting the run

_apply_pins let any exception from _pin_artifacts propagate: one broken
pin - a package's resolution bug (gh's 3-part target split) or one
target's upstream pool skew (Termux rolling pool 404 while nodejs.org
is ahead) - aborted the entire run, blocked every unrelated package,
and left lockfile.save() unreached, so any failure meant zero progress.

Catch per package, pin everything that succeeds, install the pinned
set, print a 'pinned X, failed Y' summary, and exit non-zero when
anything failed. A run where every pin fails still leaves the lockfile
untouched.

fix(mcp): read readOnlyHint from mcp 2.x snake_case annotations

mcp 2.0 renamed ToolAnnotations.readOnlyHint to read_only_hint; camelCase
survives only as a pydantic serialization alias, which is not applied to
attribute access. _annotation_read_only_hint() read the camelCase attribute
off the SDK object, so on mcp 2.x the hint was always None and every tool --
including honestly annotated read-only ones -- fell into the
"unknown = write-capable" branch.

With trust: untrusted that means the approval gate fires before every read
call (get_*, search_*, list_*), which is exactly the failure mode that
trains a user to click through the prompt without reading it, weakening the
gate on the writes it exists for.

Use mcp_field() for the object path (the helper already used across the MCP
client for this 1.x -> 2.x rename) and accept snake_case in the cache dict
too, for caches written by another client. Unknown still means
write-capable; only the field lookup changes.

Regression test covers the SDK 2.x model, both snake_case shapes, the 1.x
camelCase attribute and a snake_case cache dict.

fix(desktop): validate remembered owner hints against the row, not the foreground socket

Review finding on the resumeSession half of #97809: the staleness test
compared the remembered hint against activeGatewayConnectionId() — the
CURRENT foreground socket — but resumeSession is the function that moves
the foreground (ensureGatewayAgent below), and hints are minted from the
AMBIENT connection at create/open time (sdk openSession), which in the
all-profiles view is not the foreground. So 'names a connection that
isn't active' was true for exactly the correct hints, and a pathname-
driven resume with no capturedOwner deleted them.

Use the row as the authority instead — the same predicate as the click
path (openStoredSession) and the boot auto-restore
(repairOwnerHintsForRestore): a connection-tagged cached row pins the
hint's route; an untagged or absent row leaves no basis to trust an
explicit persisted hint, so it is dropped rather than dialed. Explicit
captures stay authoritative as given.

Tests: the two hint tests now pin the row-based contract (untagged row
drops a legacy local hint; a tagged row keeps an agreeing hint even when
the window is not looking at that connection; a disagreeing hint is
dropped), and the resets clear the persisted storage copy like the
integrations suite does.

fix(desktop): drop stale persisted session owner hints on resume

Older desktop builds persisted a `local` owner hint for sessions whose
rows carry no connection tag (the legacy primary-SSH path). Sidebar
clicks repair it (openStoredSession drops the hint for untagged rows),
but every pathname-driven resume (boot auto-restore, reconnect
re-resume, stranded-view self-heal) trusted the hint verbatim — dialing
the Mac backend for a remote session and dying with "session not
found".

Two seams now apply the same hygiene:

- resumeSession (use-session-actions/index.ts): a remembered hint is
  only honored when the connection it names is this window's live
  primary; a stale one is repaired (deleted), not just ignored, so it
  cannot re-poison the next resume or the session-scoped RPC ladder.
  An explicitly captured owner remains authoritative as given.
- useDesktopIntegrations boot auto-restore: the row ladder that
  resolves a remembered/route session now repairs the owner hint from
  the row (tagged row pins its exact route, untagged row drops the
  stale hint), matching what openStoredSession does for clicks.

fix(discord): track live voice credentials across re-keys instead of snapshotting at start()

VoiceReceiver.start() captured conn.secret_key (by value) and
conn.dave_session (by reference) exactly once. Both go stale in normal
operation:

- op 4 SESSION_DESCRIPTION rotates the transport secret_key on every
  voice (re)connect — the snapshot then fails NaCl decrypt forever.
- voice_state.reinit_dave_session() REPLACES conn.dave_session with a
  NEW DaveSession when none existed yet, so a receiver that starts
  before DAVE finishes negotiating keeps None forever and treats E2EE
  as off — every frame reaches opus as ciphertext for the whole
  session.

The failure is silent by construction: decrypt failures warn for the
first 10 packets then go dark, and shredded opus output raises nothing.
The operator-visible symptom is "the bot ignores me."

Fix — resolve, don't copy:

- Credentials live in ONE tuple (secret_key, dave_session,
  dave_protocol_version, dave_downgraded), re-resolved from the live
  connection and swapped in a single reference store; the receive
  thread reads one consistent generation per packet, so a refresh can
  never pair a new key with an old session.
- Refresh triggers: the voice-ws hook on op 4 and op 24 (the hook runs
  AFTER received_message dispatches the op, so it reads the new
  values); membership changes in the bot's channel (DAVE epoch bump)
  via the existing on_voice_state_update handler; and a
  25-consecutive-NaCl-failure streak as the catch-all, retried every
  streak window while the failure persists.
- Unmapped-SSRC hole closed without recreating it elsewhere: with E2EE
  actively on (protocol_version > 0 and outside a passthrough window),
  frames for an SSRC with no user mapping are dropped (after the
  existing sole-member inference) instead of being fed to opus as
  ciphertext.  A non-null session alone is NOT the predicate — the
  session object survives protocol downgrades to 0 and passthrough
  transitions, where plaintext is legitimate.  Passthrough windows
  mirror discord.py's own set_passthrough_mode calls: op 21
  pending-downgrade opens 120s; op 22 opens a 10s grace ONLY on the
  dave_downgraded True -> False edge (upgrade-after-downgrade), with
  replace-semantics so the short grace supersedes a residual long
  window; a receiver starting mid-pending-downgrade seeds the window
  from conn.dave_pending_transitions.
- Silence made visible: decrypt failures keep emitting one warning per
  250 after the first 10, and stop() logs decode-health counters
  (ok / decrypt_failed / dave_unmapped_dropped).

Tests: tests/gateway/test_discord_voice_rekey.py (24) — credential
resolution/rotation, the late-DAVE-session upgrade, failure-streak
refresh + reset, op 4/24/5 hook behavior, original-hook passthrough,
the DAVE-state drop predicate (downgraded-plaintext decodes, op-21
window decodes, expired window drops, upgrade edge replaces the long
window, same-version and duplicate op 22 open nothing,
mid-pending-downgrade startup seeds), unmapped-drop vs mapped flow,
sole-member rescue, tuple-generation consistency, teardown health
line.  Adjacent voice_command / voice_mixer / send / opus suites green
under the diff (111 passed).

fix(agent): unwrap data/success envelope in auxiliary LLM responses

Some OpenAI-compatible gateways (e.g. api.cline.bot) wrap non-streaming
JSON bodies in {"data": {<chat completion>}, "success": true}. The
OpenAI SDK leniently parses this into a ChatCompletion with choices=None
and keeps the envelope keys as extra fields, so auxiliary calls (vision,
compression, title generation, web extract) failed in
_validate_llm_response with a generic "LLM returned invalid response"
error. Main chat was unaffected because it streams and SSE chunks pass
through unwrapped.

Unwrap the envelope at the _validate_llm_response chokepoint: rebuild
the real completion via model_validate (SimpleNamespace synthesis as
fallback), and surface the provider's actual error message for
{"success": false, "data": {"error": ...}} envelopes. Detection is
conservative — responses with top-level choices or without a dict
"data" field are returned untouched.

fix(serve): reap orphaned host owner instead of looping observe-only

A prior backend whose session died (dead spawner, PID re-parented to
init) stays alive, so it keeps holding the host flock and its record
passes every staleness check. A fresh backend hit HELD_BY_OTHER and
returned observe-only forever; every attach retried against the same
orphan and its 10s probe timed out indefinitely.

On HELD_BY_OTHER, look the conflicting owner up in the spawn ledger
and apply the established spawner_is_dead discipline (previously wired
only into the mcp-helper reap): a provably dead-spawned owner — or a
null-spawner owner reparented to init, old past the lock-write grace,
and claimed by no Desktop SSH lock — is terminated (SIGTERM, 2s,
SIGKILL), its record discarded, and the host lock re-claimed.
Live-spawned, lock-claimed, young, interactive, self, and unprovable
owners are never touched.

fix(config): serialize .env read-modify-write cycles with a file lock

save_env_value, remove_env_value and sanitize_env_file each read
~/.hermes/.env, rewrite it in memory, then atomically replace it, with
no lock spanning the cycle. Two concurrent writers (setup wizard +
dashboard save, gateway + CLI) both snapshot the pre-write file and the
loser's replace silently drops the winner's key; a remove racing a save
can resurrect the removed key. _CONFIG_LOCK cannot help: it guards
in-memory config only.

Serialize each cycle with hermes_cli.auth._file_lock (the same fcntl
flock / msvcrt byte lock auth.json already uses), keyed on the .env
path so multiplexed profiles stay independent. The import is call-time
because hermes_cli.auth imports this module at import time. Nothing
under the lock takes other locks, so no ordering cycle exists.

fix(delegation): collect a child's real result in a grace window after the stale-heartbeat verdict

When the heartbeat's stale verdict fires (frozen activity fingerprint for the
threshold cycles), await_child used to raise FuturesTimeoutError the moment the
wait ended if the worker future had not resolved — even though a child that
already wrote its final answer often lands its recorded result moments later
while its worker thread unwinds. That synthesized timeout abandoned the real
result: in an async batch the never-collected child left the unit unable to
satisfy 'all children terminal', so the batch stayed running for hours with no
completion delivered (#113222; the reporter's 7h hang, and the follow-up traces
where a task's final line sat uncollected for 23+ minutes).

Collect instead of abandoning: after the stale verdict, signal the cooperative
stop, then wait up to _STALE_RESULT_GRACE_SECONDS (2s) for the worker to
settle. The real result wins when it lands (status completed, real summary);
only a worker that never settles falls through to the existing structured
timeout with the deferred-close drain. A configured inactivity cap
(child_timeout_seconds) keeps its teeth — it is NOT a stale verdict, so the
#116001 abandonment contract is unchanged (pinned by test_delegate_liveness_timeout).
Steering stays open across the window: the success path's _merge_late_steer (or
the failure path) remains the linearization boundary, so a concurrent steer is
never lost.

normalization: _transcribe_command_stt only checked .exists() before
substituting {input_path}. Desktop voice recordings arrive as WebM/Opus
48 kHz and providers with container/sample-rate contracts (e.g. Tencent
16k_zh) reject the raw webm, so desktop voice chat failed on every
message. _transcode_audio_for_stt (ffmpeg -> 16 kHz mono m4a) existed
but was wired only into the OpenAI path's rejection retry.

that accept any container keep the original file): when truthy, the
input is transcoded into the per-call temp dir and {input_path} points
at the normalized file. Transcode failure returns an error envelope
instead of silently feeding the raw container to a provider the user
declared needs normalization.

fix(process): a completion is published once, by its owner, with its final output

Child exit, result finalization, notice publication and output consumption are
separate steps, but several callers treated an earlier one as the last:

- A duplicate _move_to_finished set _completion_event while the owning call was
  still before its notice, so a one-shot parent could exit without the follow-up.
  Only the call that moved the session out of _running releases waiters now, and
  it always does, even when its publish raises.
- _finish_exited ran mark_exited without the session lock, so a kill committed
  between its `killed` check and its writes was overwritten with exited/0.
- After a reconcile flips `exited` ahead of a reader still on its final drain,
  wait/read_log/kill no longer consume the partial output as the completion,
  and poll no longer marks it observed. poll/read_log/kill decide that under
  the same lock hold as their snapshot, so a reader finishing in between cannot
  make an earlier partial snapshot count as the whole output.
- kill_process ignored a failed systemd scope stop. It now returns an error
  with scope_stop_failed whenever the stop fails, including when the root
  exited meanwhile (that proves nothing about detached descendants); the
  session keeps its unit so a later kill retries the stop. An already-exited
  session reports scope_stop_failed too.

Process-tree termination and post-kill survivor checks move into
tools/process_registry_termination.py (ProcessTerminationMixin) to keep
process_registry.py under its size cap. The only change in the move:
_live_descendants logs the traceback of the failure it swallows.

Refs #132358. The races were found by @andrexibiza and @jonpol01 in that thread.

fix(process): a reconcile during the reader's final drain no longer truncates the output

When poll/wait/list saw the direct child exit while the reader was still
behind, the reconcile asked the reader to finish and flipped the session to
exited at once. The reader then stopped after ONE more 4 KiB chunk, so the
rest of the pipe - up to a whole pipe buffer, the job's final lines - was
never read, and the caller had already been handed a snapshot without it
(wait() also marked that snapshot consumed, suppressing the completion).

After a finish request the reader now drains what is already buffered
(zero-timeout select, capped so a grandchild that floods the pipe still
cannot pin it), and the reconcile waits briefly for the reader to publish
before falling back to marking the exit itself.

fix(desktop): stop refusing sends from a window behind its chat

page before every send and, when this window looked behind, refused the

impossible in the backend: windows on one backend share the live session,
every turn folds rows other surfaces wrote into the model's history before
it runs (_adopt_out_of_band_turns), and a durable turn lease serializes
turns across processes. What was left was a check of what the window
showed, and it misfired in single windows for a week straight (sleep,
tool turns, approval timeouts, project moves, compaction, several chats).

Sends now always go out. The cross-window "turn finished" ping that keeps
peer windows current stays. Removes the guard module, its notice in every
locale, and the systemNotice flag only it read; the refresh graft's
tool-fold invariants keep their tests.

and the session cache still apply; an interactive `hermes chat -q` on a TTY
never sets HERMES_SINGLE_QUERY_SESSION, so it keeps its prompt. A /dev/tty
fallthrough was rejected: it prints the prompt box onto -Q / stream-json
stdout, and on Windows msvcrt blocks 45 s on a worker's hidden console.

fix(approval): protected-instruction gate hangs in `hermes chat -q` sessions

Every write to a protected agent-instruction file (SOUL.md, AGENTS.md, ...)
from a kanban worker failed with:

  BLOCKED: ... approval prompt timed out without a user response.
  Silence is not consent.

That message says a human ignored a prompt. No prompt was ever rendered.

Root cause: `HermesCLI.__init__` registers `_approval_callback` as the
thread-local CLI approval callback before it is known whether the run will
build a prompt_toolkit Application. One-shot `hermes chat -q` runs — exactly
how the kanban dispatcher spawns every worker — never build one. The callback
still looked present, so `_request_protected_instruction_approval` took the
"a CLI human is here" branch, pushed modal state into a layout nothing
renders, and blocked on a response queue only a key binding can fill. It
burned the full approvals timeout and returned "timeout".

`_run_approval_gate` learned about this context in #86878 via
`HERMES_SINGLE_QUERY_SESSION`. This gate deliberately bypasses that gate
(one-operation approval every time, no allowlist, no persistent consent, no
--yolo) and so never got the fix. Reuse the same detector rather than adding
a second mechanism: in a single-query session, skip the unreachable modal and
fail closed immediately with the honest "no interactive user or gateway is
present" reason.

Policy is unchanged and deliberately stricter than `_run_approval_gate`:
`approvals.single_query_mode: approve` does NOT auto-approve this gate. A
protected-instruction write always needs a live human. Interactive CLI users
can still approve, and the gateway path is untouched.

Measured on the reported case: pre-fix 30s+ then a bogus "timed out";
post-fix immediate with an accurate reason.

Regression coverage (tests/tools/test_protected_instruction_cli_channel.py),
verified red before this change and green after:
- interactive approve/deny through a registered callback,
- an end-to-end round trip through the real HermesCLI._approval_callback modal,
- a single-query session never dispatches to the unrenderable modal and never
  reports "timed out",
- single_query_mode approve/deny/ask never auto-approves this gate.

fix(gateway): run the plugin re-arm off the event loop and share the loader thread prefix

rearm_failed_platform takes the manager's discovery lock, which a reload sweep or a deferred load holds for its whole import, so call it through the scope-carrying executor hop like the lookup. The hung-load guard now matches the loader thread name through one _LOADER_THREAD_PREFIX constant instead of a copied literal. Gate r2 Lows (2c, efficiency, quality).

fix(gateway): run the reconnect watcher's plugin load off the event loop

Gate finding (PL1 r1 efficiency, Medium regression): after a re-arm, the
next watcher tick ran the plugin's import + register() inside the sync
_create_adapter on the event loop, and run_with_load_deadline joins for up to
plugins.load_timeout_seconds, which stalls inbound messages, heartbeats and
the control socket.

The watcher now materializes the registry entry with platform_registry.get
in the gateway executor first, using _run_in_executor_with_context so the
profile ContextVars are preserved, and _create_adapter then finds the plugin
already resolved. The rest of _create_adapter stays on the loop, as it was
on main. Builtin adapter constructors ran there before this stack and may be
loop-affine, so moving the whole call into the executor would change
unrelated behaviour.

fix(gateway): cap failed platform plugin re-arms per queued platform

Gate finding (PL1 r1 efficiency, Medium): a permanently broken platform
plugin was re-armed and re-imported on every reconnect backoff tick
forever, re-logging its load failure each time.

The watcher now counts successful re-arms in the platform's reconnect info
dict and stops after 3 (_MAX_PLUGIN_LOAD_REARMS), so a transient startup
failure still heals while a broken plugin stops being re-imported. The
platform stays queued as adapter_unavailable, as before this stack. No new
config key.

fix(plugins): never re-arm a platform whose hung load is still running

Gate finding (PL1 r1 2c/efficiency, High): a plugin whose import or
register() hangs overruns its load deadline and leaves an abandoned daemon
loader. The reconnect watcher re-armed it on every backoff tick, adding one
more abandoned thread each time, and once _MAX_ABANDONED_LOADERS (8) were
live every plugin load in the process was refused (about 25 min at the
30-300s backoff).

rearm_failed_platform now skips the platform while its
plugin-load:<manifest_key> thread is still alive in _ABANDONED_LOADERS
(checked under _ABANDONED_LOADERS_LOCK). This was chosen over "never re-arm
after a timeout": a deadline overrun caused by transient startup I/O, where
the worker eventually finishes, still heals on a later tick, and at most one
abandoned thread per plugin can ever exist.

fix(plugins): never re-arm a disabled or gated platform plugin

Gate finding (PL1 r1 2c/reuse/quality, High): rearm_failed_platform matched
any platform LoadedPlugin with an error and enabled=False. _gate_manifest
writes that same shape for its placeholders (disabled via config, not
enabled in config, removed from the catalog, legacy Relay refusal), and
the requires_hermes gate does too. The reconnect watcher therefore
imported plugins the user or the catalog had deliberately blocked.

The re-arm now re-runs gate_manifest against the current config and only
proceeds when the verdict is still defer/load, and it skips a
requires_hermes mismatch. The registry-snapshot alternative
(snapshot_registration showing a consumed loader) was probed and rejected:
a genuinely failed deferred load disposes its lease, so the snapshot shows
no loader (it would never re-arm the headline case), while a requires_hermes
skip leaves one behind (it would match the wrong case).

refactor(gateway): call rearm_failed_platform inline from the reconnect watcher

Gate finding (PL1 r1 quality, Low): _rearm_failed_platform_load was a
one-line forwarder in the handler-rewire mixin, unrelated to rewiring, and
its bool result was discarded at its only caller. Call the plugin manager
directly at the run_adapters call site instead.

fix(gateway): re-arm a failed platform plugin load from the reconnect watcher

A bundled platform plugin whose deferred load raises or overruns its load
deadline at startup (e.g. I/O contention from a state.db integrity check) has
its lease disposed, so the registry forgets the platform. The reconnect
watcher keeps it queued as adapter_unavailable, but nothing ever re-runs the
import: the platform only heals after a manual reload-plugins or a restart.

The watcher's adapter_unavailable branch now asks the current profile's
plugin manager to re-lease that platform's deferred loader (only when the
plugin is recorded as a failed platform load), once per backoff tick, so the
next pass retries the import. No new config key; the watcher already owns the
bounded backoff.

hand_over_held_inbound, which skips a None predecessor, and both runner
callers pass a candidate freshly built by _create_adapter for the same

fix(telegram): accept the update claim when a retired adapter forwards a hold

Gate finding B05-1: the successor-forward branch of _hold_inbound_event
returned before self._accept_update(). The admission ContextVar is per
adapter instance, so the successor's own _accept_update() in its hold
path reads its own (empty) var and the predecessor's in-flight claim
stays unaccepted. _release_claim then skips _record_receipt, and the
update can be replayed after a restart even though it was handed off.

Accept on the retired adapter before forwarding, and deref the successor
weakref once.

fix(gateway): hand Telegram held inbound to the rebuilt adapter

Telegram holds inbound events that PTB has already acked (offset advanced),
so dropping them means losing the message for good. The hold queue lives on
the adapter instance and drains only on that instance's _mark_connected. When
a retryable fatal (network error, polling/ingress stall) makes the runner
build a NEW adapter, that drain never runs: the reconnect path carried the
inbound dedup caches across but not the queue. Held events, plus anything
teardown salvaged onto the retired instance later, were silently stranded.

The reconnect queue entry (primary) and the secondary reconnect task now
keep the replaced adapter as "predecessor". The existing carry_inbound_dedup
seam reads its dedup caches from it before connect. A new
hand_over_held_inbound seam moves its held events at publish time
(_install_reconnected_adapter / secondary profile_map install). A candidate
that fails to connect never owns the queue, so no hand-back is needed, and
delivery waits until the replacement is registered. TelegramAdapter.
adopt_held_inbound rebinds only source._transport_adapter_ref (profile and
role authorization stay as resolved) and leaves a successor weakref on the
predecessor. Late _hold_inbound_event calls there (teardown salvage after the
replacement drained) forward to the replacement.

fix(plugins): a user model provider reports enabled only where provider discovery loads it

#133012 made status call every user `kind: model-provider` plugin enabled,
but providers/ discovery (_scan_home_layer) only loads
plugins/model-providers/<name>/ children and flat plugins/<name>/ children
whose kind is exactly `model-provider`. A provider in a category directory
(plugins/custom/foo/), or a flat one with a differently-cased kind, showed
ON in `hermes plugins list`, the TUI hub and Desktop while it never loaded.

Status now applies the loader's rule per location: flat children only when
the loader's own kind check (providers._declares_model_provider_kind)
accepts them; model-providers/ children when their kind is model-provider
(discovery imports any child there, but never registers a non-provider);
anywhere else, never.

fix(update): pack tidy never caches a partial comparison, and clears MIDX layers on Windows

A candidate compared against only the indexes that opened this run was
recorded as unique, and a healthy later run never re-checked it: one
transient mapping failure on the pack holding the copies parked a
duplicate forever (helix4u). A negative verdict is now recorded only when
every index was read; the state file carries a version so v1 verdicts are
dropped.

The incremental multi-pack-index layers were removed with
rmtree(ignore_errors=True), which on Windows silently leaves git's
read-only layer files behind. They are now made writable and unlinked one
by one, the same as pack files.

fix(update): the pack tidy lock is a kernel lock, so no takeover race exists

A stale-lock takeover by rename cannot be made exclusive: a third run can
claim the path between a taker's rename and its hand-back (helix4u's
three-taker probe got two holders). The tidy now holds a non-blocking
kernel lock (pm.filesystem.lock_fd: flock / msvcrt) on a lock file that
is never removed. The OS releases it when the holder exits, killed or
not, so there is nothing stale to judge and nothing to take over.

fix(update): a killed merge leaves no orphan pack, and a stale lock has one taker

Final-review findings on the pack tidy:
- The merged pack's payload is now published last. git ignores an index
  whose .pack is absent, so a kill mid-publish leaves only metadata, which
  the remnant sweep removes. A lone .pack (the old order) was garbage that
  neither the sweep nor git gc ever removed.
- Taking over a stale lock re-checks the age of the file it actually
  renamed; a fresh one is a racing taker's live lock and is handed back.

fix(update): pack tidy retries unreadable indexes, stays inside its deadline, drops incremental MIDX

Review on 26d3aae:
- An index that could not be opened was saved as "kept", so a healthy
  later run never checked it again. It is now skipped for this run only.
- _Index.oids() built the whole name list before the first deadline check;
  it is a generator now, checked every 1024 names.
- _drop_midx() called unlink() on multi-pack-index.d, so a repository with
  an incremental multi-pack-index refused every erase. The chain file goes
  first (git ignores the layers without it), then the directory.
fix(update): the cleanup line says duplicate packs, which is what it erases

fix(update): pack tidy erases only provably redundant packs

An independent live review of the tidy found it could lose data: a merge
under pack.packSizeLimit published only the first of several output packs
(45 of 60 commits gone), erasing "commit-free" on-demand packs dropped trees
and blobs a local branch still needed once upstream had pruned them, a
process killed mid-erase left a multi-pack-index naming a deleted pack, and
a classification timeout was cached as "holds commits" forever.

The erase rule is now proof against local packs alone: a promisor pack goes
only when every object in it is also in another promisor pack (checked by
binary search over the .idx files, no git process per pack). Nothing stored
locally can be lost and nothing depends on the remote still serving it, so
the marker heuristics and commit classification are gone. Merges run with
pack.packSizeLimit=0 and refuse anything but exactly one output; the
multi-pack-index is dropped before any pack is removed, so a kill at any
point leaves git reading; a lock file keeps two tidies from each erasing a
pack because the other still holds its copies.

.keep files written by a fetch-pack/index-pack that died (older than an
hour) no longer pin their packs. git's own repack never touches .keep'd
packs, and on a real dev checkout 53 of them held 4.5 GB of duplicated
history downloads.

fix(update): a pack that will not unlink stays whole; leftovers are finished later

Review on #132928: _remove_pack deleted the .idx before the .pack, so a
.pack unlink refused (a Windows reader mapping it) left the payload and
its .promisor without an index while the log said "skipped". The merge
step would then feed that index-less pack to pack-objects on every later
run.

- Delete the payload first: git loads a pack only when both .idx and
  .pack exist, so a refusal on .pack changes nothing and any later part
  that sticks is already invisible to git.
- Each run first sweeps such leftovers (parts whose .pack is gone, older
  than the in-flight window, since index-pack writes .promisor/.keep
  before its .pack).
- A merge input that will not retire is logged and retried later instead
  of aborting the run; the multi-pack-index is dropped whenever the pack
  set shrank, including when a step raised.

feat(update): clean up a partial clone's packs a little on every update

Each `hermes update` now spends at most 60 s on the on-demand packs a
partial clone piles up (#129712), and every finished unit is kept, so a
large checkout converges over a few updates instead of blocking one
update for 20+ minutes:

1. Erase on-demand packs (empty .promisor marker, older than an hour)
   that hold no commits. Their objects are copies of what the promisor
   remote serves; git fetches what it needs again. This frees disk,
   which the old gc fold never did. A pack holding commits is kept
   because a ref may point into it; a pack git cannot classify in time
   counts as holding one.
2. While more than 50 promisor packs remain, merge the smallest few
   with `git pack-objects --stdin-packs` (cost proportional to those
   packs, no reachability walk), marker first and index last so the
   merged pack is a promisor pack from the moment git sees it.

Verdicts and a merge batch size that halves after a timed-out merge are
remembered in .git/hermes-pack-tidy.json, so no update repeats work an
earlier one could not finish. bounded_probe_run gains `input=` for
stdin-fed git commands.

fix(approval): MCP/vault consent declines at once when no user can answer

registers that callback too, so an untrusted MCP tool or a vault card

panel nobody can answer. tests/e2e/core/mcp_plugins/

fix(update): a clashing local tag or old git no longer leaves the conversion retrying forever

Final-review findings on convert_treeless_checkout:
- A local tag that the --tags refetch would clobber made git exit non-zero
  after the objects had landed, and check=True raised before the
  completeness check ran, so every update warned and stayed tree:0. The
  offline history check is now the verdict, not the fetch's exit status.
- Git older than 2.36 has no --refetch; such a checkout is left as it is
  instead of printing git's usage text as a warning on every update.

fix(update): conversion covers the checked-out history and starts no repack

Review on 6f9a3d6 found two gaps. The refetch covered only origin's
configured refspec with --no-tags, so a release checked out from a tag no
branch reaches, or a branch fetched outside a narrow refspec, was recorded
as blobless while its history still had no trees. The refetch now takes
the tags too, checks HEAD's whole history offline (rev-list --missing=print,
about 3 s on this repo) and refetches HEAD by commit when trees are still
missing; the new filter is recorded only once that history is whole.

A raw fetch also spawned git's detached maintenance, gc --auto and a full
cruft repack of the 120 MB refetch, outside the update's time limit. The
conversion fetch now runs with per-command gc.auto=0 and
maintenance.auto=false, leaving the user's own settings untouched.

fix(install): clone blobless, convert treeless checkouts once

Installers have cloned with --filter=tree:0 since c3e9ac87a7f. A treeless
clone keeps commits only, and git requests a missing tree without telling
the server which trees it already has, so every checkout and every
path-filtered history walk re-downloads complete directory snapshots
(~0.58 MB per commit for this repo). GitHub's own guidance is that
treeless clones are for throwaway CI builds, not long-lived checkouts;
the blobless layout keeps every commit and tree local and fetches only
file contents on demand.

- install.sh / install.ps1 clone --filter=blob:none (same release tags,
  --commit pins and ancestor checks the treeless switch was made for).
- hermes update (post-update step) converts an existing tree:0 checkout once with
  `git fetch --refetch --filter=blob:none origin` (~120 MB, ~8 s
  from GitHub) and records the new filter only after it succeeds, so a
  failed refetch retries next update.
- The shallow-heal conversion unshallows as blob:none instead of tree:0.
- checkout_contains asks git with GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH: a recorded SHA the
  checkout lacks is "not contained", never a download of that commit's
  whole history.

profiles apart and follows the agent onto the threads the scheduler already
copies context into. Delegated children read None.

fix(debug): scrub any 8+ char key after a masked scheme, letters-only included

agent.redact rewrites `x-api-key: Bearer <k>` and `Authorization: *** <k>`
to `...: *** <k>` and keeps the key. The `***` scheme branch then let an
all-letter 8-19 char key (lower, UPPER or Capitalised) through as prose,
because `_NOT_WORD` treats such a run as a word; the merge base scrubbed any
`[A-Za-z0-9._~+/-]{8,}` value there (REDACT2 gate r5 2c, Medium: 3,488
head-only leaks, e.g. `x-api-key: *** qwertyuiopas`).

Put the merge base's 8+ branch first in the `***` alternation, with its own
boundary so `sk-a:b=v` shapes stay covered too. Zero head-only leaks is the
rule here; eating prose such as `configured` in `*** configured via env` is
accepted fail-closed over-redaction, so the two prose rows that pinned the
leaking behaviour go. `_NOT_WORD` and its 19-letter cap stay: the 4-7 char
and colon branches and free-text `Basic` still need them.

The key-end lookahead was copied verbatim into _KEY and _NOT_WORD; if one
copy changed, the "is it a key" and "is it a word" boundaries would drift
apart. Define it once. Compiled patterns are byte-identical before/after.

Gate r2 finding (quality Low).

fix(debug): keep RFC 6750 Bearer challenges out of the free-text token scrub

The widened _SUPPORT_BEARER_RE value class admits `=`, so challenge text
became a "token": `Bearer realm="api"` -> `Bearer [REDACTED]"api"`,
`WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm=example` -> `Bearer [REDACTED]`, which main
kept. Those params are what a 401 support bundle needs. Skip a value that
opens with a quoted auth-param (`name="`) or a known RFC 6750/7235 param name
(realm|scope|error|error_description|error_uri) followed by `=`. Tokens with
inner/trailing `=` (`abcd1234=efgh5678`, `abcd1234==x`, `Zm9v...NA==`) and a
`realmabc=...` lookalike are still masked.

Gate r2 finding (2c Low).

fix(debug): scrub the whole free-text Bearer value, inner = padding included

`_SUPPORT_BEARER_RE` matched a key-shaped prefix that had to end on a value
boundary, so `Bearer abcd1234=efgh5678 x`, `Bearer abcd1234==x` and
`Bearer Zm9vYmFyMTIzNA==X` matched nothing and leaked whole (REDACT2 gate 2c,
Medium). Free text has no header boundary: consume the value greedily
(`[KEY_CHARS=]+(:[KEY_CHARS=]+)*`), keeping the not-a-word guard and the
8-char lookahead so `Bearer tokens expire` stays prose.

fix(debug): treat a 20+ letter single-case run after a masked scheme as a key

all-lowercase or all-uppercase key after agent.redact's masked `***` scheme
(`x-api-key: *** <key>`, `--header x-api-key *** <KEY>`) reached the support
upload unredacted (REDACT2 gate 2c, Medium). Cap the word run at 19 letters:
no prose word in the kept rows comes close, and a longer single-case run is a key.

redactor, so it guarded nothing (REDACT2 gate 2ab, Low). Replace it with
`--header x-api-key *** abc1234`, which leaks on base and is scrubbed on head.

fix(debug): scrub short, colon-bearing and double-encoded support keys

Follow-up to #132270. The support-upload scrub still let some credentials
through:
- short (<8 char) keys after a scheme or a masked `***` in header/argv
  context (`x-api-key: Bearer abc1234`, `-H 'x-auth-token: Basic s3cr3t'`,
  `--header x-api-key Basic short`);
- keys with an inner colon (`Bearer sk-abc:xyz123456`, `Basic user:passw0rd`);
- double-encoded URL params (`%253Ftoken%253D<T>`, `%2526access_token%253D<T>`).
It also deleted any all-letter word of 8+ chars after a masked value
(`x-api-key: *** undefined` -> `x-api-key: ***`).

A value after `***` now counts as a key when it is key-shaped: not a plain
word (all lower, Capitalised or ALL CAPS, case-sensitive), and either 4+
chars before any colon or 6+ chars mixing letters and digits. A short word
that ends the header (`Basic short`) also counts. A trailing colon is prose
punctuation, so `*** see: documentation` and `*** time: 12:30:45` stay. The
`--header NAME` operand form uses the same scheme rule. The encoded-param
pass also accepts the `%25`-prefixed separators and writes `%252A` stars.

context window, but a request also reserves output tokens the provider
charges to that same window — the LLM service deliberately never clamps
them (`packages/llm/llm/src/index.ts`).

existing per-route warning policy rather than silently disabling proactive
compaction. The headless compaction e2e advertises a coherent capacity/cap

fix(sandbox): deny the ambient parent-delete right inside granted roots

The Low integrity label confines writes and deletes to the labeled roots,
but every granted root is labeled Low, so the integrity check alone still
let one confined child delete inside ANOTHER granted root (another
workspace, a live sibling temp directory): Windows authorizes a delete from
the parent directory's FILE_DELETE_CHILD right, which the write-restricted
intersection never reaches.

Each grant now also denies FILE_DELETE_CHILD to the world SID in the same
SetNamedSecurityInfoW call, so the capability ACE's DELETE bit is the only
delete authority inside a granted root. The idempotent skip additionally
requires the exact deny, so a root granted by an earlier build receives it
on its next provision. Delete paths inside the roots keep working; a file
whose own DACL grants no DELETE is no longer deletable through its parent's
rights, for the confined child and for the user's own processes alike.

fix(sandbox): confine Windows deletes with a Low integrity label

The write-restricted token's capability-SID intersection only covers the
write bits of the object's own access check. Windows also authorizes a
write or a delete from the parent directory's FILE_DELETE_CHILD right, and
no restricting SID has to co-sign that authority: the confined child could
therefore delete any file its ambient user SIDs control. `cmd /c del`
outside the workspace succeeded under BOTH modes, and .NET
File.Delete/DeleteFileW did too wherever the ambient DACL held Modify.

Lower the restricted token to Low integrity and apply a Low no-write-up
mandatory label to every granted directory in the same SetNamedSecurityInfoW
call that adds its capability ACE. The kernel evaluates the integrity policy
inside the access check whichever right supplied the authority, so the
granted roots stay writable while everything else becomes delete-proof as
well as write-proof. The label inherits to new children and follows the
existing standing/revocable grant lifecycle.

Also closes the Everyone-Modify ambient write boundary, and pins the delete
paths (cmd, .NET, Remove-Item, libuv) in runner.spec.ts.

Signed-off-by: Rudy Celekli <47457359+rudycelekli@users.noreply.github.com>

* fix(javascript): resolve exports against Node's full condition set

The declared-order fix selected targets against {default, import|require},
but Node's active set for the resolver that owns installed packages also
includes "node" and "node-addons". Ordering only means something against the
full active set, so a package declaring {"node", "import"} resolved to the
wrong target, and a package declaring only {"import"} reported no target
where Node resolves ./node.cjs.

Nested condition objects and fallback arrays are also valid Node targets.
They are now flattened in Node's own order: a condition object stops at its
first active key, so a null or unmatched nested target ends the search, while
an array skips the entries it cannot resolve and concatenates the rest. Node
does not fall through a target whose file is absent, so the first flattened
target stands and its absence is reported rather than skipped.

A valid exports map that matches no active condition is reported as external
with the declared condition names, and one that selects an unsupported nested
or array target no longer borrows the "not valid package JSON" reason.

The differential test installs a real package and resolves the same bare
specifier through Node and through REA, mirroring file presence between the
filesystem and the inventory. 18 of the 25 cases fail without this change.

Addresses #548 and #545.

#548: processScenarioSchema required a leading "/" for executable,
working_directory and filesystem_roots, so no process scenario could be
expressed on Windows at all. The report suggested node:path's isAbsolute, but
that answers for the host running the check: on Linux `C:\tools` is not
absolute, so a scenario captured on Windows would fail validation when it is
replayed, compared, or asserted in a test on another host. A boundary schema
must not vary with its evaluator, so the check accepts the POSIX form, a
Windows drive path and a UNC share everywhere. The rejection message now names
the constraint instead of leaving the caller to infer it from "invalid request".
The HTTP `path` field inside `checkpoints` is an URL path and is deliberately
left alone.

I checked whether this merely moved the failure downstream: containment is
enforced by isPathWithinRoot, which already uses host-aware path.relative, so
validation really was the only blocker.

#545: when a scope is inside the administrator ceiling but no grant was ever
issued, the denial still pointed at widening the ceiling -- advice that cannot
help, since the ceiling already permits the operation. The `missing` payload is
computed against candidate *grants*, so it describes what a grant must cover,
not a ceiling gap. `PermissionRemediation` gains a `grant` variant saying
exactly that, and PermissionAuthority selects it when the denial is not a
ceiling violation. An explicitly requested remediation is still honoured, and a
genuine ceiling violation still says "configure".

* refactor(config): take the environment as an input at every configuration read

Completes B-2. Every `parseConfig(process.env)` site now reads from an
injected environment, so configuration-driven behaviour is a function of an
argument rather than of the machine running it.

The twelve sites were not equivalent, and treating them as one number would
have hidden the difference:

- **src/application/ (3 sites) were genuine defects.** `runSessionStatus`
  already injected its `logger` but hardcoded `process.env` for config, so the
  MCP path's `dependencies.env` never reached it; `captureProcessScenarioFile`
  and `runAnalysis` had the same problem. `runAnalysis` gained `environment` on
  the options object it already had, which is where its other injected
  dependencies live.

- **The CLI command layer (9 sites) is a documented boundary,** where
  `process.env` is legitimate. Rather than 9 independent ambient reads, they
  now share one seam: `createCli(environment)` passes it to the seven
  registrars that need configuration, and the nested helpers (`electronContext`,
  `runtimeContext`, `loadConfiguredAuthority`, `inspectJavaScriptReplay`) take
  it explicitly.

Every new parameter defaults to `process.env`, so all existing call sites are
unchanged and production behaviour is identical. The point is that the ambient
read is now a documented default at a boundary rather than a hidden dependency
deep inside behaviour.

`process.env` now survives in `src/` only as those default parameters —
nothing reads it at the point of use.

delivered yet produced no journal entry, so the drain had nothing to wait for

timer or the listener. Dispose before aborting instead and assert the owned
timer count reaches zero, which distinguishes a released deadline from a
retained one. Verified by mutation: emptying dispose, dropping the listener
removal, and dropping the timer clear each fail the test.

Dropping the per-project `sequence.groupOrder` made every project run
concurrently. `fileParallelism: false` only serialises files inside a single
project, so `process-boundary` could still overlap with the boundary projects
that observe host process and terminal state, which is the contention that
drops input and resize echoes. The removed blanket per-project serialisation
was slower, but it was never what isolated projects from each other.

apply the ordering locally only, so CI keeps the concurrency it proves green.

startup that only lists the catalog starts no bridge work and writes no
records at all, so the assertion passed without observing anything. Reading
stderr while the child was still running also raced the pipe, and splitting
the buffer could parse a partial trailing line.

newline-delimited records, and read after the transport closes so delivery is
no longer in question. Guard the result with an explicit non-vacuity assertion
so the fatal check cannot silently stop observing anything.

now fails the test.

both its group and the aggregate left the whole file green while the catalog
regenerated without it. Structural checks cannot detect removal; only a
declared baseline can.

tool still needs no edit, while removing one now fails with a message naming
the tool. Verified by mutation: dropping a contract from its group so the
aggregate loses it too fails the floor.

* test: restore no-ceiling coverage above plausible truncation limits

Four suites claimed a result was complete at any scale while their own inputs
were bounded below where a truncation would appear, so the guarantee they
described was not actually under test. Scale independence cannot be asserted as
a relationship over a fixture smaller than the cap being ruled out.

Raise each fixture past any ceiling a regression would plausibly introduce,
which is far cheaper than the removed cases:
  referenceSourceImport  600 entries/64 KiB -> 5,000 entries with a 4 MiB member
  customProtocolCapture  generated max 40 frames -> 300..1,000
  appleApplication       12 frameworks/16 candidates -> 250/1,600
  nodeRuntimeCharacterization  assert the absent call-budget and alias bounds
    where they would be added, since the budget derives from the case count

Verified by mutation: a 1,000-entry import cap, a 500-frame capture cap, a
100-framework projection cap, a 100,000-call budget cap, and a 200-character
alias cap each fail the corresponding suite.

* fix(process): require a quiet period before declaring the target lost

Returning on the first unchanged journal sample granted a single event-loop
turn of grace. A chunk queued on a later iteration therefore still let
`target_lost` be submitted before the final terminal observation, discarding a
satisfiable reactive trigger under the same load-dependent exit scenario the
drain was added for, and `maxTicks` never bounded that because the loop exited
early every time.

Require several consecutive unchanged turns so a callback arriving on any of
the next few iterations still lands first, while keeping the overall tick bound
so a pathological stream cannot stall exit.

* fix: stop a 4 GiB fixture and measure the drain quiet period in time

The reference import fixture cycled its five sizes across all 5,000 entries,
which made a thousand 4 MiB members and nearly 4 GiB of fixture written
concurrently. It happened to fit locally but cannot fit a runner's disk. Cross
the two boundaries independently instead: entry count by volume of tiny
members, byte size by a single 4 MiB member, for about 4.2 MiB total. Verified
by mutation that a 1,000-entry cap and a 1 MiB per-member cap both still fail.

The drain check counted scheduler turns, but consecutive setImmediate turns
elapse in microseconds, so four of them finish long before a pty callback
delayed under host contention, which is when the trailing chunk matters.
Measure the quiet interval in elapsed time instead, so a late callback within
the window still lands before target loss. Verified by simulation: the
turn-count version missed any delay beyond a few microseconds, the timed
version observes delays up to the quiet interval.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: the model picker and `openclaw models list --all` list every xAI model twice, once under `xai` and once under an `x-ai` group, when the xAI plugin is enabled.

## User Impact

User impact: xAI models appear once, under `xai`. Selecting or configuring `x-ai/<model>` refs is unchanged; only the published catalog folds the alias.

## Why This Change Was Made

The xAI provider declares the runtime alias `x-ai`, so its discovery and static catalog results are also published under `x-ai`. The catalog folds runtime aliases only when the plugin manifest declares them in `modelCatalog.aliases`, which Moonshot, Fireworks and Novita already do and xAI did not. The manifest now declares `x-ai` → `xai`.

That declaration alone does not remove the duplicates when xAI discovery is unavailable. In that case the catalog publishes the static rows as fallbacks, and those rows did not go through the alias normalizer. Static fallback rows now use the same normalizer and are deduped, so the alias rows fold into the canonical provider. Moonshot, Fireworks and Novita get the same fix for their declared aliases.

## Evidence

Isolated Gateway with the xAI plugin enabled, a configured `xai` provider (dummy key, so xAI discovery reports `unavailable`) and a local remote-catalog fixture. Reads used `models.list {view, agentId:"main", refresh:true}` plus `openclaw models list --all --json`:

| read | `origin/main` | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `models.list` view `all` | `xai` 7, `x-ai` 7 | `xai` 7, `x-ai` 0 |
| `models.list` view `configured` | `xai` 7 | `xai` 7 |
| `models list --all` | `xai` 7, `x-ai` 7 | `xai` 7, `x-ai` 0 |

On this PR the `xai` rows have the same ids and fields as on main. They now follow the xAI manifest order. Every other provider's row is identical to main.

- Regression: `src/agents/prepared-model-runtime.sources.test.ts` "publishes failed-discovery static rows once under the canonical provider" sends static rows answered under a declared alias through `prepareFullCatalogFacts` and `prepareModelCatalogPublication`. It fails on main (5 rows, including the alias rows) and passes here.
- `extensions/xai/openclaw.plugin.test.ts` asserts the shipped `x-ai` catalog alias.
- `pnpm test extensions/xai/openclaw.plugin.test.ts src/agents/prepared-model-runtime.sources.test.ts src/agents/prepared-model-runtime.scoped-refresh.test.ts src/agents/prepared-model-runtime.test.ts src/agents/prepared-model-runtime.startup-static.test.ts src/agents/model-catalog.test.ts src/agents/model-catalog-view.test.ts`: 102 tests passed. The new test takes about 10–30 ms; the focused `pnpm test <file> --maxWorkers=1` run took 26 s wall time, mostly Vitest startup.
- Limit: the case where xAI discovery succeeds (the reported Gateway) was not run against the real xAI API. Those rows enter through the same catalog-entry normalizer as the fallback registry rows. The isolated repro showed that normalizer folding `x-ai` registry rows into `xai` once the manifest alias is declared.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes.

Merge danger: two-way door. The change adds a manifest declaration and normalizes provider ids on published static catalog rows. It writes no state and changes no config or protocol, so a revert undoes it fully. Blast radius: model catalog listings for providers whose manifests declare `modelCatalog.aliases` (xAI, Moonshot, Fireworks, Novita).

fix(ollama): keep ollama.com setup out of the local Ollama provider (#167433)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Ollama setup writes the hosted ollama.com catalog into the local `ollama` provider (`models.providers.ollama.baseUrl: "https://ollama.com"`) when the user picks **Ollama → Cloud only**, or passes `--custom-base-url https://ollama.com`. That duplicates the plugin's own `ollama-cloud` provider and fills the local Ollama picker group with hosted models.

## User Impact

User impact: hosted-only Ollama setup goes through the existing **Ollama Cloud** choice (`--auth-choice ollama-cloud`), which saves an `ollama-cloud` credential and defaults to `ollama-cloud/minimax-m2.7`. The **Ollama** choice now offers `Cloud + Local` and `Local only`, and rejects an `ollama.com` base URL (interactive, `--custom-base-url`, and the `--reset` preflight, so a rejected URL no longer wipes existing state first) with a pointer to Ollama Cloud.

Existing configs that already have `models.providers.ollama` pointed at ollama.com keep working unchanged; this PR does not migrate them.

## Why This Change Was Made

`Cloud only` inside the Ollama choice (#67005) predates the dedicated `ollama-cloud` provider (#88247), which is a sibling choice in the same Ollama group and owns hosted credentials, live catalog discovery and the default model. Removing the duplicate mode leaves one hosted path. Handing off from inside the Ollama method instead was rejected: onboarding scopes the following model picker to the chosen auth choice's provider (`ollama`), so hosted models would not be listed.

`Cloud + Local` is unchanged: its `:cloud` suggestions are Ollama's documented hybrid flow through the signed-in local daemon at its local base URL, so they stay under `ollama`.

Removed with the old path: the Cloud only credential prompt, its setup-time ollama.com `/api/tags` fetch, the `ollama:default` profile write, and the now-unused cloud-default table parameter in setup model building.

Follow-up, not in this PR: a Doctor migration for existing `ollama` entries at ollama.com would need to move the provider entry to `ollama-cloud`, re-home the `ollama:default` auth profile, and rewrite every `ollama/<id>` reference (agent defaults and allowlists, per-agent overrides, fallbacks, heartbeat/cron model overrides, stored session overrides). Separately, the existing `ollama-cloud` API-key method accepts an `OLLAMA_API_KEY=ollama-local` placeholder after a redacted confirm prompt (unchanged by this PR).

## Evidence

- Regression tests fail on the base source and pass here: mode prompt options (`[cloud-local, cloud-only, local-only]` on base), interactive base URL validation, non-interactive `--custom-base-url https://ollama.com` (base: "promise resolved instead of rejecting", i.e. it wrote ollama.com into `ollama`), and the reset preflight for the same URL (base: `promise resolved "true" instead of rejecting`, i.e. reset would proceed).
- Real CLI, isolated state dir, no Gateway:
  - `openclaw onboard --non-interactive --accept-risk --auth-choice ollama --custom-base-url https://ollama.com --custom-model-id kimi-k3 …` → exits 1 with ``ollama.com is served by the Ollama Cloud provider. Choose Ollama Cloud during setup, or run `openclaw onboard --auth-choice ollama-cloud`.``; no config written.
  - Same command with `--reset` against an existing config → exits 1 with the same message; the existing `openclaw.json` is byte-identical afterwards.
  - `openclaw onboard --non-interactive --accept-risk --auth-choice ollama-cloud --ollama-cloud-api-key <fake> …` → no `models` section, `auth.profiles["ollama-cloud:default"]`, primary `ollama-cloud/minimax-m2.7`.
  - `openclaw models auth login --provider ollama --method local` → `Ollama mode` shows `Cloud + Local` / `Local only`; typing `https://ollama.com` at the base URL prompt shows the Ollama Cloud message and does not proceed.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/ollama`: 31 files / 512 tests passed. `pnpm tsgo:extensions`, `pnpm tsgo:extensions:test` pass. `node scripts/check-changed.mjs` passes except the dead-export scan on `src/talk/client-voice-session-store.ts: ClientVoiceToolEffect` (untouched; `scripts/check-deadcode-exports.mts` reports the same entry on `origin/main` 4f33fe7402b).

fix(openai): new ChatGPT-login models stay hidden until an OpenClaw release (#167387)

Related: #157920

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: new ChatGPT-login models stay hidden from `/models` until an OpenClaw release, because model discovery reports a hard-coded Codex client version.

## User Impact

User impact: with ChatGPT login, models that need a newer Codex client appear in the model list once that Codex version is published to npm, with no OpenClaw release.

Example: 2026.9.8 reports `client_version=0.158.0`, so the ChatGPT backend hides `gpt-6.1-sol`. With this change, OpenClaw reports `0.161.0` (current npm `latest`) and the model appears.

## Why This Change Was Made

ChatGPT model discovery now asks npm for `@openai/codex`'s `latest` stable version and sends it as `client_version`.

- One small request to `registry.npmjs.org`, through the SSRF guard, with a 5 s timeout.
- The version is cached for 6 hours. Concurrent discoveries share one request.
- If npm is unreachable or returns something odd, OpenClaw keeps the last version it got from npm, or the bundled pin (`0.160.0`, unchanged contract test) if it never got one, and retries after 5 minutes.
- If the model-list request itself fails, the previous list stays (existing catalog retention for failed providers).
- Only stable versions are used. If OpenClaw pins a newer prerelease, the pin wins.
- This changes only the version OpenClaw *reports* for discovery. The bundled Codex binary and the Codex harness are unchanged.

Tradeoff: #113615 aligned this value with the bundled Codex pin. Reporting a newer version can list a model whose protocol the current build does not handle yet; that model then fails on its first turn instead of being hidden. We chose visible-and-explainable over silently missing. This is the same tradeoff Hermes makes (it reports `99.0.0`); a real published version is more honest and avoids out-of-sequence version handling on the backend.

## Evidence

**Backend behavior (real ChatGPT account, token kept in the browser):** visible models by `client_version`:

| `client_version` | `gpt-6.1-sol` listed |
|---|---|
| `0.158.0` (2026.9.8 pin) | no |
| `0.160.0` (current pin) | yes |
| `0.161.0` (npm `latest`) | yes |

**Real CLI flow** (`pnpm openclaw --profile <isolated> models list --provider openai --refresh --plain`, ChatGPT OAuth profile). To make the run discriminating, the fallback pin was temporarily set to `0.158.0` in a throwaway edit (reverted):

- npm reachable → `openai/gpt-6.1-sol` listed (npm `latest` 0.161.0 wins over the old pin).
- npm lookup forced to fail → `openai/gpt-6.1-sol` missing (falls back to the old pin).

**Real npm lookup through the guarded fetch:** first call returned `.../models?client_version=0.161.0` in 356 ms; the second call hit the cache in 0 ms.

**Tests:** new unit tests cover the npm version, cache reuse and expiry, shared in-flight request, fallback on HTTP error / prerelease / older-than-pin, keeping the last npm version when a later refresh fails, and the 5-minute failure retry. Existing OpenAI discovery tests pass with the resolver isolated. `node scripts/check-changed.mjs` passes.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes: `4573635c77f` (#127394) touches `openai-provider.test.ts` for account-model routing, not discovery versioning.

**Merge danger:** two-way door. No stored state, config, or schema change; a revert restores the pinned version. Blast radius: ChatGPT-login model discovery only. Worst case, a model that the current build cannot drive appears in the list and fails on its first turn.

improve(skills): learned skills keep repeatable procedures, not facts or codebase knowledge (#167404)

## What Problem This Solves

Agents saved learned skills for things that are not procedures: facts about the user (a birthday) and knowledge about one codebase (its test command, env vars, naming rules). Facts belong in memory. Codebase knowledge belongs in that repository's docs or `AGENTS.md`, and as a learned skill it loads in every session of the agent, including unrelated projects.

## User Impact

Learned skills now hold procedures for tasks the user repeats, so the agent does not work them out from scratch again. When asked to `/learn` codebase specifics or a plain fact, the agent says where that belongs instead of creating a skill. Personal procedures are still learned as before. No config or stored-data change.

## Why This Change Was Made

Skill Workshop is designed for a personal claw: its skills are agent-wide, while a repository already has an owner for its own conventions. The prompts now say so in the places that decide what gets saved:

- The shared authoring standard (used by the `skill_workshop` tool description, the background review, and `/learn`) opens with "a skill is a procedure, not memory": the method for one class of task this user repeats, so the next run starts from what worked. Facts with no method attached belong in memory.
- The do-not-capture list (background review and `/learn`) adds knowledge about one codebase, which belongs in the repository's docs or `AGENTS.md`.
- The always-on Skill Workshop system-prompt section carries both points in one clause each, so the foreground agent follows them too.

The coding rule is scoped to one codebase's knowledge, not to all coding work, so personal procedures that happen to involve code (for example "how I publish my blog") are still learned. The docs describe the same scope.

## Evidence

Real-model before/after with `openai/gpt-6-astra`. For each trial, a fresh isolated Gateway was built from either the merge base or this branch, scripted user turns were sent through the normal WebChat path (`chat.send`), and then `/learn` was sent. Every trial confirmed that the model received the server-built learn instruction. Background review was off, so any skill change came from the conversation or `/learn`. There were 3 trials per side, and the user turns were identical on both sides.

| Scenario | Base: skill saved | This PR: skill saved |
|---|---|---|
| Codebase knowledge: fix a failing test that needs a repo-specific command, env var and naming rule | 3/3 (skill contains the repo's command and prefix) | 0/3 (each reply says it belongs in the repo's docs/`AGENTS.md`) |
| Control: personal receipts-to-monthly-CSV procedure with one user correction | 3/3 | 3/3 |
| Plain personal fact (a birthday and a preference) | 1/3 | 0/3 (replies point to memory) |

A variant of the codebase scenario also required debugging a general Node test-runner issue. There, this branch kept a generic skill for that lesson with every repo-specific detail removed (no repo command, env var or naming rule). That is the intended split: general methods stay, and codebase facts go to the repository.

Full report, with per-trial results, exact commands and scripted turns: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/167404#issuecomment-6066678209

Workshop, `skill_workshop` tool and agentsapi tests pass; no test pins this prompt text.

No overlap with Pash/Sarah changes.

**Merge danger:** two-way door. The change is prompt and docs text only, and a revert fully restores the previous wording. It writes no state and changes no config or published contract. The blast radius is what agents choose to save as learned skills. Existing skills are untouched, and sessions already running keep their current system prompt until the next session.

fix(telegram): keep the progress card while a media run owes the reply (#167362)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: a Telegram chat in progress-streaming mode gets the permanent canned "I’m continuing this work and will send the result when it is ready." message, and loses its progress card, when the agent starts a background image generation and ends its turn without its own acknowledgement. This still happens on builds that include #166101.

## User Impact

User impact: while an image is being generated, a Telegram (or Discord) chat keeps its progress card with a live "Image generation: running" line instead of getting a canned message. The card goes away when the image arrives. If the image is never delivered, the card stays and shows "Image generation: failed", even on a bounded or plan-bearing card. No new messages or warnings.

## Why This Change Was Made

- The turn runs `image_generate` (a detached media run), sends no message-tool acknowledgement, and ends with empty final text. #161154 (5b846b900dd) made that an implicit continuation (`delegatedToMediaRun` → `meta.continuationPending`) on purpose, so the turn waits instead of reporting a missing reply. The reply layer then sends the default waiting status (#151032 / a1ce4e02ff0 fixed a silent chat while delegated work runs; #125106 is the original waiting reply).
